On the third night the princesses appear in a vision and tell him that if he frees them he will recover, otherwise he will die. He wakes in pain, summons his twelve sons, and laments that he cannot himself travel to the unknown Black Island. Boyislav, the youngest son and the king’s favorite, offers to go in his place; the elder brothers, who hate Boyislav, insist they all go and try to exclude him. The king resolves the dispute by drawing lots so that six sons will go and six remain; Boyislav draws a lot to go, upsetting his brothers and saddening the king, but they depart that same day. The princes travel successfully by land but lose their way at sea. Boyislav suggests sailing north, is mocked, but after weeks of wandering they follow his advice and on the third day reach the terrifying Black Island. None of the brothers dares to land except Boyislav, who takes provisions, goes ashore, and searches the bleak, rocky island for three days, sleeping one night on a bare stone. At last he finds a large, man-hewn stone, lifts it, and discovers a dark opening beneath from which a pleasant odor rises. Descending, he enters a glorious garden containing three golden castles. Three horses gallop wildly around him three times and vanish. A disembodied voice greets him three times as “Boyislav, youngest of twelve,” and he eventually discovers that the voice comes from a famished little horse hidden behind a rock. The talking horse knows Boyislav wishes to free the three princesses and gives detailed instructions: in each of the three castles a princess will greet him with great kindness and offer food and drink; he may eat but must not allow any princess to eat with him or kiss him, must take the leftovers onward from castle to castle, and must remain entirely silent throughout, as his life depends on strict obedience. Boyislav thinks this will be easy and hastens to the first castle, where a wonderfully beautiful princess runs out joyfully to welcome him, invites him in, and asks after his father and At an inn they drink heavily while he remains restrained and carefully tends his white steed. The next day, after Jalmir quietly settles the bill, they ride on. The white steed warns Jalmir that they will reach a castle ruled by a sorceress and seven daughters, where he must refuse the wine offered. details about cradles and swaddling.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The close of the story \"Helena the Fair\" is described as light content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l6706-l6848","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS. / THE FOOTLESS AND THE BLIND. / GO TO THE VERGE OF DESTRUCTION AND BRING BACK SHMAT-RAZUM. / MARYA MOREVNA.; lines 6706-6848","start":"6706","end":"6848","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ivan Tsarevich, while travelling, spares a queen-bee’s honey and a lioness’s whelp after they promise future service. He reaches Baba-Yaga’s house, surrounded by stakes topped with human heads, and agrees to herd her mares for three days to earn a heroic steed, under threat of having his head placed on the last empty stake. Each day the mares run off—into the meadows, the sleeping forest, and the blue sea—while Ivan despairs and falls asleep. A bird from beyond the sea, the lioness, and then a bee wake him and tell him the mares have already been driven home; the mares report that birds, wild beasts, and swarms of bees from all over the world attacked them and forced them back. The bee advises Ivan to hide in the stable and steal a mangy colt lying on the dung-heap at midnight. He does so, then reaches a fiery river and uses a magic kerchief to create a splendid bridge, crossing and then thinning it to a narrow span. Baba-Yaga pursues him in an iron mortar with pestle and broom, rides onto the bridge, which breaks, and falls into the fiery river, where she dies. Ivan feeds the mangy colt in green meadows until it becomes a marvellous steed, then returns to Marya Morevna. She embraces him, amazed that God has brought him back to life, but fears Koshchéi Without-Death will overtake and kill him again. Trusting his new heroic steed, Ivan persuades her to flee with him. Koshchéi’s horse senses the escape; Koshchéi pursues and overtakes them, but Ivan’s horse kills him with a kick and Ivan finishes him with a club, burns his body on a great fire, and scatters the ashes to the wind. Marya mounts Koshchéi’s horse and Ivan his own; they visit the Raven, the Eagle, and the Falcon, who welcome them joyfully and praise Marya’s unmatched beauty and Ivan’s struggle.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A speaking queen-bee asks Ivan Tsarevich not to touch her honey, promising to serve him in the future, and he leaves the honey untouched.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A lioness with her whelp meets the hungry Ivan, and after she begs him not to eat the whelp, promising future service, he agrees and continues his journey.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ivan comes to Baba-Yaga’s house, around which stand twelve stakes bearing eleven human heads, with one stake still unoccupied.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Baba-Yaga tells Ivan that if he herds her mares successfully for three days she will give him an heroic steed, but if he fails, his head will be placed on the last stake.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"On the first day, when Ivan drives Baba-Yaga’s mares a-field, they raise their tails, scatter through the meadows, and vanish, leaving him weeping and asleep on a stone until sunset.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At sunset a bird from beyond the sea flies up, wakes Ivan, and tells him that the mares are already home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Baba-Yaga’s mares report that birds from the whole world flew at them and almost picked out their eyes, forcing them to return home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On the second day the mares run into the ‘sleeping forest,’ and Ivan again sits on a stone, cries, and falls asleep until a lioness runs up and wakes him, saying the mares are driven in.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The mares explain that savage beasts from the whole world ran at them and nearly tore them to pieces, which made them come home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On the third day the mares run into the blue sea and stand there up to their necks in the water while Ivan sits on a stone, weeps, and falls asleep.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A bee wakes Ivan on the third day, tells him the mares are driven in, and instructs him not to appear before Baba-Yaga but to hide behind the manger, steal a mangy little colt lying on the dung-heap at midnight, and leave the place then.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Following the bee’s instructions, Ivan hides behind the manger, waits until midnight, steals the mangy colt, saddles it, and rides away from Baba-Yaga’s homestead.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Reaching a fiery river, Ivan uses a kerchief, shaking it three times to the right to produce a high splendid bridge over the river and then, after crossing, waving it twice to the left so that only a very slender bridge remains.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"When Baba-Yaga wakes and finds the colt missing, she pursues Ivan in an iron mortar, urging herself on with a pestle and sweeping away her trail with a broom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Baba-Yaga rides onto the bridge over the fiery river, which breaks in the middle so that she falls headlong into the river and meets a ‘savage death.’","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Ivan feeds the mangy colt in green meadows until it turns into a marvellous heroic steed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Ivan returns to Marya Morevna; she runs out to him, embraces him, and exclaims that she did not think God would bring him back to life, while expressing fear that Koshchéi might overtake and cut him to pieces again.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ivan asserts that Koshchéi will not overtake them now because he has a glorious heroic steed that ‘goes like a bird,’ and persuades Marya to come away with him on the horse.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"As Koshchéi rides home, his horse stumbles and explains that Ivan has come and taken Marya Morevna and that Ivan now has an heroic steed better than Koshchéi’s.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Koshchéi pursues and overtakes Ivan, but when he jumps down to cut Ivan with his sharp sword, Ivan’s horse strikes him with its hoof and smashes his skull; Ivan then finishes Koshchéi with a club, builds a pile of wood, burns him on a fire, and scatters the ashes to the wind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"After Koshchéi’s death, Marya Morevna mounts Koshchéi’s horse and Ivan his own, and they visit the Raven, the Eagle, and the Falcon, who receive them with joy and remark that Ivan’s struggle was worthwhile because such a beauty as Marya Morevna could not be found in the whole world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ivan Tsarevich","description":"A prince who seeks an heroic steed from Baba-Yaga, herds her mares, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l2905-l2978","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES:; lines 2905-2978","start":"2905","end":"2978","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Footnotes 54–71 to Ralston’s introductory chapter give brief notes on various Russian folk-tale episodes and terminology, including cross-cultural variants of a demon story (Finnish, Indian, Servian), a miser who endures pain better than a demon, a variant where a simpleton uses a hatchet on a greedy priest, an insect beast-epic where a spider kills a wasp and gnats and flies hold a funeral, lexical notes on euphemisms for death and an idiom for deceit, and a comment that the chort (devil-like figure) is linked with blacksmiths and functionally replaced by St Nicholas in another legend.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Russian demon (chortenok, a little chort or devil) appears in a story that is also known to the Finns.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the Finnish version of the story, the Russian demon has become the Plague.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the original Indian story, the demon formerly lived in a Brahman’s house.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the Indian story, the demon was frightened away from the Brahman’s house by the Brahman’s cantankerous wife.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the Servian version (Karajich, No. 37), the opening consists of the \"Scissors-story.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the Servian version, a vixen falls into a hole she does not see because she is intent on controverting her husband.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Afanasief’s tale ii. No. 12 was written down by a Crown Serf in the government of Perm.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Afanasief viii. No. 20 is mentioned along with the note that a copeck is worth about a third of a penny.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"One story in Afanasief is continued only a little further and its conclusion is the same as that of \"The Wise Wife.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"\"The Wise Wife\" (Book vii. No. 22) is described as a tale of magic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A Servian version of the tale related to \"The Wise Wife\" is found in Vuk Karajich, No. 7.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Afanasief v. No. 3 is noted as being from the Novgorod Government.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The phrase literally meaning \"has bid to live long\" is a conventional euphemism for \"has died.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The phrase \"Remember what his name was\" is sometimes added to the euphemism for death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In a referenced story, a miser holds out against pain which a scalded demon is unable to bear.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Professor de Gubernatis remarks that an unnamed figure may sometimes be called \"the first Brutus of popular tradition.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Afanasief v. No. 53 is cited without further detail.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The idiom \"zavtrakami podchivat\" means \"to dupe.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The word \"zavtra\" means \"to-morrow\" and \"zavtrak\" means \"breakfast.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"One of the inferior members of the Russian clerical body, though not of the clergy proper, is mentioned in connection with a tale.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"In one variant of a story, a pope or priest appears and immediately claims a share in the spoil.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"In that variant, the Simpleton makes use of his hatchet in response to the priest’s claim.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Priests are often nicknamed goats by the Russian peasantry, perhaps because of their long beards.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Afanasief ii. No. 8 and v. No. 5 are linked with similar tales by Khudyakof (No. 76), Grimm (No. 34 \"Die kluge Else\"), Haltrich (No. 66), Asbjoernsen and Moe (No. 10), and Dasent (No. 24 \"Not a Pin to choose between them\").","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Afanasief ii. No. 5 was written down by a crown-peasant in the government of Perm.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"\"Mizgir\" is a venomous spider like the Tarantula, found in the Kirghiz Steppes.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"In another story with the same title (v. 39), the spider lies on its back awaiting its prey.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"In that story, \"the honorable widow,\" the wasp, comes and falls straight into the spider’s trap.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The spider beheads the wasp.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Gnats and flies assemble, perform a funeral service over the wasp’s remains, and carry them off on their shoulders.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"The insects carry the remains to the village of Komarovo, whose name derives from \"komar\" meaning gnat.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"These insect and spider tales are presented as specimens of the Russian \"Beast-Epos.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"Afanasief’s \"Legendui\" No. 31 is taken from Dahl’s collection, and Russian legends are discussed further in Chapter VI.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"\"Baruinya\" is the wife of a \"barin\" or seigneur.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:35","text":"In a certain legend, the chort is described as akin to the devil, whom traditions frequently connect with blacksmiths.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:36","text":"Ralston suggests that the chort’s prototype in the original form of the story was probably a demigod or demon rather than the Christian devil.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:37","text":"In the legend \"The Priest with the Greedy Eyes,\" the role played by the chort in the other legend is instead played by St. Nicholas.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:38","text":"\"The Wise Wife\" is explicitly identified as a magical tale centered on a wise wife figure.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Russian demon (chortenok, chort)","description":"A demon or little devil appearing in a Russian story, related to the chort figure later described as akin to the devil and linked with blacksmiths.","role_refs":["role:1","role:17"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:18"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Plague (Finnish version)","description":"In the Finnish version of the Russian demon story, the demon is transformed into or identified with the Plague.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Brahman’s cantankerous wife","description":"A quarrelsome wife who frightens a demon away from the Brahman’s house in the Indian version of the story.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Brahman householder","description":"The Brahman whose house the demon formerly inhabited in the Indian story.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Vixen","description":"A female fox who, while intent on contradicting her husband, fails to see a hole and falls into it in the Servian version.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Vixen’s husband","description":"The husband engaged in a dispute with the vixen in the Servian \"Scissors-story\" opening.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Miser","description":"A miser who is able to endure severe pain which a demon cannot bear.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Scalded demon","description":"A demon that has been scalded and is unable to endure the pain as well as the miser.","role_refs":["role:1","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Simpleton","description":"A simpleton who, in one variant of a story, responds to a greedy priest’s claim on the spoil by using his hatchet.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Priest (pope) and priests in general","description":"A cleric who claims a share of the spoil in one tale variant, and priests in general who are nicknamed goats by Russian peasants.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Professor de Gubernatis","description

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l14854-l14961","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING. / THE HEDGEHOG, THE MERCHANT, THE KING, AND THE POOR MAN.; lines 14854-14961","start":"14854","end":"14961","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The Hedgehog asks a poor man he calls father to lend him money and instructs him to buy a black cock and a cast-away saddle at the market, paying double for each, since the cock will be his steed. The poor man does so. The Hedgehog saddles the cock and rides to the rich merchant he once led out of a great wild wood, reminding him of his promise to give the Hedgehog the best of his three daughters and three sacks of coin. The merchant summons his three daughters and tells the Hedgehog to choose; the Hedgehog selects the second daughter, said to be the most beautiful. The merchant loads three sacks of gold, silver, and copper into a coach with four horses, places his daughter inside, and sends her off with the Hedgehog riding beside the coach on his black cock. On the journey the Hedgehog sees the bride crying. When he asks why, she says that God has punished her with such a nasty being as him and that she does not know whether he is a man or a beast. The Hedgehog responds that if that is her only trouble he will keep the three sacks of coin and send her back to her father, since she is not worthy of him. He does so and takes the money to the poor man, who becomes extremely rich. The Hedgehog then rides his black cock to the king whom he had also led out of a great wild wood and reminds him of his promise to give his most beautiful daughter and three coaches of coins. The king calls his three daughters, explains that the Hedgehog saved him from certain death in the wood, and asks which will marry the Hedgehog. The two elder daughters turn away, but the youngest and fairest agrees, saying that if her father has promised, she will marry the Hedgehog and that God’s will be done. The king praises and kisses her, then measures out three coaches of gold, silver, and copper coins, seats her in a chariot of gold and glass, and sends her off with the Hedgehog riding alongside on his black cock. They travel across forty-nine kingdoms. When the Hedgehog looks into the chariot, he sees that the princess is cheerful rather than weeping. She calls him her heart’s beautiful love and invites him to sit beside her on the velvet cushion, saying she is neither afraid nor disgusted and that, if God has given him to her, he should be hers. The Hedgehog calls her his only and most beloved wife, shakes himself, and is transformed into a charming twenty-four-year-old king’s son with golden hair, mouth, and teeth. {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l7693-l7800","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA.; lines 7693-7800","start":"7693","end":"7800","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A peasant blessed by the Lord with an abundant rye harvest fills his granary, while a mouse and a sparrow come five times a day for three years to eat the grain together until almost all is gone. When only a small amount remains, the mouse secretly gnaws a hole in the floor at night and lets all the remaining rye fall to her, leaving the sparrow hungry. The sparrow flies to the lion, Tsar of beasts, to petition for justice, but the lion dismisses him, so he goes to his own Tsar, the eagle, and complains both of the mouse’s theft and the lion’s failure to judge. Angered, the eagle summons the lion and his army of beasts to battle; the beasts and the birds fight in an open field for three hours and three minutes until the eagle’s birds win, covering the field with the bodies of beasts. The wounded eagle withdraws to a slumbering forest and perches on a lofty oak, pondering how to regain his strength.

Long afterward, a merchant and his wife, who have no children, live in that land. The merchant tells his wife of a troubling dream in which a huge bird fastens upon him and must be fed an entire ox and a pailful of drink at a time, and he decides to walk in the forest. Taking his gun, he goes into the forest and comes to an oak where he sees the eagle and prepares to shoot it. The eagle speaks in a human voice, begging the merchant not to kill him but instead to take him home and feed him for three years, three months, and three days so that his wings may regrow and his strength return, promising to repay the merchant with good. After the eagle repeats this plea three times, the merchant takes pity, carries the bird home, kills an ox, and pours out a pail of mead, which the eagle consumes in a single meal, nearly ruining the merchant.

Seeing his host’s loss, the eagle advises the merchant to go to an open field where many beasts lie dead and wounded, take their rich furs, and sell them in town. The merchant follows this advice, sells the furs for much money, and becomes well provided for. After a year, the eagle has the merchant take him in a wagon to a place with lofty oaks; he flies above the clouds and crashes into an oak, splitting it in two, but says he has not fully regained his former strength and must be fed another year. After another year, he repeats the trial, this time smashing an oak into small pieces, yet again says that his old strength has not completely returned and asks the merchant to feed him for yet content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l8536-l8653","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA. / CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE.; lines 8536-8653","start":"8536","end":"8653","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Boyislav, traveling with a wise talking horse, is instructed to throw apples into the sea, which causes long roads to rise from the waves. Riding these roads, they reach Green Island, where Boyislav poses as a suitor for the king’s daughter but insists he must consult his father before choosing. Refusing the king’s rich gifts, he cleverly asks instead for the humble tablecloth from which he has eaten, which produces sumptuous food, and obtains it despite the king’s reluctance. Ordered to throw another apple, Boyislav and the horse reach White Island, where all the inhabitants, including the king, queen, and the most beautiful princess under the sun, lie in enchanted sleep sustained by an ever-burning taper. The horse instructs Boyislav to admire the princess but secretly take the taper without letting it go out. In the silent, luxurious city and golden palace, Boyislav becomes entranced by the sleeping princess’s beauty and nearly quenches the taper to awaken everyone, but the horse’s fierce neigh stops him. He takes the taper, then impulsively kneels to kiss the princess’s hand, causing her to blush and smile, and writes his name on a table before leaving. At the city gate a gust extinguishes the taper, the city awakens with a great shout, and the horse rescues Boyislav. After he throws in the last apple, another sea-road appears, bringing them back to firm land at dawn before the road sinks again.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At the horse’s command, Boyislav throws the second apple into the sea, and a five-hundred-mile road rises from the waves along which the horse carries him toward a distant city.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The horse tells Boyislav that the road leads to Green Island, ruled by a king who has a daughter described as neither beautiful nor ugly.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The horse instructs Boyislav to say he is seeking a bride but must first consult his father, and to refuse jewels and other gifts, asking instead for the tablecloth from the table where he eats.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On Green Island, Boyislav is welcomed by the king and presented to the princess; he tells the king he is in search of a bride but must speak with his father before deciding, which displeases the king and princess though he remains courteous.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The king leads Boyislav to a supper-chamber where a small table with a poor-looking cloth bears the choicest food and drink, from which Boyislav eats.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the meal, the king shows Boyislav a treasure-chamber and offers him rich presents, but Boyislav refuses, claiming his father has many treasures and he prefers to travel unburdened.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When pressed to take a keepsake, Boyislav asks for the tablecloth from the supper table; the king is ashamed and reluctant, offering another finely woven cloth instead, but finally gives up the original cloth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Boyislav leaves the king and princess with the tablecloth, rejoins the horse waiting outside the city, and the horse praises him for acting correctly before racing back across Green Island to the sea.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The horse orders Boyislav to throw the third apple into the sea; Boyislav hesitates, regretting to lose it forever, but obeys, and another five-hundred-mile road rises from the waves leading toward another great city.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The horse explains that they are nearing White Island, where a king with the most beautiful daughter under the sun reigns and where all people sleep because of a taper in the king’s palace that never burns out; they must sleep until someone quenches it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The horse instructs Boyislav to go to the palace, look at the princess as much as he wishes, take the taper, and ensure it The Snake’s Wife then pursues him, trying to swallow him, but Ivan and his brothers trick her with salt; later, Ivan hides in the forge of Kuzma and Demian, where the smiths seize the Snake’s Wife by her tongue, beat her to death, burn her body, and scatter her ashes, followed by a feast. An editorial note then summarizes a variant skazka of Ivan Buikovich (Bull’s son), in which multi-headed dragons called Chudo-Yudo are slain over successive nights, linked to the dragon killed by Slavonic St. George, and explicitly compared to the Lernaean Hydra for their regenerative heads; Ivan’s brothers sleep through the battles until awakened by gloves and a cap hurled at their hut, and the widows of the Chudo-Yudo monsters play roles analogous to the Snake’s daughters in the first tale.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After killing the Snake, Ivan Popyalof remembers he has left his gloves behind, tells his He contrasts the relatively uniform comic and animal tales of Europe with the more individualized supernatural beings of each people, especially the gloomy dark powers of Slavonic tradition, and identifies key Russian male and female embodiments of these powers of darkness, including the Snake, Koshchei the Deathless, the Morskoi Tsar, Baba Yaga, the Witch, and the Female Snake.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The chapter is devoted to mythical skazkas, whose selection aims to illustrate the distinctively content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l9328-l9447","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE. / THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG. / THE KING OF THE TOADS.; lines 9328-9447","start":"9328","end":"9447","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A fisherman who lives with his wife in a cottage by the sea is only allowed by the king to fish once a week, on Mondays, and must supply the royal kitchen. One Monday, after working all morning without catching anything, he makes a final attempt and hauls up a tightly sealed copper kettle instead of fish. When he opens it, black smoke pours out and turns into a fiery man who says the fisherman has helped him and that he will help him, but also destroy him. The frightened fisherman demands a reward and asks how the being could live inside such a small vessel. The fiery man demonstrates by turning back into smoke and re-entering the kettle; the fisherman quickly seals the lid, trapping him. From inside, the spirit begs for release and promises a reward. The fisherman first makes him swear never to destroy him, then releases him. The fiery man leads him to a high cliff with steps cut in the rock, plucks a herb, and gives it to him with instructions: if he steps on a certain step he will be carried to a high mountain overlooking a great lake rich in fish, where he may fish as much as he likes, but only on Mondays, and to return he must climb to the top. The spirit vanishes. The fisherman follows the instructions, is borne by a mighty wind to the mountain, and sees an unknown land covered in dark forests with a broad lake and no human dwellings. At the lake he finds a boat already equipped with fishing gear. He casts his net twice without success, but on the third throw he catches three strange fish unlike any he has seen. Deciding they are fit for the king rather than for himself, he returns via the mountain and wind and heads home, where his wife has dinner ready and is waiting impatiently. The narrator notes that the fisherman loves domestic peace and quietly does whatever his wife wants while concealing his obedience. His wife scolds him for being late and threatens to eat without him. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l8174-l8301","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA.; lines 8174-8301","start":"8174","end":"8301","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ivan the merchant's son must recognize his bride Vassilissa the Cunning through three tests set by the Tsar of the Sea: choosing correctly among three identical mares, three doves, and three maidens. After Ivan succeeds, the Tsar gives him Vassilissa and they marry. Later, Ivan and Vassilissa flee by night toward Ivan's homeland. Pursuers sent by the Tsar are twice fooled when Vassilissa magically transforms Ivan and herself into a garden and cabbage, then into a well and falcon. The Tsar of the Sea then pursues them himself, but Vassilissa uses a brush, comb, and towel that transform into an impassable forest, a lofty mountain, and finally a great sea, which forces the Tsar to turn back. Near home, Ivan goes ahead to tell his parents, despite Vassilissa's warning not to kiss his godmother or he will forget her. Ivan kisses his godmother and forgets Vassilissa, who waits in vain and eventually takes service with an old woman in town. Ivan finds a new bride and prepares a feast for the whole world. Vassilissa, dressed as a beggar, comes to the merchant's house and receives a burnt cake, while a perfect small cake is served at the feast. When the feast cake is cut, two pigeons fly out; the male repeatedly asks the female for a kiss, and she refuses, citing how Ivan forgot Vassilissa. This dialogue reminds Ivan of his first wife; he recognizes the beggar as Vassilissa, claims her before his parents, and dismisses the new bride with gifts. Ivan then lives with Vassilissa, gains wealth, and avoids further trouble.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Tsar brings out three mares that look exactly alike, places them in a row, and tells Ivan to choose one.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ivan examines the mares, notices that one bridle has a dim spangle, seizes that mare, and declares, \"This is my bride.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Tsar then releases three identical doves, scatters buckwheat before them, and Ivan chooses the one that is constantly shaking her wings, again calling it his bride.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Tsar finally presents three maidens identical in face, stature, and hair; one waves her handkerchief and Ivan seizes her hand, declaring her his bride, after which the Tsar gives Vassilissa to Ivan and they have a joyous wedding.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After some time Ivan decides to escape with Vassilissa to his own country; they saddle their horses and ride away at night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In the morning the Tsar discovers their flight and sends a party of pursuers after them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"At Vassilissa's instruction, Ivan lies down on the damp earth to listen and hears the neighing of horses approaching.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Vassilissa turns Ivan into a garden and herself into a head of cabbage; the pursuers find only a garden with a cabbage and return to the Tsar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Tsar, suspecting a trick, orders the pursuers to bring him the head of cabbage they saw in the garden.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On a second pursuit Ivan again listens at Vassilissa's request and hears horses; Vassilissa turns herself into a well and Jalmir, distressed, consults his talking white steed, who advises him to ask the king for three hundred loaves of bread, three hundred kegs of wine, and three hundred slaughtered oxen. The king provides these and promises rich reward if Jalmir succeeds. Jalmir travels a long time with wagons of provisions until he reaches the sea shore. There he rescues a large fish stranded on the beach at his horse’s prompting; the fish gives him a whistle to summon its aid. Jalmir next encounters three giants on the shore, gives them the food and drink, and they roast the oxen over a fire. Jalmir also feeds a great eagle, which thanks him and promises to help him later. After eating, the giants ask Jalmir’s true wish. He explains that he must bring back a princess from a golden castle out in the sea, which the giants point out. In return for the provisions, the giants break pieces from a cliff and in three days build a dam across the sea so that one can walk dry-shod to the castle. On the fourth day Jalmir crosses the dam, enters the golden castle, and asks the princess to share his king’s throne and crown. She agrees, provided Jalmir will remain at court as viceroy. She mounts a black horse, he his white steed, and they ride back along the dam. During the journey Jalmir becomes troubled by his growing attraction to the princess, while she looks at him with special delight. They arrive at the king’s castle. The king meets them, leads a solemn procession, and asks the princess to be his spouse. She replies that she must first have her golden castle. The astonished king looks imploringly at Jalmir, who volunteers to fetch it. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l9227-l9325","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA. / CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE. / THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG.; lines 9227-9325","start":"9227","end":"9325","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this concluding portion of the tale, the king keeps Yanek’s miraculous food-producing table and has craftsmen make an indistinguishable copy, sending the counterfeit back. When Yanek finds the table no longer provides food, he smashes it and vows to break down the king’s castle. The king, disturbed by dreams, musters his army. Yanek arrives with a magic pack, summons an immense army from it, and so terrifies the king that he sues for peace, promising to return the true table and give Yanek his daughter in marriage. The princess appears, Yanek declares the wedding will take place that day, recalls the magical army into the pack, and they celebrate with an endless feast from the table. That night Yanek uses a magic bag to conjure the most beautiful castle in the king’s garden. At dawn, the new castle blazes with gold, silver, and precious stones, and the astonished king gives Yanek his whole kingdom. Yanek becomes a powerful and benevolent king, fortifying his borders with castles from the bag and garrisoning them with troops from the pack; the magic table sustains him. He rules long as a father to his people, keeps his treacherous brothers away, and cares devotedly for his mother. The magical table, pack, and bag are kept on a golden throne in the most beautiful chamber. After Yanek’s death, his descendants rule increasingly badly. Ashamed of their peasant origins and fearing ridicule if the true source of their power is known, they hide the magical items in a dark, damp cellar. The table and bag rot, mice gnaw the pack, and the great kingdom collapses. In later hardship, a king searches for the items, but they crumble at his touch, leaving only fragments.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The king receives Yanek’s table via the chamberlain, is delighted by its food, and decides to deceive Yanek instead of returning it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The king summons joiners, carvers, and turners to make an exact copy of Yanek’s table, then identifies the real one and sends the counterfeit to Yanek.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When Yanek commands the returned table to provide food, it trembles but produces nothing, so he smashes it and tells the chamberlain to inform the king that he will destroy the castle the next day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The king hears Yanek’s threat, initially feels secure, but after troubling dreams orders his army to assemble before the castle ready for battle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Yanek comes with his pack, counts the royal troops, again asks for his table, and is mocked by the king.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Yanek opens the pack and commands “a thousand times a thousand” infantry and cavalry to come out, and an enormous army pours forth, filling the land before the castle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Confronted with Yanek’s vast army, the king raises a white flag, approaches Yanek, admits a mistake, and offers to return the table and give his daughter in marriage to make peace.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Yanek agrees to peace on the wedding feast, the table provides abundant meat and drink until evening.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At night Yanek goes to the king’s garden with his bag and commands the most beautiful castle in the world to emerge; such a castle appears that even Yanek is astonished.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Yanek refuses the old king’s prepared chambers, saying he has his own household, and leads his bride to the new castle, which she greatly admires.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At sunrise people tell the king about the new castle blazing with gold, silver, and precious stones, and the king, impressed, gives Yanek everything he can, including his kingdom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Yanek becomes a powerful king able to wage war against the whole world, sets castles from the bag along the boundaries, garrisons them with troops from the pack, and is supplied with excellent food by the table.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Yanek reigns long as a ‘real father’ to his subjects, keeps his brothers away as punishment, and cares so well for his mother that she lives to a great age.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The pack, bag, and table are placed on a golden throne in the most beautiful chamber of Yanek’s castle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After King Yanek’s death he is mourned by all, and his eldest son succeeds him but rules less well; later kings are even worse.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Yanek’s successors are ashamed of their peasant ancestry and, to hide the true source of royal power, throw the table, pack, and bag into a dark, damp cellar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"In the cellar the table and bag rot, mice gnaw the pack, and with this decay the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l11121-l11233","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE KING OF THE TOADS. / THE MOUSE-HOLE, AND THE UNDERGROUND KINGDOM. / THE CUIRASSIER AND THE HORNED PRINCESS. / THE TREACHEROUS BROTHERS.; lines 11121-11233","start":"11121","end":"11233","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After the brothers escape the sorceress, she cannot harm them beyond the boundary of her castle lands and curses herself over her dead daughters. The brothers ride until the castle vanishes, then rest and learn from Jalmir that he has saved them from certain death; he reveals his identity as their youngest brother, after which they grow cold toward him. Jalmir’s white steed reproaches him for revealing himself, foretells that they will all enter the service of a mighty king, and offers ongoing advice. The brothers thereafter avoid Jalmir but flatter him at inns so he will pay their expenses. They reach a great city, go first to an inn where the brothers drink to excess, and later present themselves to the king, who makes them courtiers with good pay and little work and shows growing favor to Jalmir, provoking his brothers’ jealousy. While idly exploring the royal castle, the brothers discover a room full of books and read that the king has no birds in his kingdom and that birds for his table are extremely costly. They plot to tell the king that Jalmir knows about birds so he will be sent to fetch them, and they urge the king to insist firmly. The king summons Jalmir, angrily commands him to bring birds despite his protests of ignorance, and Jalmir departs in distress to consult his white steed. The horse tells him not to grieve and promises that at dusk they will go for the birds. At night Jalmir mounts the white steed and rides swiftly to the sorceress’s castle, where the horse instructs him to pass by chambers filled with silver, golden, and diamond bird-cages without touching them, and instead to take only a wooden cage holding a mean-looking bird from a fourth chamber, warning that touching the others will shake the castle and allow the sorceress to seize and kill him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the brothers cross the boundary of the sorceress's castle lands, she has no more power over them, must return home, and curses herself above the dead bodies of her daughters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The brothers ride without stopping until wise.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Jalmir's white steed drops behind of its own accord and speaks privately to its master, reproaching him for revealing year.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The eldest brother suggests that they tell the king that Jalmir knows about birds so the king will send him for them, and ignorance.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The king summons Jalmir, states that he has no birds in his kingdom, and commands Jalmir to bring them; when Jalmir {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l4719-l4826","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 4719-4826","start":"4719","end":"4826","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An old woman, under threat from the king, promises to make the bride’s wedding ring but actually relies on Prince Ivan, who already has the ring and later secretly provides the wedding-dress and seamless shoes. The old woman delivers these items to the bride, each time accepting only one ducat and claiming she made them herself. When the wedding day arrives, Ivan has the old woman warn him when the bride is about to be married; he then reveals his princely identity, enters the church before his brothers arrive, stands beside the bride, and marries her. The king rejoices at Ivan’s return, learns of the treachery of his elder sons, banishes them, and makes Ivan heir to the throne.

The editor then summarizes another tale, "Prince Arikad," in which the Queen-Mother is carried off by the Whirlwind (Vikhor). Her youngest son climbs a hill using iron hooks, kills Vikhor, rescues his mother and three ladies, and lowers them with a rope made of hide; his brothers cut the rope to prevent his descent and later force the ladies to swear not to betray them, with the oath accompanied by the eating of earth. The same formality appears in another story, and its sacred nature is suggested as a reason for the reticence found in such tales.

Finally, several descriptions of Koshchei’s death are given. In one, he is killed by a blow on the forehead from a mysterious egg that is the last link in the magic chain binding his life. In another version of the same story, told of a Snake, the fatal blow comes from a small stone found within the yolk of an egg inside a duck inside a hare inside a stone on the fabulous island Buyan. In another variant, Koshchei initially deceives his captive about where his "death" resides, naming a besom and a fence that she decorates with gold. He then confesses that his death lies in an egg inside a duck inside a log floating on the sea. Prince Ivan obtains the egg, tosses it from hand to hand, causing Koshchei to rush around wildly, and finally breaks the egg, whereupon Koshchei falls and dies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An old woman dresses herself, goes to the king, and volunteers to make the wedding ring; the king content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l9777-l9859","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE. / THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG. / THE KING OF THE TOADS.; lines 9777-9859","start":"9777","end":"9859","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A woman (in this context, the king's supposed beloved) asks the King of the Toads to restore the enchanted country's former shape, promising that once her former husband dies, the Toad King will take his place and she will marry him publicly. When he agrees and embraces her, he is struck with a twig, frozen to the earth, then denounced as a \"serpent of hell\" by the king, who cuts him into pieces and throws them into the water, where frogs devour him. The lake drains, treetops rise as the water recedes, and a park, city, and crowds of freed people appear; they praise the king as he reaches the castle, where he beheads the hated queen despite an old man (the liberated king) pleading for her. The liberated king gives his realm to his deliverer and soon dies. The new king is accepted by the people, rides a fiery steed to proclaim the succession, then later returns to his former palace to find that many years have passed and only an aged former body-guard recognizes him. After selling his old castle, he summons the fisherman, who describes how the water vanished under his boat, trees sprang up, a great city appeared, and he wandered for a long time before reaching home to find his wife dead. The king consoles the fisherman, takes him into his service, and they all move to the restored kingdom, where they live happily until their deaths.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A woman tells the King of the Toads that once her former husband dies the Toad King will take his place and they will reign together, but she asks him first to restore the kingdom from its enchanted state to its former shape in exchange for marrying him publicly.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The King of the Toads agrees to the request, embraces his supposed beloved, and is struck three times with a twig in the dark, which freezes him to the earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The king calls the King of the Toads a \"Serpent of hell,\" threatens to enchant him for eternity, draws his sword, cuts him into countless pieces, and throws the pieces into the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After the Toad King is dismembered and thrown into the water, frogs rush in from all sides, croaking loudly, and greedily swallow the pieces of his body.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Once the frogs have devoured the Toad King, the water begins to drain from the lake; by moonlight over a mountain summit the king sees tree-tops rising as the water recedes until the lake disappears, leaving a splendid park in its place.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Multitudes of people appear in the restored park, praise the king, and hurry toward the castle; he joins them and must pass through a large city and many streets to reach the castle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Inside the brightly lit castle filled with people, an old man in the last chamber is preventing the crowd from hacking the queen to pieces when the king intervenes by cutting off her head, saying she deserves it; the old man sheds a few tears for his former wife.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After the queen’s execution, universal rejoicing begins, but the liberated king withdraws from the celebrations, calls his deliverer, says his hours are numbered, and grants him the whole kingdom to rule in his place; by morning the old king is dead.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The new king mounts a fiery steed, rides to the city, announces the former ruler’s death and last will, and the people grieve briefly before joyfully greeting him as their new king; after the old monarch’s burial he inspects the kingdom and decides to remain there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When the new king travels back toward his former palace, the road is much longer than before and he must ride several weeks; no one recognizes him because several years have passed while he was in the enchanted kingdom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"An old grandfather, who identifies himself as the last surviving member of the body-guard that once accompanied the king to a cliff, recognizes the king and begs to be taken into his service again.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The people accept the grandfather’s testimony, gather around the king, kiss the hem of his garment, and he sells his castle, loads his belongings onto wagons, and prepares to leave; he inquires after the fisherman, learns he returned only yesterday, and has him summoned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The fisherman reports that while he was fishing the water suddenly disappeared beneath his boat, leaving him on dry land, so he ran away as trees rapidly grew under him, their branches striking his face in the night; at dawn he found that a forest had become an enormous city with a great palace.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The fisherman says he then wandered a day, two days, a week, a month, and a year without finding his cottage, and only yesterday returned home to discover his wife dead and himself alone in the world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The king tells the fisherman not to cry and offers to keep him with him; the fisherman responds in tears, and the group journeys safely to the new kingdom, where they live happily until they die.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"King of the Toads","description":"Supernatural king associated with the enchantment of the country, deceived during an embrace, struck with a twig, dismembered with a sword, and thrown into the water, after which frogs devour his body and the enchantment ends.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"New king / deliverer king","description":"Human king who poses as the Toad King’s beloved, strikes and kills the King of the Toads, witnesses the restoration of the kingdom, beheads the queen, is granted the realm by the liberated king, proclaims his rule, later returns to his former palace after years have passed, and takes the fisherman into his household.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Liberated old king","description":"Former ruler of the enchanted kingdom, found as an old man in the castle, who tries to shield the queen from the mob, mourns her as his former wife, is described as the liberated king, and then gives his kingdom to his deliverer before dying.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Queen, former wife of the liberated king","description":"Queen whom the crowd wants to hack to pieces and whom the king beheads instead; she is described as deserving her fate and is referred to as the former wife of the old king.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Frogs","description":"Numerous frogs that rush from all sides with terrible croaking and greedily swallow the dismembered pieces of the King of the Toads’ body.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"People of the restored kingdom","description":"Crowds of people who appear when the lake drains, praise the king, hurry to the castle, try to take vengeance on the queen, rejoice at their liberation, later grieve briefly for the old king, accept the new king, and kiss the hem of his garment.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Grandfather body-guard","description":"An aged man who identifies himself as the only surviving member of the king’s former body-guard from the journey to the cliff and who recognizes the king when others do not, asking to reenter his service.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Fisherman","description":"Man connected with the enchanted lake, summoned by the king, who recounts how the water vanished beneath his boat, trees grew rapidly around him, an enormous city and palace appeared, he wandered for a long time before returning home to find his wife dead, and who is taken into the king’s service.","role_refs":["role:8","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Fisherman’s wife","description":"Unseen character mentioned by the fisherman as his wife, whom he finds dead upon finally returning home after his prolonged disorientation.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Fiery steed","description":"Horse described as fiery, used by the new king to ride quickly to the city to announce the old king’s death and last will.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"monstrous_enchanter_king","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The woman speaks of the whole country being enchanted and asks the King of the Toads to restore its former shape, and his death immediately ends the enchantment, implying he is the ruler responsible for it.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"heroic_deliverer_and_new_king","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"He tricks and strikes the King of the Toads, calls him a serpent, dismembers him, thereby ending the enchantment, executes the queen, and is formally granted the entire kingdom by the liberated king and accepted by the people as their ruler.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"liberated_old_king","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"After the enchantment ends, an old man in the castle is later described as the liberated king who had been ruler; he mourns his former wife and then transfers the kingdom to his deliverer before dying.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"condemned_treacherous_queen","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"Crowds in the castle are eager to hew the queen to pieces, the king instead beheads her, and he states that she deserved her fate; she is identified as the old king’s former wife.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"agents_of_nemesis","assigned_to":["fig:5"],"basis":"Frogs appear after the Toad King is dismembered and greedily devour the pieces of their own former king, described as their destroyer.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"role:6","label":"subjects_of_kingdom","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"They emerge when the lake drains, praise the king, join the celebration, seek vengeance on the queen, mourn briefly for the old king, and then acclaim the new king, even kissing the hem of his garment.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"loyal_surviving_retainer","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"The old grandfather identifies himself as a member of the former body-guard from the cliff expedition, notes that all his comrades are dead, and begs to be taken again into the king’s service.","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"role:8","label":"helper_and_beneficiary","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"The fisherman is sought out by the king, recounts his ordeal linked to the enchantment’s end, and, after losing his home life, is given a place with the king for the rest of his days.","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9","ev:10"]},{"id":"role:9","label":"bereaved_widower","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"He explains that after his long wandering he returned home to find his wife dead and says he is alone in the world.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:10","label":"deceased_spouse","assigned_to":["fig:9"],"basis":"She is mentioned only as the fisherman’s wife, whom he finds dead upon finally returning home.","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"role:11","label":"magical_mount","assigned_to":["fig:10"],"basis":"The horse is called a fiery steed and serves as the swift mount by which the new king reaches the city to proclaim the succession, suggesting an extraordinary or magical quality.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Enchanted lake water draining to reveal the kingdom","literal_form":"Lake water covering the kingdom that drains away after the King of the Toads is slain, revealing a park and city.","associated_figures":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3","fig:6","fig:8"],"taxonomy_refs":["water"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:9"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Rising treetops and rapidly growing forest","literal_form":"Treetops rising from the receding water and trees that quickly grow under the fisherman, striking his face.","associated_figures":["fig:2","fig:6","fig:8"],"taxonomy_refs":["tree"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:9"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"Moon over mountain summit during restoration","literal_form":"The content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l5030-l5149","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 5030-5149","start":"5030","end":"5149","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A human girl has lived for three years in an underwater realm with her husband Osip and their two children. Allowed to visit her mother on the surface, she learns that to summon him she must stand at the dike and call his name. Her mother tricks her into revealing this, then while the daughter sleeps, the mother sharpens an axe, calls Osip from the water, beheads him as he appears, and the pond darkens with blood. The next day the daughter tries to return, finds only her husband’s severed head floating in the water, realizes her mother has killed him, and in grief transforms her daughter into a wren, her son into a nightingale, and herself into a cuckoo. A scholarly note explains that serpent‑spouse stories are widespread, referencing Indian Panchatantra tales, Balkan and other European versions, and suggesting a link to Apuleius’s Cupid and Psyche. Another note states that the snakes in this story resemble Indian Nagas of the underground world and may be related to merfolk, Rusalkas, Vodyanies, Nixies, and similar European water-spirits, among whom a kind of popular cult still exists.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The girl has lived \"down there\" with her husband for three years and during that time has had two children, a son and a daughter.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"To let her visit her mother, the husband brings the girl up to the surface of the water and ashore.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Before she leaves, the husband tells her that to summon him she must go to the dike and call, \"Osip, Osip, come here!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The daughter goes to her mother’s house carrying her little girl and leading her boy; her mother greets her joyfully, talks with her, and feeds her dinner.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The daughter tells her mother that she has been living very well with her husband below, and that her life there is better than her mother’s life on the surface.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The mother asks the daughter for her husband’s name and how she will get home, and the daughter reveals that his name is Osip and that she will call him at the dike with the summoning formula.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the daughter lies down to sleep, the mother sharpens an axe, goes to the dike, calls out \"Osip, Osip, come here!\", and when Osip appears she beheads him, after which the pond water becomes dark with blood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The next morning the daughter leaves her mother’s house with her children, goes to the dike, calls for Osip repeatedly, but he does not come.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Looking into the water, the daughter sees a head floating and realizes that her mother has killed her husband.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In her grief on the bank, the daughter declares that her little girl will henceforth fly as a wren, her boy as a nightingale, and that she herself will fly as a cuckoo crying \"Cuckoo!\" forever.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The commentator states that stories about serpent-spouses are common and that there are many transformation tales in which a husband or wife appears in the form of a snake.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"According to the commentator, in some tales a serpent-husband removes his serpent skin, the wife seizes and burns it, and this usually benefits both spouses but not always.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The commentator claims that a story of the serpent-spouse type likely underlies Apuleius’s legend of Cupid and Psyche, and he mentions Albanian, Roumanian, Wallachian, and Servian snake-husband tales as wild versions of the motif.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The commentator writes that the snakes in this story resemble the Indian Nagas, serpents who inhabit Patala or the underground world, can take human shape, and often associate with mortals.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"He adds that these snakes may also be related to mermen and mermaids, and to various European water-beings such as Rusalkas, Nereids, female Nixies, and male water-sprites called Vodyanies, Nix, Nek, and Naekke, around whom popular belief and even a form of cult still persist in some regions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Unnamed girl / human wife","description":"A human girl who has lived for three years in an underwater realm with her husband Osip, has a son and daughter, visits her mother on the surface, discovers her husband’s murder, and turns herself and her children into birds.","role_refs":["role:1","role:5","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Osip, underwater husband (serpent-like being)","description":"The girl’s husband named Osip, who lives under the water, fathers two children with her, allows her to visit her mother, can be summoned from the dike by his name, and is beheaded by the girl’s mother; the commentator identifies the story’s snakes as akin to serpent beings like the Indian Nagas.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Old woman / girl’s mother","description":"The girl’s mother, who welcomes her daughter and grandchildren, learns her son-in-law’s name and summoning call, then treacherously lures him to the dike and kills him with a sharpened axe.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Little girl (daughter’s daughter)","description":"The young daughter carried in her mother’s arms during the visit, who is later transformed by her mother into a wren.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Boy (daughter’s son)","description":"The young son led by the hand or following his mother, who is transformed by her into a nightingale.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Indian Nagas","description":"Serpent beings said to inhabit Patala or the underground world, able to take human form and mix with mortals, to whom the story’s snakes are compared.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Mermen and mermaids","description":"Aquatic humanoid beings of the sea-coasts mentioned as possibly related to the snakes or water-spirits in the story.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Rusalkas","description":"Water-nymphs in South-Russian belief, closely resembling Greek Nereids and female Nixies, cited as analogous beings to the story’s water-snakes.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Vodyanies","description":"Male water-sprites venerated in parts of Russia, described as almost identical with German Nix, Swedish Nek, and Finnish Naekke and linked to the same family of water-beings as the story’s snakes.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Nereids and female Nixies","description":"Sea and fresh-water nymphs of Greek and Northern European tradition, mentioned as resembling Rusalkas and as related to other water-spirits.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"German Nix, Swedish Nek, Finnish Naekke","description":"Male water-spirits from German, Swedish, and Finnish folklore, described as almost identical with the Russian Vodyanies.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:12","name_or_label":"Cupid and Psyche","description":"The divine lovers in Apuleius’s legend, which the commentator suggests was founded upon a serpent-spouse type folktale.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Human wife living in underwater otherworld","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The girl has lived for three years \"down there\" under the water with her husband and children before returning to visit her mother.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Serpent-like or water-spirit husband","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Osip lives under the water, emerges when summoned from the dike, and the commentator explicitly treats the story’s snakes as comparable to serpent beings like Nagas and other water-spirits.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Murderous mother-in-law who betrays supernatural son-in-law","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"After
