content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6442-l6588","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6442-6588","start":"6442","end":"6588","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Baba Yaga returns home with Vasilissa, feasts, and sets the girl difficult household and grain-sorting tasks under threat of being eaten if she fails. Vasilissa feeds her doll with the scraps and prays; the doll promises help and secretly performs the work. Each morning Baba Yaga departs in a magical mortar with pestle and broom, accompanied by personified riders of Day and Sun, while at dusk a rider of Night and skulls with glowing eyes light the yard. Baba Yaga’s invisible servants, three pairs of hands, grind wheat and later press oil from poppy seed. On the second day, after the doll again completes the tasks, Baba Yaga questions Vasilissa, identifies the white, red, and black riders as her bright Day, red Sun, and dark Night, warns that excessive questioning is dangerous and claims to eat over‑inquisitive people. When Vasilissa attributes her success to her mother’s blessing, Baba Yaga angrily expels her, saying she does not want blessed people in her house.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The gates opened, Baba Yaga drove in whistling with Vasilissa following, they entered the sitting-room, and Baba Yaga lay at full length and ordered Vasilissa to fetch what was in the oven because she was hungry.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Vasilissa lit a splinter at one of the skulls on the fence, took a large quantity of meat from the oven and drinks from the cellar, and Baba Yaga ate and drank everything, leaving only a crust of bread and a morsel of sucking-pig for Vasilissa.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Before going to sleep, Baba Yaga ordered Vasilissa to cleanse the courtyard, sweep the room, cook dinner, get the linen ready, and to take four quarters of wheat from the corn-bin and clear it of other seed, threatening to eat Vasilissa if all was not done.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After Baba Yaga began to snore, Vasilissa set the remnants of the hag’s supper before her doll, cried, explained that Baba Yaga had given her a heavy task and threatened to eat her, and begged the doll for help.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The doll replied to Vasilissa, telling her not to fear, to eat, say her prayers, and go to bed, and stating that 'The morning is wiser than the evening.'","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Early the next morning Vasilissa saw the light in the skull’s eyes going out, then a white horseman appeared and all was light. Baba Yaga went into the courtyard and whistled, whereupon a mortar with a pestle and a broom appeared. Then the red horseman appeared, the sun rose, and Baba Yaga seated herself in the mortar and drove out of the courtyard, shooting herself along with the pestle and sweeping away her traces with the broom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Left alone, Vasilissa examined Baba Yaga’s house, wondered at the abundance, and hesitated over which work to start. She then saw that all the work had already been done and that the doll had cleared the wheat to the last grain. Vasilissa thanked the doll as her preserver, and the doll told her only to cook dinner, slipped into her pocket, and advised her to cook in God’s name and rest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Towards evening Vasilissa prepared the table and waited for Baba Yaga. As it grew dusky, a black rider appeared at the gate and everything became dark, with only the skulls’ eyes giving light. The trees began to crack and the leaves to rustle, and Baba Yaga drove up, whereupon Vasilissa went out to meet her.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Baba Yaga asked if everything was done, and Vasilissa invited her to inspect it. Baba Yaga examined everything, was vexed that there was nothing to be angry about, and said, 'Well, well! very good!'","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Baba Yaga summoned 'My trusty servants, zealous friends' to grind her wheat, and three pairs of hands appeared, gathered up the wheat, and carried it out of sight. After supper Baba Yaga went to bed and ordered Vasilissa to repeat the day’s work and additionally to clean earth from poppy seed grain by grain because someone had mixed earth with it out of spite. Baba Yaga turned to the wall and snored, and Vasilissa fed her doll, which again told her to pray, go to sleep, and that the morning was wiser than the evening.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The next morning Baba Yaga again drove out of the courtyard in her mortar, and Vasilissa and her doll immediately did all the work. When Baba Yaga returned she called on her faithful servants to press oil from the poppy seed, and three pairs of hands appeared, gathered up the poppy seed, and took it out of sight. Baba Yaga sat down to dinner and ate while Vasilissa stood silently nearby.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Baba Yaga asked Vasilissa why she stood silent 'like a dumb creature.' Vasilissa answered that she had not dared to speak but, if permitted, wanted to ask about something. Baba Yaga allowed her to ask but warned that not every question brings good and quoted, 'Get much to know, and old soon you’ll grow.'","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Vasilissa asked who the white rider on a white horse in white clothes was that passed her as she came, and Baba Yaga replied that this was her bright Day.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Vasilissa asked who the red rider on a red horse in red clothes was that passed her later, and Baba Yaga answered that he was her red Sun.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Vasilissa asked who the black rider was that passed her at the gate, and Baba Yaga replied that he was her dark Night and that they were all her trusty servants.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Vasilissa thought about the three pairs of hands but stayed silent. Baba Yaga asked why she did not continue to question her. Vasilissa replied that she had asked enough and repeated Baba Yaga’s saying that getting too much to know makes one grow old. Baba Yaga stated that it was good Vasilissa had only asked about what she saw outdoors, because she hated having 'dirt' carried out of doors and said she eats over‑inquisitive people.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Baba Yaga asked how Vasilissa managed to accomplish the work she was set. Vasilissa answered that her mother’s blessing assisted her. Baba Yaga reacted by telling Vasilissa to get out of her house, calling her a blessed daughter and saying she did not want blessed people.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Baba Yaga","description":"A hag or witch-like figure called 'granny' and 'hag' who arrives whistling, lives in a house with skulls on the fence, rides in a mortar with pestle and broom, commands personified riders of Day, Sun, and Night and invisible hands, eats large amounts of food, sets Vasilissa difficult tasks under threat of being eaten, warns against over-inquisitiveness, and expels those she calls blessed.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:5","role:8","role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l5436-l5581","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 5436-5581","start":"5436","end":"5581","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Prince, having taken leave of the Yaga, goes to a sea-shore and hides in bushes. Twelve spoonbills arrive, strike the wet earth, and turn into fair maidens to bathe. The Prince steals the shift of the eldest, who is Vasilissa the Wise, so that eleven maidens put on their shifts, become birds, and fly away, leaving her behind. Vasilissa begs for her shift and promises to help the Prince when he comes to the house of her father, the Water King; he returns it and she becomes a spoonbill and flies away. The Prince then meets three heroes—Obedalo, Opivalo, and Moroz Treskum—who join him as he goes to the Water King. The Water King welcomes him but immediately commands him, on pain of death, to build a great crystal bridge in a single night. The Prince despairs, but Vasilissa asks why he cries, tells him to sleep, and summons carpenters and workmen by a powerful whistle; they build and ornament the bridge overnight. In the morning the Prince pretends to be finishing the job as the Water King inspects and praises it. The King then orders a second task: a large, shady garden with singing birds, blossoms, and ripe fruit must appear by the next day under the same threat. Vasilissa again tells the Prince to sleep, summons gardeners, and by morning the garden stands complete; the Prince tidies it as the Water King inspects and praises it. The King sets a third trial: the Prince must choose a bride from among his twelve daughters, all identical in appearance, and must identify the same one three times or die. Vasilissa secretly instructs him on three signals she will give (waving a handkerchief, arranging her dress, and a fly above her head), enabling him to pick her correctly three times. He marries Vasilissa, and a great wedding feast is prepared. The Water King orders that all the abundant food be eaten, threatening the Prince if anything remains; the Prince asks that his ‘old fellow’ Obedalo join them, and Obedalo consumes everything yet remains unsatisfied. The King then produces forty tubs of strong drink and orders them emptied; Opivalo drinks them all and asks for more. Seeing he cannot destroy his son-in-law this way, the King has an iron bath-house heated with twelve loads of firewood until its stove and walls glow red-hot. The Prince asks that his ‘old fellow’ Moroz Treskum bathe first. Moroz enters, blows in the corners, and makes icicles hang there, cooling the room. After him the young couple bathe safely, are scrubbed, and then go home.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Prince bids the Yaga farewell and goes to an appointed spot on the sea-shore, where he hides behind bushes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Twelve spoonbills arrive at the sea-shore, strike the moist earth, turn into fair maidens, and begin to bathe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Prince steals the shift of the eldest maiden and hides with it while the maidens bathe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Eleven maidens put on their shifts, turn back into birds, and fly away, leaving only the eldest, named Vasilissa the Wise, without a shift.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Vasilissa the Wise begs the Prince to return her shift and promises to do him good service when he comes to the house of her father, the Water King.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Vasilissa identifies the Water King as her father and implies that the Prince is already destined to visit his house.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Prince returns Vasilissa’s shift; she immediately turns into a spoonbill and flies away after her companions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On his way the Prince meets three heroes named Obedalo, Opivalo, and Moroz Treskum, and he takes them with him to the Water King’s.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Water King greets the Prince, says he has grown weary waiting for him, and orders him to build a great crystal bridge in one night under threat of beheading.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Prince weeps over the impossible bridge task, saying he does not even know how to handle an axe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Vasilissa the Wise speaks to the Prince from an upper window, asks why he is crying, tells him to lie down and sleep, and says that ‘the morning is wiser than the evening.’","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Vasilissa goes out onto the steps and whistles loudly, summoning carpenters and workmen from all sides, who level the ground, carry bricks, and build an ornate crystal bridge during the night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the morning Vasilissa wakes the Prince and tells him the bridge is ready; he takes a broom, sweeps, and tidies the bridge as the Water King comes to inspect it and praises him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Water King sets a second task: by the next day the Prince must produce a big, shady garden with singing birds, blossoming flowers, and ripe apples and pears, or be put to death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The Prince again weeps, and Vasilissa repeats her counsel to sleep while she summons gardeners by whistling; they plant a green garden with birds, blossoms, and ripe fruit overnight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In the morning Vasilissa wakes the Prince, who goes to the garden, sweeps a path, and trains a twig as the Water King comes to inspect and praises his service.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Water King commands the Prince to choose a bride from among his twelve daughters, who are said to be exactly alike in face, hair, and dress, and to identify the same one three times or be put to death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Vasilissa tells the Prince how to recognize her among the twelve daughters by three signals on three successive trials: she will wave her handkerchief, then arrange her dress, and finally there will be a fly above her head.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Prince successfully picks out Vasilissa the Wise three times in succession and marries her; a wedding feast is prepared.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The Water King prepares more food than a hundred men could eat and orders his son-in-law to see that it is all eaten, threatening him if anything remains.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"At the Prince’s request, Obedalo is allowed to join the feast and eats everything that has been prepared, yet is still not satisfied.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The Water King sets out forty tubs of strong drinks and orders the Prince to see that they are all emptied; at the Prince’s request, Opivalo drinks them all and asks for more.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The Water King, seeing he cannot harm the Prince that way, orders an iron bath-room to be prepared and heated with twelve loads of firewood until the stove and walls are red-hot, so hot that it is impossible to approach within five versts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The Prince asks that Moroz Treskum go first into the bath-room; Moroz enters, blows in different corners, and in a moment icicles are hanging there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"After Moroz Treskum, the young couple enter the cooled bath-room, are lathered and scrubbed, and then go home safely.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"By marrying Vasilissa, the Prince becomes the Water King’s son-in-law.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Vasilissa is repeatedly called ‘the Wise’ and consistently takes the initiative, giving advice, summoning supernatural workers, and signaling the Prince during the tests.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Across the episode, the Prince faces a series of escalating life-threatening tasks imposed by the Water King and survives each by relying on Vasilissa and the three extraordinary heroes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Prince","description":"A prince who leaves the Yaga, travels to the Water King’s realm, is given impossible tasks under threat of death, and ultimately marries Vasilissa the Wise.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Vasilissa the Wise","description":"The eldest of the bathing maidens, daughter of the Water King, a shapeshifter who appears as a spoonbill and as a maiden, who aids the Prince with his tasks and becomes his wife.","role_refs":["role:2","role:8","role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Water King","description":"A king associated with water, father of Vasilissa and father-in-law.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Yaga","description":"A figure called ‘the Yaga’ whom the Prince Har explains that all men who fall in battle come to Odin and are fed on the endlessly regenerating boar Sahrimner, cooked by Andhrimner in the kettle Eldhrimner. Odin himself gives his meat to his two wolves Gere and Freke and lives only on wine. Two ravens, Hugin and Munin, sit on Odin’s shoulders and fly over the world each day to bring him news, earning him the name Raven-god. Har describes the drink in Valhal: the goat Heidrun, feeding on the tree Lerad, produces mead from her teats to fill a vessel large enough for all the einherjes; the hart Eikthyrner, also eating from Lerad, has horns from which drops fall into Hvergelmer, the source of many rivers flowing around the abodes of the gods. Har details the vastness of Valhal with its 540 doors, through each of which 800 einherjes can pass when they go to fight the wolf. He also describes the einherjes’ daily routine of arming themselves each morning, fighting and slaying one another for sport, then returning to Valhal to drink together. A verse then names Ygdrasil ash as foremost of trees, Skidbladner of ships, Odin of the gods, Sleipner of steeds, Bifrost of bridges, Brage of skalds, Habrok of hawks, and Garm of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l7802-l7937","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA.; lines 7802-7937","start":"7802","end":"7937","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After three years, three months, and three days, an eagle asks the merchant who had fed him to carry him to some lofty oaks. There the eagle regains his full strength by smashing the largest oak, then has the merchant leave his horse, sit on his wings, and flies with him high above a blue sea. Three times the eagle drops the merchant toward the water and catches him, shrinking the apparent size of the sea each time, and finally asks if the merchant has now felt mortal terror, comparing it to the fear the eagle felt when the merchant once aimed a gun at him. The eagle then carries the merchant beyond the sea to the copper kingdom of his eldest sister. Striking the damp earth, the eagle turns into a gallant hero. The sister joyfully welcomes him, feasts the guests, and shows vast treasures of gold, silver, and precious stones, offering the merchant anything he desires. Following the eagle’s prior instructions, the merchant refuses the riches and asks only for a copper casket, which the sister refuses, saying it is not suited to him. Angered, the brother resumes eagle form, seizes the merchant, and flies away while the sister calls after them that she will give the casket, but he tells her she is too late. In flight the merchant sees fire behind them and flowers ahead; the eagle explains that the copper kingdom is in flames, and the flowers belong to the silver kingdom of his second sister. The same pattern repeats there: the eagle becomes a hero, the sister welcomes and feasts them and offers treasures, the merchant asks only for a silver casket, she refuses with a warning that it is the wrong morsel for him, the eagle angrily departs with the merchant, and the sister belatedly offers the casket. Again they see fire behind and flowers before; the eagle explains that the silver kingdom is burning and the flowers are from the golden kingdom of his youngest sister. In the golden kingdom, the youngest sister welcomes them warmly, feasts them, and shows her treasures. When the merchant asks only for the golden casket, she freely gives it, saying she owes him for saving her brother from hunger. The merchant stays for a time feasting in the golden kingdom. When he departs, the eagle tells him to part on good terms and warns him not to open the casket until he reaches content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l7939-l8046","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA.; lines 7939-8046","start":"7939","end":"8046","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A merchant carrying a golden casket pauses to rest in a meadow that belongs to the Tsar of the Sea. When he opens the casket, a richly painted castle with many servants appears on the Tsar’s land. The Tsar sends messengers to demand that the intruder leave. Unable to return the castle to the casket, the merchant accepts the Tsar’s offer: the Tsar will restore the palace to the casket if the merchant swears to give him whatever the merchant has at home but does not yet know of. The merchant swears, receives the palace in the casket, and goes home, where his wife greets him and reveals that a son was born during his absence. The merchant realizes this child is what he unwittingly promised and becomes sorrowful, though he and his family live prosperously in the castle from the casket. After more than ten years, the son, Ivan the merchant’s son, now wise and handsome, has a troubling dream in which the Tsar of the Sea commands him to come, saying it is time to \"know his honor.\" His parents weep, bless him, and send him away to a strange land. Ivan travels along broad roads, fields, and steppes until he reaches a dreamy forest with a small cabin facing the forest. At his words the cabin turns to face him. Inside lies Baba-Yaga, boneleg, who comments on the arrival of \"Russia\" and asks Ivan’s origin and destination. Ivan reproaches her for asking news before offering hospitality, so she feeds him, gives him drink, and lets him rest. In the morning, after hearing his story and his request to reach the Tsar of the Sea, Baba-Yaga warns that the Tsar is very angry and gives him detailed instructions: he must go to a lake, hide behind a tree, and wait for three beautiful doves, the daughters of the Tsar of the Sea, who will remove their wings and dresses to bathe. Ivan must seize the many-colored wings of one dove and only return them when she agrees to marry him. Ivan follows the path, hides by the lake, and witnesses the three doves become maidens and bathe. He steals the many-colored wings. After bathing, two maidens dress, become doves, and fly away; the third searches for her missing wings, singing that if the taker is an old man he will be a father, if of middle years an uncle, and if a good youth she will marry him. Ivan reveals himself and returns the wings. The maiden, naming herself Vassilissa the Cunning, asks his origin and destination. He says he is Ivan the merchant’s son going to the Tsar of the Sea. The wolf carries Ivan swiftly to Tsar Dolmat’s garden and warns him to take only the Fire-bird and not its golden cage. Ivan steals the Fire-bird but, tempted by the cage, takes it and triggers a wire alarm. Watchmen seize him and bring him before Tsar Dolmat. Ivan explains that he is Tsar Vwislav Andronovich’s son, sent because the Fire-bird was stealing golden apples from his father’s favorite tree. Dolmat rebukes Ivan’s theft, claims he would have given the Fire-bird honorably, and offers to forgive him and give the bird if Ivan will travel beyond the thrice ninth land to Tsar Afron and bring back Afron’s golden-maned steed; otherwise he will brand Ivan a dishonorable thief. Ivan agrees, sorrowful, and returns to the Gray Wolf, who reproaches him for ignoring the warning but still offers help.

The Gray Wolf carries Ivan to Tsar Afron’s kingdom by night and instructs him to take the golden-maned steed from the white-walled stables but not the golden bridle hanging on the wall. Ivan again yields to temptation, takes the bridle, and sets off another string-triggered alarm. The grooms seize him and bring him to Tsar Afron. After questioning his identity, Afron chastises him, states he would have given the steed honorably, and proposes to pardon him and grant the steed if Ivan will go beyond the thrice ninth land to the thirtieth kingdom and bring Princess Yelena the Beautiful, whom Afron has long loved but cannot obtain. Otherwise, Afron will denounce him as a dishonorable thief. Ivan promises to bring Yelena, leaves in tears, and returns to the Gray Wolf, who again reproves his disobedience but still offers to carry him wherever needed.

The Gray Wolf runs with Ivan as swiftly as an arrow to Yelena the Beautiful’s distant kingdom. Reaching the golden fence surrounding her marvelous garden, the wolf tells Ivan to dismount, retrace his steps, and wait in a field under a green oak content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l3397-l3451","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"TO THE FOOLING OF GYLFE. / CHAPTER I. / CHAPTER II. / IDUN AND HER APPLES.; lines 3397-3451","start":"3397","end":"3451","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Odin, Loke, and Honer travel hungry over mountains and heaths, find a herd of cattle, and take an ox to boil, but the broth repeatedly fails to cook. A very large eagle in an oak above them reveals he is preventing the cooking and demands a share of the ox; when he takes most of the best meat, Loke angrily strikes him with a pole that sticks to the eagle and to Loke’s hands. The eagle flies off dragging Loke over rough ground and will not release him until he promises to lure Idun and her apples from Asgard. Later, Loke entices Idun out of Asgard into a forest under the pretext of comparing apples, and the giant Thjasse, in eagle form, seizes her and carries her to his home in Thrymheim. Without Idun, the Asas grow gray-haired and old; in council they discover Loke was last seen with her, seize him, and threaten him with death or torture. Frightened, Loke promises to bring Idun back if Freyja lends him her falcon-guise. Using the guise, he flies to Jotunheim, finds Thjasse away at sea and Idun alone, transforms her into a nut, and carries her off in his claws. When Thjasse returns, he takes eagle form and pursues Loke, gaining on him. The Asas, seeing the falcon with the nut and the pursuing eagle, prepare bundles of shavings at Asgard’s wall, light them as Loke arrives, and the eagle flies into the fire, burning his feathers so he falls. The Asas kill the giant Thjasse within the gates of Asgard, and the slaying is said to be very famous.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Odin, Loke, and Honer go on a journey over mountains and heaths while unable to find anything content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l2252-l2301","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LOKE AND HIS OFFSPRING. / CHAPTER X. / THE GODDESSES (ASYNJES). / CHAPTER XI.; lines 2252-2301","start":"2252","end":"2301","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage recounts how the giant Gymer and his wife Orboda of the mountain giants have a daughter, Gerd, described as the fairest of women. Frey sits in the holy high seat Hlidskjalf and looks out over all the worlds. Looking north, he sees a hamlet with a beautiful house; when a woman comes to the door and raises her hands to open it, the sky and sea gleam and the whole world is brightened. For his audacity in sitting in that sacred seat, Frey departs full of grief and, back home, refuses to speak, sleep, or drink. Njord sends Frey’s servant Skirner to ask what troubles him. Frey admits he has seen a beautiful woman and is so lovesick he cannot live unless he gets her; he orders Skirner to woo her and bring her to him, whether or not her father consents, promising rich reward. Skirner agrees but demands Frey’s excellent sword, which fights by itself, and Frey gives it to him. Skirner travels, courts Gerd, and wins from her a promise to come in nine nights to Bar-Isle to marry Frey. On Skirner’s return, Frey laments how long the remaining nights seem. The narrator then explains that this is why Frey later lacked a sword when fighting Bele, whom he killed with a hart’s horn. Ganglere remarks on the imprudence of giving away such a weapon and assumes Frey regretted it; Har answers that Frey’s meeting with Bele was of little importance, but that he will be in greater danger without his sword when the sons of Muspel go forth to battle. Editorial footnotes equate the story in brief with the Niblung legend and identify Frey’s lament as a stanza from the Elder Edda poem Skirner’s Journey.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Gymer is married to Orboda, who belongs to the race of the mountain giants, and they have a daughter named Gerd.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gerd is described as the fairest of all women.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Frey goes into Hlidskjalf and from there looks out upon all the worlds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"From Hlidskjalf Frey sees toward the north a hamlet with a large, beautiful house.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When a woman approaches the house and raises her hands to open the door, the sky and sea glisten, and she makes all the world bright.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Because of his audacity in sitting in the holy seat, Frey leaves full of grief.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After returning home, Frey neither speaks, sleeps, nor drinks, and no one dares to speak to him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Njord sends Frey’s servant Skirner to ask Frey why he is so angry and silent; Skirner expects to receive harsh words.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Frey tells Skirner that he has seen a beautiful woman and is so filled with grief for her sake that he cannot live unless promising to reward Skirner well.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Skirner agrees to go but demands that Frey give him his excellent sword, which wields itself in Ivan announces it is time to leave because his brothers wait under the mountains and he must rescue three Tsaritsas held in Whirlwind’s castles. They visit the Tsaritsa of the Golden Kingdom and her sisters of the Silver and Copper Kingdoms, taking them and supplies, and come to a place where they must descend a mountain using linen. Ivan lowers his mother, Yelena the Beautiful, and the two other Tsaritsas to where his elder brothers wait below. The brothers secretly plot to abandon Ivan, take the women and their mother to their father, and claim they found them, intending that Pyotr marry Yelena, Vassili marry the Silver Tsaritsa, and a general marry the Copper Tsaritsa. When Ivan is to come down, they tear away the linen, leaving him stranded atop the mountain. He weeps and wanders over the Copper, Silver, Golden, and Diamond Kingdoms without meeting anyone until he finds a whistle on a castle window. When he blows it, beings called Lame and Crooked appear and ask what he wants. At his request they provide a table with excellent food and then a bed. They explain that whoever blows the whistle will be served in everything, that they formerly served Whirlwind, and that Ivan must keep the whistle with him. Ivan then wishes to be in his own kingdom and instantly appears in the middle of the market square. There he meets a merry shoemaker carrying shoes to sell and offers to enter his service, claiming he can make shoes and clothes. Given fine leather to work, Ivan summons Lame and Crooked, who disparage the leather and later produce beautiful shoes overnight. The shoemaker is astonished at the workmanship and sells the shoes at market. At the palace, three weddings are being arranged: Pyotr is to marry Yelena the Beautiful, Vassili the Tsaritsa of the Silver Kingdom, and the Tsaritsa of the Copper Kingdom is to be given to a general. Yelena needs shoes, and the shoemaker’s pair surpasses all others. She says such shoes are made only in the mountains, pays him well, and orders another pair, richly sewn and covered with precious stones and diamonds, to be made without taking her measure and finished by the next day on pain of hanging. The shoemaker, despairing of fulfilling the task, spends what he believes to be his last night drinking and reveling with many friends, then returns home drunk with a keg of spirits, tells Ivan his plight, and asks to be awakened when they come to hang him. During the night Ivan blows the whistle, Lame and Crooked appear, and he orders that the demanded shoes be ready. Frigg is first and owns the hall Fensaler. Saga dwells in the large hall Sokvabek. Eir is the best healer. Gefjun is a maiden, and those who die as maidens become her handmaidens. Fulla is a maiden with loose hair and a golden band; she carries Frigg’s chest, cares for her shoes, and knows her secrets. Freyja, ranked with Frigg, is married to Oder and mother of the beautiful Hnos, whose name is applied to all fair and precious things. Oder goes far away; Freyja weeps for him, her tears being red gold, and she roams among many nations in search of him, changing her name and being known by several epithets; she owns the Brising necklace and is called Vanadis. Sjofn turns men’s and women’s hearts to love. Lofn, with permission from Alfather or Frigg, unites men and women despite obstacles, and love and beloved things take their name from her. Var hears oaths between men and women, gives her name to such vows, and punishes those who break them. Vor is extremely wise and searching so that nothing can be hidden from her; a saying links becoming ‘vor’ with becoming wise. Syn guards the hall door against those who should not enter and protects legal suits against falsehood; a saying mentions ‘syn is set against it’ when something is denied. Hlin guards those whom Frigg wants protected from danger; a proverb notes that one ‘hlins’ when forewarned. Snotra is wise and courtly; wise people are called Snotras after her. Gna is Frigg’s messenger to various worlds; she rides the horse Hofvarpner, which runs through air and over sea. When some Vanir see her riding in the air they question what flies there, and she answers in verse that she is gliding through the air on Hofvarpner, offspring of Hamskerper and Gardrofa. A saying uses Gna’s name for things that fare high in the air. Sol and Bil are also counted among the goddesses but are described elsewhere. The text then names other female beings who serve in Valhal, bearing drink and ale-horns to the einherjes; Grimner’s Lay lists several by name. These are called valkyries. Odin sends valkyries to all battles to choose the slain and determine victory. Gud and Rosta, along with the youngest norn Skuld, always ride to sway battle and choose the slain. In the evenings, while they eat skimmed milk, the father repeatedly tells Martin that he will inherit the cottage but must not cheat his mother or brothers. Martin greedily picks out all the bread from the milk, while Mihal is surprised and Yanek is saddened by his father’s talk and does not eat. When the father is dying, he gathers the family, again instructing Martin to keep the cottage and, turning to Yanek—whom he loves most—says that though Yanek is simple, the Lord has given him a good heart; he urges him to remain kind and to obey his brothers, then dies. Martin and Mihal lament loudly, but Yanek is stunned and later goes to the garden, sits under a tree, and cries. After the funeral, Martin and Mihal decide to go into the world to seek fortune, planning to leave Yanek with his mother, but she insists they take him so he will not lose his chance. Martin and Mihal pack food into bags; Yanek takes nothing, and they all set out. On the road, Yanek talks about meeting fortune, and his brothers snap at him, resentful that he carries nothing. After a hot half-day’s walk, they rest under a roadside tree; Martin and Mihal eat while Yanek sits apart and cries. They mock him for laziness, but Yanek rebukes them for stripping their mother of everything when they are supposed to go out to earn for her. Surprised, they invite him to eat, mainly to lessen their own guilt, and continue traveling. In the evening they reach a cottage, where a cottager offers lodging and supper. Martin boastfully claims he has his own provisions. The cottager and his wife eat, while Yanek, with downcast face, sits hungry in a corner. The wife notices and kindly invites him to the table, asking if he is their servant; Martin explains he is their brother but lazy. Yanek at first refuses but finally accepts. Soup, Martin’s favorite dish, is served to Yanek, while Martin has only bread and cheese; Martin hates Yanek for enjoying the soup and later dreams of him eating it. The next morning, the brothers depart before breakfast so that Yanek will not eat. Martin leads them through a forest, hoping they will find no house all day. After walking all morning, they reach open country, climb a small hill, and see in the valley a huge castle as tall as ten houses stacked together. Yanek laughs at the sight, Martin claims they have lost the road and should turn back, but Mihal argues that any direction is equally part of the wide world. A man’s wife turns into a cannibal man-eater with a craving to eat him. A wise talking dog, described as a kind of brother, warns the man, who flees south until he reaches a deep river where an old man can make a bridge by stretching his neck across the water. The man crosses on the old man’s neck. The bridge-maker promises to delay the pursuing wife and throw her into the river, where monsters will devour everything except her stomach, which contains her life and would float away and revive her unless it is destroyed. The man continues west to two witch aunts who agree to help. When the wife arrives, the old man forces her to cross on the narrow edge of his neck, then jerks her into the river; monsters eat her, leaving only the stomach, which floats downstream. The witch aunts retrieve the stomach, cut it up, and burn it, ending the man-eater. The man then meets a gentle young woman gathering fuel, marries her, and goes to live with her and her malicious grandmother. The grandmother takes him to hunt on an island in a lake and strands him there. After dark, the lake water rises, flooding the island. The man climbs the highest tree as the water and hungry, savage creatures rise around him. In distress he calls to the Morning-star, who once appeared to him in a dream promising rescue. The Morning-star, after confirming the earlier promise through a boy attendant, commands daylight to come; dawn arrives immediately, the waters fall, and the man survives. He hides by the landing. When the grandmother returns by canoe expecting to find his bones, he seizes the canoe, escapes, and goes home to his wife. Later the grandmother herself is trapped on the island as the waters rise. She falsely claims the Morning-star once promised to save her, but the star denies this and refuses to hasten daylight. His master, who had expected execution if the shoes were not finished, cannot remember making them but takes them to the palace. Yelena the Beautiful recognizes that spirits must have made them for Ivan and tests the shoemaker by ordering a wedding robe of gold and precious stones to be ready by morning, on pain of death. The despairing shoemaker drinks heavily with his friends, saying he cannot possibly complete the task and expects to be beheaded. After he falls asleep, Ivan summons his supernatural helpers, Lame and Crooked, with a whistle; they promise and deliver the robe overnight, which shines like fire and lights the room. Again the shoemaker barely remembers anything and brings the robe to Yelena. She pays him well but sets an even greater task: by the next morning a Golden Kingdom must stand on the sea seven versts from shore, connected to the palace by a golden bridge covered with velvet, with wonderful trees and song-birds along its railings, or the shoemaker will be quartered. He drinks again with his friends, explains the hopeless task to Ivan, and falls into a drunken sleep. Ivan calls Lame and Crooked, who agree to complete this work by morning. At daybreak a golden castle gleaming like fire stands on the sea with the described bridge, trees, and birds. Ivan wakes the shoemaker, who is astonished and barely remembers anything. They go to the golden castle full of untold wealth. Ivan gives his master a wing to dust the bridge and a letter to hand over if anyone asks who lives in the palace. Meanwhile, Yelena sees the golden castle and bridge and runs to tell the Tsar. The Tsar sends messengers to inquire whether a hero has arrived; they find the shoemaker, who gives them the letter. In it Ivan reveals to his father the Tsar how he freed his mother, won Yelena the Beautiful, and was betrayed by his elder brothers. He then turns from American myths to the nations whose myth-tales he treats: Russians, Chekhs, and Magyars. He briefly characterizes Russia’s historical ‘key-note’ from the time of Olga and Vladimir, then digresses into a broad historical sketch: Rome is presented as the first great assimilating power to create a true State, followed by a ‘new Rome’ with wider ambitions, ruling in the name of God and morality and seeking to convert the Slavic ‘youngest brothers of the Aryan race.’ The Teutonic/German peoples inherit Western Roman civilization and, acting often as agents of the Catholic Church, drive an aggressive, long-term movement eastward, Christianizing and conquering while seeking temporal lordship. This leads to a defensive struggle of Slavs against Germans, the ethnological destruction and Germanization of many Western Slavs, the loss and partition of Poland’s Baltic lands, and Slavic failures in Great Moravia and farther south. The fall of the Western Slavs is attributed to political immaturity rather than personal inferiority. Poland and Russia remain in the East, and their opposition is described as a great modern tragedy whose causes, the author argues, are widely misunderstood: Western opinion wrongly blames Russia for Poland’s downfall, while he emphasizes internal Polish social structure and persistent German expansion. At a swollen stream he sees Gjalp, Geirrod’s daughter, standing across the river and causing the flood. Thor throws a stone at her and escapes the water by pulling himself up with a shrub, giving rise to the proverb that a shrub saved Thor. At Geirrod’s hall Thor and his companion are given a single seat; as Thor sits, it rises toward the roof, but he braces himself with the staff Gridarvol against the rafters and forces the seat down, breaking the backs of the hidden Gjalp and Greip beneath it. Thor later recalls this in verse, saying the giant’s daughters wanted to lift him to heaven.

Geirrod then invites Thor into the main hall, where great fires burn. Geirrod seizes a red-hot iron wedge with tongs and hurls it at Thor, who catches it with his iron gloves and throws it back so forcefully that it pierces an iron pillar, Geirrod’s body, the wall, and into the ground.

A skaldic poem (Thor’s Drapa) retells and expands the story. Loki, called the Midgard-serpent’s father and a great liar, exhorts Thor to leave home and follow supposedly green paths to Geirrod’s enclosure. Thor and Loki set out from Odin’s home to visit Ymir’s giant offspring. Gjalp, described as a perjured daughter of Geirrod, prepares magic. Thor and his warlike companions reach the land and confront a roaring, snow-swollen, venomous stream. Thor, called the troll-woman’s disgracer and giants’ foe, wades the torrent using a staff for support while the stones ring beneath it. The flood rises over his shoulders, but he strains his neck strength until the water diminishes. Thjalfe and another companion cling to Thor’s belt to keep their heads above water while Geirrod’s daughters make the stream more dangerous for the staff.

Thor and his oath-bound companions, protectors of Asgard, wreak havoc among the giants. Geirrod’s giants are routed. There is wailing among cave-dwelling giants as Thor strikes a giant’s head and presses Gjalp and Greip’s eyes against the roof, breaking their backs. A dwarf-kin giant, identified as the father of Greip, throws a forge-heated iron beam at Thor, who catches it in mid-air. Geirrod’s hall trembles when the giant strikes his head against a house column, and Thor swings the iron beam against the giant’s head. Thor, the crusher of hall-dwelling troll-women, wins a bloody victory over Geirrod’s kin. He instructs one companion to sell the pears only to the princess, at a price discouraging ordinary buyers. The princess sees the beautiful pears as she leaves church, buys them, and at home eats them with a golden knife; immense horns grow on her head, disfiguring her and causing great distress. The king and queen summon doctors, who fail to remove the horns, which grow back whenever they try to saw them off. The king then proclaims that whoever frees the princess from the horns will marry her and gain the kingdom. \n\nThe man with the apples dresses as a doctor, is admitted to the princess, and tells her she must have angered God and must confess her sins before he can help. She admits to avid card-playing, humiliating male opponents by having them flogged, and stealing a magic purse, cap, and mantle from two men. The doctor demands that she return the stolen property, which she does, giving him the purse, cap, and mantle to deliver to their owners. He leaves with the items and later returns, saying she must have eaten something that produced the horns. She mentions only having eaten the pears. He agrees to cure her on condition that he receive her and the kingdom, as the king has proclaimed. They consent. He then cuts an apple into four pieces, has her lie down and eat them; when she finishes the four quarters, her horns fall off at once. There is great rejoicing, a marriage contract is drawn up, and the wedding is celebrated. The young king’s two friends attend, and he promises them the highest rank at his court. Returning shortly, he examines her and suggests she has eaten something that caused the horns. She says she has eaten nothing harmful except a few beautiful pears. Each day Yarmil despairs and lies down, but at midday his princess brings him food, comforts him, and lets him sleep with his head on her lap. She then takes a powder from her bosom, mutters mysterious words, and throws it into the air, summoning invisible hands that complete the tasks quickly. The sorceress struggles to hide her rage yet acknowledges that Yarmil has completed the first and second years of his service.

When a black darkness rushes from the castle, Yarmil strikes its darkest point; the darkness turns into the sorceress, and his sword pierces her heart. She dies cursing, and Yarmil and the princess ride away swiftly.

After a long journey, they return to Yarmil’s father’s castle, where their reunion brings great joy. The queen is terrified, and when Yarmil tells his father all that has happened, the king has the queen burned without mercy. Once the feasting there is finished, Yarmil and his wife travel on to their own kingdom. The mouse-hole they had known is now a magnificent gate into a great city with a golden castle on a hill at its center. Crowds of people and courtiers greet the royal couple with applause and thank Yarmil for freeing them. He recalls his thesis that all myths share a common origin and parallel structure up to the level reached by the least developed peoples, proposing Morning-star myths as an illustration. He notes that American Indians have many stories where the Morning-star is a Light-bringer, comparable to Latin 'Lucifer'. He then narrates his own changing perception of Lucifer: from a terrifying demonic being in childhood, to discovering in Virgil that 'Lucifer' simply means Morning-star and herald of the sun. He recounts a powerful experience watching the Morning-star over Lake Michigan, imagining it as the chieftain of night and Prince of Darkness leading the hosts of heaven against the Lord of Light, whose sunrise establishes the kingdom of light and casts down the dark powers forever. Finally, he summarizes a Modoc Morning-star myth: a sky-sun personage (an old man with an indestructible golden disk in his back) is destroyed, often by fire, every evening, but is resurrected each morning when the Morning-star, his attendant spirit or 'medicine', summons him. The golden disk is identified with the sun, and Curtin concludes that the Modoc Morning-star is the same character as the Latin Guests agree, while Yarmil’s brothers and mother envy his success. The next day the king orders that in a year and a day the princes must return with their princesses so he can celebrate their weddings. The elder brothers depart east and west, but Yarmil travels through a magic mouse-hole to a white castle, receives a white steed from a white lady, and rides to a golden castle. There he goes to the twelfth chamber, expecting his wondrous princess, but finds instead the ugly toad he has been washing three times a day. The more he bathes it, the uglier and mangier it becomes, and his strength wanes as the deadline approaches. Despairing at the thought of bringing such a creature to his father, he discovers the toad has vanished, searches the castle and garden, and finally returns to find the once-poor chamber transformed into a paradise-like room with a beautiful lady, even fairer than the portrait. Yarmil obeys, despite the horrifying cries, and on his return passes a man nailed to the door by his tongue who begs to be freed. After a brief inner struggle, Yarmil resists and shuts the door without helping him. The lady explains that the twelve shirts are her twelve toad skins and the tapers that burned her continuously; by extinguishing them he has liberated her, though it will take three years for her to be completely free. She reveals she is a mighty king’s daughter whom the monstrous man nailed to the door, a wizard, transformed into a toad because she refused to marry him. A more powerful witch punished the wizard by nailing him to the door, but the witch still holds the princess under her power. The princess now makes Yarmil promise that for three years he will tell no living soul what creature she was or how many skins she had, warning him especially not to reveal this to his mother, who is herself a witch, hates him, and will try hard to learn the secret. Despairing, he receives a mysterious letter on his writing-table in black letters from the princess, professing love, urging patience, and telling him to take a gift casket from the pan for his father and to put her back in the pan. Yarmil goes to the twelfth chamber, finds a diamond-set casket in the pan, replaces the toad, and rides a white flying steed to a white castle, where a white lady exchanges the mounts. Passing through a great gate, he sees only a mouse-hole behind him and reaches his father’s castle at the same time as his brothers. Before assembled guests the king asks for gifts from their princesses. The elder brothers present small and smaller mirrors that nevertheless show the king’s whole person, which he attributes to human workmanship. Yarmil timidly offers his casket, which proves full of diamonds of greater value than the kingdom and contains an even smaller mirror from which a puppet leaps to hold the glass whenever the king looks into it, vanishing when he stops. The king declares no human hand could have made this and embraces Yarmil lovingly, while the brothers and their witch mother secretly rage. The king then orders the princes to depart and return in a year and a day with portraits of their princesses. Yarmil fears bringing a portrait of the ugly toad, refuses to deceive his father by painting a beautiful lady despite his skill, and hopes for the toad’s help. He rides back beyond the town, where the ground opens at a mouse-hole to admit him. At the white castle the white lady again provides the white steed, which flies to a golden castle. In the twelfth chamber Yarmil removes the diamond pan’s covers, takes the toad to his bosom, and now bathes it twice daily, though it grows uglier, deepening his worry. Near the deadline he finally finds another letter on his writing-table, written in silver letters, in which the princess again professes love, urges patience, and tells him that her portrait lies in the pan in a casket, instructing him to give it to his father and replace her in the pan. Yarmil finds a yet richer casket in the pan, replaces the toad, rides the white steed to the white castle, receives his own horse, and again, after passing the gate, sees only a mouse-hole behind. He arrives with his brothers at his father’s gate at the same time. The horse warns him that his father the king has pronounced a death sentence against him, but Boyislav refuses to believe it. When he enters the city he is seized by the townspeople on the king's orders, taken to the castle, and thrown into a dark dungeon, while the horse is penned and the captor rewarded.

The narration explains that Boyislav's brothers, after he rescued the princesses of Black Island, abandoned him by sailing away, forced the princesses on oath to claim the brothers as their liberators, and slandered Boyislav as having stayed with a worthless woman and mocked his father. They planned to cast lots for the princesses as wives, but the women refused. The king, restored to health when the princesses were freed, believes their forced story, orders Boyislav's death, and offers a reward for his capture. The princesses grieve in silence, while the brothers deflect the king's questions and continue to inflame his anger against Boyislav.

After Boyislav is imprisoned, the brothers persuade the king to forbid anyone on pain of death from asking mercy for him. Many pity the prince, but only an old warrior and former commander openly weeps and decides to intercede, reasoning that he is near death anyway. He goes to the king, asks for Boyislav's life, and is himself sentenced to death for defying the royal order, but he boldly tells the king he fears death less than the shame of seeing the king give his own blood to the hangman. Struck by this, the king reconsiders: he admits that Boyislav's guilt is uncertain in light of the princesses' strange behavior and decides not to have him hanged, but instead orders that Boyislav be confined with lions so that they may tear him to pieces.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Boyislav rests with his horse in a green content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l10633-l10758","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG. / THE KING OF THE TOADS. / THE MOUSE-HOLE, AND THE UNDERGROUND KINGDOM. / THE CUIRASSIER AND THE HORNED PRINCESS.; lines 10633-10758","start":"10633","end":"10758","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A princess who enjoys defeating people at cards plays with a man whose magic purse produces ten ducats whenever he shakes it. Astonished by his inexhaustible money, she watches and discovers the source. She brings him wine, secretly drugging his goblet with a sleeping powder, and while he sleeps under the table she steals the magic purse, leaving a normal one with only ten ducats. When he wakes and finds the purse no longer produces money, she dismisses him without flogging, though he has lost much. He returns to his comrades in distress, saying he has lost the purse, and they worry about their debts. The comrade who owns a magic mantle vows revenge on the wicked princess, borrows another friend’s cap of invisibility, and plans to seize her as she goes to church. Wearing the cap and mantle, he snatches the princess from the street, flies with her through the air to distant wild mountains, and sets her down by a pear-tree laden with beautiful fruit. The princess asks him to climb the tree and shake it so she can eat pears. He climbs while keeping the cap and mantle with him, hanging them on a branch before shaking. When the tree is shaken, the cap and mantle fall to the ground; the princess quickly puts on the cap, wraps herself in the mantle, and vanishes, leaving the man stranded on the tree in the wilderness. Alone in the wild mountains, he groans, wanders, and eats some pears. Immediately gigantic horns grow from his head, so large he can barely move through the woods. With great difficulty he drags himself to a deep ravine where a hermit named Wind lives. This Wind says he is not strong enough to carry the horned man home but directs him to his stronger brother nearby, who can remove the horns. The man struggles on to the brother’s cave, kneels, and implores help. The elder Wind says he must ask the Lord how forcefully Wind may blow, since the journey home is far. He goes to the Lord, who commands him to blow mightily. Returning, the elder Wind instructs the man to climb an apple-tree, pluck an apple, cut it into four parts, and eat it; this will make his horns fall off. The man climbs with difficulty, eats the apple, and is freed from the horns. He takes extra apples and pears, then Wind carries him swiftly back to the inn where his friends are waiting and rejoice at his return, asking about his adventures.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The princess has the man brought in to play cards and is pleased to have someone she can They repeatedly flee from Koshchei the Deathless, but Koshchei’s prophetic steed warns him, and after forgiving Ivan twice, Koshchei finally catches him, dismembers him, seals the pieces in a barrel, and throws it into the blue sea while carrying Marya away. At the same time, the silver token left with Ivan’s brothers-in-law (the Eagle, Falcon, and Raven) turns black; they retrieve the barrel, reassemble Ivan’s body, and revive him with the Waters of Death and Life. Ivan resumes his quest for Marya, who learns from Koshchei that his marvelous steed came from Baba Yaga beyond a fiery river, reached by a magical handkerchief that raises a bridge. Marya steals the handkerchief for Ivan, who crosses the fiery river toward Baba Yaga’s realm, and along the way he spares the young of an outlandish bird, a hive of bees, and a lioness after each mother promises future help.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Raven tells Prince Ivan it will be hard to find Marya Morevna and asks content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l4136-l4287","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 4136-4287","start":"4136","end":"4287","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Prince Ivan spares a lioness, who promises to repay him. Hungry and faint, he reaches Baba Yaga’s house, ringed by twelve poles bearing eleven human heads, and agrees to guard her mares for three days in exchange for a heroic steed, under threat that his head will occupy the twelfth pole if he fails. Each day the mares flee—first across the meadows, then into thick forests, and finally into the blue sea—while Ivan weeps and falls asleep on a stone. Animal helpers (an outlandish bird, the lioness, and a bee) gather the mares and wake him. On the third day the bee also tells him to hide from Baba Yaga, steal a sorry colt from the stable, and escape at midnight. Ivan does so, rides to a fiery river, and uses a magic handkerchief to create and then thin a bridge; Baba Yaga pursues in an iron mortar with pestle and broom but falls into the fiery river when the bridge breaks and dies. Ivan fattens the colt in green meadows until it becomes a wondrous steed, rides to Marya Morevna, and they flee together, though she fears Koshchei the Deathless will kill him again. Meanwhile Koshchei’s horse stumbles and explains that Ivan has carried off Marya, and Koshchei decides to pursue despite the other steed’s superiority.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A lioness speaks to Prince Ivan, begging him to let her alone and promising that she will do him a good turn sometime.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Prince Ivan consents to the lioness’s request and spares her, saying, \"Very well; have it your own way.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hungry and faint, Prince Ivan wanders until he reaches Baba Yaga’s house, around which stand twelve poles in a circle, each of eleven bearing a human head while the twelfth is empty.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Baba Yaga tells Prince Ivan he may earn a heroic steed by taking good care of her mares for three days, warning that if he fails his head will be set on the twelfth pole.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Baba Yaga gives Prince Ivan food and drink and sends him to drive her mares afield; they immediately cock up their tails, scatter across the meadows, and vanish from his sight, causing him to weep, sit on a stone, and fall asleep.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Near sunset on the first day an outlandish bird flies to Prince Ivan, wakes him, and tells him that the mares are already at home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the mares return on the first evening, Baba Yaga storms at them, and they reply that birds from every part of the world nearly pecked their eyes out; she orders them that next day they must disperse amid the thick forests instead of galloping over the meadows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On the second day the mares again cock up their tails and disperse into thick forests; Prince Ivan again sits on the stone, weeps, and falls asleep until the lioness runs up, wakes him, and announces that the mares are all collected.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"On the second evening Baba Yaga rages more than before, and the mares explain that beasts of prey from all parts of the world almost tore them to pieces; she orders them to run into the blue sea the next day.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On the third day the mares disappear into the blue sea and stand there up to their necks in water; Prince Ivan again sits on the stone, weeps, and falls asleep until a bee flies up at sunset, wakes him, and tells him that the mares are all collected.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The bee instructs Prince Ivan to avoid being seen by Baba Yaga when he returns, to hide behind the mangers in the stable, to steal a sorry colt rolling in the muck, and to ride away at midnight.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"When Ivan returns on the third evening, he hides behind the mangers while Baba Yaga storms at the mares; they explain that countless bees from all parts of the world stung them until the blood came, and afterward Baba Yaga goes to sleep.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At midnight Prince Ivan steals the sorry colt from Baba Yaga’s stable, saddles it, rides to the fiery river, and waves a handkerchief three times on his right hand, whereupon a splendid bridge suddenly appears high in the air across the river.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After crossing the fiery river, Prince Ivan waves the handkerchief twice on his left hand, leaving only a very thin bridge across the river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Baba Yaga pursues Prince Ivan at full speed in an iron mortar, urging it on with a pestle and sweeping away her traces with a broom; at the fiery river she drives onto the bridge, which breaks in two when she is halfway across, causing her to fall into the river and die a cruel death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"After escaping, Prince Ivan fattens the colt in green meadows until it turns into a wondrous heroic steed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Riding the wondrous steed, Prince Ivan goes to Marya Morevna; she runs out, embraces him, and asks by what means God has brought him back to life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Prince Ivan tells Marya Morevna how he returned and urges her to come with him; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l10565-l10691","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SOZH AND DNIEPER. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER IV. / MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT.; lines 10565-10691","start":"10565","end":"10691","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Princess Anna the Fair has Katoma’s feet cut off and orders him set on a tall tree-stump, while she ties Prince Ivan to her carriage and returns to her kingdom, where she makes him herd cows under her supervision. Katoma sits helpless on the stump for three days without food or drink, near a dense forest inhabited by a mighty but blind hero who lives by hunting game by smell and cooking it at a wood fire. Chasing a fox, the blind hero crashes into the stump, uproots it, and frees Katoma. They exchange stories, learning that the same princess blinded the hero and maimed Katoma. They decide to live together: the blind man carries Katoma on his back and supplies feet, while Katoma guides him with his eyes, and they hunt successfully in the forest. Later Katoma proposes they abduct a rich merchant’s charitable daughter to keep house for them. They drive a cart into the merchant’s yard, lure the daughter out as she comes to give alms, seize her, and escape pursuit. In their forest hut they ask her to be as a sister, cooking and washing for them; she stays, and they treat her with affection and respect while she manages the household. After some time, a Baba Yaga begins secretly visiting the hut whenever the heroes go hunting, making the maiden dress her hair while she sucks the girl’s breasts, causing her to grow weak and thin. Forbidden by the Baba Yaga to tell, the maiden initially remains silent, but after persistent questioning by her adoptive brothers she reveals everything, describing the old woman’s evil face and grey hair. The blind hero identifies the visitor as a Baba Yaga and proposes they stay home from the hunt to entice and capture her.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Princess Anna the Fair has both of Katoma’s feet cut off and orders her servants to set him on a tall tree-stump.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Princess ties Prince Ivan to the carriage by a cord, turns the horses around, and drives back to her own kingdom, leaving Katoma on the stump.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In her kingdom, Princess Anna the Fair assigns Prince Ivan to take care of the cows, while she sits on the balcony in the evenings to ensure their number is correct.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Katoma remains sitting on the stump for three days without food or drink and cannot get down, expecting to die of starvation.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Near the stump there is a dense forest where a mighty hero lives who is completely blind.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The blind hero hunts by smell, chasing passing animals such as hares, foxes, and bears, and is so swift that no wild beast can escape him;
