content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l290-l378","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE                                 34 / A HOPI (MOKI) MAIDEN                                   184 / THE PINNACLES OF THUNDER MOUNTAIN                      344 / INTRODUCTION; lines 290-378","start":"290","end":"378","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"In all of these languages a strange similarity in cosmology is observed, in that it is a cosmology of regions or worlds.\"","summary":"The passage explains the Amerindian concept of a pervasive magical power (here termed \"orenda\"), to which unexplained phenomena, disease, and magical efficacy are attributed. It describes how orenda can be transferred from a serpent to an arrow through ritual, notes Cushing's ethnographic work on orenda, and recounts an Iroquois myth in which a god planning the rivers is thwarted by his wicked brother. The text states that birds and humans exercise orenda through song, making worship largely dance-based. It discusses shamans (prophets, priests, medicine-men), their initiation, revelations, and the risk of being condemned as witches. The passage then outlines Amerind creation myths explaining distinctive traits of animals and natural phenomena, and a common cosmology of multiple worlds or regions: a central midworld, an upper and lower world, and four cardinal worlds inhabited by various classes of beings and attributes that travel to the center. Finally, it compares this to a three-region heaven–earth–hell cosmology in \"civilized\" folk-lore, suggesting that expanding such moral geography helps one understand Amerind cosmology.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In different Amerindian language families, a term exists for magical power: orenda (Iroquoian), wakan or wakanda (Siouan), hube (in the language referred to), and pokunt (Shoshonean); the author adopts \"orenda\" as a generic term.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"All unexplained phenomena are said to be attributed to orenda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The venom of the serpent is described as orenda, and this orenda can pass from a serpent to an arrow, making the arrow charmed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A rattlesnake may be stretched beside an arrow and an invocation performed to convey orenda from the snake to the arrow.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Alternatively, the serpent may be made into a witch’s stew and the arrow dipped into the brew to transfer orenda.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Cushing is credited with major contributions to understanding the doctrine of orenda and has discussed how forms and decorations of implements and utensils have orenda as their motive.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"An Iroquois god, described as one of the ancients, planned the streams of earth by his orenda so they would run up on one side and down on the other, allowing men to float up or down by crossing the river.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The god’s wicked brother interfered and made the streams run down on both sides, illustrating that orenda may thwart orenda.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The bird that sings is said to be exercising its orenda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When human beings sing, they are also considered to exercise orenda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Song is described as a universal accompaniment of Amerindian worship, and all such worship is characterized as fundamentally terpsichorean (dance-based) aimed at pleasing supernatural beings to induce them to grant favors.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"All diseases and ailments of humankind are said to be attributed by tribal people to orenda.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Amerindian mythology is characterized as a theory of magic.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Many tribes teach tales about some method of introducing death and disease into the world by which supernatural agencies can cause sickness and death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Prophets, who are also priests, wonder-workers, and medicine-men, are referred to as shamans in scientific literature and as medicine-men in popular and frontier parlance.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Shamans are usually initiated into a guild, often through elaborate tribal ceremonies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Individuals sometimes have revelations and then set themselves up to prophesy, expel diseases, and teach as priests.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"If such individuals gain a following they may exert much influence and be greatly revered; if they fail, they may gradually be regarded as wizards or witches, accused of black art, and in extreme cases put to death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"All Amerindians are said to believe in shamancraft and witchcraft.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Myths of cosmology are usually called creation myths, and sometimes any myth that accounts for things, even trivial ones, is so called.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Every striking phenomenon noticed by Amerinds, such as the horn of the buffalo, the tawny patch on the rabbit’s shoulders, the blue-jay’s crest, the magpie’s tail, the chameleon’s sheen, and the snake’s rattle, has a myth explaining its origin.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Each Amerindian language has its own different set of myths, making the folk-tales appear inexhaustible.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Across these languages, a similarity in cosmology is observed: a cosmology of regions or worlds surrounding the tribe’s home world.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The regions are described as a central (home) world, an upper world, a lower world, and four worlds at the cardinal points: northern, southern, eastern, and western.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Animals of the tribes, including human animals, tree animals, star animals, water animals (bodies of water), and stone animals (mountains, hills, valleys, rocks), have appropriate habitations in the zenith world, nadir world, or one of the cardinal worlds.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Their dwelling in the center world is explained by myths of travel from their proper regions to this midworld.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"All bodies and attributes, including colors of clouds, the rainbow, and other objects, are assigned a proper place in the six regions from which they come to the midworld.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"In the folk-lore of \"civilization\" there are described only three regions: heaven, earth, and hell.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"In this three-region cosmology, all good things are said to come from heaven and all bad things from hell, though enlightened people interpret moral good and evil as attributes of individuals rather than literal To illustrate fortune and favour, a tale is told of Shah Mahmud, who uses his ‘fortune’ to fill a poor boy’s net with fish; after the Sultan’s shadow passes over the net, every cast brings abundant fish. Finally the Nightingale, drunk with ecstasy from the Rose, boasts of his unique key to Love and a song that overpowers reason and even David’s song, ensnaring souls and moving the garden. He describes his anguish during the Rose’s absence and his joy at her New Year return, calling her his bride whose crimson volume records his notes; the Rose dies yet revives each year. He insists he will remain devoted to this present Rose rather than seek the more distant beloved others speak of, before a sterner voice cuts him off.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A voice from Heaven declares that the Royal Road is not for all to tread and the Royal Palace is not for the rabble, who may reach it yet be shut out.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The heavenly voice says that the blaze from its Harim window frightens the roadside rabble and that though many knock at the portal, only one in thousands enters.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Tajidar is presented as the speaker of this message, and the winged crowd beneath his word bow in silence and clap in acclamation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The birds’ hearts and eyes are kindled by the ‘Firebrand of the Wise’; they feel their degradation, believe they can be retrieved, and in the hope of consummation forget the cost.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The multitude of birds cry that they long to follow Tajidar wherever he leads, even through flood, fire, or snow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Some birds listen with cold, disdainful air, content with their state or fearful that the time and travel might be wasted; they come forward one by one with unwise objections, which Tajidar answers with reproof, argument, and allegory.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Pheasant is the first to object, questioning by what right Tajidar is raised to pre-eminence over other birds when he seems like the rest except for a lofty crest such as the Pheasant also has.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Tajidar replies that he was chosen by Sulayman not by any virtue of his own but by Sulayman’s choice alone, likening it to the free largess of Sulayman’s eyes rather than the gold and silver of his own sighs.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Tajidar teaches that Allah’s grace comes and goes as it wills; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-archive-l1916-l2162","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/bird-parliament-attar-fitzgerald.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Bird Parliament; lines 1916-2162","start":"1916","end":"2162","translation":"Bird Parliament","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After the Tajidar has spoken, fear and doubt spread among the birds, who worry how to approach a Monarch greater than Sultan Mahmud without material gifts. Tajidar tells them that the true offerings are the ‘gold dust’ of a long pilgrimage, the ‘ruby’ of a bleeding heart, and the giver’s own naked soul, seeking no reward but the Monarch’s presence. To illustrate this, he recounts a story: Shah Mahmud, disguised and out walking, visits a poor furnace-stoker at the baths, silently eats his bread and drinks his water, and is invited back freely. Pleased, Mahmud returns many nights, then reveals himself and offers any reward, even a throne. The poor man asks only to remain as he is if the Shah will continue to visit his humble home, whose presence makes it more royal than a throne. The tale rekindles the birds’ desire for the quest; they forget the dangers, longing for restoration to their ancient rank and the Monarch’s robe of grace. They cry for the Road and for a guide, choose Tajidar, and then draw lots to confirm Heaven’s will; the lot falls on Tajidar, whom they crown as Khalif of their long-lost Khalif and set on a pulpit-throne to organize the march. Tajidar describes an unprecedented Road no wing or foot has ever traveled: across waterless deserts and shoreless waters, through valleys and cloud-high mountains with valleys deeper than seas, where dust is adders, vapour is fire, the elements are hostile, famine and toil are deadly, and the way is strewn with the bones of those who failed. The journey demands ever-increasing self-sacrifice; many may endure yet gain nothing or never return. The first stage is the Vale of Search, an endless maze of branching paths with only one right way, beset with pitfalls, gulfs, precipices, burning dust and fiery air, and haunted by hyenas, snakes, and ghouls.   "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "A youth prepares provisions and rides upon his Eagle companion, who carries him upward from his town into the sky through a great opening. They reach the Mountain of Turquoises in the sky-world, where the Eagle sheds its coat and becomes a beautiful maiden. She leads the youth to the pure white city of her winged people, who can appear in different guises. In a great building there, an old winged man welcomes them and declares that they shall be wife and husband, and they agree, so the youth marries the Eagle-maiden.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "The youth bids good-night to his Eagle, goes into the house, takes parched flour, dried and pulverized wafer-bread in a large bag, and other hunter foods, and makes them into a firm package.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "The youth sleeps until late morning and does not arise until his brothers have departed for their fields of corn.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "After a hasty breakfast, the youth slings the package of food over his shoulders and descends to the cage of the Eagle.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "The Eagle is waiting in the cage, comes out with a smile in its eyes when the youth opens the wicket, settles on the ground, spreads its wings, and invites the youth to mount.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "The Eagle tells the youth to sit on its back, grasp the base of its wings, and rest his feet above its thighs so he will not fall off, and asks whether he is ready and has enough food.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "The Eagle rises slowly, circling wider and higher above the town as it ascends.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "While circling above the town, the Eagle says it will sing a farewell song to the youth's people so they will know of their final departure and sings a song whose words are given.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "Hearing the Eagle's song from above, the people exclaim that the Eagle and the youth are escaping and leaving them and call out to be saved.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },

She warns him that she is going on a long journey and that spirits can be seen only in darkness, urging him to return to his fathers, but he insists on following her out of love. The maiden-spirit instructs him to prepare prayer-sticks with feathers as gifts to the Fathers, food for four days, much prayer-meal, and a light downy feather dyed red, then to return at midnight and tie the feather over her forehead at dawn. After he prepares these offerings and meets her again, he ties the red plume above her forehead; as sunrise light rises behind a great mountain, the spirit disappears and only the feather remains, moving ahead like a dancer’s plume through streets, fields, and to a river toward the land of evening. The young man follows the plume westward, becoming exhausted as it glides swiftly and sometimes waits when he calls to his bride, passing forests of piñons and cedars. When the night is divided he sees a red camp-fire-like light on a hill-top and finds the maiden-spirit seated there; she greets him and he, weary, falls asleep beside her while she, as a spirit, does not sleep.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At night, when a light shines, the maiden-spirit, described as more beautiful than ever, comes out of the grave-bed and sits by her lover.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The maiden-spirit urges the young man to return to his fathers and says she is going on a long journey, visible only in darkness because spirits are not seen in daylight.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The maiden-spirit laments that her husband did not recognize her, did not love her, and therefore killed her despite her hope for love.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The young man tells the maiden-spirit that he loves her and wants to accompany her wherever she goes, regardless of the difficulty of the journey, even if he can only see her at night.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The young man explains that he killed the maiden because he failed to recognize her while trying to save her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The maiden-spirit says, \"I am a spirit, and thou art unfinished,\" distinguishing her condition from the young man’s living state.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The maiden-spirit instructs the young man to plume many prayer-sticks, select a light downy feather and dye it with ocher, her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"At sunrise the young man gathers feathers of summer birds, cuts many prayer-sticks, and binds feathers to them with cotton as gifts to the Fathers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The young man selects a beautiful downy feather from an eagle, dyes it red with ocher, and ties to it a darkness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The maiden-spirit again suggests he go back but acknowledges his reason for accompanying her and tells him to watch as day comes, since he will no longer see her and must instead look where the plume goes and follow it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The young man takes the bright red plume from among the feathers of sacrifice and ties it above the maiden-spirit’s forehead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"As light rises from behind a great mountain, the red glow fades from the grave-sands and the young man can no longer see the maiden-spirit.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A light downy evening.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The young man follows the red feather, growing weary as it glides swiftly and occasionally leaves him far behind; when he He finds her imprisoned \"in fire\" in the cellar of an enchantress whose death is hidden in a blue rose-tree standing in a deep lake. With the aid of a magic ring he uproots the tree, the enchantress sickens, and when he throws the rose-bush into the cellar the building turns into an island inhabited by people formerly sitting in Hell, who thank Prince Ivan. A second story mentions a prince whose heart is taken by a witch and kept seething in a magic cauldron, tormenting him. A third tells of a Queen-Maiden who loves Ivan; his stepmother puts him into a magic sleep so the Queen-Maiden departs. A friendly witch later explains that the Queen-Maiden's love is hidden inside an egg enclosed in a duck, in a hare, in a coffer on an oak beyond the ocean. Ivan obtains the egg, the witch has it served to the Queen-Maiden, and when she eats it her love returns and she marries him. Ralston then comments that monstrous beings such as Koshchei, Chudo Yudo, Usuinya, and especially the many-headed snake Zmei Goruinuich typify evil in tales, but actual snakes in Russian peasant belief are good omens fed with milk and not to be harmed, which he links to an older cult of household snake gods similar to one attested in Poland and Lithuania. The passage ends with the beginning of the story \"The Water Snake\": an old woman's daughter bathing at a pond promises to marry a snake in exchange for her shift; after a week a troop of snakes breaks into the cottage, seizes her despite her mother's distress, carries her into the pond, and under the water they all become men and women while the mother mourns on the bank.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A prince has loved and lost a princess who is so beautiful that no man can look at her without fainting, and he goes in search of her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The prince comes to the home of an enchantress who invites him to tea and allows him to look through her house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the enchantress's cellar the prince sees the beautiful princess he loves \"in fire.\"","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The princess tells the prince that her love for him has brought her into this fiery captivity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The prince learns that he cannot free the princess unless he discovers where the enchantress's death lies, so he asks his hostess about it that evening.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The enchantress says that in a certain deep lake stands a blue rose-tree, unreachable by any man, and that her death is there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A magic ring enables the prince to reach the lake, where he sees the blue rose-tree with a blue forest around it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After several attempts the prince pulls up the blue rose-tree by the roots, and the enchantress immediately begins to sicken.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The prince returns, finds the enchantress near death, and throws the rose-bush into the cellar where the princess is crying, causing the building to shake and turn into an island.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The new island is inhabited by people who had been sitting in Hell, and they offer thanks to Prince Ivan.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In another Russian story a witch torments a prince by having taken his heart and keeping it perpetually seething in a magic cauldron.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In a third story a Queen-Maiden falls in love with the young Ivan, and after they are betrothed she wishes to take him to her own land and marry him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ivan's stepmother throws him into a magic slumber so that the Queen-Maiden must return home without him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"When Ivan awakes and learns that the Queen-Maiden has gone, he grieves greatly and sets out in search of her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A friendly witch tells Ivan that the Queen-Maiden's love is hidden far away: beyond the ocean stands an oak, on the oak a coffer, in the coffer a hare, in the hare a duck, and in the duck an egg which contains her love.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Ivan gains possession of the egg, and the friendly witch arranges for it to be placed before the Queen-Maiden at dinner.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"When the Queen-Maiden eats the egg, her love for Ivan returns fully; he appears, and she joyfully takes him to her land content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6991-l7100","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6991-7100","start":"6991","end":"7100","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage first notes that the episode of baking and eating a witch’s daughter in a Russian tale has many parallels in German, Norse, Servian, Modern Greek, Albanian, Baltic Kashoubian, and Turkic (Tardanak vs Seven-Headed Jelbegen) traditions. It then describes a Chernigof variant in which an old, childless couple place a wooden log in a cradle and rock it while singing until it becomes a baby, who later rows a silver boat with a golden oar (or the reverse in another variant). A White-Russian variant replaces the witch’s daughter with a witch’s son who lures village children with toys and devours them. Buslaef’s study of Kulish’s version is said to compare it with the romance of \"The Knight of the Swan.\" Further variants tell how Ivanushka, son of a lady, is carried off in a whirlwind by Baba Yaga and is repeatedly sought by his three sisters or by three servant-maids; the successful rescuer bribes the cat Jeremiah with butter and smears pitch on the sleeping Baba Yaga’s eyelids, so the cat refuses to scratch her eyes open. This comparison shows how closely related the Witch and Baba Yaga figures are. Another class of stories portrays the Vyed’ma as the daughter of ordinary royal parents who, without clear cause, begins to destroy and devour all living things, as if possessed by an evil spirit. The opening of the tale \"The Witch and the Sun’s Sister\" then recounts a king and queen whose only son, Prince Ivan, is mute until age twelve; warned by his groom friend that his unborn sister will be a terrible witch who will eat her parents and their subjects, Ivan asks his father for the best horse and rides away to escape the foretold danger.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the referenced Russian story there is an episode involving the baking and eating of a witch's daughter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The editor states that this baking-and-eating episode is well known in many lands and occurs in Grimm’s \"Haensel und Grethel,\" Norse tales \"Askelad\" and \"Smoerbuk,\" the Servian story \"The Stepmother,\" Modern Greek stories, the Albanian story \"Augenhuendin,\" a Baltic Kashoubian tale about a giantess, and the song of Tardanak describing the killing of the Seven Headed Jelbegen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the Servian story \"The Stepmother,\" two Jews are tricked into eating their baked mother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Modern Greek stories mentioned, the hero bakes a Drakaena while her husband the Drakos is at church, and in another story bakes a Lamiopula during the absence of her mother, the Lamia.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6205-l6305","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6205-6305","start":"6205","end":"6305","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage surveys several Baba Yaga folktales and begins the tale of Vasilissa the Fair. In one story, a childless couple hatch forty-one sons from eggs collected from every house; the weakest later becomes a hero who saves his brothers from Baba Yaga, whose daughters they marry, by tricking her servants into killing her daughters instead. The youths display the severed heads on spikes and escape Baba Yaga's fiery pursuit via a magic bridge-creating kerchief. Other stories describe girls sent to serve Baba Yaga, receiving arduous or impossible tasks such as heating a bath with dead men’s bones, fetching water in a sieve, and bathing Baba Yaga’s hideous children who appear as vermin. A kind girl, aided by a sparrow, succeeds and is rewarded with a blue coffer of money, while a conceited stepsister fails, mistreats the helpers and vermin-children, and is punished with a red coffer that releases fire and burns her and her mother. The narrator then notes that the skazka 'Vasilissa the Fair' is similar in many features and in its catastrophe to this story, and begins that tale: a merchant’s dying wife gives their eight-year-old daughter Vasilissa a secret doll that will, when fed, advise her in misfortune. After the mother’s death, the merchant remarries a widow with two daughters who become Vasilissa’s jealous, cruel stepfamily, overworking her while they idle. Vasilissa remains beautiful and thriving because the doll secretly helps her with her tasks, which she repays by sharing her food with it at night.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Baba Yaga is usually described as living alone, but she sometimes appears in the role of a house-mother.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A childless old couple are advised to collect one egg from each house in their village and place them under a sitting hen, resulting in forty-one sons.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Of the forty-one sons, forty grow into strong men while the forty-first remains for a long time a weak, diminutive \"Hop-o'-my-thumb\"-like figure.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The forty-one brothers set out to seek brides and eventually marry the forty-one daughters of a Baba Yaga.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"On the wedding night, Baba Yaga intends to kill her sons-in-law.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The formerly weak youngest brother, now a mighty hero, advises all the brothers to exchange clothes with their brides before lying down to sleep.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Following the clothing exchange, Baba Yaga's servants cut off the heads of her daughters instead of those of her sons-in-law.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The young men place the severed heads of their brides on iron spikes around Baba Yaga's house and ride away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When Baba Yaga sees her daughters' heads on spikes, she becomes enraged, takes a burning shield, pursues her sons-in-law, and begins burning everything on all four sides with the shield.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A magic kerchief that can create a bridge allows the fugitives to escape from Baba Yaga.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In one story, a heroine is ordered to swing the cradle of Baba Yaga's infant son and to address him respectfully while singing lullabies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In other stories, a heroine is instructed to wash Baba Yaga's many children, whose appearance is usually unattractive.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In one example, a girl is ordered by Baba Yaga to heat a bath, but the fuel provided consists of dead men's bones.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A sparrow advises the girl where to find wood so she can overcome the difficulty of using bones as fuel.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The same girl is then told to fetch water in a sieve, and again the sparrow advises her to line the sieve with clay so it will hold water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The girl is sent to wait upon Baba Yaga's children in the bath-room, where worms, frogs, rats, and other insects enter and are identified as Baba Yaga's children; she bathes them and then bathes Baba Yaga herself.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Pleased with the girl's service, Baba Yaga shares tea with her and sends her home with a blue coffer that is full of money.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The generous gift of the blue coffer arouses the stepmother's greed, and she sends her own daughter to Baba Yaga hoping for similar treasure.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Baba Yaga gives the second girl the same tasks, but the girl cannot make the bones burn or the sieve hold water and slaps the sparrow when it offers advice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"When Baba Yaga's vermin children enter the bath-room, the conceited girl crushes many of them, and the survivors complain to their mother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"As a result, Baba Yaga gives the second girl a red coffer instead of a blue one, and when it is opened, fire comes out and consumes both the girl and her mother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The narrator states that the skazka 'Vasilissa the Fair' is similar in many features and in its catastrophe to the preceding Baba Yaga story.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"In 'Vasilissa the Fair,' a merchant lives twelve years with his wife and they have only one child, Vasilissa the Fair; the mother dies when Vasilissa is eight years old.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"On her deathbed, the merchant's wife takes a doll from under the bed-clothes, gives it to Vasilissa, and instructs her to keep it secret, feed it in times of misfortune, and ask its advice; after eating, the doll will tell her how to remedy her troubles.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"After blessing and kissing her daughter, Vasilissa's mother dies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Following a period of mourning, the merchant decides to remarry and chooses a middle-aged widow with two daughters about the same age as Vasilissa, expecting her to be a good housekeeper and mother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"After the marriage, the merchant's new wife proves unkind to Vasilissa, whose stepmother and stepsisters are jealous of her beauty and burden her with exhausting outdoor work to ruin her appearance while they remain idle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Despite the harsh treatment, Vasilissa becomes ever plumper and prettier, while the stepmother and her daughters grow thin and lose their looks, attributed to the effects of their own spite.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The narration explains that Vasilissa is able to endure and complete her tasks because her doll helps her.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Vasilissa saves the most delicate part of her meals for her doll and, at night in her small chamber, feeds it in secret.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Baba Yaga","description":"A supernatural old woman who usually lives When the youth returns to his Eagle people, he finds that the message has already arrived and his Eagle-maiden wife, sorrowful at the doorway, rebukes him for having gone out of curiosity into a fearful country against the advice of herself and his grandparents, the Storks. She explains that the invitation to visit the city he saw, described as the most fearful of all cities and the city of the damned, cannot be refused, and that he must go with the Eagles. She implores him to prove his love by obeying a strict condition: during the visit he must not laugh or even smile once, and she will sit by his side and watch him; if he does this, all may yet be well and he may remain happily with her.

The youth promises repeatedly and, when night comes, goes with the Eagle people to the city. The city appears beautiful and bustling, with high stone walls, many small windows glowing with red firelight, smoke and sparks rising from chimneys, beacon fires on the roofs, and lively sounds and cries of life everywhere. They are ushered into a great dance hall (kiwitsin) where an audience is already assembled, and the fires blaze so that the room is as bright as day.

Maidens, mostly, enter as dancers, beautiful and richly clothed, with bright eyes and merry faces. Descending ladders into the room, they dance down the middle of the floor, jostling one another, playing grotesque pranks and assuming comical postures. As they dance they point at one another and cry in shrill but not unpleasant voices, “Hapa! hapa! is! is! is!” glossed as “Dead! dead! this! this! this!”, repeating this baleful expression even while full of life and joy. The youth watches their long dance, finds their antics amusing, and is puzzled that such lively maidens call one another dead, but he keeps his promise and does not smile.

A second group of dancers, even merrier, then enters. Among them are two or three girls of surpassing beauty, and one maiden in particular continually looks coquettishly toward the youth, directing her smiles and merriment at him while pointing to her companions and repeating the same cry. The youth becomes absorbed in watching her. Finally, when she jostles another dancer in an especially amusing way, he laughs aloud. The coquettish maiden runs to him with two others, seizes his hands, and drags him into the dance.

At this moment the Eagle-maiden lifts her wings, utters a cry of woe, and flies away with her people. The youth, carried away by merriment and the company of the beautiful maidens, pays no heed to their departure. He dances up and down the great lighted hall with the girls, imitating their strange postures and joining in their exclamations of “Hapa! hapa! is! is! is!”, whose true meaning he still does not understand.

As the fire burns low, the maidens invite the youth to stay the night with them instead of returning home, insisting that they are merry companions and laughing and jostling one another as they repeat their cry. They lead the willing youth into a distant room, large and fine like the others, where he lies down on soft blankets. The two form an alliance, abduct a princess afflicted by a mysterious disease caused by a Snake that enters via the chimney and sucks her strength, and seize the Snake, which leads them to a healing lake. There they and the princess are cured, she is returned to her father, and Ivan later returns to the Enchantress Queen who maimed him and beats the magic out of her with red-hot iron bars. A Tula variant is then mentioned, in which a wicked wife blinds her trusting husband and cuts off the feet of his companion, is killed by a hero, and Healing Waters are again found with the aid of a snake. The text then transitions to the theme of supernatural steeds, noting that the magical horse tamed by Katoma belongs to a common equine type in skazkas, and begins the tale of Princess Helena the Fair. An old man teaches his three sons literacy and instructs them to read prayers over his grave after his death. When he dies, news comes from the King that Princess Helena the Fair sits in a specially built shrine with twelve columns and twelve rows of beams, awaiting as bridegroom the youth who can, with a single bound of his swift steed, leap high enough to kiss her on the lips. While the two tall, strong elder brothers prepare themselves and their horses for this challenge and neglect their father’s wish, the undersized youngest son, Ivan (Vanyusha), alone reads prayers at the grave for three nights. When his brothers ride off without him, Vanyusha weeps and goes to his father’s grave. The dead father rises from his coffin, comforts him, whistles up a supernatural horse that shakes the earth and breathes flame, and tells it to serve his son. Vanya crawls into one ear of the horse and out the other, becoming an incomparable hero, then rides like a falcon to Helena’s shrine, and after three increasingly high leaps finally reaches and kisses her on the lips. The onlookers fail to stop the unknown hero. She lifts the lid and, addressing the insects as her children in a prayer-like way, orders them to bite a young man hoeing in the riverside corn-field so that he will flee. The insects agree and swarm out, biting the young man until he abandons his work and runs home. A boastful youth from the northern Tented Pueblo then attempts to woo the maiden and likewise flees from the insects, as does a wealthy young man from the River Town who brings many gifts. After these failures, other men fear the shame of being driven off by insects and delay seeking the maiden, unaware that she is a Passing Being. In the Ant Hill town Hálonawan lives a poor but handsome young man, son of the priest-chief, who confides in his gentle, crafty grandmother that he longs for the beautiful, wise maiden and wishes to woo her, valuing her tests of character over wealth. His grandmother warns that the maiden thinks of men only as brothers and sends the insects, who are disguised beings, to drive suitors away. Although she advises him not to go, she ultimately instructs him in a protective ritual: he must go to the mountains, scrape bitter bark from the finger-root, bake it into a small loaf and hide it in his belt, hoe in the corn-field until he is sweaty, then rub his body with the bark. She explains that the bark is as bitter as bad salt in bad water and that the various biting insects (\"horn-wings,\" \"long-beaks,\" and \"blue-backs\") avoid such bitterness. He wipes sweat from his face, rubs his shins with sand, slaps his sides, rolls in the dust, and cries out, invoking the Moon Mother and calling the insects little beasts that cause thoughts, but finally grabs his blanket and breakfast and runs toward his home.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:5","type":"summary","locator":"636-651","quote_or_summary":"A young man from the Tented Pueblo to the north laughs when he hears how the lover fared, mocks him as a little boy, and boasts that he will show what a Hámpasawan man can do by visiting the maiden of Mátsaki. His elders say, “Be it well,” and he goes as the other had gone, but he fares no better and is also driven away.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"651-662","quote_or_summary":"A young man from the River Town hears of the failures, laughs, and calls the other two fools, saying girls are not in the habit of asking much when one’s bundle is large. Being wealthy, he makes a bundle of presents as large as he can carry, but it does him no good and he too runs away from the insects.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"662-674","quote_or_summary":"Many days pass before anyone else tries to woo the maiden of Mátsaki. Men say that failure brings a ‘sick satisfaction’ of shame and prefer to wait to see what others will do. They do not know that she is a Passing Being and that others have failed because of mosquitoes, may-flies, and little black gnats.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:8","type":"summary","locator":"674-686","quote_or_summary":"In Hálonawan, the Ant Hill, lives a handsome but poor young man, son of the priest-chief, who thinks many days and then tells his gentle grandmother that his longing for the maiden of Mátsaki is killing him. He praises her beauty and wisdom and says he does not wonder she asks hard tasks of her lovers, since she cares about the men themselves more than their bundles. He resolves to strengthen his thoughts with manliness, harden his heart against weariness, and go speak to her.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:9","type":"summary","locator":"686-701","quote_or_summary":"The grandmother, very soft to her grandson, calls him her poor boy and warns that the maiden is as wonderful, wise, and beautiful as he says, but thinks of men only as brothers and friends. She believes it is the maiden who sends the may-flies, gnats, and mosquitoes to drive men away and calls the insects disguised beings. She compares the shame of failure to being covered with water in a rain-storm and urges him not to go, but he insists that he must go because of his longing.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:10","type":"summary","locator":"701-702+","quote_or_summary":"The grandmother concedes that the maiden will test him and advises him to go to the mountains to scrape bitter bark from the finger-root. He is to make a small loaf of the bark, hide it in his belt, hoe hard until sunrise, and when covered with sweat, rub every part of his body with the root-bark. She says the bark is as bitter as bad salt mixed with bad water and that horn-wings, long-beaks, and blue-backs (various biting insects) fly far from such bitter salt.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."},{"id":"ev:11","type":"summary","locator":"footnote within 674-686","quote_or_summary":"A footnote explains that the ancient pueblo of Zuñi itself was called Hálonawan, the Ant Hill, whose ruins lie opposite the modern town, and that the present pueblo was known in ancient songs and rituals as Hálona-ítiwana, the “Middle Ant Hill of the World,” often spoken of simply as the Ant Hill.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text, summarized."}],"confidence":{"extraction":"high","motif_candidates":"medium","comparison_claims":"uncertain","notes":"Core narrative details and roles are explicit; motif family assignments involve some interpretive mapping to the provided taxonomy and should be reviewed."},"reviewer_status":{"status":"needs_review","reviewer":"","reviewed_at":"","notes":""},"extracted_by":"gpt-4.1","extracted_at":"2026-07-18","notes":"Passage depicts a sequence of failed suitors repelled by insect agents sent by a supernatural maiden, followed by a poor but resolute youth who receives ritual protection advice from his grandmother; the footnote about Hálonawan situates the story in a cosmological center setting."}

{"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6006-l6113","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6006-6113","start":"6006","end":"6113","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""And it became a wide, such a wide river!"","summary":"In a Baba Yaga tale, the witch discovers that a girl has escaped and beats her cat and other household beings for not stopping her. Each helper (cat, dogs, doors, birch-tree, servant-maid) protests that Baba Yaga never gave them anything, whereas the girl had fed or cared for them. Baba Yaga, described as bony of limb, pursues the girl in a flying mortar, steering with a pestle and sweeping away her tracks with a broom. The girl repeatedly listens for her pursuer by putting her ear to the ground and, when Baba Yaga nears, throws down a towel that turns into a wide river and then a comb that becomes a dense forest. Baba Yaga fetches oxen to drink the river dry but cannot gnaw through the forest and has to turn back. The girl’s father returns home; after she explains that her stepmother sent her to her "aunt," who is actually Baba Yaga and wanted to eat her, the father angrily shoots his wife. He and his daughter then live on and prosper.

The editor summarizes a variant in which a heroine is sent by her husband’s mother to Baba Yaga. The husband’s advice saves her: while Baba Yaga goes to another room to sharpen her teeth, the girl escapes, having first spat under the threshold on the advice of a cat she has rewarded with butter. The spittle answers for her in her absence, like various substitute tokens in other tales (drops of blood, blood-soaked rags, apples, eggs, beans, stone images, wooden puppets).

The magical comb and towel that enable the girl’s escape recur in many similar Russian tales, along with a brush from whose bristles a wood springs up, sometimes mountains, and a bath whisk that becomes a forest. The towel can also create or destroy a bridge. Analogous sets of small objects appear in many other traditions: the brush, comb, and mirror of a German water-sprite; the rod, stone, and pitcher of water of a Norse troll; the knife, comb, and salt that save Asterinos and Pulja from their fiendish mother in a Modern Greek story; the twig, stone, and bladder of water from a filly’s ear that save her master from a Gaelic giant; the brush, comb, and egg (which becomes a frozen lake) that cause the death of a pursuing Old Prussian witch; a wand that raises a river and a mountain between a youth and a Rakshasa in a Deccan story; and, in a similar episode in Somadeva’s tale of the Prince of Varddhamana, a handful of earth, a cup of water, and dry sticks and a match that create impeding obstacles and destroy a Rakshasa.

The commentator interprets these instruments as symbolizing the power over the elements attributed to the supernatural beings who own them and as examples of a "like produces like" logic: in a Sanskrit form of the story, a handful of earth becomes a mountain and a cup of water becomes a river; metaphorically, a brush can be seen as a tiny wood (as in the word "brushwood"), and the indented outline of a comb can resemble a serrated mountain range. This perception is reflected linguistically in German, where Kamm means both comb and mountain ridge, similar to Spanish sierra.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"When Baba Yaga discovers the girl has escaped, she beats the Cat for not scratching out the girl’s eyes, but the Cat replies that Baba Yaga never gave it so much as a bone, whereas the girl gave it bacon; the dogs, doors, birch-tree, and servant-maid similarly complain that Baba Yaga never rewarded them, but the girl gave them food, oil, a ribbon, or a handkerchief.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Baba Yaga, described as bony of limb, jumps into a wife that the girl has gone to her aunt’s, then soon sees his daughter arrive and learns that the stepmother sent her to Baba Yaga, who wanted to eat her; the father becomes angry, shoots his wife, and thereafter lives and prospers with his daughter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In a variant of the story, the heroine is sent by her husband’s mother to Baba Yaga; her husband gives her advice that saves her life.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In that variant, Baba Yaga goes into another room to sharpen her teeth before eating the heroine; meanwhile the heroine, following a Cat’s advice and after giving it butter, spits under the threshold, and the spittle answers for her in her absence while she escapes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The spittle’s answering role is compared to that of drops of blood, rags dipped in blood, apples, eggs, beans, stone images, or wooden puppets in other folk-tales, which similarly serve as substitutes for an absent person.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The magic comb and towel with which the girl escapes are said to occur frequently in Russian tales of this class and always to produce the desired effect.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Other Russian variants use a brush, from each bristle of which a wood springs up, or in one case mountains, and a bath-room whisk (golik) that turns into a forest; the towel may also be used to construct or annihilate a bridge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Similar sets of "Prince of Varddhamana," a handful of earth, cup of water, and dry sticks and match that impede and ultimately destroy a up.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In the Old Prussian tale, the magic egg produces a frozen lake with a "mirror-smooth" surface on which the pursuing witch slips and dies.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The commentator states that these magic instruments typify the influence which their supernatural owners were believed to exercise over the elements and that the transformations operate according to a principle of "like produces like."","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In a Sanskrit form of the story, a handful of earth turns into a mountain and a cup of water turns into a river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The commentator suggests that metaphorically a brush can be treated as a tiny wood, as shown by the word "brushwood," and that a comb’s indented outline may resemble a serrated mountain range; German Kamm means both comb and mountain ridge, similar to Spanish sierra.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"In the main tale, the helpers explain that Baba Yaga has never rewarded them during the time they served her, whereas the girl has given them bacon, rolls, oil, a ribbon, or a handkerchief.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The stepmother lies to the father about the girl’s whereabouts, and after hearing the truth the father kills his wife and then lives happily with his daughter.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"In the variant, the heroine is endangered by her husband’s mother but is saved by her husband’s advice and the help of a Cat rewarded with butter.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Across the cited tales, magic objects typically belong to or are associated with supernatural pursuers such as Baba Yaga, a German water-sprite, a Norse Troll, a fiendish mother, a Gaelic giant, an Old Prussian witch, and Rakshasas, and are used to raise elemental obstacles between them and human fugitives.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The girl in the main tale calls the house of Baba Yaga her "aunt’s" when explaining her journey home, clarifying that the supposed aunt is Baba Yaga who wanted to eat her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The girl twice listens for Baba Yaga by putting her ear to the ground before throwing her magic towel and comb.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"In the Deccan and Somadeva episodes, the wand or the At midnight the coffin lid falls, the princess rises, threatens him, and conjures terrifying illusions, including what seems to be a fire engulfing the church, but he continues reading without looking back. Near daybreak she returns to her coffin and the horrors vanish. In the morning the king finds the coffin open with the princess lying face down. After hearing the youth's account, he orders an aspen stake driven into her breast and her body thrust into a hole in the ground, then rewards the priest's son with money and lands. The narrator then introduces another story from Little Russia, noting that Gogol, in his story \"Vy\" (translated as \"The King of the Gnomes\"), closely followed such popular traditions. The new tale, \"The Soldier's Midnight Watch,\" begins: a soldier has served God and the Tsar for fifteen years without seeing his parents. When the Tsar grants leave to some soldiers, he returns toward his home near Kief, visiting the Lavra and holy relics on the way. On the road he meets an extraordinarily beautiful merchant's daughter from his town and exchanges flirtatious banter with her. At home he happily reunites with his family, including a very old white-haired grandfather. When the soldier describes the girl and her teasing words, the grandfather warns that she is an awful witch who has killed several young men. He instructs the soldier to stay inside with a bridle and a thick aspen cudgel; the witch will come at night and try to say a spell first to turn him into a horse and ride him to death, but if he speaks first she will become a mare whom he must bridle, ride, and beat with the cudgel until she dies. The soldier follows these instructions: at midnight, as soon as the witch enters, he utters the prescribed words, she becomes a mare, and he rides her over rough country while beating her with the aspen cudgel until she collapses and he kills her. He returns at daybreak, tells his grandfather he has beaten her to death, and then sleeps deeply until the old man wakes him in the evening.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At midnight in the church, the coffin lid falls to the ground, the princess jumps up, cudgel and to sit quietly in the izba at night, explaining that the witch will come and, if she manages to say \"Stand still, my steed!\" first, he will immediately turn into a horse which she will ride to death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The grandfather further explains that if the soldier manages to say \"Tprru! stand still, jade!\" before the witch The Squirrel climbs into it and stretches its topmost bough until it reaches the young man’s feet, restraining him from jumping on it too soon. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l9767-l9909","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL. / SOZH AND DNIEPER. / FOOTNOTES:; lines 9767-9909","start":"9767","end":"9909","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A series of scholarly footnotes explains Slavic and related folkloric terms and beliefs. Notes describe the ambivalent Russian adjective and noun 'likhoi/likho' and Polish 'licho', linking them with misfortune, unevenness, unlucky odd numbers, an evil spirit, and a proverb about not awakening Likho. Other notes gloss 'Kruchina' (grief) personified as male, and 'Spasibo' and 'Good-bye' as contractions of religious blessings. Russian personifications of Luck and Bad-luck (Schastie and Neschastie) are said to be exact counterparts of Indian Lakshmi and Alakshmi, and a tale from the Hitopadesa is summarized in which the Fortune of King Sudraka appears as a beautiful woman and foretells his death due to the queen's fault. Additional notes explain weekday names and recount an English legend about a ship named 'The Friday' that vanished, illustrating Friday superstition. Another note quotes an English nursery rhyme addressing a lady-bird whose house is on fire. A long comparative note identifies Russian personified Wednesday and Friday as counterparts of Lithuanian Laumes, describes Lithuanian taboos on spinning during 'Laume's Eve' (Thursday evening) when Laumes come at night to work and steal spinning, and notes similar attributions to modern Greek Neraides (related to Nereids). It remarks that Neraida resemble Lamia and share features with Laume, and tentatively asks whether the names Laume/Lauma and Lamia are connected. Finally, it explains that Russian 'Nedyelya' originally meant Sunday, the non-working day, and later came to mean 'week'.","language":"English","quote_policy":"

With a massive mace and the cap, Nikita defeats the warriors of Helena the Fair, turns her fiery ambush against her by burning her women’s chambers, and secretly takes the king’s place during three lethal bridal strength tests until she submits. When Helena discovers the deception, she maims Nikita, degrades the king to a swineherd, and blinds Nikita’s brother Timofei; later the brothers obtain Healing and Vivifying Waters from Baba Yaga that restore limbs and sight, the Witch-Queen is put to death, and Nikita becomes the king’s prime minister, with the distinct effects of the two waters carefully described.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the Indian tale, a king’s daughter is born with three breasts, and he considers her presence unfortunate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Indian king offers one hundred thousand purses of gold to anyone who will marry his three-breasted daughter and take her away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A blind man, led by the hunchback Mantharaka or Cripple, marries the three-breasted princess, receives the gold, and goes far away with her and his friend to live in one house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The wife falls in love with the hunchback and conspires with him to kill her husband by boiling a snake in order to poison him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"As the blind husband stirs the snake-broth while it cooks, the rising steam cures his blindness; he then pretends to remain blind and watches his wife and friend embrace in his presence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The husband seizes the hunchback by the legs and dashes him against his wife; the blow drives the wife’s third breast out of sight and beats the hunchback straight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In a Russian variant, a king promises vast wealth to anyone who will find him a bride ‘fairer than the sun, brighter than the moon, and whiter than snow.’","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The peasant Nikita Koltoma offers to show the king where such a princess lives and sets out with him in search of her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In one forge, Nikita finds fifty smiths torturing an old man for an unpaid debt of fifty roubles; ten hold him by the beard with pincers while the others hammer his ribs, and Nikita ransoms the greybeard, obtains a heavy war mace weighing fifty poods, and leaves the forge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The old man, who has been under this punishment for thirty years, later runs after Nikita, thanks him for his rescue, and gives him a Cap of Invisibility in gratitude.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Nikita, accompanied by the king and his followers, reaches the palace of Helena the Fair; she sends warriors to capture or slay them, whom Nikita kills with his mace, and then prepares a gigantic bow with a fiery arrow to annihilate her guests, but Nikita, wearing the Cap of Invisibility, shoots the arrow into her women’s chambers, setting the whole upper story ablaze so that she submits and marries the king.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Nikita warns the king that for three nights Helena will test his strength by pressing her hand on his breast so hard he cannot bear it; each night the king slips out and lets Nikita take his place, and Nikita endures her pressure, finally throwing her down so violently that she abandons her attempt to squeeze her husband to death and accepts conjugal submission.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After discovering she has been tricked, Helena casts Nikita into a twenty-four-hour slumber, has his feet cut off, and sets him adrift in a boat, then turns the king into a swineherd and puts out the eyes of Nikita’s brother Timofei.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In time the brothers obtain from Baba Yaga the Healing Water and the Vivifying Water, use them to recover the feet and eyes they had lost, the Witch-Queen is put to death, and Nikita lives as the king’s prime minister.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The Healing Water restores whole but motionless legs and perfectly formed but sightless eyes, while the Vivifying Water then restores movement to the legs and sight to the eyes.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Indian king (father of three-breasted princess)","description":"King in the Panchatantra tale whose daughter is born with three breasts; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l2421-l2553","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE TRIAL OF LOVERS: / THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE / THE POOR TURKEY GIRL / HOW THE SUMMER BIRDS CAME; lines 2421-2553","start":"2421","end":"2553","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A divine-ancestry boy living with his mother pretends he is going to hunt small animals but instead seeks out dangerous monsters. First he visits the den of the Misho Lizards, who politely invite him in and then cover him with venom. Because he is the child of the gods and prepared, the venom does not harm him. He thanks them and throws a lump of rock salt into their fire, which explodes and kills the lizards. He takes two of their hearts, goes home, and hangs them beside a bear’s heart already displayed near the ladder. His mother sees this and scolds him for his disobedience and for risking her becoming completely alone. That evening he pesters her until she tells him of another monster: a giant with a hair-knot on his forehead who lies across a narrow cliff trail, politely inviting travelers to step over him and then kicking them off the precipice to feed his children in a den below. The boy feigns horror and says he will never go there, but at dawn he again lies to his mother, takes his war-club, and goes straight to the cliff. The sun’s yearly path is described as climbing a series of poles that join earth and sky. Different versions say that the bearer of the sun rides a turquoise animal or that the Sun himself dons a robe of cloud, takes a son under each arm, and rises into the heavens, travelling to a sky-hole where a sacred meal of mixed pollens and water is eaten before the brothers descend. Geographic notes locate Warm Spring and a nearby mythic lake. The origins of the monsters (anáye) are given in two versions: all conceived in the fifth world and born from one granddaughter of First Woman, or sent by First Woman after she is offended with man. Yéitso, a giant, is said to appear over various hills, utters a satisfied exclamation, and is struck so that his armor is rent; dead demons are said to become useful to humans, and Yéitso’s armor is conjectured to have turned into flint tools. The names of the twin War Gods, Nayénezgani and To`-ba-dzis-tsí-ni (Child of the Water), are etymologically explained and said to have been given after their first victory and scalp-dance celebration. Navaho storytellers identify the volcanic hill El Cabezon and neighboring cones as the heads of Yéitso and other giants slain in a storm raised by the War Gods. One giant’s formulaic cry, Yiniketóko!, is likened to “Fee Fa Fum!” in European nursery tales.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"One informant described sixteen poles in the east and sixteen in the west joining earth and sky, while others said there were thirty-two poles on each side.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The annual progress of the sun is explained as the sun climbing different poles between winter and summer solstices, spending about an equal number of days at each pole.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Many versions say the bearer of the sun rode a domesticated or pet animal (lin), now especially understood as a horse; in Version A this animal was made of turquoise and larger than a horse.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Version A the sky is said to dip down and touch the earth so that the horse carrying the sun can ascend to the sky.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Version B

{"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l1140-l1247","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"H. HALLIDAY SPARLING. / TRANSLATORS' PREFACE. / THE STORY OF THE VOLSUNGS AND NIBLUNGS. / CHAPTER V. Of the Slaying of King Volsung.; lines 1140-1247","start":"1140","end":"1247","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"King Volsung and his sons sail in three ships to Gothland at King Siggeir's invitation. That night Signy secretly warns her father and brothers that Siggeir has gathered an overwhelming army and intends to betray them, urging them to withdraw and later return with greater force. Volsung recalls a vow made before his birth never to flee from fire or sword and refuses to retreat, declaring that all must die once and that he will not live in dishonor. He insists that Signy return to her husband Siggeir. At dawn Volsung leads his men ashore, and Siggeir attacks with his army. After a fierce battle in which Volsung and his sons cut through Siggeir's men eight times, Volsung and his followers are slain, and his ten sons are captured. 

Signy, learning of her father's death and her brothers' capture, asks Siggeir not to kill the brothers quickly but to set them in stocks so she may see them alive for a time; Siggeir agrees, pleased that their suffering will be prolonged. The ten brothers are bound with a mighty beam on their feet in the wild-wood. Each midnight an old, great, evil-looking she-wolf comes from the woods, killing and eating one brother, while Signy sends a trusted man each morning to learn the news and grieves that she cannot help them. After nine nights, only Sigmund remains. Before the tenth night, Signy sends her trusted man with honey to smear on Sigmund's face and put in his mouth. When the she-wolf comes, she licks the honey from his face and puts her tongue into his mouth; Sigmund bites and holds it fast. As the wolf pulls back, bracing against the stocks, she tears them apart but loses her tongue, which is torn out by the roots, and she dies, freeing Sigmund. A tradition says this she-wolf was Siggeir's mother, who turned herself into this form through troll-lore and witchcraft.

After his escape, Sigmund dwells in the woods. Signy sends men to confirm he is alive, hears his account of the wolf, and then visits him herself. Together they build a house underground in the wild-wood, where she hides him and sends what he needs, while King Siggeir believes all the Volsungs are dead.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"King Volsung and his sons travel to Gothland in three well-manned ships at King Siggeir's bidding and arrive late in the evening.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Signy comes at night to a secret meeting with her father and brothers to speak privately.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Signy reports that King Siggeir has drawn together an army that no one can face and intends to deal guilefully with Volsung and his sons.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Signy advises Volsung and his sons to sail back home, gather the greatest power they can, and then return to Gothland to avenge themselves instead of facing Siggeir's trap immediately.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"King Volsung declares that before his birth he made a vow never to flee in fear from fire or sword and that he has kept this vow all his life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Volsung says he will not now depart from GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 7212-7296","start":"7212","end":"7296","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Nati'nesthani, a poor Navaho man living with a turkey, repeatedly tries to locate a mysterious distant fire. After using two forked sticks and a straight stick to aim at the flame, he follows the indicated direction to an eastern mountain, where a rock shelf leads to two fine huts. Ashamed of his ragged possessions, he hides them in a juniper tree and enters one hut, finding a young woman sewing an ornate buckskin shirt. Her father arrives carrying Nati'nesthani's old clothes, publicly calling him \"son-in-law\" and seating him on fine skins beside the woman. The father repeatedly asks for tobacco; Nati'nesthani initially claims to be poor and without tobacco, though he belongs to the People up on the Earth (Ninokádine`). He then produces a decorated pouch containing a mixture of tobacco and other plants, fills a clay pipe made from wood-rat earth, lights it with the sun, and gives it to the old man, who smokes, sweats heavily, and collapses in a swoon. The daughter obtains a large quantity of goods from her mother, promising them to Nati'nesthani if he restores her father to life. They lay the old man on his side with his head to the north and face to the east. Using a composite medicine called ké`tlo, Nati'nesthani lights it with sunbeams in a pipe, blows smoke to earth and sky and then onto the patient from the four cardinal directions. The old man begins to revive, and the medicine is further soaked with water in an earthen bowl and rubbed on his body, in a manner said to underlie current ritual practice.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Nati'nesthani finds that he has marked the same spot as before and makes a third journey to seek the distant fire, returning disappointed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"During the day Nati'nesthani, accompanied by his turkey, sets traps for wood-rats and other small animals.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After dark he again sees the distant flame and sets a second forked stick in the ground with a long straight stick laid between the forks and aimed at the fire before going to sleep.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The next morning he carefully notes the spot toward which the straight stick points and tells his turkey he will seek the distant fire once more, for the last time.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When Nati'nesthani speaks of his last attempt, the turkey turns its back on him and behaves like a pouting child, showing anger.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Following the direction indicated by the stick, Nati'nesthani travels to an eastern mountain, finds a rock shelf that seems to run back some distance, climbs it, and discovers two nice huts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Feeling ashamed of his ragged bark blanket, wood-rat-skin pipe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Nati'nesthani pushes aside the curtain of one hut and sees a young woman inside making a fine buckskin shirt ornamented with fringes and shells.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ashamed of his appearance, Nati'nesthani hangs his head and advances, looking at the young woman under his
