Sigrun explains that her father has promised her in marriage to Hodbrod, son of King Granmar, but she has vowed to reject Hodbrod and asks Helgi to oppose him in war and take her away, declaring she would rather share Helgi’s bed than Hodbrod’s. Helgi vows to fight Hodbrod and pledges his life on the matter, then sends out messengers with money to summon his followers. A great host gathers at Red-Berg, with more forces and ships coming from Hedinsey and Norvi Sound. Helgi consults his ship-captain Leif, who reports many thousands of warriors. The fleet sails into Varin’s firth and is struck by a fierce storm; Helgi orders the sails raised higher instead of reefed, and the ships nearly founder before reaching land. Sigrun arrives on the beach with a great army and guides Helgi’s fleet to a safe haven called Gnipalund. Local landsmen come to the shore. The brother of King Hodbrod, lord of Swarin’s Cairn, calls out asking who commands the army. Sinfjotli stands forth, splendidly armed with helm, bright byrny, spear, banner, and gold-rimmed shield, and declares that the Volsungs and King Helgi are present, insulting Hodbrod as one who prefers to stay at home feeding swine and kissing handmaids by the fire. Granmar answers with harsh insults, accusing Sinfjotli of lying about lords, being reared on wolf-meat in the wild woods, killing his brothers, and sucking the blood of corpses. Sinfjotli responds with further taunts, claiming that Granmar was a witch-wife on Varinsey, later a Valkyria in Asgarth, and that Sinfjotli fathered nine wolf-whelps on that body. Granmar replies that Sinfjotli is a liar and likely father of nothing, having been gelded by the giant’s daughters of Thrasness; he calls Sinfjotli the stepson of King Siggeir, who lived with wolves in the wild and slew his brothers. King Helgi intervenes, saying it would be more fitting to fight than to speak shameful words, and acknowledges that Granmar’s sons, though hostile, are hardy men. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 8192-8289","start":"8192","end":"8289","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Navaho man is stranded in an eagle’s cave high on a cliff after using a basket to ascend. The Pueblo people below first call to him affectionately for two days, urging him to throw down the eaglets and tempting him with food, but he refuses to respond. On the third and fourth days they grow angry, shoot fire-arrows into the cave, and verbally abuse him, yet he remains silent and throws out the arrows. At his request the eaglets shake out many small feathers, which fall on the people below; he believes these feathers bring disease. Finally, the Pueblos abandon him to die of hunger and thirst after four days. That night, weakened and despairing, he hears a rushing sound four times as first the male and then the female Eagle arrive. They thank him for not throwing down his “younger brother” and address him as Donikí, later naming him Kinníki, after the chief of the eagles. The male Eagle produces a small cloth bundle with cornmeal, a tiny white shell bowl whose contents never diminish while the Navaho eats, and a jointed water-plant filled with water, from which the Navaho drinks his fill. The great Eagles sleep beside him, removing their single-piece robes of plumes and revealing humanlike forms, keeping him warm. At dawn, a voice from the top of the cliff calls to them and many eagles and hawks gather outside the cave and on the rock above, singing about Kinnakíye sitting there and how they will see him when they fly up.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Pueblo people see the empty basket swinging, wait for the Navaho to return, and when eagles.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Navaho sits silently in the cleft or cave and does not answer the Pueblo people despite their persistent calling until not.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On the second day the Pueblo people gather again at the foot of the cliff, repeat their entreaties, use endearing terms, and The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy.; lines 1799-1912","start":"1799","end":"1912","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"King Eylimi asks his daughter Hjordis to choose a husband between King Sigmund and King Lyngi, promising that his counsel will follow her choice. Hjordis selects the older but more renowned Sigmund, is betrothed and wedded to him, and King Lyngi departs. After the wedding feast, Sigmund returns with Hjordis’s father to Hunland and rules his realm. King Lyngi and his brothers then gather an army to attack Sigmund and openly announce their coming. Sigmund agrees to meet them in battle, while Hjordis is taken into the wood with a bondmaid and great wealth to wait out the fighting. Vikings land from their ships, and Sigmund and King Eylimi set up banners and sound horns; Sigmund blows a horn once owned by his father and fights fiercely, protected by his spae‑wrights so that he takes no wound while killing many foes. In the midst of the battle a one‑eyed man in a blue cloak and slouched hat appears, armed with a bill, and breaks Sigmund’s sword with his weapon. After the sword shatters, Sigmund’s luck departs, slaughter turns against his side, and both Sigmund and Eylimi fall along with most of their followers. An endnote identifies the one‑eyed man as Odin, who comes to change the ownership of the sword he had given Sigmund. King Lyngi then goes to Sigmund’s abode hoping to seize the king’s daughter and his wealth, but finds neither and sets his men over the realm, thinking he has destroyed the Volsung kin. That night Hjordis walks among the slain and finds Sigmund still alive. She asks whether he can be healed, but he refuses, saying his good fortune has left him and Odin no longer wills him to draw sword, since the weapon that was both his and Odin’s is broken. Hjordis wishes he could live to avenge her father, but Sigmund says that vengeance is fated for another man. He tells her she is already pregnant with a man‑child who will be the noblest and most famed of their kin, whose name will endure as long as the world. He instructs her to keep the shards of his broken sword so that a fine sword, Gram, can be forged for their son, who will accomplish great deeds. Sigmund says he grows weary of his wounds and will go to see their kin who have gone before, and Hjordis sits over him until he dies at daybreak. Seeing many ships approach, Hjordis proposes that she and her bondmaid exchange clothing and that the servant take her name and claim to be the king’s daughter. They do so. Vikings led by Alf, son of Hjalprek, king of Denmark, land, observe the battlefield full of dead men, and bring the two women before the king. The bondmaid answers Alf’s questions, telling him of the fall of Sigmund, Eylimi, and other great men and of those who wrought the deed. The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy.; lines 1666-1797","start":"1666","end":"1797","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Helgi and the Volsungs come with a great host to battle; King Hodbrod gathers allies, but Helgi breaks through his forces at Wolfstone. In the fight, people see shield-maidens like burning flames, among whom is Sigrun, a king’s daughter. Helgi kills King Hodbrod under his banner; Sigrun thanks him, promises they will share the land, and Helgi later weds her and rules the realm with renown. A note explains that valkyries are women sent by Odin to choose those fated to die in battle and join the Einherjar in Valholl. 

After the Volsungs return home, Sinfjotli again goes to war. He falls in love with a very fair woman who is also wooed by the brother of Queen Borghild. The rivals fight and Sinfjotli kills Borghild’s brother, then continues raiding successfully and returns in autumn with ships and wealth. When Sinfjotli tells his deeds to his father Sigmund and to Borghild, she orders him to leave the realm and refuses to see him. Sigmund refuses to drive his son away and offers Borghild atonement in gold and wealth for her brother’s death, saying he has never before paid weregild but does not wish to uphold wrong against a woman. She outwardly yields and, with Sigmund’s counsel, arranges a splendid funeral feast for her brother, summoning many great men.

At the feast Borghild carries drink around. She offers Sinfjotli a great horn, calling him her fair stepson, but he refuses, saying the drink is charmed, and Sigmund drinks it instead. She taunts Sinfjotli for letting another man drink his ale and brings the horn again; he again refuses, calling it guile, and Sigmund again drinks. A third time she challenges him to drink if he has the heart of a Volsung. He says there is venom in the drink, but Sigmund, now very drunk, urges him to let his lip strain it. Sinfjotli drinks and falls dead. 

Sigmund is almost slain with grief. He takes Sinfjotli’s corpse into the woods and comes to a firth, where a man in a little boat offers to ferry him across. Because the boat is too small for both, they first lay the corpse in it while Sigmund walks along the shore;

Of the Birth of Sinfjotli the Son of Sigmund. / CHAPTER VIII. The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy. / CHAPTER XV. Of the Welding together of the Shards of the Sword Gram. / CHAPTER XVI. The prophecy of Grifir.; lines 2238-2377","start":"2238","end":"2377","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sigurd visits his maternal uncle Grifir, a man famed for knowing fate, and insists on learning the whole course of his life, which Grifir reveals. Returning home, Sigurd meets Regin, who urges him to fulfill his promise to slay the dragon Fafnir, but Sigurd insists that he must first avenge his father Sigmund and other slain kinsmen. Sigurd then addresses the kings with whom he has been staying, thanks them for their favor and gifts, and asks for their support in a campaign against the sons of Hunding to show that the Volsungs are not all dead. The kings grant his request and prepare a great army, ships, and war-gear; Sigurd himself steers the largest and finest dragon-prowed ship with richly decorated sails. As they sail with a fair wind, a violent sea storm arises and the waves resemble the foam of men’s blood, but Sigurd orders that the sails not be shortened and instead set even higher. Sailing past the rocky point of a ness, they are hailed by a man on the cliffs who asks who leads the fleet and is told it is Sigurd, son of Sigmund, the most renowned of young kings’ sons. The man praises Sigurd’s fame and asks to be taken aboard. When asked his name, he sings that he is called Hnikar, that he once gladdened Huginn and went to battle with the bright son of Volsung, and that he may now be called Feng or Fjolnir. They land and take him aboard. Sigurd then asks Hnikar, who knows the fates of gods and men, what signs best foreshow good fortune in battle. Hnikar gives a series of poetic counsels about battle omens: a dark-winged raven is a good companion to a warrior; seeing two men standing, eager for fame, in a forecourt when setting out well-equipped is favorable; hearing a wolf howling beneath ash boughs is a good sign before fighting; a warrior should not turn his face against the low, late-shining ‘moon’s sister’ during battle, as victory belongs to the one who can best see through the sword-play and shape the ranks; stumbling feet are dangerous when going to battle because the Dísir, guileful female beings, stand about on both sides and desire the warrior’s wounding; and warriors should be fair-combed, well washed, and have food in the morning, since no one can command the return of evening and it is base to grovel before fate. After this, the storm abates and the fleet reaches the realm of Hunding’s sons, where Fjolnir disappears. Sigurd and his men then ravage the land with fire and sword, killing men, burning homes, and laying waste before them. Refugees flee to King Lyngi and report the devastating onslaught, saying Hunding’s sons were wrong to think they need no longer fear the Volsungs, since Sigurd son of Sigmund commands the army. Lyngi sends the war-message throughout his realm, refuses to flee, gathers allies, and with his brothers leads a great host against Sigurd. A fierce battle ensues in which spears and arrows fly, axes bite, shields are split, armor torn, helmets shattered, skulls cloven, and many men fall The Wooing of Brynhild.; lines 3542-3681","start":"3542","end":"3681","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this passage Gudrun and Brynhild quarrel bitterly over their husbands’ honor and past deeds. Gudrun defends Sigurd, recounting how he slew Fafnir and rode the flaming fire to Brynhild, lay beside her, and took from her hand the ring Andvari’s-loom, which she now shows as proof. Brynhild recognizes the ring, becomes deathly pale, and withdraws in silence. That night Gudrun consults Sigurd, who fears that trouble will come and warns her not to question Brynhild about whom she loves most. The next morning in the bower Gudrun presses Brynhild to explain her sorrow. Brynhild accuses Gudrun of cruel intent, vows that Gudrun will pay for having Sigurd and his wealth, and claims she and Sigurd swore oaths together which Gudrun helped to betray. They dispute which husband is nobler, Brynhild insisting that Sigurd’s slaying of Fafnir and riding of the fire outweigh King Gunnar’s might, while Gudrun praises Gunnar as king and notes that Sigurd alone dared the fiery ride when Gunnar did not and Grani would not bear him. Brynhild speaks ill of Grimhild, accusing her of giving Sigurd an evil drink that erased his memory of Brynhild, an accusation Gudrun rejects as a lie. Brynhild curses Gudrun to have joy of Sigurd in measure of the deceit used against her, yet also says she now loves Gudrun’s brother alone and tries to end their angry exchange. The narrator remarks that great misfortune arose from the earlier going to the river and recognition of the ring. In the following chapter Brynhild lies in bed like one dead, and Gunnar, hearing she is sick, visits and presses her for an explanation, but she answers nothing at first.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Brynhild tells Gudrun that her father is mightier than Gudrun’s, that her true love has done Guttorm makes three attempts on Sigurd: twice he retreats before Sigurd’s fierce eyes, but the third time he stabs Sigurd as he sleeps in bed. Hogni notes the fulfillment of Brynhild’s soothsaying, and Gudrun laments that her kinsmen have slain her husband and future support. In an ancient song, Gudrun sits in silent, near-fatal sorrow over Sigurd. Earls and their gold-adorned brides come to comfort her, each recounting her own grief. Giaflaug, Giuki’s sister, details the loss of five husbands, daughters, sisters, and eight brothers. Gudrun remains silent. Brynhild refuses him, saying she will not have him nor any other man. Brynhild declares she will not live, saying Sigurd has betrayed her and Gunnar by being allowed into her bed. He calls his brother Hogni and says he must slay Sigurd because Sigurd has failed him where he trusted him, so they may be lords of the gold and the realm.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","rights_note":"Public domain (Project Gutenberg); summarized for analysis."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"3986-4015","quote_or_summary":"Hogni replies that it ill behoves them to break their oaths with wrong, notes that Sigurd is a great aid, and says no kings shall be as great as they if the King of the Hun-folk lives. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 8632-8652","start":"8632","end":"8652","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Among a crowd of pueblo people, a dancing Navaho sings a song they find strange. As they watch, he begins to rise slowly from the ground. First his head, then his shoulders, chest, waist, and finally his whole body rise above the level of the crowd. Only then do they realize that they are about to lose him along with the great shell of Kintyél and the combined wealth of many pueblos in shell-beads and turquoise that he carries and wears. They scream and address him with affectionate kinship terms such as father, brother, and son, begging him to come down, but the higher they call the higher he rises. When his feet are above them, they see a streak of white lightning under his feet, like a rope hanging from a dark cloud that has gathered above. The narrator states that it is the gods who are lifting him and that this is the way, according to the legends, that the gods lift mortals to the sky. When persuasion fails, some of the people call for ropes to pull him down, but he rises beyond the reach of their longest rope. Others call for arrows to shoot him, but before they can reach him he vanishes into a black cloud and is never seen on earth again.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The pueblo people consider the Navaho's song strange and wonder what it content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l5098-l5174","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XXXVII. The Battle in the Burg of King Atli. / CHAPTER XXXVIII. Of the slaying of the Giukings. / CHAPTER XXXIX. The End of Atli and his Kin and Folk. / CHAPTER XLI. Of the Wedding and Slaying of Swanhild.; lines 5098-5174","start":"5098","end":"5174","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"King Jormunrek sends his son Randver and his counsellor Bikki to King Jonakr to woo Swanhild, daughter of Sigurd Fafnir’s-bane, whom Jormunrek desires as his wife. Jonakr accepts the honorable alliance, while Gudrun warns against trusting in luck. Swanhild’s betrothal is arranged and she sails with Randver, sitting beside him. Bikki encourages Randver to desire Swanhild for himself, and the two exchange affectionate words. Upon their return, Bikki falsely tells Jormunrek that Randver has seduced Swanhild. The king orders Randver bound to the gallows-tree. As Randver is led to execution, he plucks the feathers from his hawk and has it shown to his father, who interprets the featherless bird as a sign that his own honor has been stripped away and orders Randver’s release, but Bikki has already caused Randver’s death. Bikki then urges Jormunrek to avenge himself on Swanhild, and she is bound in the gate of the burg while horses are driven at her to trample her. When she opens her eyes wide, the horses refuse to trample her, so Bikki orders a bag drawn over her head, and she is killed. A note adds that in the Prose Edda version the king spontaneously rides over Swanhild as she washes linen, believing her to be the cause of his misfortunes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Jormunrek is described as a mighty king, and Randver is named as his son.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Bikki is identified as Jormunrek’s counsellor and accompanies Randver on the journey to King Jonakr.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Swanhild, daughter of Sigurd Fafnir’s-bane, is said to be nourished at King Jonakr’s abode and is described as the fairest maiden under the sun.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Jormunrek desires Swanhild as his wife and sends Randver and Bikki to woo her from King Jonakr.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Randver agrees that it is fitting for him to go on his father’s errand.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Randver and Bikki travel to Jonakr’s abode, see Swanhild, and consider her beauty as a treasure.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Randver tells King Jonakr that Jormunrek wishes to be his brother-in-law by marrying Swanhild, claiming she should not be given to any mightier man.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"King Jonakr responds that the marriage alliance with Jormunrek is of great honor because Jormunrek is a man of fame.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gudrun comments that trust in luck is wavering and may change.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The wooing is accomplished, and Swanhild goes to the ship with a goodly company and sits in the stern beside Randver.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Bikki tells Randver it would be good and right if Randver himself had such a lovely woman as wife rather than the old king.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Randver finds Bikki’s suggestion good, speaks sweet words to Swanhild, and she replies similarly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Upon returning, Bikki reports to Jormunrek that Randver has gained Swanhild’s full love and calls her Randver’s harlot, urging the king to avenge the supposed wrong.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Jormunrek, who has often followed Bikki’s ill counsel, orders that Randver be taken and tied up to the gallows-tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"As Randver is led to the gallows, he plucks the feathers from his hawk and has it shown to his father.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Seeing the featherless hawk, Jormunrek says that his son deems his honor to be gone away from him as the feathers from the hawk, and he orders Randver to be delivered from the gallows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Before the release can be carried out, Bikki has already arranged for Randver to be slain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Bikki then tells Jormunrek he has wrongs to avenge against Swanhild and advises that she be given a shameful death; the king agrees to follow this counsel.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Swanhild is bound in the gate of the burg, and horses are driven at her to tread her down.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"When Swanhild opens her eyes wide, the horses do not dare trample her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Bikki orders that a bag be drawn over Swanhild’s head, and after this is done she loses her life.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"A note states that in the Prose Edda version, the king, returning from hunting, sees Swanhild washing linen and suddenly decides she is the cause of his woes, so he and his men ride over her and slay her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Jormunrek","description":"A mighty king who desires Swanhild as his wife, sends Randver and Bikki to An anecdote illustrates the fear of fish contamination. Traditional hunting methods are described, such as driving deer and antelope over a mesa. Several place- and gens-names are linguistically analyzed, including a saline-water locality, a possible totemic gens name, and a wood-related place-name. A large birch-tree in a legend is identified as an actual standing tree. The winter-night lodge game Ke-si-tsé (moccasin game) is described, with its use of buried moccasins, a chip representing night, guessing a hidden stone, and its associated songs and a myth about day- and night-hunting animals. Notes outline how Navahoes were once poorly clothed and fed, lacked many arts, and later acquired sheep from Spanish invaders and weaving from Pueblo tribes, as well as other useful arts from adopted outsiders. Technical clarification is given about the fibrous tissue used on bows, often miscalled sinew. The use of caves and rock-shelters as non-residential store-houses is mentioned. An alternative migration story explains the naming of a woman \"Base of Mountain\" and her descendants after a decision to follow the mountain base instead of a valley. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l4383-l4514","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XXVI. Sigurd comes to the Giukings and is wedded to Gudrun. / CHAPTER XXVII. The Wooing of Brynhild. / CHAPTER XXXII. Of the Ending of Brynhild. / CHAPTER XXXIII. Gudrun wedded to Atli.; lines 4383-4514","start":"4383","end":"4514","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"And at that feast drinks Atli his bridal with Gudrun; but never did her heart laugh on him, and little sweet and kind was their life together.\"","summary":"The passage tells how Gudrun mourns Sigurd, wanders in despair, and finds temporary refuge in King Alf's hall in Denmark, where needlework partly soothes her grief. Learning of her whereabouts, Grimhild and her sons organize a splendidly armed embassy to atone for Sigurd's killing, offering gold and using a powerful, rune-marked drink that makes Gudrun forget their guilt. Reconciled in feeling by the potion, Gudrun is pressed by Grimhild to marry the mighty king Atli; though Gudrun foresees evil and yields only under compulsion, the marriage is agreed. Gudrun is then brought with great ceremony to Atli's high-built hall, where they celebrate their bridal feast, yet her heart never rejoices in him and their life together is unhappy.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Listeners say that no one like Sigurd remains in the world and that his name will never diminish in the North while the world stands.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Gudrun says life was better when she had Sigurd, whom she compares to gold over iron, leek over other grass, and hart over other wild things.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Gudrun says her brothers begrudged her Sigurd and could not sleep until they had slain him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When Grani saw Sigurd sore wounded he made huge clamour, then drooped down to the earth because he knew Sigurd was slain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Gudrun says she spoke to Grani as if speaking with a man when she saw his grief for Sigurd.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Gudrun goes into the wild woods, hears wolves howling all around, and deems death merrier than life.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gudrun comes to King Alf's hall in Denmark and stays there with Thora, Hakon's daughter, for seven seasons with good welcome.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Gudrun sets forth her needlework, embroidering swords, byrnies, royal gear, King Sigmund's ship sailing along the land, and the fight of Sigar and Siggeir south in Fion.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The needlework and her stay in Denmark somewhat solace Gudrun of her grief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Grimhild learns where Gudrun dwells, calls her sons to talk, and asks if they will make atonement to Gudrun for her son and her husband, saying it is meet and right.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Gunnar says he will atone for Gudrun's sorrows with gold.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Grimhild and her sons send for their friends, array horses, helms, shields, byrnies, and war-gear, and set out on their journey with no great champion staying home; their horses wear mail-coats and helms are adorned with gold or silver.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Grimhild accompanies the journey, saying their errand would not be fairly brought to pass if she sat at home.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"About five hundred noble men ride with them, including Waldemar of Denmark, Eymod, and Jarisleif; in King Alf's hall they are awaited by Longbeards, Franks, and Saxons wearing war-gear and red fur-coats, as described in a song.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Gudrun's kinsmen choose good gifts for her and speak softly, but she trusts none of them.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Gunnar brings Gudrun a drink mingled with hurtful things which she is compelled to drink; after drinking she no longer remembers their guilt against her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The horn that holds the drink has all kinds of letters cut on its surface and reddened with blood.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The drink is described as beer in which are mingled many ills, including a ling-fish, wheat-ears, wild beasts' inwards, blood of all the wood, brown-burnt acorns, black dew of the hearth, god-doomed dead beast's inwards, and sodden swine's liver.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"After Gudrun drinks, their hearts are brought near to each other and they make great cheer.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Grimhild greets Gudrun, offering her gold, dear-bought rings, and bed-gear of the maids of the Huns, saying Sigurd is thus atoned for and that Gudrun shall be given to Atli the mighty king to be mistress of all his might; she urges Gudrun not to cast her friends aside for one man's sake.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Gudrun answers that she will never wed Atli the King and calls it unseemly for them to have offspring between them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Grimhild tells Gudrun not to nourish her wrath and promises it will be to her as if Sigurd and Sigmund were alive when she has borne sons.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Gudrun says she cannot take her heart from thoughts of Sigurd, whom she calls the first of all men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Grimhild says it is shaped that Gudrun must have this king and none else.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Gudrun warns that if she is given to Atli, evil will come upon Grimhild's kin from him, that Atli will deal evil to his own sons, and that he will be repaid with a grim revenge.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Grimhild becomes fierce at Gudrun's words and bids her obey, promising great honour, friendship, and the steads called Vinbjorg and Valbjorg.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"The narrative states that such might was in Grimhild's words content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l151-l218","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"WITH EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA / SELECTED BIBLIOGRAPHY: / RECOMMENDED READING-- / INTRODUCTION; lines 151-218","start":"151","end":"218","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage is a historical-literary overview of Scandinavian expansion and Viking activity. It describes how Scando-Gothic peoples moved south and west over Europe, clashing with Greeks and Romans and founding kingdoms, until their landward advance was checked in Charlemagne’s time. With southern land routes closed, the Viking Age begins: for over two centuries Vikings raid by sea, circling the Western Isles, invading Normandy, harrying the coasts of France, England, and Ireland, and exacting tribute from closely related Anglo-Saxons. In Ireland, amid the breakdown of older civilization, Vikings found kingdoms at Limerick and Dublin; Olaf the White, first king of Dublin, is said to descend from Sigurd the Volsung, and the kingdom persists until the English invasion, when it is taken by other men of Viking stock. A long citation from the anonymous \"Wars of the Gaedhil with the Gaill\" describes, in highly rhetorical terms, the extreme suffering of the Gaedhil at Viking hands and emphasizes the invaders’ superior arms and armor and their hunger for the rich, river-filled land of Erinn. The editor notes that this picture is exaggerated, meant to magnify the enemy in order to glorify the chronicler’s own people, the Dal Cais, who under Brian Boroimhe checked the Northmen’s inroads. The passage then mentions Viking earldoms in the Orkneys, Faroes, and Shetlands, and gives an example of Earl Sweyn Asleifsson of Orkney, who into the late 12th century followed a regular yearly pattern: intensive spring farming and sowing, followed by a \"spring-viking\" raiding voyage, a return for harvest and storage of grain, and then an \"autumn-viking\" voyage lasting until just before winter.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Scando-Gothic peoples migrated southward and westward over Europe, shaking empires and founding kingdoms.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The northward incursions continued until the landward march of the Northmen was stopped by their own kin in the time of Charlemagne, closing their southern road by land.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After their land route south was closed, a period began in which Vikings, under many brave leaders, conducted widespread sea-raiding and for over two hundred years \"held the world at ransom.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Vikings sailed around the Western Isles, invaded Normandy, harried the coasts of France, and eventually appeared on most shores of the known world.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Vikings exacted tribute from the Anglo-Saxons, who were said to be closely related to content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l3280-l3394","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE POOR TURKEY GIRL / HOW THE SUMMER BIRDS CAME / THE SERPENT OF THE SEA / THE MAIDEN OF THE YELLOW ROCKS; lines 3280-3394","start":"3280","end":"3394","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In ancient times, when several ancestral villages were inhabited, a very beautiful maiden, daughter of the high priest in the Village of the Yellow Rocks, was born with magical knowledge of hunting and of all game animals. Selfishly deciding to keep this power for herself, she used her understanding of the animals’ habits and language to charm and gather deer, antelope, rabbits, and other wild game into a huge corral she built on a nearby mountain marked with ancient deer carvings. As a result, the hunters of the surrounding villages could find no game and returned empty-handed, while the maiden’s family always had ample meat and buckskins. Many young men desired her; the first to act was a youth from the Village of the Winds. Declaring to his parents that he was going courting, he prepared a bundle of fine women’s garments and ornaments and traveled to Yellow Rocks. He identified the maiden’s house by its beauty and distinctive sacred ladder: a carved cross-piece hung with a fringe of black hair and hollow stalactites from a sacred cave on the Colorado Chiquito, which tinkled like bells when the wind blew or the ladder was touched. As the youth climbed, the bells sounded and the people inside announced a visitor’s arrival. He used the formulaic phrase ‘Draw me in,’ indicating he had brought a gift bundle, which the maiden took and dropped inside, signaling his courtship intent. That night, by the fireplace, the high priest asked his purpose, and the youth declared his wish to rest his thoughts and hopes on the maiden. She served him food and took a few bites herself, a customary sign of favorable disposition, though the narration notes her seeming acceptance did not match her true feelings. The father then gave them his blessing and sacred speech and formally adopted the youth as his child—explained as the entirety of the marriage ceremony. Later, the father noted the son’s long journey and weariness. The maiden led the youth to an upper chamber but told him he was not yet her husband; she wished to test him. She instructed him to rise early, when deer were most plentiful, go out and kill a fine deer for her, and only then would they commit their thoughts and hopes to one another for life.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The story is set 'in the days of the ancients' when several villages, including the Village of the Yellow Rocks, Salt City, Village of the Winds, Village of the White Flowering Herbs, and Village of Odd Waters, were inhabited.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the Village of the Yellow Rocks lived a very beautiful maiden who was the daughter of the high priest.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The maiden was endowed by birth with magic knowledge of the hunt and knowledge of all the game animals that sustain humans.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The text notes that, although she was a woman, she possessed this extraordinary hunting knowledge.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The maiden was selfish and decided that, since she possessed this knowledge above all others, she would keep all the game animals to herself.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Using her knowledge of the animals’ habits and language, the maiden communicated with and charmed the game animals.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On the top of a mountain, where ancient figures of deer are cut in the rock, the maiden built a huge corral.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The maiden gathered into this corral all the deer, antelope, and other wild animals of the surrounding country.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hunters from the various villages trailed deer and antelope but always lost the trails and returned with no game.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The maiden and her family always had plenty of meat and buckskins for clothing, while other people lacked meat and wore out One poor young hunter fails her test. The situation becomes notorious, and two small gods who live with their grandmother on Thunder Mountain, at the site of a sacrificial altar, decide to court the maiden themselves. Outwardly ugly, childish pigmies yet inwardly magnificent shapeshifters, they defy their grandmother’s scolding and prepare to visit the maiden. After discarding a bundle of worthless objects meant as a gift, they kill and string many wood-rats as a present, while considering the needs of their ‘children’ in the nearby villages. Reaching white cliffs opposite the maiden’s village at noon, they wait until evening because the elder god insists it is improper to court before night, while the younger is impatient. Near dark they approach the village, identify the maiden’s house by its tall ladder with bells, and climb up cautiously. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l3396-l3520","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE POOR TURKEY GIRL / HOW THE SUMMER BIRDS CAME / THE SERPENT OF THE SEA / THE MAIDEN OF THE YELLOW ROCKS; lines 3396-3520","start":"3396","end":"3520","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A maiden who secretly controls a herd of deer via a river path tests would‑be husbands by requiring them to bring her game. The first suitor spends the day hunting in the forests and mountains but finds no deer while the maiden checks her hidden deer corral, and she sends him away when he returns empty‑handed. The next day a wealthy, conceited young man named Hálona arrives with a heavy bundle of gifts and is welcomed by the maiden’s father as a prospective son‑in‑law. At night the maiden tells him she will only accept a husband who proves himself a good hunter by bringing back deer or an antelope. Though he rises eagerly at dawn, calling the Sun his father, and hunts along the river, he too finds no game while the maiden again guards her deer upriver, and she dismisses him as a suitor. A third young man from the City of Salt, hearing that many suitors are turned away, prepares even more gifts and sets out to court her.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A youth staying with the maiden agrees to her condition, sleeps, then rises early; she gives him food and he goes into the forests and mountains with bow and arrows to hunt deer, following a strong track that disappears so that he finds no game.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"While the first young man is out hunting, the maiden goes into the river and follows it against the current beyond the village, past marked rocks and up a canyon to where her deer are gathered, to make sure none of them get out.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The deer in the maiden’s corral up the canyon are described as peaceful and contented.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The narrative states that there were no tracks of the girl when she went to the deer corral, so no one could follow where she went.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After hunting all day and finding no game, the first young man returns at night tired and hungry; the maiden asks about his luck, and when he says he found no game she tells him they cannot rest their thoughts and hopes on each other for life, returns his bundle, and he goes home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The next day a young man named Hálona hears what happened, calls the first suitor a fool for not taking enough presents to please the maiden, and says he will take a bundle that will make things right; he is described as very conceited.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hálona, who is wealthy, fills a very heavy bundle with everything a woman could reasonably want, puts on his best clothes, paints his face, and sets out for the maiden’s home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On arriving, Hálona’s foot touches the lowermost rung of a ladder; stalactites above jingle as he climbs, and his heavy bundle lands on the roof with a thud, prompting people below to remark that somebody has come.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The maiden acknowledges the visitor, pulls the huge bundle into the room from above, places it on the floor, and the young man follows it down into the house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"An old man sitting by the fire greets the visitor, comments that strangers do not come to another’s house without thoughts, and asks what he is thinking.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Hálona silently admires the maiden as a magnificent creature and assumes she will become his wife, then tells the old man aloud that he came thinking of the daughter and wishes to rest his hopes and thoughts on her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The old man explains that it is the custom of their people, and of all people, that young men and maidens marry and establish themselves in houses so they may possess dignity and be heads of households; he says he has no objection and asks his daughter, who also says she has no objection, and the suitor eats his meal with satisfaction.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After the meal the father lays out corn-husks and tobacco and they smoke together; he then refers to the stranger as his son and tells his daughter that the visitor has come a long way and should not be kept sitting up late.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The daughter leads Hálona to another room while he thinks about how gentle she is and how softly she steps up the ladder.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"At the doorway the maiden says they will say good-night there; when Hálona asks what is the matter, she explains that she wishes to know of her husband at least that he is a good hunter who can provide food and buckskins, and therefore asks him to go out in the morning and hunt deer or bring her an antelope; he agrees and lies down to rest.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The next morning Hálona cannot wait for daylight and wants the Sun, called his father, to rise before its time; when the Sun rises he jumps out of bed, straps on his quiver, takes his bow and a small luncheon the maiden has prepared, and starts off while she watches from the top of the house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"As Hálona goes down the river and sees the maiden watching from the rooftop, he runs until he is out of sight to show how fine a runner and good hunter he is, since he is reputed to be strong and active; he hunts repeatedly but finds no deer or even tracks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Meanwhile the maiden goes up the stream as before to watch over the corral where her deer are gathered; Hálona’s experience matches that of the first young man, and he returns at night without game, though he is less downcast because he is more self-reliant.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"When Hálona returns, the maiden asks whether he has any deer; he answers no, and she says that under the circumstances she does not see how they can become husband and wife, so he carries his bundle home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The next day a young man in the City of Salt hears that day after day young men go to court the maiden and she turns them all away; he assumes they did not take enough with them, so he makes up two bundles and goes to her home, telling himself that this time it will be all right.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The old man is explicitly identified as the maiden’s father and refers to the visiting suitor as \"now my son\" after accepting him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The maiden and each suitor speak in terms of becoming husband and wife, but she rejects those who return without game despite earlier indications that she and her father had no objection to the match.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:7","ev:9","ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Hálona refers to the Sun as \"his father\" when impatiently waiting for dawn.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Maiden with secret deer corral","description":"Young woman who owns or controls a herd of deer kept in a secluded corral reached by following the river against the current; she is being courted by many young men and sets conditions for marriage.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:7","ev:9","ev:12","ev:13","ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"First unnamed young man (first suitor)","description":"A youth who stays with the maiden, hunts for deer in the forests and mountains without success, and is sent away when he returns without game.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Hálona (second suitor)","description":"A wealthy and conceited young man who believes gifts will win the maiden; he brings a heavy bundle of presents, is initially accepted as a potential husband, but fails the hunting test and is rejected.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Old man, father of the maiden","description":"Household elder who sits by the fire, questions the visiting suitor, explains marriage customs, agrees to the match, and refers to the suitor as his son.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Household people below","description":"Unspecified people inside the house who hear the noise of Hálona’s arrival and note that somebody has come.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Young man from the City of Salt (third suitor)","description":"A young man living in the City of Salt who hears that the maiden rejects many suitors, concludes they did not bring enough gifts, prepares two bundles, and goes to court her.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Sun","description":"The Sun, which Hálona impatiently wishes to rise and which is referred to as his father when he prepares to go hunting.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Keeper of secret deer herd","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The maiden goes by a hidden route up the river to a canyon where her deer are gathered and ensures none of them escape.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:12"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Potential bride and test-giver","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"She is courted by young men, discusses the possibility of marriage, and sets the condition that any husband must prove himself a good hunter by bringing back deer or antelope.","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:7","ev:9","ev:13","ev:14"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"First suitor and unsuccessful hunter","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"The first unnamed youth stays with the maiden, hunts at her request, fails to find game, and is dismissed as a potential husband.","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"Second suitor Hálona, wealthy but content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l2555-l2682","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE TRIAL OF LOVERS: / THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE / THE POOR TURKEY GIRL / HOW THE SUMMER BIRDS CAME; lines 2555-2682","start":"2555","end":"2682","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After a giant is slain, his many little Top-knots gather to devour his body and only realize he is their father when they reach the top-knot on his head. The boy cuts out the giant’s heart, carries it, then descends to the young Top-knots and kills all but two. Taking the two surviving, childlike Top-knots, he wrings the neck of one and throws it into the air, where it becomes a falcon-like bird; he swings the other and throws it so that it becomes an owl. He declares that though born for evil, they are changed for good and will become the means for his descendants to sacrifice to the gods. He returns home at dusk, hangs the giant’s heart on the cross-piece of the ladder beside other hearts, and is scolded by his worried mother, who knows he has gone to the forbidden dangerous place. He presses her to reveal whether any other terrible creatures exist. After denying it repeatedly, she finally tells him of Awiteli Wakashi, a fearsome four-fold Elk or Bison who lives near the little Cold-making Hill, so huge and violent that people avoid traveling through that region. Though he promises not to go, the next morning the boy sets out even earlier with his bow and arrows, crying and sniffling on the trail as if in fear. Near the hole of his grandfather, an old Gopher, the animal hears the weeping, recognizes his grandson, enlarges his tunnel, and invites the boy inside. The boy admits he wanted to see and even kill the four-fold Bison but is frightened. The Gopher offers help, telling him not to attempt it alone, then digs a long underground tunnel towards the beast, packing it firmly. Reaching the area near the Bison’s heart, he hears its heartbeat, sees the long hair that would stop arrows, and cuts the hair away to reveal a light patch of bare skin. He returns and instructs the boy to crawl through the tunnel, shoot the exposed patch above the heart, then turn and run back as fast as possible, diving into the Gopher’s hole. The boy obeys: he crawls to the upward turn, sees the light patch, looses an arrow, and flees. The four-fold Bison roars, collapses, then rises, snorting and bellowing, and rips the tunnel open with its horn like a flash of fire just as the boy tumbles into his grandfather’s deeper hole. The Gopher exclaims that the monster nearly caught him but reassures the boy and goes to see whether the Bison is dead.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the Giant falls, numerous little Top-knots gather around his body and voraciously eat it until reaching the top-knot on his head, when one cries out that the corpse is their own father.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"While the young Top-knots are still crying, the boy cuts out the Giant’s heart, slings it over his shoulder, and climbs down the cliff toward them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The boy kills all of the young Top-knots except for two that are described as still young, like little children.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boy grasps one of the two surviving young Top-knots by the throat, wrings its neck, and throws it into the air, where it becomes a winged creature that flies away crying “Peep, peep, peep,” like the falcons of today.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The boy swings the second surviving Top-knot around by the neck and flings it into the air, and it flies away heavily, crying “Boohoo, boohoo, boohoo,” becoming an owl.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The boy says of the transformed creatures that they were born for evil but changed for good, and declares that they shall be the means by which future children will sacrifice to the gods.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After returning home, the boy hangs the Giant’s heart on the cross-piece of the ladder beside other hearts already hanging there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The boy’s mother, troubled by his late return, scolds him and asserts that he went to the dangerous place she had mentioned, which he admits.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The boy repeatedly asks his mother whether there is any other terrible creature; she initially denies this, but after he persists, she reveals the existence of a fearful four-fold Elk or Bison named Awiteli Wakashi living near the little Cold-making Hill and frightening travelers away from that region.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Although he tells his mother he will not go, the next morning the boy sets out even earlier than before, carrying his bows and arrows toward the four-fold Bison.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"As he walks along the trail, the boy cries and snivels, moving slowly as if filled with dread, until he nears the hole of his grandfather, an old Gopher who is digging and hears the crying.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Gopher recognizes the crying as his grandson’s, emerges partway from the hole he is digging, calls the boy, enlarges the hole when the boy puts his foot in, and invites him down inside.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Inside the hole, the Gopher tells the boy to dry his eyes and asks what is wrong; the boy explains that he was going to look for the four-fold Bison and even thought of trying to kill it but became frightened.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Gopher offers to help and digs a long underground tunnel toward the Bison, carefully packing the top and sides so the tunnel will not collapse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Following the sound of the creature’s heartbeat, the Gopher reaches the area near the four-fold Bison, sees the long hair covering its body where arrows cannot penetrate, and cuts the hair off until the white skin shows.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Gopher returns and instructs the boy to crawl through the tunnel until it turns upward, to look for the light patch of exposed skin over the Bison’s heart, to shoot exactly in the middle of that spot, and then to run back and tumble into the Gopher’s hole as quickly as possible.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The boy follows the Gopher’s instructions: he crawls through the tunnel, finds the light patch where the hair has been cut away, shoots an arrow at it with all his might, and then runs back through the tunnel.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The four-fold Bison roars with a into his grandfather’s deeper hole.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Gopher exclaims that the monster almost caught the boy, tells him to rest, and goes to He is to place sweetened meal of parched corn, plumed prayer-sticks, and sacred corn pollen inside, then seal himself within so his people can roll the log into a great river. Traveling within this log, he will meet strange beings, choose a companion, and proceed to the great mountain where the Sun enters. The Deer-being vanishes and the youth returns home. His sister anxiously waits for him at sunset, then serves him food; at his request she summons their father. The young man recounts his encounter with the magnificently dressed Deer-being, and the father declares that, since the Sun-father has directed the Deer-being, the instructions must be followed. The father orders the Priest of the Bow to inform the elders and priests that their strong-handed deer hunter will go to the Sunset world to greet the Sun-father, and that they must gather at the sacred houses with prayer-sticks, twine, feathers, plumes, and treasures for the Sun-father, Moon-mother, Great Ocean, and Prey-beings. The next day the people work in the kiwetsiwe and sacred houses making prayer-plumes, while the sister and her relatives prepare sweet parched cornmeal and gather pollen. By evening preparations are complete. The young man calls his relatives, chooses four uncles to accompany him, prepares a bundle of cotton, a large sack of sweet meal, and small sacks of sacred red and black warrior paints, then bids farewell to his lamenting people and rests. The next morning, escorted by priests, he leaves town in embroidered white cotton garments, carrying plumes, and travels with his four uncles over the mountains. On the third day they reach a forest by a great river and camp. The young man goes alone into the forest, selects the greatest tree, cuts it down over two days with his large flint knife, finds it partly hollow, and completes the hollowing, making the round door and top hole, padding the interior thickly with cotton and placing his food and plumes inside. He then calls his uncles, explains that he is to journey in this hollow log to the western home of the Sun-father, and instructs them that once he has sealed the door and plug they must, without thinking of him, roll the log to the river’s high bank and push it into the water. To rid herself of both kinds of "pests," she announces that she will marry and cherish any man who can drive away the corn‑eating animals so they never return. Many young men attempt this but fail, and the offer becomes widely known.

A very poor and extremely ugly young man from an outer town, mocked by women but possessing bright twinkling eyes, hears of the offer. Though he has no gift to present, he admires the girl deeply and visits her house in the evening. He is politely received; she serves him bread and her father smokes with him. When questioned, the young man admits he wishes to be accepted as a suitor. The father refers the decision to the girl, who agrees she would be satisfied, but privately explains that he must first rid her cornfields of the pests forever. He says he will try, though it is difficult, and she replies that this is why she asks it.

The next day he goes quietly to her cornfields near the northern mesa. Using a sharp stick and a bone shovel, he digs a deep pit with smooth sides, lays poles from the mountain across the opening, covers them with earth, replaces corn‑stalks so the ground looks undisturbed, and spreads highly tempting bait over the weakly supported center.

At night, coyotes begin to sing and a whole host of animal pests—Bears, Badgers, Gophers, and others—comes slowly down from the mountain into the field. Swift Coyotes arrive first. One Coyote, sniffing around and watching for danger, discovers the bait, leaps toward it, and crashes through the flimsy covering into the pit, landing at the bottom with sticks, dirt, and bait. The boy repeatedly asks to live apart from his parents so he can travel and hunt freely. Though they consider him careless and forgetful, they eventually consent on condition that his younger sister, Waíasialuhtitsa, live with him to keep house and remind him of his duties. The siblings move into lofty rooms in the upper pueblo. Heásailuhtiwa hunts daily and always brings back game, which his sister cooks, but he never sacrifices to the Deer he kills or to the Gods of Prey who aid hunters; he is described as forgetful and careless. One day he travels north over a mountain to the Waters of the Bear, startles a great buck, and follows its trail far north past mesas and mountains until he reaches a great river flowing west. The deer’s tracks lead into cottonwood thickets toward the river. Thinking he sees the deer beneath a large tree, he circles to approach between the river and the thicket. There he finds instead a richly dressed, handsome young man under the tree, who greets him and questions him. When the boy explains he is following a deer’s tracks from the Waters of the Bear, the stranger points out that the tracks lead to him and reveals, “I am the Deer,” explaining that he lured the boy there. The Deer-being rebukes him for repeatedly killing his ‘children’ and eating their flesh without ever providing offerings to comfort their souls, despite his good fortune in hunting. He says Sun-father has heard the deer’s supplications and ordered that the boy be brought there and commanded to visit Sun-father in his house at the western end of the world. The Deer-being instructs the youth to hurry home, tell his priest-chief father to summon the Priest of the Bow (Pithlan Shíwani) and his children to the rooms of sacred things, and prepare plumed prayer-sticks for Sun-father, Moon-mother, and the Great Ocean, as well as red plumes of sacrifice for the Beings of Prey, so that the boy can bring these as payment for his forgetfulness and carelessness when he visits Sun-father’s home. He further tells the boy to have his sister prepare sweetened parched cornmeal and corn pollen for his journey and his mother to prepare much new cotton, to bundle these, summon some relatives, and return to the same tree on the fourth day. He asks whether the boy has flint knives, and the boy answers that his father has many. The youth and the dogs then attack, mauling and clubbing the warriors until the whole band is killed or mortally wounded. The youth leisurely scalps the fallen, gathering a long, heavy string of scalps, then departs over the hills with his provisions and trophies, followed by some dogs while others stay behind to feed on the corpses. Reaching a great spring by the Black Mountains, the youth and his dogs build a fire, cook his provisions, and he thanks the dogs as his friends and brothers, feeding them grease-cakes and other delicacies he had set aside as their reward. Afterward he ties the scalps to a long pole, carries it over his shoulder, and walks toward Moki singing a song of victory. The dogs, glutted and excited, run around him calling him father, but the short-legged beagle dogs fall behind, so the swifter dogs ask the youth to slow down for their tired brothers, and they all reduce their pace. In Moki, people are puzzled by the disappearance of almost all their dogs and suspect devils or wizards, until near evening they hear the uproar of returning dogs and the youth’s victory song. Looking down from the mesa, they see all the dogs covered in blood and dirt and are unsure what has happened until they recognize the tall, lank vagabond youth among them. The young men previously rejected by a certain beautiful maiden react with shame and anger, while the elder men, recognizing the great valor of the once-neglected youth, answer his song with songs of victory and convene a solemn council to receive him as an honored guest. The narrative describes him as an outcast youth who went to Zuñi and returned as the hero of the Moki nation. After ceremonies of initiation and purification are performed over him, the beautiful maiden willingly accepts him as her husband. This newfound praise of someone formerly despised, and especially his possession of such a wife, arouses intense jealousy among many jilted lovers who unite in the common cause of undoing him. Other pretty maidens imitate their ‘lucky sister’ and declare they will marry no one who does not prove at least somewhat heroic like the youth from the dog-holes, so that the young men of Moki become Long ago, a village of Prairie-dogs lived in this basin in fairly peaceful relations with Rattlesnakes, Adders, Chameleons, Horned-toads, and especially Burrowing-owls, whom they regarded as grave and sacred and whose ceremonies they never disturbed. One morning the Burrowing-owls hold an elaborate Foam-dance, each dancer balancing a bowl of foam on the head while dancing with crooked legs in unison without spilling any. A Coyote, out hunting near the Prairie-dog town and living with his old grandmother among rocks to the west, hears the owls’ music and song, approaches, and watches with great curiosity. He politely greets the old Owl who serves as master of ceremonies and asks about the dance. The Owl explains that it is a very sacred performance of a sacred society whose initiated members can do strange things. He tells Coyote that what looks like foam is actually the dancers’ grandmothers’ heads, and that their limp comes from having their legs broken, which brings them good luck and lets them perform a unique dance. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l11522-l11650","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA / THE TALE; lines 11522-11650","start":"11522","end":"11650","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The divine twins Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, described as chief gods under the Sun who delight in conflict and deathly scenes, are sitting by a deep pool when they hear troubling sounds from below. The younger twin identifies the disturbance as war-cries and wails of people in the Underworld and urges that they descend to investigate. They invert their magical cord-shields, cover their heads, close their eyes, and step into the pool, using darkness and their special thought-magic to travel dry through the waters down to an Underworld village. There they first smell decay and assume the inhabitants are dead, but then realize the odor comes from cooked food that has been discarded. Hiding to watch, they see the Underworld people place fine, steaming food in low trenchers and gather only to inhale the steam and savor while carefully avoiding touching the food itself, as if it were refuse. The elder twin infers that such beings, who feed on savor, will be especially sensitive to faint sounds, and even demons would not know how to fight them. The Underworld people nonetheless detect the twins, raise a war alarm, rush out like swarming ants, and pursue the intruders with a war-cry song. The twins laugh, shoot arrows through the crowd, and find that the arrows pass through the Underworld people without felling anyone, to the elder twin’s surprise. Editorial notes explain the twins’ status as the Sun’s right- and left-hand gods of war and games, the cloud-spun nature of their shields within a layered cosmos supported by waters and clouds, the etymology of an exclamation involving death, and the jargonistic, possibly borrowed nature of the war-cry The Horned-toad finally hooks a horn into Coyote’s heart, killing him, then exits the body and goes to the nearest water-pocket. After the surrounding water recedes they bury her in front of the door. Within four days a strange plant grows from the burial spot, bearing bright green leaves and long red pods. The boys interpret the plant as springing from their grandmother’s heart and carrying the color and fiery quality of her scolding tongue. They decide to scatter the seeds so men may find and plant them, saying that although they have lost their beloved grandmother, people have gained a new burning but pleasing food—peppers—whose seeds first arose from the fiery heart of the grandmother of Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma. They crush the pods, delight in their pungent odor, scatter the seeds, and some take root; humans later find the plants, esteem them as food, and cultivate them, including in the pepper gardens of Zuni. The mountain where the gods lived with their grandmother is thereafter called Thunder Mountain and is associated with frequent lightning, thunder, and rain. A variant report says that when the boys were asked how they stole the lightning-shaft and thunder-stone, they blamed their grandfather, the Centipede. The beloved Gods of the Rain then gave him the lightning-shaft to handle differently, and it burned and shriveled him so that he became small and fringed, explaining the appearance of centipedes today. A new story is then introduced: the tale of the Twins of War and Chance, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, and their dealings with the unborn-made men of the Underworld. The translator explains his editorial choices, references an essay on Zuni Creation Myths, and introduces Waíhusiwa, a priestly Zuni storyteller who has already told many tales of the four directions, the Above, the World-embracing Waters, a youth and his eagle in the Sky-world, and a hunter who married a Serpent-maiden and went to the Mountain of Sunset. Prompted by the elder Pálowahtiwa, Waíhusiwa agrees to tell a story of the Underworld about people who cannot digest because they lack proper insides, after a formal call-and-response opening. The Zuni introduction then describes the Underworld as containing villages of \"unborn-made\" people, beings between the living and the dead, likened to smoke, mist, and stages of corn, partly embodied yet unfinished and unfixed, contrasted with the dead who are like the wind and can take form by their own wills.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Crows rush in and flap against a light, fail to extinguish it, grow blacker and blacker, and thus become as black as present-day crows; eagles become speckled with brown and black.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In the Sacred Drama Dance, old Mítsina streaming.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A new tale is titled \"HOW THE TWINS OF WAR AND CHANCE, ÁHAIYÚTA AND MÁTSAILÉMA, FARED WITH THE UNBORN-MADE MEN OF THE UNDERWORLD,\" and is noted as reprinted from the Journal of American Folk-Lore.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The translator states he had withheld single relation to dance and dramaturgic ceremonies.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Waíhusiwa, of the priestly kin of Zuni, is identified as one of the translator’s chief corn.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"These \"unborn-made\" people are said to be \"dead in a way\" because they have not yet begun to live as surface people content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l12126-l12242","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE TALE / THE COCK AND THE MOUSE / ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER; lines 12126-12242","start":"12126","end":"12242","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The translator describes towering stone pillars in Southwestern canyons that resemble giants with their young, which in moonlight and mist seem to move and to drink clouds. He notes that the Zuñi tell etiological stories about such rocks from a creation time when all things were soft, and that the following legend explains the great rock column known as “El Capitan” in Cañon de Chelly. The story introduces Häki Suto (Foretop Knot), a giant Cloud-swallower who devours men and drinks the cloud-breaths of gods and the souls of the dead from which rains descend, causing snow, rain, mists, and waters to vanish so that corn withers and people starve. After many failed attempts by human heroes, the Twin Gods of War, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, decide to destroy him; on their way they meet their tiny grandmother, Spider (Spinner of Meshes), who knows the monster’s habits and plans to sew his eyes shut with down-cords. She runs ahead to where Häki Suto lies across the cliff-trail like a fallen tree, pretending to be old and rheumatic and politely inviting travellers to pass under his legs so that he can seize them and hurl them over the cliff to feed his young Forehead-cresters.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In Southwestern canyons there are It introduces the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, small immortal youths living with their grandmother on Twin Mountain, who keep a large turkey flock. At their grandmother’s urging they reluctantly release the turkeys to feed, and the birds wander beyond the woods toward Háwikuh. The flock enters a valley north of Háwikuh where villagers have cornfields; young men resting from hoeing hear and see the unusually large flock, run to the pueblo calling out their discovery, and inform the Priests of the Bow. The priests climb to the house-tops and summon the people to arm themselves with bows, arrows, boomerangs, and strings to hunt the turkeys and increase their own flocks and plumes, and the people rush The elder uses a war-club and the younger uses plume-grass to defeat their pursuers, who are easily felled and terrified even by grass. The twins rebuke them and demand food, then eat in a shocking, voracious way that makes the people physically ill and afraid that such eating will be fatal. When a puff of wind is interpreted as the gods shooting arrows, the twins decide the people must be hardened and taught to eat, then fall asleep. The people, thinking them dead, try to remove their bodies as dangerous refuse; the twins feign death and then suddenly rise, terrifying the villagers, who see the supposedly dead come back to life. A flock of deadly jays arrives; their mere landing kills the people, who flee in panic. The twins snare, kill, roast, and eat the jays, impressing and frightening the villagers, who then grant them lodging. The next day a boiling cooking-pot with onion earrings chases and kills people with splattering mush. The narrator explains that the harsh onion symbolizes the vigor and invincibility of the twin gods. The twins deride the idea of fearing food, eat the onion earrings and the mush, and kick the lethal pot to
