content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l12521-l12636","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 12521-12636","start":"12521","end":"12636","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The Eagle tells the priest-chief’s daughter to bathe at dawn, don her finest clothes, and be ready when the ceremonial dance appears four times; then he will carry her on his back to the Sun, who awaits them, though the journey may prove fatal. That night she gathers the basket-trays she made for her father’s sacred plumes and, by firelight, divides them by color among the six world regions (north, west, south, east, upper, lower). She tells her priest-chief father he will see her no more, and he accepts this as the will of the gods. As morning nears she bathes, sleeps while the Eagle watches, and is awakened when the great star rises, heralding the Sun. Outside, two war-priests call the people to prepare and eat for the dance. The girl dresses in many garments and four white mantles, then brings out bowls of finely ground cornmeal in six colors. Addressing \"my children,\" she explains that these meals will beautify and protect them and guide their life-paths, and leaves them as an inheritance before departing for an unknown region where she may live or die. When the drum sounds for the first appearance of the dance, the Eagle has her lie lengthwise on his back, gripping his shoulders and bracing her feet on his thighs, then flies with her up through the roof opening into the sky. As the dancers below come and go, the Eagle and maiden circle high above, unseen. She asks him to slow so she can sing a farewell song to her earthly children; the people in the plaza hear it, lament her departure, and rebuke the two gods leading the dance for letting her escape. Some remember the song, others do not. On the third emergence of the dancers, the gods ask where the pair are, and the people answer that they are in mid-heaven, nearing the home of the Sun-father. The Eagle encourages the girl that with one more emergence they may reach their father’s home, while dancers below move ever more vigorously, some ignoring the people’s complaints. At the fourth and final emergence, the two gods lead the dance with faces blackened in war paint and with bows and arrows ready to slay the priest-chief’s daughter, but when they reach the plaza center the people point out that she and the Eagle are already high in the sky, almost at the Sun’s content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l9956-l10077","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 9956-10077","start":"9956","end":"10077","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage closes an earlier tale by explaining how events involving Áhaiyúta, Mátsailéma, their grandmother, and their grandfathers the Rainbow-worm and old Turtle Etawa account for the present small size of rainbow-worms and of local turtles, and the marked shells and larger size of distant turtles. A new story then begins: in K’iákime, the handsome young son of the priest-chief runs around Thunder Mountain each pre-dawn in elaborate dance regalia before praying. An old Tarantula living in a den at the mountain’s base covets his fine apparel, lures him into exchanging clothes under the pretense of letting him see how handsome he looks, dresses in the youth’s garments, backs to the lip of his den while asking how he looks, and finally dives into his hole with the clothing. The young man, forced to don the Tarantula’s ugly garments, returns home late and tells his worried elders and father what happened.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma are said to have an old grandmother and two grandfathers: the Rainbow-worm and the old Turtle.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Because their great-grandfather Rainbow-worm blew all his substance away at the Háwikuhkwe, present-day rainbow-worms are described as being no bigger than a finger.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Great turtles in the far-away Waters of the World are said to be larger than turtles living \"here\" and to have many marks on their shells where arrows once glanced off the shield of their great-grandfather.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Old Turtle Etawa, after serving as a great master of ceremonies, became proud, despised his old pond, and left to seek a new home in the Western Waters of the World.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After Etawa left, his grandchildren and their descendants living \"here\" are said never to have grown any larger and to remain small.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In K’iákime, a handsome young man, son of the town’s priest-chief, regularly dresses as for a dance and runs entirely around Thunder Mountain each morning before sunrise, before saying his prayers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The young man’s costume includes painted red and green moccasins, white leggings with fringes like those of a Master of Dances, embroidered white cotton skirt, mantle, and coat, sacred white shell anklets, long blue turquoise earrings, a multicolored headband, and blue, red, and yellow macaw feathers in his hair.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"At the southeastern end of Thunder Mountain stand two broad rock columns called Ak’yapaatch-ella, and beneath them in the base of the mountain an old Tarantula has his den.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Each morning as the young man runs past in his fine dress, the old Tarantula hears the horn-bells attached to the youth’s belt and sees him pass.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Tarantula covets the young man’s fine apparel, thinking how fortunate it would be to obtain it, and decides to wait for him the next time he passes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"On the next morning at sunrise, the Tarantula thrusts his head out of his den, calls out to the young man to stop despite his saying he is in a hurry, and insists that he come over.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Tarantula tells the young man that if both remove their clothing and place it in heaps before each other and the Tarantula then puts on the youth’s apparel, the young man will be able to see how handsome he is.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The young man accepts the Tarantula’s proposal, removes all his ceremonial garments one by one, and lays them in a heap before the Tarantula.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Tarantula removes his own gray-blue, woolly, dirty clothing—leggings, skirt, breech-cloth, coat, and mantle—and then dresses himself in the young man’s handsome garments.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After dressing, the Tarantula stands upright on his hind legs and repeatedly asks the young man, \"How do I look?\" while backing toward the entrance of his den, and each time the youth replies that he looks more handsome, finally saying he looks perfectly handsome when the Tarantula stands on the lip of his hole.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"At the moment the young man declares him perfectly handsome, the Tarantula turns around and plunges headfirst into his den, taking the garments with him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The young man laments the trick, decides he cannot go home naked, puts on the Tarantula’s remaining gray-blue breech-cloth and skirt, and runs home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The young man returns home much later than usual, when the sun is already high, so the old people have been thinking that something must have happened to him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"When questioned by his elders, the young man explains that the Tarantula living under Ak’yapaatch-ella stripped him of his garments and ran into his hole with them, and his father says they had suspected something of the kind.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Áhaiyúta","description":"A figure mentioned as one of the grandchildren of the Rainbow-worm and the old content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10519-l10623","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10519-10623","start":"10519","end":"10623","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two sisters from the Town of the Cliffs argue about going out; the elder insists and they descend the steep path of the great mesa to wash their clothes at a spring and pool below, carrying cotton garments and yucca-root for soap. Above the town, in a deep cave called the Cave of Átahsaia, lives the huge cannibal demon Átahsaia, armed with claws, a mountain-oak bow, and a great flint knife, dressed in lion and bear skins. Seeing the young women at the spring, he calls them his lunch and utters his war-cry, which the Echo-god Teshaminkia repeats so that the maidens hear and momentarily flee before returning to wash; Átahsaia then descends the mountain with his weapons toward them. The narrative then introduces the divine twins Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, who dwell on nearby Twin Mountain. They are described as twin sons of the Sun-father and the Mother Waters of the World, hatched from a foam-cup on the Great Ocean that once covered the earth. After the Sun dries the waters from the highlands, the twins deliver humans from the bowels of the Earth-mother and guide them toward their father’s home, later to the Middle of the World where the people now live. When war and hostile beings arise, the eight Stern Beings change the twins’ hearts to the medicine of war, making them the Boy-gods of War who protect the Corn-people with rainbow and thunderbolt weapons. Having overcome most enemies, they teach chosen followers the songs, prayers, and organization of a warrior society called the Priests of the Bow and breathe war-medicine into the nostrils of its wisest members. To this day, people renew their remembrance by making images of the twins and placing them each year at mid-sun on the Mountain of Thunder and the Mountain of the Beloved so that the twins will guard the Land of Zuni from sunrise to sunset and block the paths of enemies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Two sisters, an elder and a younger, discuss going out; the elder calls the younger timid, and they decide together to go down to the pool despite the younger’s fear.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The sisters gather their cotton mantles and other garments into bundles, take a bag of yucca-root (soap-weed), and start down a steep, crooked path to a pool at the foot of a great mesa to wash clothes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The setting includes a great mesa with a steep path, a spring and pool at its foot, and the Town of the Cliffs on high shelves of the mesa.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Far above the Town of the Cliffs, among red-gray and yellow rocks shaped like a boulder-like mountain, there is a deep cave called the Cave of Átahsaia where the demon lives.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Átahsaia is described as a huge, ugly demon with a body as big as the biggest elk, a shaggy breast, long brawny limbs covered with black-and-white speckled scales, coarse hair, bulging eyes, a wide mouth full of yellow fangs, red puffy lips, and a wrinkled, rough face.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Átahsaia’s weapons include long finger-nails like bear claws, a bow made from a mountain-oak sapling with two arrows ready, and a great flint knife as broad as a man’s thigh and twice as long, which he also uses to push back his hair.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Átahsaia is said to devour men and women for meat and the children of men as sweetbread, and his forelocks are covered with the blood of those he has slaughtered.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Although Átahsaia is ugly and can only speak with chattering teeth and laugh like a wolf, he is described as very polite but also as a great liar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Átahsaia wakes, looks out of his cave, sees the two young women at the spring, and mutters that they will be a good lunch, then howls his war-cry \"Ho-o-o-thlai-a!\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Teshaminkia, the Echo-god, repeats Átahsaia’s war-cry so that the maidens hear it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The younger sister, called a háni, clutches the elder sister’s arm in fear when she hears the cry, regrets having come out, and the two temporarily run away before returning to the spring when they hear nothing more.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After the sisters return to the spring, they wash their clothes on flat stones.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Átahsaia arms himself with his weapons and clambers down the mountain toward the maidens, again muttering that they will be a good lunch.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Around the corner of the great mesa are two towering buttes called Kwilli-yallon (Twin Mountain), on whose top live Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma are twin children of the Sun-father and the Mother Waters of the World, hatched from a foam-cup on the face of the Great Ocean, which then covered the earth.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Sun dries away the waters from the highlands of the earth, after which the twins deliver men forth from the bowels of the Earth-mother and guide them eastward toward the home of their father, the Sun.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"When war and strange beings arise to destroy humans, the eight Stern Beings change the hearts of the twins to sawanikia, the medicine of war, after which they are known as Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, \"Our Beloved,\" the \"Terrible Two,\" Boy-gods of War.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Even after becoming Boy-gods of War, the twins continue to guard the ancestors, guide them to the Middle of the World, and become invincible guardians of the Corn-people of Earth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The twins are said to possess hearts of the medicine of war and wisdom almost equal to the Sun-father’s; they wield the rainbow as their weapon and thunderbolts, lightning-shafts pointed with turquoise, as their arrows, and are the greatest warriors of the new era.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"After conquering most enemies of men, the twins teach chosen followers the songs, prayers, and organization of a warrior society called their children, the Priests of the Bow, and breathe sawanikia into the nostrils of the two wisest, a practice continued with their successors.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Each year at mid-sun, people make anew the semblance of the twins and place these images on the top of the Mountain of Thunder and the Mountain of the Beloved so the twins know they are remembered and so they will guard the Land of Zuni from sunrise to sunset, cutting off the pathways of enemies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The Land of Zuni is portrayed as a territory guarded by the twins from sunrise to sunset against enemies’ pathways.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Elder sister","description":"The elder of two sisters from the Town of the Cliffs, bold and sister (háni)","description":"The younger sister, called a háni, who is timid and fearful about going out, clutches her elder sister’s arm when she hears Átahsaia’s war-cry, and briefly runs away before returning to wash clothes.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Átahsaia","description":"A huge, ugly demon living in a deep cave above the Town of the Cliffs who devours adults and children, carries a mountain-oak bow and an enormous flint knife, wears lion and bear skins, is outwardly polite but a liar, and descends the mountain intending to eat the two maidens.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Teshaminkia (Echo-god)","description":"The Echo-god who repeats Átahsaia’s war-cry so that the maidens hear it.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Sun-father","description":"The Sun, father of the divine twins, lover of the earth.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Áhaiyúta","description":"One of the divine twin brothers, originally hatched with his brother from a foam-cup on the Great Ocean as a child of the Sun-father and Mother Waters, later transformed into a Boy-god of War; he helps deliver humans from the Earth-mother, guides them to the Middle of the World, guards the Corn-people, wields rainbow and thunderbolt weapons, founds the Priests of the Bow, and is honored by annual placement of his semblance on sacred mountains.","role_refs":["role:7","role:8","role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Mátsailéma","description":"The other divine twin brother, sharing Áhaiyúta’s origin as son of the Sun-father and Mother Waters, his transformation into a Boy-god of War, his guardianship of humans and the Corn-people, his use of rainbow and thunderbolt weapons, his role in founding the Priests of the Bow, and his continued veneration on sacred mountains.","role_refs":["role:7","role:8","role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Eight Stern Beings","description":"A group of eight beings who change the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l11269-l11376","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 11269-11376","start":"11269","end":"11376","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mítsina, an old gambler, invites two elder War-gods to play cane-cards after they rescue their small, unfortunate War-god brothers from the fire. He stakes all his fine possessions and even the younger brothers against the War-gods’ powerful lightning war-knife, and repeatedly loses. In his gambling frenzy he finally wagers and loses his own body parts, ending with his eyes. The War-gods, deciding not to kill him but to reform him, gouge out his eyes so he will stop causing trouble, then free their younger brothers and carry off Mitsina’s ill-gotten treasures to transform them into blessings for faithful humans, leaving him unconscious. Mitsina eventually awakes blind, confirms by sunlight that his loss and blinding are real, and discovers a packet of pitch at his window. Lighting it from the coals in his hearth, he inhales the fumes, which restore to him a kind of non-physical vision. He can no longer see his home as before but perceives instead the way to the great City of the Gods and Souls (Kothluellakwin). Renouncing his possessions and former bad inclinations, he follows the pitch-light westward, singing a mournful song. Birds gather at his song, mock his blindness, and try to put out his light. The tale notes that eagles and crows were once white as the foam of warring waters; when the strong eagles (and other birds) repeatedly flap into Mitsina’s light to extinguish it, they fail and only singe and blacken their wings and tails with smoke, ruining their white plumage, so they abandon the attempt.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mítsina is inside his house pitching cane-cards and talking to himself, having tired of watching the little War-gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The two elder War-gods haul their unfortunate younger brothers away from the fire, climb the ladder, and look into Mitsina’s house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mítsina sees the two War-gods, invites them to a game, and they accept his challenge cheerfully.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Mítsina offers to bet all his fine things hanging on the north side of the house, and the War-gods ask that the “ugly little devils” they saw sizzling by the fire be included, offering to wager everything they have.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The War-gods scramble out, drag their wretched little brothers in by the heels, dump them on the floor, and sit down to play, showing indifference to them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The War-gods stake their war-knife, described as the point of lightning, capable of splitting mountains and overcoming demons and men alike.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On learning the power of the War-gods’ weapon, Mitsina becomes doubtful but decides to play and loses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Mítsina continues to gamble, putting up the rest of his goods, including turquoises, necklaces, and the objects he plays The warrior priest proposes digging Old Tarantula out of his den and publicly commands all townspeople—men, women, and children—to bring digging tools and baskets to help. They tunnel into Tarantula’s hole all day, carrying out earth in baskets until a hillock is formed, but when they reach the solid rock foundations of the mountain and see the hole yawning like a cave, they abandon the effort and go home in despair. That evening the elders meet again and decide to send for Great Kingfisher, described as wise, crafty, and swift, who can dive into water and seize what he wants. The warrior priest sends Young Swift-runner to summon him. Great Kingfisher comes to the council, hears how Old Tarantula stripped Swift-runner of his garments and how the people dug to the foundations of the mountain without reaching him, and agrees, despite Tarantula’s cunning and sharp sight, to attempt to recover at least some of what was stolen. The next morning he hides between forked rock columns at Ak’yapaatch-ella, watching the opening of Old Tarantula’s hole with only his beak showing. At dawn Old Tarantula peers out with his many sharp eyes, spots Great Kingfisher, and mockingly calls him a skulker. Great Kingfisher dives at him with great speed but only brushes the plumes of Tarantula’s head-knot as the creature plunges back into his hole. Inside his dark, deep room, Old Tarantula congratulates himself, dances and sings a song, admires his fine fluttering garments—Swift-runner’s stolen dress—and begins another dance, boasting of his handsomeness.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At the urging of the other old ones, the priest-chief sends for his warrior priest to men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The warrior priest calls on the whole town, including women and children, to turn out and help dig out Old After heavy rain, a skull is washed into a stream and carried to his fields. Each dawn the priest-chief’s beautiful elder daughter goes to gather squash-flowers for feast bread. One morning she hears a voice singing among the vines and finds a handsome young man where a skull had lain. He offers to help her pick flowers if she will take him home. She agrees; but when the Sun’s first rays touch him, he sinks away and becomes a hideous old skull. Keeping her promise, she carries the skull home, lays it on cotton in a new water-jar, and covers it with a stone. At sunset a voice from the jar asks to be taken down; as darkness falls, the skull becomes the same handsome youth, richly adorned as the Sun-father had dressed him. The girl is delighted and says she will marry him. At sunrise he again becomes only a skull, which she returns to the jar. While she goes to the spring, her curious younger sister uncovers the carefully sealed jar and sees a great rattlesnake coiled over the white skull; terrified, she calls their father. The priest-chief, described as very wise, rebukes her for meddling, then addresses the being in the jar as both child and father, asking it to cease hiding in hideous forms and be as it truly is. The skull rattles assent. The priest-chief consents to its marrying his daughter and says they will close the room so it will never come forth; again the skull clatters in glad assent. When the elder daughter returns, the voice instructs her to close all doors and windows and bring raw cotton, since her father has agreed to the marriage and the being will now throw off its disguise. She brings much cotton. That night, at the voice’s command, she takes the jar down and the youth appears more handsome than ever; they marry and are happy. The next morning, when the Sun rises, he no longer changes but remains in human form, spinning cotton marvellously fine and weaving beautiful blankets and mantles, excelling in everything as a child of the Sun-father and a god. Meanwhile the Sun-father looks down through the windows in sorrow, lamenting that his son does not come to speak with him but declaring he will yet come. In time the priest-chief’s daughter bears two boys described as like the children of the deer. {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10305-l10409","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10305-10409","start":"10305","end":"10409","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Lesser Falcon returns to the council of old men with only Old Tarantula’s head-plume, explaining that Tarantula retreated into his den. The old priest praises the value of the plume from Summerland. The people decide that, since the wisest and swiftest birds have mostly failed, they must seek help from the Gods. They summon the youth Swift-runner, noted for his faithful service to the Gods, and instruct him to climb Thunder Mountain to the home of the two War-gods, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, who live there with their grandmother at the Middle Place of Sacrifice.

The town priests prepare sacrificial plumes and treasures and give them to Swift-runner as offerings and greetings for the Gods. The next morning he climbs the steep path to their dwelling. The grandmother, on the roof, calls him inside and summons her grandsons from below. The two War-gods abandon their playful behavior, solemnly greet the youth, and ask his purpose. Swift-runner, showing reverence, brings greetings and offerings from his town and explains his trouble: Old Tarantula stole his clothing, the elders’ attempts to use various birds to retrieve it have largely failed, and so they have sent him to the War-gods, called the fathers of the people in times of difficulty and strife.

The younger brother War-god orders his grandmother to grind rock flour. She grinds white calcareous sandstone (kétchïpawe) into fine powder, makes dough with water, and the two Gods skillfully shape the dough into two deer and two antelope images. They tell Swift-runner to place these figures on a sacrificial rock-shelf on the southern side of Thunder Mountain, pray over them, then return home and explain their instructions to the elders. They say the figures will become living beings on the rock-shelf and that he should greet them in the morning and lead them toward Old Tarantula’s den to lure him out, since Tarantula loves to hunt and kill.

Swift-runner follows their directions, sets the figures on the shelf, and then returns home to report to the elders. His father, the old priest-chief, consults the warrior priest about taking the war-path when Tarantula is tempted out, and then calls from the rooftop for the young men and warriors to prepare for war, relying on the sacred images made by the Two Beloved for Swift-runner. The people eagerly arm themselves and spread out over the foothills under Thunder Mountain. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10625-l10741","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10625-10741","start":"10625","end":"10741","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Twin brothers Áhaiyúta (elder) and Mátsailéma (younger) live with their grandmother on the top of Twin Mountain. One morning they prepare to go out hunting despite their grandmother’s anxious warnings about the dangers abroad. As they descend the rocks, the younger brother hears the cry of the demon Átahsaia and identifies him as the source of sorrow, saying he is hunting the two maidens of Héshokta who have gone to the spring. The brothers decide Átahsaia must be killed and, following the younger brother’s cautious plan, wait on a rock overlooking the pathway within bow-shot of the demon’s cave. Meanwhile, as the two girls wash, Átahsaia rushes toward them. They try to hide among the rocks, but he outflanks them and confronts them with bloodshot eyes and a jagged flint knife, then lowers the knife, smiles, and approaches gently like a young man. The younger sister clings to the elder in terror. Átahsaia claims to be their grandfather and says he means no harm; the elder sister quickly believes him and reassures the younger. When the younger continues to sob, Átahsaia angrily brandishes his knife and threatens to cut off the light of her life if she does not stop. The elder sister urges obedience, saying it is better to live in fear than die, since no one knows where the trails of death lead. The narrator explains that in the speech of the gods and ancients, to have one’s light cut off means to die and go to a dividing-place of life. Átahsaia then again speaks gently, calling the girls his granddaughters, claiming to be a lonely old hunter whose people are gone, and inviting them to his home above to share his abundant venison and sweet-bread and to help fill his water-jars. Reassured, the elder sister agrees to go with him and to fill his jars. Átahsaia praises her but calls the younger sister a fool, saying his knife makes the world wiser by killing fools, then leads the way toward his home while the elder sister drags the reluctant younger along.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma live with their old grandmother on the top of Twin Mountain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Áhaiyúta is called the elder brother and Mátsailéma the younger brother, and they share the same grandmother.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The brothers decide to go hunting on a fine day, and the younger puts on an elk-hide helmet and takes a mountain-lion-skin quiver from an antler near the ladder.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Their grandmother calls up through a trap-door, asking where they are going and complaining that they worry her by going abroad when even open spaces are full of danger like thick war.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The brothers laugh, reassure their grandmother that they are only going out to hunt, tighten their bows and straighten their arrows before the fire, and then skip down the rocks toward the cliffs below.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The younger brother hears and identifies a cry as that of Átahsaia, calling him an old wretch who is abroad to cause tears.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The brothers agree that Átahsaia must be stopped and must die that day because he is pursuing the two maidens of Héshokta, {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10849-l10955","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10849-10955","start":"10849","end":"10955","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two divine twin brothers stand over a dying demon they have defeated and recite a prayer, saying that through the power of sawanikia and with the Sun-father’s help they have "seen" (killed) an enemy who caused many bereaved families. A note explains that to "see" an enemy in Zuñi mythology means to take his life. The rescued maidens, realizing who saved them, respond with a blessing and breathe upon their hands. 

The twins then tell the maidens that the slain being is the last enemy of men and that their father, the Sun, has truly accomplished the deed through them. They instruct the girls to return home to Héshokta, inform their father, and have him teach their words to his priests. The twins announce that they will separate their paths from those of humans, mingling only in spirit, and will depart to their everlasting homes in the mountains—one to the Mountain of Thunder and the other to the Mount of the Beloved. From there they will guard, from sunrise to sunset, the land of the Corn-priests so that foolish men do not break into and lay waste the Middle Country of Earth. They say they will still require from their "children" the plumes with which they dress their thoughts and the forms of their being so that men may renew them each year at mid-sun. The tale explains that henceforth two stars will be seen at morning and evening, one going before and one following the Sun-father: Áhaiyúta as his herald and Mátsailéma as his guardian, both warriors and fathers of men. The twins bid the maidens go happily home.

The maidens bow, breathe from the twins’ hands, and return to the Town of the Cliffs, where they tell their father what happened and repeat the words of the Beloved. The old man recognizes the twins as Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, offers a prayer of thanks, and casts white meal of the seeds of earth, shells from the Great Waters, pollen of flowers, and war paints upon the winds. He declares that in four days he will gather his warriors to cut, paint, and feather plume-sticks and place them on high mountains so that the Beloved Two Warriors may take them unto themselves through their knowledge and power of medicine.

After the maidens depart among the rocks, the brothers laugh, shout, and Áhaiyúta kicks the ugly carcass of the demon Átahsaia, mocking him. They wonder what to do with the body and decide to skin it. They flay the body from foot to head as one skins a fawn for a seed-bag, insert sticks in the limbs, tie strings, stuff it with grass and moss, and prop it against a cliff so that it looks like the living demon. They remark on his ugliness and gleefully anticipate frightening their grandmother with the stuffed skin.

They then dismember the corpse. Áhaiyúta cuts off the demon’s head, calls it a liar that spoke a falsehood for every life it took, and condemns it to become a "lying star" whose nightly appearance will show its guilt to all people. He spins the bloody head and hurls it into the sky, where it becomes a great red star that rises in summer and announces the coming morning when it is still midnight, called Mokwanosana, the Great Lying Star. Mátsailéma slits the abdomen, tears out the intestines, and declares that because they consumed the flesh of men over the world, they will be stretched from one end of the earth to the other so that the children of the demon’s victims can look up each night, see them, and mock them. When he slings the entrails into the air, they extend across the sky and become the Great Snow-drift of the Skies, identified as the Milky Way. The remainder of the carcass is thrown into the chasm where the demon had cast his victims. Rattlesnakes come out and feed on the flesh until their fangs turn yellow with putrid meat, and the story notes that their descendants’ fangs remain yellow and poisonous. Finally Mátsailéma calls for "fun," asking Áhaiyúta to dance around with the stuffed skin so he can see how it Following the bird’s instructions, he builds a large divided chest filled with meat and water for the journey. The bird takes the chest and the prince on her back, flies some distance, and leaves him at his destination. The prince, now so worn and altered that no one recognizes him as royal, enters the service of a tailor as a servant. He learns that in this country two princes (his brothers) have brought back brides from the other world, but the brides refuse to marry until they receive wedding clothes identical to those they had in the other world, made without measurements—an impossible task that no craftsman will accept. The disguised prince persuades his tailor-master to promise the King that he can supply what is required. After the King provides money, the prince tells the tailor to pray and sleep. At midnight he goes into the fields, uses three eggs given him earlier by maidens to create three palaces, enters each, takes the maidens’ robes, then turns the palaces back into eggs and returns home, where he hangs the robes on the wall. In the morning the tailor finds the magnificent robes, brings them to the King, and the princesses recognize them as their own clothes from the other world and guess that Prince Ivan is in this world, though they keep silent. The prince leaves the tailor, repeats a similar pattern with a shoemaker and other artisans, and through his hidden help all are enriched by the King as the princesses receive their full wardrobe. When the princesses have all their clothes and can no longer delay marriage, they weep because the prince has not come. On the eve of the wedding, the youngest bride asks her father the King for permission to give alms to beggars. As she distributes alms and scrutinizes the beggars, she notices on one of them the ring she had given the prince in the other world, along with her sisters’ rings, and recognizes him. She seizes him, brings him into the hall, and tells the King that he is the one who brought them out of the other world and that his brothers forbade them to say he was alive, threatening to kill them. The King punishes the deceitful sons, and three weddings are celebrated. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l12404-l12519","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 12404-12519","start":"12404","end":"12519","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“Tell her to bathe herself and put on her finest garments tomorrow morning. Then, when the time comes, mount her upon thy shoulders and bear her up to me.”","summary":"The twin war gods promise the priest-chief’s war-priests that they will lead the Óinahe dance: it will come forth three times, but on the fourth time the priests’ wish will be fulfilled. The Eagle overhears this and becomes sad. The next morning, at the maiden’s window, he refuses her food and explains that her father’s war-priests and the people of the town under the mountain are longing to see her, so they have ordered the Óinahe to tempt her out and have petitioned Áhaiyúta and his younger brother on Thunder Mountain. The gods have decreed that on the fourth day of dancing the people’s wish will be fulfilled and that the maiden shall be no more. The Eagle, calling the girl his mother, urges her to free him so he can seek help. She loosens his bonds and he flies straight up to the Sun at the zenith. In the Sun’s splendid home the Eagle, calling the Sun his father, explains that the people dance daily to tempt the maiden forth, that the Twain’s powers are surpassed only by the Sun’s, and that they have commanded that either the wish be fulfilled or the maiden perish on the fourth dance. The Sun confirms this knowledge and instructs the Eagle to return, tell the maiden to bathe and dress in her finest garments the next morning, mount her on his shoulders, and attempt to carry her up to the Sun’s house, though he warns that the powerful twins’ word may still come to pass during the journey. The Sun says he will watch when the Eagle reaches the mid-heavens. The Eagle departs. Then a commentary explains that demons enter the corpses of wizards and great sinners, forming bloodthirsty vampires who value their coffin-lids and shrouds. The beginning of the tale \"The Coffin-Lid\" follows: a daring moujik near a graveyard sees a corpse emerge holding a coffin-lid, steals the lid, and forces the undead—who has killed village children—to begin revealing how the victims can be brought back to life.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A lazy and talkative village As they argue, Frost numbs their hands and they grow seriously cold, noticing each other's blue faces. Little-Russians describe a vampire that gnaws its way out of the grave with steel-like teeth, kills babies and older household members, and can be tracked back to its grave by salt sprinkled on the floor. Kashoubes tell of a Vieszcy vampire that awakens in the grave, gnaws its own hands and feet, causing relatives and neighbors to sicken and die, then rises at midnight to destroy cattle or ring a deathly bell, and usually drinks the blood of sleepers, leaving a small wound over the heart. Lusatian Wends say that a corpse which chews its shroud or sucks its own breast causes all its kin to die. Wallachians describe a murony, a hybrid of werewolf and vampire, that can take animal and insect forms, and when exhumed shows fresh long nails and blood streaming from its face. A Russian story details a peasant led by a stranger (a vampire) who opens the backs of two sleepers and drains their blood into pails to drink. Folk-tales (skazkas) and their parallels prescribe depriving vampires of power by staking the corpse (using aspen or thorn wood); stories of a Bohemian and an Istrian vampire show stakes failing. Burning the body or decapitating it with a grave-digger's shovel are said to be the only certain means of destruction; Wends add that hitting such a vampire on the back of the head with a shovel makes it squeal like a pig. The origin of vampires is discussed: they may be wizards, witches, suicides, victims of violence, or the cursed dead; victims of vampires or corpses over which animals leap or birds fly may become vampires; some are destined from birth as children of unholy unions, fathered by the Evil One or an animated corpse. Vampire corpses torment neighbors until transfixed, and the stake must be driven with a single blow, as a second would restore life. as he gnaws, first relatives and then neighbors sicken and die. After finishing his own flesh, he rises at midnight to destroy cattle or sound a bell in a belfry, whose ill-omened tones cause those who hear them to die. When exhumed, it has long nails of recent growth on hands and feet, and blood streaming from eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:5","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"A Russian story recounts a peasant conducted by a stranger into a house where an old man and a youth sleep. The stranger places a pail near the youth, strikes him on the back so it opens and blood flows into the pail, which the stranger drinks; he then does the same to the old man, drinks, and remarks that day is breaking and they should return to his dwelling.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"The author notes that many skazkas contain directions for depriving a vampire of its power: a stake must be driven through the murderous corpse, in agreement with their parallels elsewhere. An Istrian strigon vampire transfixed with a sharp thorn cudgel near Laibach in 1672 reportedly pulled it out of his body and threw it back contemptuously.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:8","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"The passage asserts that the only certain methods of destroying a vampire are either consuming him by fire or chopping off his head with a grave-digger’s shovel. Wends add that striking a vampire over the back of the head with such an implement makes him squeal like a pig.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:9","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"The origin of the vampire is described as obscure, but in modern times it has generally been a wizard, witch, suicide, person who died violently, or someone cursed by the Church or by parents, who reappears in a troubling way to surviving relatives and acquaintances.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:10","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"Even honorable dead may become vampires by accident: in some countries, a person slain by a vampire is supposed to become a vampire; the leaping of a cat or other animal across a corpse, or the flight of a bird above it, may transform the dead into a ravenous demon.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:11","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"Sometimes a man is thought to be destined from birth to be a vampire, as the offspring of an unholy union. In some cases the Evil One himself is the father of such a doomed victim; in others, the father is a temporarily animated corpse.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Ralston, via Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:12","type":"summary","locator":"13717-13791","quote_or_summary":"Regardless of the cause of vampirism, a corpse that has become a vampire is said to give neighbors no rest until transfixed. THE HASTY WORD                                            370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 718-855","start":"718","end":"855","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston comments on the term skazka (folk-tale) within Russian narratives, giving brief examples: a boy abducted by the witch Baba Yaga is found being entertained by a story‑telling cat, and a foolish caretaker (Durak) kills village children by boiling them while attempting to wash them. He then describes Russian winter social gatherings where skazkas are sometimes told and introduces the tale "The Fiend" as a story about evil spirits, said to be traceable to Eastern sources.

In "The Fiend," an old couple have a daughter, Marusia. In their village, St. Andrew's feast (November 30) is celebrated with week‑long gatherings of girls who bake pampushki; lads join in the evenings with music, liquor, dancing, and revelry. At one such vechernitsa a particularly handsome, richly dressed youth arrives, treats everyone with his gold, dances best of all, and attaches himself to Marusia. When they part he proposes marriage, calling himself a merchant’s clerk from a nearby place, and Marusia accepts in principle.

At home, Marusia tells her mother about the wealthy suitor. The mother advises her to take a ball of thread to the next gathering, slip a noose over one of his buttons when seeing him off, and quietly unroll the thread to discover where he lives. Marusia does so the following night: she fastens the thread to him, lets it unwind as he walks away, then follows the thread, which leads from the road across hedges and ditches to the village church, whose door is locked.

Circling the church, Marusia finds a ladder, sets it against a window, climbs in, and sees her "betrothed" beside a grave devouring a corpse left in the church overnight. Terrified, she makes a small noise, flees home imagining pursuit, and is nearly dead with fear on arrival. Next morning, when her mother asks whether she saw the youth, Marusia admits only that she saw him, concealing the rest.

Marusia debates whether to attend the gathering again; her mother urges her to go and amuse herself. She goes, finds the Fiend (Evil One) already there, and festivities resume while the other girls remain unaware of his true nature. When they start to go home, the Evil One again asks Marusia to see him off. She is too afraid to move, and the other girls reproach her for refusing. THE HASTY WORD 370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 1854-1991","start":"1854","end":"1991","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Conclusion of the tale of the Bad Wife and the peasant, followed by the satirical story of the Golovikha and an editorial transition to the tale 'The Three Copecks.' The peasant leads his quarrelsome wife to a currant bush where she falls into a bottomless pit. After three days he returns, lowers a cord, and pulls up a little demon who begs not to be sent back because a 'Bad Wife' has descended and torments the demons. The peasant frees the demon, who proposes they go to Vologda: the demon will possess merchant wives and daughters, while the peasant will appear to cure them and receive fees. This scheme makes the peasant rich. The demon then warns him not to cure the Boyar's daughter when possessed, or he will eat the peasant. When the Boyar's daughter becomes violently insane and cannibalistic, the Boyar summons the peasant. The peasant arranges for all the townspeople and coachmen outside the house to crack whips and cry 'The Bad Wife has come!' Inside, he tells the demon the Bad Wife is arriving. Terrified, the demon rushes to the window, hears the shouting, and asks where to hide; the peasant advises him to return to the pit. The demon flees back there, and the Boyar rewards the peasant with his daughter in marriage and half his property. The narrator adds that the Bad Wife still sits in the pit, in Tartarus.\nThe next story, 'The Golovikha,' satirizes a bumptious woman who insists on being chosen as Golova, or head of the village association. After her husband reports her wish, the elders elect her. As Golova she settles disputes, takes bribes, and drinks spirits at the peasants' expense, but fails to collect the poll-tax. When a Cossack arrives to enforce collection, she hides by having her husband tie her in a bag and place her among five sacks of seed-corn. The Cossack slashes the sacks with his whip, and the woman, beaten through the bag, cries that she will no longer be Golova. After this, she obeys her husband. The editor notes that this tale is an example of stories that satirize women and that it sheds light on Russian communal institutions, explaining the term 'Golovikha.' He then announces that he will give a tale that praises a good and wise wife, identifying it as a variant from which, in his view, the English story of 'Whittington and his Cat' is derived, and suggesting that an incense-burning feature in it points to a Buddhist origin. The tale is called 'The Three Copecks.'","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The peasant leads his wife to a currant bush; she jumps into it while shouting a threat at an imagined thief and falls into a bottomless pit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The peasant stays home for three days after his wife falls, then on the fourth day returns to the pit, lowers a long cord, and pulls up a little demon.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The demon begs the peasant not to send him back into the pit, saying that a bad wife has come there, has devoured and tormented the demons by pinching and biting them, and that they are exhausted by her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The demon promises to do the peasant a good turn if released, and the peasant lets him go free into the The main tale, \"The Two Friends,\" tells of two young men in a village who are close companions and agree that whoever marries first will invite the other to his wedding, whether he is alive or dead. About a year later one dies; months afterward the survivor becomes a bridegroom and, with his kinsmen, drives to fetch his bride. Passing the graveyard, he remembers his promise, stops the horses, and goes to his friend's grave to invite him to the wedding. The grave yawns open, the dead man rises, thanks him for keeping his word, and urges him to enter \"my abode\" and share a glass of drink. Though the marriage procession is waiting, the bridegroom jumps into the grave. The corpse pours three cups of liquor; after each cup, the story states that a hundred, then two hundred, then three hundred years pass away. When the dead man takes leave, the coffin lid falls and the grave closes. Emerging, the bridegroom finds that the graveyard has become waste ground overgrown with nettles and tall grass, the road and his companions have vanished, and the nearby village's houses and inhabitants are unfamiliar. He consults the priest, who is not the man he knew; searching the church-books, the priest discovers that three hundred years earlier a bridegroom went to the graveyard on his wedding-day and disappeared, and that his bride eventually married another. A footnote connects this theme of prolonged absence and a changed world with Washington Irving's \"Rip van Winkle,\" which is said to rest on folk-tales corresponding to the Christian legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus and an older tale, and with a legend of a monk who listens to a bird singing in a convent garden and remains entranced for many years (including a Russian version). The note then summarizes a closely similar Norse story, \"Friends in Life and Death,\" in which a bridegroom knocks long on his dead friend's grave until the occupant appears, accompanies him to and from church, and later grants him a view of the world beyond the grave by placing on his head a sod cut from the graveyard; after witnessing strange sights, the bridegroom waits, becomes overgrown with mosses and shrubs, and returns to find that everything in the outer world has changed. Finally, the author remarks that such sketches of life within the grave show ghosts preserving memories and behaving genially, but contrasts them with other Russian tales in which the visitor from the other world is a terrifying vitalized corpse with human appetites, superhuman strength, and malignity, clothed in grave garments he cannot relinquish, and introduces the story \"The Shroud\" as an An editorial transition introduces a new story that explains how a vampire (here called a warlock) operates and how to destroy it. A soldier on furlough walks toward his native village and visits a miller friend. As night falls, the miller warns him that a terrible warlock who died now rises from his grave at night, haunts the village, and terrifies even the boldest. The soldier, insisting that as \"crown property\" he cannot be drowned in water or burned in fire, refuses to stay and continues his journey, passing a graveyard where he sees a great fire on one of the graves and the warlock sitting by it sewing boots. The warlock invites him to a village wedding. At the feast, the warlock drinks, revels, drives out all guests and relatives, puts the bride and bridegroom into a magical sleep, pierces their hands with an awl, and draws their blood into two phials. On the way back, the soldier learns from the warlock that this will cause the couple’s death and that only he knows the method of reviving them by cutting their heels and pouring their own blood back into the wounds; he carries the bridegroom’s blood in his right pocket and the bride’s in his left. Boasting of his powers, the warlock explains that he can only be truly overcome if someone builds a huge pyre of aspen boughs, burns him, and throws onto the fire all snakes, worms, reptiles, and carrion birds that emerge from his body; if even a single maggot escapes, he will survive in that form. At his grave, the warlock turns on the soldier, intending to tear him to pieces to prevent him from revealing these secrets. They fight until the cocks crow, at which moment the warlock falls lifeless. The soldier takes the phials of blood from the warlock’s pockets and goes to his family’s house, where he hears of a haunting warlock and of a wedding at the home of a rich peasant whose bride and bridegroom have mysteriously died during the night. At midnight the window opened. At the window appeared a witch all in white. She took a sprinkler, passed her arm into the cottage... the Cossack suddenly gave his sabre a sweep, and cut her arm off close to the shoulder.","summary":"A fool uses a magic formula invoking a Pike to ride a stove to the king. The king wants to kill him, but the king's daughter insists on marrying the fool. Enraged, the king has the couple sealed in a tarred tub and cast into the sea. Using the Pike's power, the fool has the tub thrown ashore, escapes with his wife, and conjures a marble palace opposite the king's own. The king discovers his daughter there, pardons the couple, and they prosper. Afanasief and Ralston then discuss the Pike's wide importance in northern mythology, citing a Russian Christmas song about a wealth-bringing pike from Novgorod, its connection to the pike-form of Andvari the dwarf in Scandinavian legend, the Lithuanian lake-monster pike Strukis, and a gigantic pike in the Kalevala. The text then turns to Russian beliefs about witches, wizards, and vampires who gain powers from compacts with evil spirits and continue to harm people after death. In the opening of the tale \"The Witch Girl,\" a Cossack lodges with a terrified family who expect \"Death\" to visit their cottage that night. He stays awake and at midnight sees a witch in white reach in with a sprinkler. He cuts off her arm with his sabre, saving the household.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The King's runners come for the fool and tell him the King will give him red boots, a red caftan, and a red shirt.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The fool is seated on the stove when he utters the formula, \"By the Pike's command, at my request, do thou, O stove, go to the King!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The stove moves and carries the fool to the King's residence.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The King intends to put the fool to death.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The King's daughter takes a strong liking to the fool and begs her father to give her in marriage to him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The King, angry, has his daughter married to the fool and then orders both to be placed in a tub, the tub to be tarred over and thrown into the water, which is done.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The tub floats on the sea for a long time with the fool and his wife inside.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"While in the tub, the fool's wife begs him to do something to get them cast ashore.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The fool again speaks a formula invoking the Pike, asking that the tub be cast ashore and torn open.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The tub is cast ashore and torn open, and the fool and his wife step out of it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After leaving the tub, the wife implores the fool to build some kind of house.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The fool commands, by the Pike's power, that a marble palace be built immediately opposite the King's palace, and it appears at once.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the morning, the King sees the new palace, sends to find out who lives there, learns it is his daughter and her husband, summons them, pardons them, and they live together and prosper.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Afanasief is quoted as saying that the Pike is a scales, a back woven with pearls, and a diamond in its head instead of eyes; the song promises wealth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Russian wealth-bringing Pike is connected by the commentator to the Scandinavian pike-shape taken by Andvari, the dwarf-guardian of a famous treasure mentioned in the Voelsunga Saga and the Nibelungenlied.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A Lithuanian tradition says a certain lake is ruled by a monstrous pike named Strukis, which sleeps only once a year for a single hour, formerly on St. John's Night.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"In the Lithuanian story, a fisherman once used Strukis's sleep to appears in the Finnish epic Kalevala.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The narrator states that Russia is rich in stories about the Black Art and that peasants strongly believe in witches, wizards, turnskins, and vampires.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Some witches are described as supernatural beings belonging to the powers.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"These human witches and wizards are described as terrors to their districts during life and as becoming vampires after being buried, leaving their graves at night to drink blood.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The narrator says such Slavonic sorcery stories resemble western tales about sorcery but are more savage, especially in their thirst for blood.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"One evening, a Cossack rides into a don't fear death!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The Cossack puts his horse in the stable, feeds it, and then enters the cottage.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Inside the cottage, the Cossack sees men, women, and little children weeping, praying to God, and afterwards putting on clean shirts.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The master explains that in their village Death goes about at night, and in any cottage she looks into, all responds with the saying, \"Without God's will, no pig gets its fill,\" and the household lies down to sleep while he keeps watch and does not close his eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"At midnight, the window opens and a witch dressed all in white appears, extending her arm with a sprinkler into the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l3381-l3496","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 3381-3496","start":"3381","end":"3496","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Prince Ivan has a leather rope made long enough to reach the \"other world\" beneath the earth, where he descends through a stone opening to fight the beast Norka. In the underworld he finds a talking horse and three enchanting sisters who live in copper, silver, and golden palaces; they are Norka's sisters and help Ivan, the youngest giving him a sword and Water of Strength to behead Norka as it sleeps on a stone in the middle of the blue sea. After killing Norka, Ivan takes the three sisters—who love him—and their palaces transformed into eggs to be hoisted to the upper world, but his brothers betray him by cutting the rope; he survives by tying the rope to a stone. Wandering in a storm, he shelters under a tree, covers some soaked nestlings with his coat, and is thanked by their gigantic bird-mother, who offers to grant any desire in return.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Prince Ivan asks his father to have a leather rope plaited long enough to reach to the other world, and his father orders this to be done.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A leather rope is made that is long enough to reach to the other world beneath the earth.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Prince Ivan, his brothers, servants, and provisions for a year go to the place where the Beast disappeared under a stone, build a palace there, and live in it for some time.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A very large stone, described as big as a hill, covers the place where the Beast disappeared; the elder brothers cannot move it, but the youngest brother easily flings it aside.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Prince Ivan offers to go into the other world to overcome Norka and instructs his brothers to lower him with the rope and to pull it up when it is jerked.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ivan is lowered by his brothers into the other world, described as underneath the earth, and he sets out walking there.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the underworld Ivan sees a richly caparisoned horse which speaks to him, greeting him by name and saying it has long awaited him.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ivan rides the horse to a copper palace, enters, eats a prepared dinner, and lies down on a bed before a beautiful lady arrives and classifies possible guests as father, brother, husband, grandmother, mother, or sister depending on age and sex.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The lady in the copper palace is described as more beautiful than can be imagined except in a skazka.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The lady in the copper palace says that the beast Ivan wants to overcome is her brother Norka and that she bound up three of the wounds Ivan gave him earlier.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ivan later visits a second sister in a silver palace; she hosts him and says Norka is staying with their youngest sister.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ivan visits the youngest sister in a golden palace; she tells him Norka is asleep on the blue sea, gives him a steel sword and a draught of the Water of Strength, and instructs him to cut off Norka’s head at a single stroke.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Norka sleeps on a stone in the middle of the blue sea, and when it snores the water is disturbed for seven versts around.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ivan crosses himself, approaches the sleeping Norka, and cuts off its head with the sword; the head exclaims, \"Well, I'm done for now!\" as it jumps off and rolls far into the sea.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After killing Norka, Ivan returns, gathers the three sisters, and intends to take them to the upper world; they all love him and do not wish to be separated from him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Each of the three sisters, being an enchantress, turns her palace into an egg, teaches Ivan how to turn the eggs into palaces and back again, and gives the eggs to him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Ivan and the three sisters go to the place of ascent, where there is a rope; he fastens the maidens to the rope, jerks it, and his brothers haul them up and are amazed at the wondrous maidens.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ivan’s brothers privately agree to lower the rope for him, pull him partway up, and then cut the rope so he may be killed and they can keep the beauties as wives.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Suspecting their plan, Ivan ties the rope to a stone and jerks it; the brothers hoist the stone, cut the rope, and the stone falls and breaks, while Ivan remains below, weeps, and walks away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"As Ivan wanders, a storm breaks out with lightning, thunder, and torrential rain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Ivan seeks shelter under a tree and sees young birds being drenched; he takes off his coat and covers them, then sits under the tree himself.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"A very large bird, mother of the nestlings, flies in, so big that it darkens the light even further.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The giant bird asks who wrapped up her nestlings, sees Ivan, thanks him, and offers to do anything he desires in content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l15423-l15510","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING. / THE HEDGEHOG, THE MERCHANT, THE KING, AND THE POOR MAN.; lines 15423-15510","start":"15423","end":"15510","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An unnamed advisor who calls the king's son his \"younger brother\" explains how to obtain an object from an enchanted castle by using a golden rod to open it, running straight to a silver lake in the garden, ignoring voices, beautiful maidens offering food and drink, piles of treasure, and swarms of snakes and toads, and circling the lake three times before escaping. The king's son, called Yanoshka, follows these instructions: he opens the castle, resists the tempting maidens, passes the treasures without touching them, runs through the snakes and toads without fear, circles the silver lake three times, and barely escapes as the stone wall closes, losing the heel of his boot. When he returns home, the silver lake now flows through the flowery garden, where precious golden fish leap in the water, alongside the already famous marble palace, sounding tree, and sweetly speaking bird. These wonders become renowned throughout \"seven worlds,\" drawing many visitors. The king learns of them, vows not to eat or drink until he sees the garden, refuses black coffee from the old witch, and rides there in a golden carriage with his wife, the queen. As the king and queen enter the garden, a brother and sister rush out, panting, and kiss their hands; the queen remarks that the girl looks just like the king, and he says the boy looks like her. The royal couple admires the garden, especially the sounding tree and speaking bird. The boy swiftly climbs the tree, plucks two golden apples, and gives one to each parent. They also admire the silver lake with golden fish and tour seven chambers of the marble palace. In the most beautiful room, the king asks his \"little servant\" (the prince) why a picture is covered with velvet and what it depicts. The prince says nothing but pulls aside the covering, revealing an image by which the king and queen recognize their own children, whom they have never seen before. They embrace the children, weeping and laughing, while the world-sounding tree and sweetly speaking bird are heard. The old witch, called an old sinner, becomes sad as the king has her seized, bound to a tree, and burned over a fire of
