{"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l5298-l5434","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 5298-5434","start":"5298","end":"5434","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A King is being carried by an Eagle. The Eagle uses the contrast of sky above, earth below, and the directions right and left to orient him and points out the house of his second sister. They visit her; she seats the Eagle hospitably but leaves the King outside and sets greyhounds on him. The angry Eagle snatches up the King and flies away; the house is seen burning behind them. They then visit the Eagle's mother and eldest sister, who welcome both Eagle and King and treat the King with respect. The Eagle tells the King to stay awhile and promises to repay what he has eaten at the King's house; he gives the King a ship and two coffers, one red and one green, with instructions not to open them until home, and to open the red coffer in the back court and the green in the front court.

Sailing home, the King stops at an island, becomes curious about the forbidden coffers, and opens the red one. An uncountable number of cattle pour out and fill the island. Despairing, the King wonders how to fit them back into the small chest. A man emerges from the water, offers to repack the herd in return for "whatever you have at home that you don't know of," and the King, thinking he knows everything at home, agrees. The man restores the cattle to the coffer, and the King sails on.

Back home the King learns that a son has been born during his absence. He rejoices but secretly weeps, fearing the boy must be given up to pay the debt. He later opens the red coffer in the back court and releases multitudes of cattle, and opens the green coffer in the front court, which becomes a splendid garden filled with many trees. Delighted, he forgets his obligation.

Many years later, as the King walks by a river, the same man rises from the water and reminds him of the unpaid debt. The King goes home in grief and tells the Queen and the now-grown Prince everything. All mourn, but they decide they must surrender the Prince. They take him to the mouth of the river and leave him there.

The Prince follows a footpath away from the river, trusting God to lead him, and reaches a dense forest with a hut inhabited by Baba Yaga. He enters, she feeds him, and he tells her his story and purpose. Baba Yaga directs him to the sea-shore where twelve spoonbills will arrive, transform into fair maidens, and bathe. She instructs him to steal the eldest maiden's shift and make terms with her, then proceed to the Water King, taking along three beings he will meet on the way—Obedalo, Opivalo, and Moroz Treskum—who will be useful helpers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Eagle orients the King in mid-flight by saying that above them is the sky, below them the earth, and that on the right is an open plain and on the left a house where his second sister lives.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Eagle and the King land in a wide courtyard at the second sister’s house; she welcomes the Eagle and seats him at an oaken table but leaves the King outside and releases greyhounds to attack him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Angered at the treatment of the King, the Eagle seizes the King from the courtyard and flies away; as they fly, the King sees a red house burning behind them, identified as the second sister’s house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Eagle then brings the King to the house where his mother and eldest sister live; they receive the King with cordiality and respect.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Eagle asks the King to stay with them for a time and promises to give him a ship and repay what he had eaten in the King’s house, wishing him Godspeed home afterward.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Eagle gives the King a ship and two coffers, one red and one green, and instructs him not to open them until he gets home, specifying that the red coffer should be opened in the back court and the green in the front court.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The King sails along the blue sea in the ship; when he reaches an island and his ship stops, he becomes consumed with curiosity about the contents of the coffers and the prohibition on opening them.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Unable to resist, the King opens the red coffer on the island, and an enormous quantity of cattle of many kinds pours out, filling the island so that there is scarcely room for them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Seeing the vast herd, the King becomes deeply sorrowful and weeps, lamenting that he cannot possibly fit all the cattle back into the small coffer.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A man emerges from the water, approaches the King, and asks why he is weeping so bitterly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The King explains that he does not know how to get the huge herd of cattle back into the tiny coffer.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The man from the water offers to pack up all the cattle on the condition that the King give him whatever he has at home that he does not know about; the King reflects, assumes he knows everything at home, and agrees.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The man from the water packs all the cattle back into the coffer, and the King sails homeward with the coffer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"When the King reaches home, he learns that a son has been born to him during his absence; he kisses and caresses the child while shedding tears.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The Queen asks why the King is weeping; he claims that it is for joy, concealing that the Prince is the unknown thing he has promised away.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Later the King opens the red coffer in the back court, releasing multitudes of cattle that fill the sheds and pastures, and opens the green coffer in the front court, which becomes a great and glorious garden with many trees.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Delighted by the cattle and the beautiful garden, the King forgets about his promise to give up his son.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Many years pass; while walking by a river, the King encounters the same man from the water, who rises from the river and reminds him that he is in the man’s debt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The King returns home in deep grief and tells the Queen and the Prince the whole truth about his bargain and the obligation to surrender the Prince.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The King, Queen, and Prince all mourn and weep but decide that the Prince must be given up; they take him to the mouth of the river and leave him there alone.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Left at the river, the Prince sees a him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The twelve spoonbills are explicitly said to turn into fair maidens and begin bathing at the In the Russian tales, a poor man rids himself of Need by trapping her and throwing her away, becoming prosperous, while his rich brother later takes Need and is ruined. Another variant shows Need living behind the stove, advising a poor couple how to obtain a gift for a rich brother and later being expelled in a pitcher through an ice-hole after gold unexpectedly appears. In a chap-book story, Kruchina steals a poor man's crust of bread but compensates him with a duck that lays daily golden eggs. Little-Russian belief in Zluidni describes them as small beings bringing evil to households; in one tale a poor man who has given his brother a fish sells his \"thank you\" (spasibo) to an old stranger and receives a purse of gold, then tricks his Zluidni into carrying mill-stones and shoves them off a bridge into a deep river. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l14320-l14433","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 14320-14433","start":"14320","end":"14433","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston explains how the Christian Prophet Elijah (Ilya) in Russian and other Slavic traditions has assumed the functions of the old thunder-god Perun, being linked to harvest, drought and rain, and pictured as riding a flaming car, destroying devils with stone arrows and sending thunder, lightning and hail that can bless or ruin crops. Various regional customs are described: peasants set grain on their gates, attend special services, and sacrifice a communal beast on Ilya's day; Novgorod once had twin churches \"Ilya the Wet\" and \"Ilya the Dry\" for processions seeking changes in weather; disease spirits and cattle-plague are fought by Ilya through angelic warriors. Servian and Bulgarian beliefs depict storms as Ilya's battle with the devil or Lamia fiend, clouds as his heavenly sheep, and hail as produced by spirits of dead Gypsies to scourge sinners. St. Nicholas, who has taken over the role of an ancient water ruler, is portrayed as gentler and is compared with Odin, while Ilya is likened to Thor. A legend then contrasts their characters: a moujik faithfully keeps Nicholas's day but neglects Elijah's. Elijah and Nicholas walk over his flourishing cornfields; Elijah vows to destroy them with lightning and hail to punish the moujik, while Nicholas instead warns the moujik to sell his standing crop to Elijah's priest. A storm later devastates the field, which now belongs to the priest, illustrating Nicholas's mild but crafty intervention against Elijah's harsher judgment.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Church day of the Prophet Elijah falls on July 20 and occurs at the beginning of the harvest season.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Peasants are said to have connected the new Christian saint Elijah with the old thunder-god Perun, who had been considered Lord of the Harvest.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Elijah is described as a prophet associated with drought and rain, whose enemies are consumed by fire from above and who was taken into heaven by a whirlwind in a chariot of fire with horses of fire.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Russian tradition portrays the Prophet Ilya as thundering across the sky in a flaming car and striking the clouds with lightning darts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the Vladimir Government, Ilya is said to destroy devils with stone arrows.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The stone arrows of Ilya are explicitly compared to the hammer of Thor and the lance of Indra.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On Ilya's day peasants expect thunder and rain, set rye and oats on their gates, and ask clergy to praise Ilya so that he may bless their cornfields with abundance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In some districts people collectively attend church on Ilya's day, then kill and roast a beast bought by the community, cut its flesh into small pieces, and sell these portions so that the money goes to the church.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Staying away from the Ilya-day ceremony or failing to buy a piece of the meat is considered a great sin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Mowing or making hay on Ilya's day is believed to risk Elijah smiting the field with thunder or burning the crop with lightning.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Old Novgorod is said to have had two churches dedicated to Elijah, one called \"Ilya the Wet\" and the other \"Ilya the Dry.\"","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Cross-bearing processions were made to \"Ilya the Wet\" in times of drought and to \"Ilya the Dry\" when rain was harming the crops.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Diseases are regarded as evil spirits, and invalids are said to have prayed to the thunder-god for relief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A spell against the Siberian cattle-plague implores the \"Holy Prophet of God Ilya\" to send thirty angels in golden array with bows and arrows to destroy the plague.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Servian tradition holds that at the division of the world Ilya received thunder and lightning as his share, and that the crash and blaze of a storm show his contest with the devil.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Servians say the faithful should not cross themselves when thunder peals lest the devil take refuge behind the protecting cross from the heavenly weapons.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Bulgarian tradition says forked lightning is Ilya's lance, with which he chases the Lamia fiend, and that summer lightning comes from the sheen of the lance or the fire issuing from the nostrils of his celestial steeds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Bulgarian tradition calls the white clouds of summer Ilya's heavenly sheep and says he forces the spirits of dead Gypsies to make pellets of snow, i.e., hail, with which he scourges the fields of sinners.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"St. Nicholas is said to have succeeded to the place formerly held by an ancient ruler of the waters and to have a milder character than Ilya.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The passage states that Ilya is the counterpart of Thor and that Nicholas in some respects resembles Odin.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"A moujik is described as always keeping Nicholas's day holy, lighting a taper and having a service performed, but not keeping Elijah's day and even working on it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Elijah and Nicholas are said to walk over the moujik's land and see his cornfields, where green blades are growing splendidly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Nicholas remarks that there will be a good harvest, praises the moujik as honest and pious, and says the harvest will fall into good hands.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Elijah replies that he will burn all the moujik's land with lightning and flatten it with hail so that the moujik will learn to keep Elijah's day holy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"After Elijah and Nicholas quarrel and part, Nicholas goes to the moujik and tells him to sell all his standing corn to the Elijah priest, warning that otherwise hail will beat the crop flat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The moujik bargains with the Elijah priest, sells his whole crop, receives the money, and goes home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"A stormcloud later rolls up and empties itself over the moujik's cornfields with heavy rain and hail, cutting down the entire crop.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The next day Elijah and Nicholas walk past the devastated cornfield; Elijah says he has destroyed the moujik's field, but Nicholas responds that the field now belongs to the Elijah priest.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Perun","description":"An old Slavonic thunder-god, considered Lord of the Harvest, whose functions are said to have been taken over by the Christian Prophet Elijah.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Prophet Elijah / Ilya","description":"Biblical prophet and Christian saint who in Russian and other Slavonic traditions acts as a thunder-god, riding a flaming car, wielding lightning and hail against devils, diseases, and sinners, and associated with drought, rain, and harvest.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:3","role:4","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:9","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Peasants / lay worshippers","description":"Russian rural people who connect Elijah with Perun, expect thunder and rain on Ilya's day, perform gate and church rituals, participate in the sacrificial feast, and fear punishment on their crops.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Clergy / priests (general)","description":"Christian clergy asked to laud Ilya's name on his day and who receive money from the sale of the sacrificial beast's meat.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Invalids / sick petitioners","description":"People who, viewing diseases as evil spirits, pray to the thunder-god for relief and use spells invoking Elijah and angels against cattle-plague.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Thirty angels in golden array","description":"Angelic warriors requested in a spell to be sent by Elijah, armed with bows and arrows, to destroy the Siberian cattle-plague.","role_refs":["role:18"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Siberian cattle-plague","description":"A livestock disease treated in the passage as an evil spirit to be destroyed by Elijah's angels.","role_refs":["role:16"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"Servian believers / tradition","description":"Servian people or their tradition, which say Elijah received thunder and lightning and that storms show his contest with the devil, and advise against crossing oneself during thunder.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Bulgarian believers / tradition","description":"Bulgarian people or their tradition, which interpret The discussion then turns to Russian tales in which a youngest prince descends into an underground world or ascends to an enchanted upper realm, and whose elder brothers repeatedly try to kill him as he returns. One variant explains their behavior by fear of a severed snake’s head the hero is carrying, but the author considers this an ad hoc invention. He instead explains such fraternal hostility by reference to \"oriental\" polygynous family structures, where the hero is the son of a younger wife and is hated by his half-brothers, citing an Indian analogue to Norka and the biblical story of Joseph. First, a city called Troyan receives a miraculously appearing deep lake from the Lord, but it is guarded by a terrible monster that demands a maiden each day in exchange for access to water. After three years the king’s daughter, called the Troyan Andromeda, is exposed on the lake shore as a sacrifice. A \"Perseus\" in the form of St. George comes to save her, falls asleep with his head on her knees as she combs his hair, is awakened by her tears as the monster approaches, kills the monster, and converts the inhabitants of Troyan to Christianity. Next, St. Nicholas is described as a kindly helper of peasants, contrasted with St. Kasian. In one story a peasant’s cart is stuck in muddy road; Kasian refuses to help to keep his heavenly clothes clean, while Nicholas helps and becomes muddy. The Lord later questions them and decrees that Kasian will be honored by men only once every four years, whereas Nicholas will be honored twice a year, explaining current prayer customs. Another story tells of two moujiks, one rich and one poor. The poor man borrows money from the rich man with St. Nicholas’s icon as surety and cannot repay. The rich man abuses the icon, carting and flogging it, until a young merchant pays the debt and rescues the picture, hanging it in honor with a lamp burning before it. An old man then becomes the merchant’s manager and brings him prosperity. Meanwhile, an evil witch enchants a king’s daughter so that she lies dead by day and rises at night to eat people; she is shut in a coffin in a church and promised, with half the kingdom, to anyone who can disenchant her. Guided by the old manager’s instructions, the merchant keeps watch, undergoes adventures, and succeeds; the narrator reveals that the old man was St. Nicholas himself. Finally, the beginning of a legend titled \"The Priest with the Greedy Eyes\" is given: in St. Nicholas’s parish lives a Pope (priest) with \"pope-like\" eyes, who serves Nicholas until he is destitute. Out of spite he gathers the church keys, strikes Nicholas’s picture with them, leaves the parish following his greedy eyes, meets an unknown man on the road who asks to be his companion, and they travel together, sharing biscuits and loaves. After a hailstorm devastates the field, the Prophet Elijah promises to restore it and make it twice as good, while St. Nicholas quietly advises the peasant to buy back the ruined crop for half price, which the priest gladly accepts. The field miraculously regenerates: new shoots grow, timely rain falls, and an abundant, weed-free crop of rye ripens like gold. Elijah later assumes he has rewarded the priest, but Nicholas points out that the land now belongs to the peasant. Elijah then declares that he will ‘take the profit out of the corn’ so no matter how many sheaves are threshed, only a peck of grain will emerge at a time. Nicholas warns the peasant and tells him to thresh only one sheaf at a time; thus, each sheaf yields a peck, filling all his bins and barns and prompting him to build new barns for the surplus. Seeing this prosperity, Elijah accuses Nicholas of revealing everything to the peasant and threatens that the peasant will not forget him, prompting Nicholas to sense danger and instruct the peasant to buy two wax tapers, a large and a small, and to use them in a specific way. Elijah and Nicholas, disguised as wayfarers, meet the peasant carrying a big rouble taper and a tiny copeck taper; the peasant says he will offer the large taper to Elijah for the doubled harvest and the small one to Nicholas. Nicholas uses this to show Elijah that the peasant credits Elijah most, and Elijah is appeased, abandoning his threat. The peasant prospers and thereafter honors both Elijah’s Day and Nicholas’s Day equally. The commentary then notes that the thunderous power once attributed to the pagan god Perun is now shared among various Christian saints. Prophet Ilya (Elijah) is one bearer of this power; others include St. George, who pierces monsters with his lance, and St. Andrew, who strikes places given over to witchcraft with his mace. A legend from the Chernigof Government tells of a village with over a thousand witches who stole the holy stars until none remained to light the sinful world. He asks, \"Woe, is that you that’s helping me to sing?\" A voice answers, \"Yes, master, it’s I that’s helping you,\" and after he invites Woe to go on together, Woe replies that it will never depart from him.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","rights_note":"Public domain (Project Gutenberg; Ralston translation)."},{"id":"ev:8","type":"summary","locator":"lines 8155-8330","quote_or_summary":"When they reach home, Woe urges the peasant to go to the pot-house. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l15309-l15468","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 15309-15468","start":"15309","end":"15468","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The editor introduces a legend illustrating the Russian belief that a hasty or angry word can place a person in the power of the Evil One during life and after death. He notes that the tale is a variant of stories about a youth who visits the Water King and elopes with the monarch's daughter, differing mainly in that a devil replaces other mythical figures such as Slavonic Neptune or an Indian Rakshasa. The legend itself tells of a poor old couple with an only son. The mother repeatedly asks neighboring peasants in two villages to give their daughters in marriage, but all refuse. Distressed, the son asks his parents' blessing to seek his fate wherever his eyes lead him. Weeping along the highway, he laments that no girl will marry him and declares that he would even accept a bride from the devil. Immediately an old man rises from the earth, questions him about his words, reassures him, and leads him to a lake. When the youth turns his back to the lake and walks backwards, he suddenly finds himself beneath the water in a richly furnished white-stone palace. There the old man feeds him and presents twelve maidens, each more beautiful than the last, offering any of them as a bride. The youth asks for time until morning to choose and is taken to a private chamber. As he lies awake, a beautiful maiden enters, explains that he has become the devil's guest, and warns that his life depends on following her instructions so he can return to the \"white world.\" She tells him that the fiend will present twelve identical maidens and that he must choose her, recognizable by a fly above her right eye. She then reveals that she is the daughter of a priest from another village who vanished at age nine: after her father, in anger, exclaimed \"May devils fly away with you!\" she went out crying on the steps and was seized by fiends who brought her to live with them in the underwater palace. The next morning the old man presents twelve identical maidens and orders the youth to choose his bride; using the fly as a sign, he correctly identifies the same maiden three times despite the fiend's attempts to confuse him by shifting their positions.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The narrator states that in Russian belief a hasty word can place its utterer or its victim in the power of the Evil One, not only after death but also during life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The narrator says that this idea of the hasty word has given rise to numerous Russian legends and still exists as a living faith among the peasantry.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The narrator remarks that the story will be recognized as a variant of tales about a youth who visits the Water King and elopes with one of that monarch's daughters.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"He explains that the main difference is that a devil of the Satanic type is substituted for a mythical personage, such as Slavonic Neptune or Indian Rakshasa, who plays a similar part in other skazkas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the legend, an old couple living in great poverty in a village have one son.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The old woman tells the old man that it is time to get their son married.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The old man tells his wife to go and ask for a wife for their son.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The old woman goes to a neighbor and then to other peasants asking for their daughters as a wife for her son, but each refuses and she is eventually turned away from every house in the village.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"She returns home and tells her husband that no one will give their daughter to their son, calling him an unlucky fellow.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The old man says that summer is approaching and they have no one to work for them, and advises his wife to seek a bride in another village.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In another village the old woman again visits every house but everyone refuses, and she returns saying that no one wants to become related to them as poor beggars.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The old man replies that there is no use in wearing out her legs and tells her to jump up on to the polati.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The couple's son is sorely afflicted and entreats his parents to give him their blessing so that he may go and seek his fate, saying he will go where his eyes lead him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The parents give their son their blessing and let him go wherever it pleases him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Walking along the highway, the youth weeps bitterly and laments that he must be worse than other men since no girl is willing to marry him, saying that if the devil himself would give him a bride he would take even her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Suddenly a very old man appears as if rising from the earth, greets the youth, and asks what he was saying just now.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The old man tells the youth not to be afraid, says he will not harm him and may help him out of his trouble, and urges him to speak boldly.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The youth explains his situation and repeats that in his misery he said that if the devil offered him a bride he would take even her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The old man laughs and tells the youth to follow him, promising to let him choose a lovely bride for himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"They reach a lake, where the old man instructs the youth to turn his back to the lake and walk backwards; after a couple of steps the youth finds himself under the water in a white-stone palace with splendidly furnished and decorated rooms.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"In the palace, the old man gives the youth food and drink and then introduces twelve maidens, each more beautiful than the other, telling him to choose whichever he likes and that whichever he chooses will be bestowed upon him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The youth says the choice is puzzling and asks for time until the next morning to think about it, and the old man agrees and leads him to a private chamber where he lies down to sleep and think.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"As the youth lies thinking about which bride to choose, a beautiful maiden enters his chamber, asks whether he is asleep, and he replies that he cannot sleep because he is always thinking which bride to choose.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The maiden says she has come to give him counsel, tells him he has become the devil's guest, and warns that if he wants to go on living in the white world he must follow her instructions, otherwise he will never get out of the place alive.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"She instructs him that the fiend will bring twelve maidens exactly alike and that he must carefully choose her, marked by a disappeared from home at nine years old, and recalls that one day her father, angry with her, said, \"May devils fly away with you!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"She recounts that after her father's curse she went out on the steps and began to cry, whereupon fiends suddenly seized her, brought her to the underwater palace, and she has been living with them there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The next morning the old man brings in twelve fair maidens, each exactly like the others, and orders the youth to choose his bride.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The youth selects the maiden above maiden.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"youth / son","description":"Only son of a poor old couple who cannot obtain a bride through his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l15060-l15187","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 15060-15187","start":"15060","end":"15187","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Dark is it in the forest without Byelun\"; \"The devil take thee!\"","summary":"Ralston notes that the old gods of the Slavonians have mostly vanished but survive in peasant sayings about a benevolent White or bright god, Byelun, who guides travellers and gives gold, and a malevolent Black god cursed in imprecations. He then describes a belief that infants cursed before birth, suffocated, or dying unchristened (or christened by a drunken priest) become prey to demons, and a ritual by which a mother can recover the soul of a suffocated child by standing for three nights within a priest-traced circle in a church until the cocks crow and the demons return the child. Emphasizing the power and irrevocability of parental curses, he introduces two tales: in the first, an old hunter near Lake Onega sells his dog to a stranger and later visits the Mian mountain, where he finds a city of devils and obtains a captive youth instead of payment, who proves to be the son of a merchant whose wife cursed him and thus caused the devil to carry him off. In the second tale, an old couple’s son, cursed by his mother before birth, grows up, marries, and disappears; a beggar in a forest hut hears a nightly horseman lament that the Lord should judge his mother for cursing him unborn. The father meets and follows this rider to a frozen river, where the son rides into an ice-hole and vanishes; the parents fail to recover him, but the young wife follows him, removes her cross at his request, jumps into the ice-hole, and finds herself in a vast hall beneath the water where Satan is seated and her husband identifies her as his wife.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ralston states that the old gods of the Slavonians have passed away but leave scant traces in peasant traditions and proverbial expressions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Among the peasants of White Russia there is a memory of a white or bright being now called Byelun, who leads belated travellers out of forests and bestows gold on men who serve him well.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Peasant sayings include the phrases \"Dark is it in the forest without Byelun\" and, of a fortunate man, \"He must have made friends with Byelun.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The memory of a black or evil god survives in imprecations such as the Ukrainian curse \"May the black god smite thee!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"It is said that infants cursed by their mothers before birth, suffocated in their sleep, or dying unchristened or christened by a drunken priest become the prey of demons.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Russian peasants are reported to believe that to rescue the soul of a suffocated babe from fiends, the mother must spend three nights in a church, standing within a circle traced by a priest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the cocks crow on the third morning, the demons are said to give the mother back her dead child.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ralston remarks that great stress is laid in skazkas and legends on the terrible power of a parent's curse, whose \"hasty word\" can condemn even an innocent child to slavery among devils and is irrevocable once uttered.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ralston comments that, despite the fearful efficacy of such curses, they have not silenced bad language, contrasting this with the fictional Vril that made war impossible among the Vril-ya in \"The Coming Race.\"","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the first tale, an old man living near Lake Onega supports himself and his wife by hunting.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A well-dressed man meets the hunter, buys his dog, and tells him to come for his money to the Mian mountain the next evening.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"When the hunter goes to the top of the Mian mountain, he finds a great city inhabited by devils and locates the house of his debtor.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the devils’ bath-room the hunter is served by a young man, who, after the bath, falls at his feet and begs him not to accept money for the dog but to ask for the youth instead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The hunter agrees and asks for the young man to serve him as a son, and the devils are compelled to give the youth to him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"At the youth’s direction, the hunter goes to Novgorod and asks a merchant whether he has any children.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The merchant replies that he had an only son whose mother cursed him in a passion, crying \"The devil take thee!\", whereupon the devil carried him off.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"It is revealed that the youth rescued from the devils is the merchant’s son, and the merchant rejoices and takes the hunter and his wife to live with him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"In the second tale from the Vladimir Government, an old couple have an only son whom the mother cursed before he was born; he grows up and marries, but then suddenly disappears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A hut stands in a nearby forest, and an old beggar spends the night there, lying on the stove.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"During the night a horseman arrives, dismounts, enters the hut, and spends the night there, muttering repeatedly, \"May the Lord judge my mother, in that she cursed me while a babe unborn!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The beggar reports this to the old couple; the father then hides behind the stove in the hut, recognizes the horseman as his son when he arrives, and follows him on foot at his command.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Father and son reach a frozen river with a hole in the ice, and the youth rides straight into that hole so that both he and his horse disappear under the ice.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The father lingers by the ice-hole, later tells his wife he has found their son but that he lives in the water; the mother visits the hut the next night but also fails to get him back.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"On the third night, the son's young wife goes to the hut, hides behind the stove, and when he enters, she declares she will never part from him and follows him to the ice-hole.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"At the edge of the ice-hole, the wife states that if he goes into the water, she will follow; he tells her to take off her cross, and she does so and leaps into the hole.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"After leaping into the ice-hole, the young wife finds herself in a vast hall where Satan is seated, and her husband identifies her to Satan as his wife.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Old gods of the traditions.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Byelun (White or bright god)","description":"A white or bright being remembered among White Russian content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l5151-l5296","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 5151-5296","start":"5151","end":"5296","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston describes recurring figures in Russian skazkas: beautiful maidens who live under the waves and can transform into birds (often called Swan-Maidens). They are usually daughters of the Morskoi Tsar or Water King, a somewhat undefined underwater monarch who dwells in splendid halls beneath the sea and at times seizes human victims, typically boys who later marry one of his daughters and escape with her to the upper world. The Water King’s role sometimes overlaps with that of Koshchei or a Snake. Ralston notes that the following skazka has incidents similar to West-European folk-tales. The story “The Water King and Vasilissa the Wise” then begins: a King fond of hunting aims at an eaglet perched on an oak. Three times the eaglet begs him not to shoot and to take it home and feed it for three years, promising future service. After the third plea the King relents, brings the eaglet home, and feeds it; over two years it devours all his cattle. The bird, now an eagle, twice asks to be released; the first time it cannot yet fly and demands a third year of feeding even if the King must borrow cattle. After the third year the eagle can fly and invites the King onto its back. During their flight the eagle three times drops the King into the sea (to his knees, girdle, and neck) and rescues him each time, asking whether he was frightened. The King admits fear but says he hoped God and the creature would pull him out. The eagle explains that this repays the King’s three attempts to shoot it and that the King has now experienced the fear of death. They then fly beyond “thrice nine lands.” The eagle has the King describe what he sees above, below, and to either side: sky above, earth below, an open plain to the right, and a house to the left, which the eagle identifies as his youngest sister’s. They visit; the sister warmly welcomes her brother and seats him at a table, but leaves the King outside and sets greyhounds on him. The enraged eagle seizes the King and flies off. Looking back, the King sees a red house; the eagle says it is the sister’s house burning because she mistreated the King. The flight continues as the eagle again asks what lies above and below.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The skazkas mention beautiful maidens who usually live beneath the wave and can transform themselves into birds and fly wherever they please.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"These bird-transforming maidens are, for the most part, daughters of the Morskoi Tsar or Water King.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Water King is described as a patriarchal monarch of somewhat shadowy form, living in subaqueous halls of light and splendor, who sometimes emerges to seize a human victim, generally a boy.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Stories usually represent the captured boy as obtaining the hand of one of the Water King’s daughters and escaping with her to the upper world with difficulty.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The role usually filled by the Water King is sometimes allotted instead to Koshchei or to the Snake in Slavonic popular fiction.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ralston states that many features of the skazka about to be told closely resemble those of various well-known West-European folk-tales.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the skazka, a King who is very fond of hunting and shooting goes out hunting and sees an eaglet sitting on an oak and prepares to shoot it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Three times the eaglet begs the King not to shoot, asking him instead to take it home and feed it for three years, promising that it will someday be of service or use to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After the third entreaty, the King relents, takes the eaglet home, and feeds it; over two years it eats so much that it devours all his cattle, leaving him without cows or sheep.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After two years the eagle asks to be set free, but when released it cannot yet fly and demands that the King feed it for one more year even if he has to borrow cattle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The King borrows cattle from people around him and feeds the eagle for a third year, after which the eagle can fly and invites the King to sit on its back so they can fly together.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"They fly until they reach a blue sea, where the eagle shakes the King off so that he falls into the sea and sinks up to his knees; the eagle then catches him on its wing and asks if he was frightened, and the King replies that he thought he was going to drown outright.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Over a second sea, the eagle drops the King in the middle so that he sinks up to his girdle, then rescues him again; the King says he was frightened but thought that perhaps God and the creature would pull him out.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Over a third sea with a great gulf, the eagle drops the King so that he sinks up to his neck and again rescues him onto its wing, asking each time if he was frightened.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The eagle tells the King that these actions were in payment of an old score, reminding him of the three times he had been about to shoot the eaglet, and adds that now the King has felt what the fear of death is like.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"During the falls into the sea, the King thinks to himself that perhaps the eagle will pull him out and at one point explicitly thinks, ‘please God, the creature will pull me out.’","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After these trials, the eagle and the King fly beyond ‘thrice nine lands’ for a long time.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"While flying, the eagle asks the King what is above and below them; the King answers that above is the sky and below is the earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The eagle asks what is on the right and left; the King sees an open plain on the right and a house on the left, which the eagle says belongs to his youngest sister.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"They fly to the house, whose mistress comes out, cordially receives her brother the eagle and seats him at an oaken table, but does not look at the King and leaves him outside, where she releases greyhounds and sets them at him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The eagle becomes exceedingly angry at his sister’s treatment of the King, jumps up from the table, seizes the King, and flies away with him again.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"As they fly away, the eagle tells the King to look back; the King sees a red house, and the eagle explains that it is his youngest sister’s house on fire because she did not receive the King and set greyhounds at him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"After leaving the burning house behind, they continue flying, and the eagle again asks the King what is above and below THE HASTY WORD 370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 2430-2540","start":"2430","end":"2540","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage surveys simpleton-tales and then introduces the animal story \"The Mizgir.\" It first describes a widely known tale about over-anxious people who weep over misfortunes that might befall their as-yet-unborn grandchildren, giving a Scottish version (two old maids imagining a grandchild falling from a window and dying) and a Russian version about Lutonya, whose parents grieve over a purely hypothetical grandchild supposedly killed by a dropped log. Offended by their foolishness, Lutonya leaves home, vowing not to return until he finds people more foolish, and in one Russian story he witnesses various absurd acts (raising a cow to a grass-covered roof, forcing a horse into its collar, and a woman fetching milk from a cellar one spoonful at a time) but the story ends before he succeeds. In another Russian tale, Lutonya departs after his mother is cheated by a sharper; he helps carpenters who try to stretch a too-short beam, encounters reapers who bite off ears of corn because they lack sickles, fashions a sickle they mistake for a monstrous worm and try to drown by sending a man on a log into a river, where he drowns while onlookers worry only about his leggings, and finally meets a man who, like a well-known Irish anecdotal figure, forgets to count himself when counting his party. The narrator remarks that many such Russian tales parallel English fool stories (wise men of Gotham, an old woman tricked by a pedlar named Stout, and other inhabitants of \"Fool-land\") and German exaggeration stories (Lügenmärchen) behind Baron Munchausen. The passage then quotes the beginning of an animal tale, \"The Mizgir.\" In ancient times gnats and flies swarm, biting people and drawing blood, until a bold Spider appears and spins webs along roads to catch them. A Gadfly is snared; she begs for mercy for the sake of her many offspring, and the Spider releases her. She then summons gnats and flies to hide under an ash-tree's roots from the Spider. The Spider finds a Cricket, Beetle, and Bug and instructs them to act as snuff-taking crier, drummer, and herald to proclaim falsely that the Spider has been executed in Kazan and no longer lives. The insects, reassured by the Bug's proclamation, rejoice, cross themselves three times, fly out from under the ash tree, and are immediately caught in the Spider's webs, as the Spider begins to Reaching a sea, the grateful pike forms a bridge so he can cross to an oak where Koshchei's death is hidden in a casket. When Ivan opens it, a hare escapes; the spared wolf catches it. A duck flies out of the hare; the crow catches it, enabling Ivan to obtain an egg that contains Koshchei's death. After Ivan drops the egg in the sea, the pike retrieves it and again bridges the water so he can return to his mother. She hides him when Koshchei returns; Ivan tortures Koshchei by squeezing the egg and finally kills him by smashing it. Ivan and his mother take what they want, collect a princess Ivan is to marry, and head home. At a hill where Ivan's brothers are waiting, the princess sends Ivan back for a forgotten wedding robe, ring, and seamless shoes. Ivan first sends his mother and the princess down a ladder; his brothers cut it and coerce the women into concealing his role, then return home where their father rejoices at their return but mourns missing Ivan. Ivan retrieves the bride's possessions, discovers the ring can summon twelve youths who carry him down from the hill, and travels to his home city. He lodges with an old woman and learns that his mother and brothers have returned with a princess. The eldest brother wishes to marry her, but she demands her betrothal ring; a proclamation has failed to find anyone who can supply it. The father-in-law wanted to take it away with him...\" and a West Highland scene \"how a youngest sister took service in a house where a corpse lay\" and watched a dead man who rose three times at night before she struck him with a stick and later received gold, silver, and a vessel of cordial.","summary":"The excerpt concludes a Russian skazka episode in which, after a repeated confrontation, a woman lays a cross on a male assailant as he rushes at her, causing him to fall down dead. Looking into a coffin, she finds a large amount of money; her father-in-law wants to take it or at least ensure that only someone more cunning than himself receives it. The narrator then cites a West Highland Celtic tale, \"The Girl and the Dead Man,\" where a youngest sister takes service in a house containing a corpse. While sewing and watching the dead man at night, she sees him rise and grin at her three times; she threatens him, and on the third rising strikes him with a stick, which adheres to him along with her hand, and they go out. Eventually she gains a peck of gold, a peck of silver, and a vessel of cordial, and returns home. When he later claims a field of corn as his own, it begins to burn until he corrects himself and names it as Militsa's, after which the fire ceases. Another story tells of Ivan the Unlucky, whose failures lead him to seek help from the king; the king's daughter proposes that marriage might give him a new Fortune, and the king angrily orders her to marry him, after which Ivan becomes lucky. In another tale, a poor man meets two ladies, Fortune and Misfortune, who attempt to help him with gifts of money that his wife unwittingly gives away, until they give him two farthings to pass to fishermen \"for his luck\"; the resulting catch of a fish brings him wealth. A final story describes a young merchant's son whose extreme bad luck ruins all his ventures and employers; a king then names him \"Luckless,\" marks his forehead, and decrees that he be exempt from taxes and always fed and housed but never allowed to stay more than one day in any place, so he wanders, always received and then expelled. He argues that folk-songs may strongly reflect national character, but European folk-tales often consist of modern adaptations of old, foreign themes transplanted from other climates, so they give only a partial picture of national life. He describes the bulk of Russian and other Indo-European folk-tales as centered on adventures of fairy princes and princesses and on combats between heroes and giants, trolls, ogres, snakes, dragons, and other monsters, set in a Fairy-land where relations between mortals, immortals, humans, animals, and the spiritual and material worlds are far less restricted than in modern Europe. Some commentators interpret these heroic combats as typifying ancient struggles between aboriginals and invaders. Ralston notes that stories common across Europe vary more with geography than moral character, and that style changes greatly as tales travel. He highlights Russian Skazkas as stylistically characteristic of the Russian people, praising Russian peasants’ narrative and acting talents, the simple and quaint language, natural humor, vivid content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l5583-l5712","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE THREE KINGDOMS. / VASSILISSA GOLDEN TRESS, BAREHEADED BEAUTY. / THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS. / THE FOOTLESS AND THE BLIND.; lines 5583-5712","start":"5583","end":"5712","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Vassilissa Kirbítyevna cleverly decorates Koshchéi Without-Death’s broom and then his goat to provoke him into revealing where his death is hidden. Mocking her supposed stupidity, Koshchéi finally explains that his death lies far away: on an island in the sea, under an oak tree, in a buried chest containing a hare, inside a duck, and finally in an egg. After he departs to hunt, Vassilissa tells Ivan Tsarevich, and with their strong companion Bulat they set out to find this hidden death. When they run out of provisions, Bulat repeatedly wants to kill animals for food—a mother dog with her whelps, an eagle with eaglets, and a lobster on the seashore—but each animal begs for mercy, promises future service, and is spared. The companions cross the sea in a fisherman’s boat to the island, where Bulat uproots the oak and uncovers the buried chest. A hare leaps out and runs, but the spared dog catches it; Bulat tears it open, releasing a duck that flies upward, only to be caught and brought by the spared eagle. When Bulat rends the duck, an egg falls into the sea, and the spared lobster retrieves it. They take the egg to Koshchéi and strike him on the forehead with it, and he dies at once. Ivan takes Vassilissa with him, and they travel homeward with Bulat. On three successive nights Bulat stands guard while Ivan and Vassilissa sleep in a tent. At midnight twelve doves arrive each night, strike wing against wing, and become maidens, who identify Koshchéi as their brother and Vassilissa as their sister-in-law. They foretell that when Ivan returns home, his favorite dog, then his favorite horse, and finally his favorite cow—whose milk nourished him in childhood—will each in turn break free and kill him. They add that whoever hears these warnings and tells Ivan will be turned to stone: first up to the knees, then up to the girdle, and finally entirely. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l15062-l15196","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING. / THE HEDGEHOG, THE MERCHANT, THE KING, AND THE POOR MAN.; lines 15062-15196","start":"15062","end":"15196","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A little boy has won a magical flower-garden and marble palace and receives a golden rod that can transform them into a portable golden apple. Guided by a little golden bird, he and his sister return \"home,\" where the bird instructs them to restore the palace and garden, reveals that they are the king's son and daughter, and gives them a picture in a golden frame showing their arms and names, to be hung in the palace and kept hidden under velvet until their father asks about it. The fame of the marble palace and flowery garden spreads through the kingdom, drawing visitors from afar and reaching the king, who resolves to see it. An old woman drugs the king so he falls ill and cannot travel, then offers to visit the palace and garden in his stead; she intends to destroy the children but her weapons break and she fails. At the garden she praises its beauty but claims it would be seven times more beautiful if it had the world-sounding tree. When the boy asks how to obtain it, she says it stands in an enchanted palace at a specified place and that they must go and bring it. From then on the boy is restless; he bids his sister a tearful farewell and sets out alone. He travels across forty-nine kingdoms to a dark enchanted castle guarded by a big, lame, hairy devil with a fearful whip. This first guardian devil angrily questions him, learns he is Yanoshka and seeks the world-sounding tree, but says he has not heard of it and sends him onward to a brother at another enchanted castle. At the second dark castle, another big, lame, hairy devil likewise questions Yanoshka, knows nothing of the tree, and directs him to their eldest brother at a third castle. At the third enchanted castle, a similar devil finally acknowledges the world-beautifully sounding tree in the garden of that palace. He gives Yanoshka a golden rod and detailed instructions: strike the castle wall three times to open a door, find the tree in the middle of the garden, walk around it three times, then flee swiftly before the stone wall closes. If Yanoshka fails and is shut inside, he will be turned to stone and never again see the bright sky or day.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The little boy wins the flower-garden and marble palace and is given a golden rod, as well as shown where the garden and palace are located.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Using the golden rod, the boy strikes the side of the garden and palace three times, and they turn into a golden apple that he can carry in his pocket.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The little golden bird flies ahead of the boy and girl as they travel home with the golden apple.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The golden bird tells the children they have reached home and instructs them to place the golden apple on a spot and strike it three times so a marble palace and flower-garden will appear there.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The golden bird says that the palace and garden will speak to the seven kingdoms, their report will spread, and the king himself will come to look at them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The golden bird reveals that the little boy is the king's son and the little girl is the king's daughter, and provides a picture in a golden frame showing their arms and THE HASTY WORD                                            370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 632-716","start":"632","end":"716","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"We cross the threshold, a spot hallowed by many traditions, and pass, through what in more pretentious houses may be called the vestibule, into the 'living room.'\"","summary":"Ralston explains that Russian fairy tales, though limited in scope, provide an incomplete but fairly accurate idea of the mental characteristics of the peasantry and of Russian village life. He notes that the tales give little explicit information about religious views or social relations under serfdom, but scattered realistic vignettes amid idealized adventures allow readers to construct a mental picture of a Russian village. He describes the landscape (corn-land, forest, river) and its seasonal changes, the single-street village with wooden barn-like huts, and the contrasting appearance of the land in spring, summer, harvest-time, and winter snow. He then sketches Sunday and holiday life with churchgoing, girls' songs and summer choral dances, winter social gatherings, peasant weddings, and funeral parties going to desolate burial nooks. Working days show peasants driving out with carts to till the soil and wield tools, girls laughing by a stream or pool in summer, the frozen water with an ice-hole frequented by wives and daughters in winter, and the picturesque night-time look of the houses. Above all he emphasizes cottage interiors: better-class homesteads with fences, gates, barns, cattle-sheds, gardens for fruit and vegetables, a threshold hallowed by traditions, a living room with a cellar under the wooden floor, an honored corner containing holy pictures, and a large stove described as the heart of the house and the family's sleeping place. He contrasts this with poverty-stricken huts resembling cattle sheds, where smoke escapes through a tattered roof and much suffering is borne with patience and resignation; even there domestic virtues, family affection, filial reverence, and parental love are evident. Lamps burning before holy pictures in many poor homes suggest that the peasants are sometimes lifted by lofty thoughts and noble aspirations above their hard lives. The chapter selects such stories for their graphic village descriptions and their illustration of Russian sentiment and humor, likening them to a painter's rough notes that can still give a true content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l4100-l4220","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON. / WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH. / THE FOOTLESS AND BLIND CHAMPIONS. / THE THREE KINGDOMS.; lines 4100-4220","start":"4100","end":"4220","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Peerless Beauty repeatedly coaxes Koshchéi Without-Death to reveal the location of his death, first tricking him when he falsely claims it is in a broom and an oak fence, and eventually learning that his death is in an egg inside a duck in a stump floating on the sea. While Koshchéi rides off to war, she instructs Ivan Tsarevich, bakes him cakes, and sends him to seek this hidden death. Ivan travels to the distant sea, runs out of food, and repeatedly spares a hawk, a bear, and a pike who beg for mercy and promise later help. A magical rising of the sea forces him up a tree; when the waters recede, a stump is left on shore. The bear breaks open the stump, releasing a duck; the hawk catches and tears the duck so that an egg falls out, and the pike retrieves the egg from the water and gives it to Ivan. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l2904-l3023","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON. / WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH.; lines 2904-3023","start":"2904","end":"3023","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ivan Tsarevich seeks the thirtieth kingdom to see a beautiful maiden from whose hands and feet healing water flows. A giant who has guarded her kingdom for a hundred years boasts of killing mighty heroes and blocks the way, so Ivan turns aside. In a forest cabin an ancient woman greets him, learns his purpose, and gives him magic herbs and a rolling ball. She instructs him to burn the herbs so their smoke will put the giant into a deep sleep, then cut off his head and follow the ball to the maiden’s golden castle, where she leads an army of maidens, spends nine days amusing herself in the meadows, and then sleeps a hero’s sleep for nine days and nights. Ivan follows her instructions, uses the herbs’ smoke to fell the giant, decapitates him, and follows the ball to the golden palace. He hides in a thicket and watches the maiden and her all-female army sport in the meadows for nine days. On the tenth day he enters the palace and finds the maiden and her army asleep; healing water flows from her hands and feet. He fills a flask with the water, falls in love with her beauty, and rides home. When the maiden wakes after nine days she rages, pursues Ivan on her swift mare, overtakes him, and kills him with a sword blow to the breast. Pitying his beauty, she uses her healing water to close his wound and revive him, then asks him to take her as his wife. He agrees, and she tells him to go home and wait three years. As he approaches his home kingdom, his elder brothers, who have set guards to watch for him, intercept him, drug him, steal the flask of healing water, and throw him into a deep pit from which he emerges into an underground kingdom. There he travels until a storm with lightning, thunder, and rain forces him to take shelter under a tree where young birds sit soaked in a nest. He covers them with his coat. Their enormous mother returns, darkening the sky, and, seeing her chicks protected, blesses Ivan and offers a reward. At his request she agrees to carry him to the upper world, asking him first to prepare a double box filled half with game and half with water to feed her during the flight. He does so, rides in the box on her back, and she bears him to the upper world before departing. Ivan goes to his father the Tsar, who, influenced by his elder sons’ lies, dislikes him and sends him into exile. Ivan wanders for three years. Then the beautiful maiden arrives by ship at the Tsar’s capital and sends a letter demanding the man who stole the healing water, threatening to burn and destroy the kingdom if he is not produced. The Tsar sends his eldest son to her ship. Two small boys, the Tsar’s grandsons, see him and ask their mother if he is their father; she says he is their uncle and tells them to take whips and flog him back home, which they do, and he returns disgraced.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ivan Tsarevich declares that he is going to the thirtieth kingdom to see a beautiful maiden from whose hands and feet healing water flows.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A giant says he has guarded the maiden’s kingdom for a hundred years, boasts of defeating many great heroes, and mocks Ivan as a weak \"little worm.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ivan, realizing he cannot overcome the giant directly, turns aside from that path.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ivan comes to a sleeping forest where there is a cabin containing an ancient woman who greets him by name and asks why God has brought him there.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ivan explains his situation to the old woman, who gives him magic herbs and a ball and explains how to use them to put the giant to sleep and find the maiden’s golden castle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The old woman instructs Ivan to make a fire in an open field, throw the herbs on it while standing to windward, so the smoke will cause the giant to sleep a deep sleep; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l7137-l7259","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MARYA MOREVNA. / VARIANT OF THE RESCUE OF IVAN TSAREVICH AND THE WINNING OF THE COLT. / YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS.; lines 7137-7259","start":"7137","end":"7259","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An old man and his old wife, long childless, pray to God for a child to help them in their old age. After seven years of prayer the Lord grants them seven sons, all named Simeon. When the parents die, the sons are left orphans at about ten years old and plough their own land. Tsar Ador passes their village, marvels at the small boys doing heavy field work, and sends his chief boyar to question them. Learning they are seven orphan brothers all called Simeon, he summons them to his palace. There he consults his boyars about educating the boys; on their advice, he asks each brother what science or art he wishes to pursue. Each Simeon instead claims an extraordinary craft: the eldest can forge a pillar to the sky if given a forge; the second can climb such a pillar and see all lands; the third can create a ship by striking with an axe; the fourth can seize a ship and take it to an underground kingdom and back to avoid enemies; the fifth can shoot a bird at a hundred versts; the sixth can catch any bird his brother shoots before it falls and bring it to the Tsar; the seventh is a master thief surpassing all others. The Tsar welcomes the first six talents but is enraged by the seventh’s thieving art and asks how to put him to death. His boyars advise sparing the thief, reminding the Tsar that for ten years he has failed to obtain Tsarevna Yelena the Beautiful, losing armies and treasure, and suggesting that Simeon the thief might be able to steal her for him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An old man and his old wife lived to a great age without children and The king notices his condition and, after hearing of the woman's unrivaled beauty, goes himself to see her and is overwhelmed, as is everyone who beholds her. Deciding she is destined to be his queen rather than a soldier's wife, the king orders the mayor to find a way to get rid of Fedot, threatening him with the gallows if he fails. Wandering miserably through back lanes, the mayor meets Baba-Yaga, who already knows his thoughts and offers help. She devises a plan: tell the king about an island beyond the thrice-ninth land in the thirtieth kingdom where a deer with golden horns lives, have a rotten old ship refitted and manned with fifty drunkard sailors, and send Fedot on a six-year voyage to fetch the deer, expecting the ship to sink and all aboard to drown. The king accepts the plan, orders the ship prepared, and summons Fedot, commanding him under threat of beheading to bring back the golden-horned deer alive. Fedot goes home in deep distress; his wife learns the cause, calls the task an exploit rather than a mere service, and tells him to pray and sleep, saying the morning is wiser than the evening. While he sleeps, she opens a magic-book; two unknown youths appear and ask what she needs. She sends them beyond the thrice-ninth land to seize the golden-horned deer and bring it back. They fly like a whirlwind, capture the deer, deliver it to the house before dawn, and vanish. She wakes Fedot, shows him the deer now in their yard, and instructs him to cage it, take it aboard the ship, sail five days out, and turn back on the sixth. Fedot cages the deer, has it loaded secretly onto the ship, and tells the sailors it is supplies and medicine for the long voyage. On the day of departure a crowd and the king gather at the wharf; the king appoints Fedot chief of the sailors, and the ship sails until the shores disappear. Offering to divide the items, the soldier instead has them fetch vast quantities of pitch and a huge kettle, pours boiling pitch down the mountainside, and tricks them into racing after a rolling stone so that all three are crushed and embedded in the pitch; he then takes the magical items for himself. Using the flying carpet and cap of invisibility, he begins searching for his \"fair princess,\" visiting in turn two remote huts where old, toothless Baba-Yagas live; the first and second sisters cannot help him but direct him onward. He finally reaches the hut of the eldest Baba-Yaga at the end of the world, beyond which lies only outer darkness; she summons all her stormy winds, who blow from every side, to ask if they have seen the princess. When the tardy South Wind arrives, it reports that the beautiful princess lives in a new kingdom where her husband has vanished without news and many kings and princes are courting her; South Wind explains that it can carry a man there in three hours if it blows. The narrative shifts to Vassilissa's mother, the Tsaritsa, who, while mourning her lost children, drinks from a garden spring and accidentally swallows a pea that causes her to conceive and bear Ivan Goroh, a boy who grows with miraculous speed into a mighty champion by the age of ten. Learning how his sister was carried off by a whirlwind and his brothers vanished seeking her, Ivan insists on going to find them despite his parents' objections, and they eventually bless and send him on his way. Ivan travels until he reaches a dark forest where a cabin on hen's legs stands; by reciting a formula he makes it turn toward him, meets an old woman inside, and learns that the supposed whirlwind is actually the Savage Serpent. She warns him of the danger but asks him, if he survives, to bring back from the serpent's castle a water that restores youth, and she directs him toward a bald mountain and the serpent's kingdom. Ivan travels west for a year, passes three kingdoms, reaches the serpent's land, and at the town gate gives alms to a lame, blind beggar, who confirms that Tsarevna Vassilissa Golden Tress is there
