While the Tsar despairs of going further, Nikita asserts he will find the Tsar a bride and tears down the iron fence after the others fail. They ride into the court, pitch white woven, gold-embroidered tents on the green meadow, and sleep; Nikita, lacking a tent, builds a hut from bark mats and keeps watch. At dawn, Yelena the Beautiful notices the tents and broken paling, becomes enraged, and sends a powerful hero to kill the uninvited guests and seize their tents. Nikita defeats the hero with his iron staff but spares his life, sending him back with a message that Yelena should abandon her pride and marry their terrible Tsar. Approaching with outward grace and honor, she conceals the weapon behind her. Recognizing the trap, Nikita puts on the cap of invisibility, takes the bow, and shoots the arrow at Yelena’s chamber, knocking off the top of her castle. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l8767-l8893","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA. / CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE.; lines 8767-8893","start":"8767","end":"8893","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Boyislav is secretly taken from prison and shut in a lions' den on his brothers' advice; the doors are walled up, leaving only a small opening. Using a magical taper and tablecloth hidden in his bosom, he conjures food, feeds the lions until they become tame, and spends a year living safely among them. Meanwhile, the princess of White Island travels the world with an army seeking the prince who freed her kingdom, insisting he must come from a royal family with twelve sons. Reaching Boyislav's father's kingdom, she demands her liberator. Two of Boyislav's brothers falsely claim the deed; each fails a test involving the taper and is beheaded, after which the remaining three confess. The old man who once saved Boyislav reveals he is alive in the lions' den. The king opens the den and begs Boyislav to leave, but Boyislav refuses until he hears that the princess of White Island threatens to destroy the city. He then leaves with his magical items and is recognized and lovingly reproached by the princess, who recalls an earlier kiss and declares their betrothal. A feast and wedding are planned, but the princesses of Black Island remain sad and three princes who had gone there are terrified. In the midst of the celebration Boyislav asks for his trusty horse, finds him half-starved in a pen, and embraces him. The horse speaks, explaining that a cord from Red Island has become hay and kept him alive, and then urges Boyislav to cut off his head to free him. After initial reluctance, Boyislav obeys, and the horse disappears, replaced by a beautiful prince. At supper the youngest princess of Black Island rushes into this prince's arms, and her sisters welcome him. He explains that he is the only son of a powerful king, transformed into a horse by a witch-queen whose daughter he refused to marry; the princesses of Black Island were also enchanted, turned into horses for part of each day. Boyislav had freed the princesses earlier and has now freed him, lifting the spell from Black In the kitchen, the cook and chamberlain attempt to prepare the fish, but as they are buttered the whole palace shakes, an invisible force strikes the men senseless, and one fish stands up, speaks to the others, and all three vanish. The king demands that more such fish be obtained from the fisherman, who can catch them only on Mondays; using a magical herb, the fisherman is transported via a cliff to a mountain and then to a lake where he catches three fish on his third cast, and his wife again brings them to the king and receives more gold, bringing peace and prosperity to the household, for which the fisherman thanks the fiery man who helped him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The fisherman's wife hurries to the king's palace after dinner carrying three fish and causes confusion among the servants as she tries to find the king.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A heavily bearded guard grabs the fishwoman roughly by the hand and pushes her back when she attempts to rush into the king's chamber, prompting her to scream that they are killing her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When the king appears, the fishwoman calls him \"Royal Grace\" and tells him she has only three fish but that they are so wonderful she has never seen their like.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The king, being in good humor, orders the woman to give the fish to his cook instead of to him and rewards her with a handful of gold pieces for the road.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Overjoyed by the money, the fishwoman falls at the king's feet and nearly knocks him down before taking the fish to the kitchen and running home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the woman leaves, the king goes to the kitchen, shows the fish to his cook, and orders that they be prepared in a special manner, warning the cook that he will answer with his head if anything goes wrong.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The cook, though usually brave at cutting off other people’s heads, trembles with fear when his own head is threatened and asks how he should prepare the fish.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The king says the manner of cooking is the cook’s affair and announces he will send his chamberlain to look after the fish, after which the chamberlain arrives in the kitchen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The confused cook, not knowing how to unconscious.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"While the cook and chamberlain lie unconscious on the floor, one of the fish stands on its tail in the pan and speaks brief conversation in the pan, all three fish vanish, and the narrator notes that no one knows where they went.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The cook wakes from his involuntary slumber before the chamberlain, and when both rise and discover the fish gone, they worry about what the king will say.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The chamberlain reports the disappearance of the fish and the strange events in the kitchen to the king, who says he cannot believe it but offers forgiveness if more fish like those can be obtained from the fisherman.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The fisherman tells the chamberlain that he can catch such fish only on Mondays, which makes the king very angry, though anger cannot change the situation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"There is great joy in the fisherman's cottage because of the money received, and the fisherman's wife impatiently waits for Monday, wakes her husband early, gives him a special breakfast, and urges him out to get more of the strange fish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The fisherman obeys the king's command, going to a cliff with a 'wonderful herb' in his bosom, and as soon as he stands on a certain step he is carried to a mountain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"From the mountain the fisherman rushes to a lake where a boat is waiting, catches nothing on his first and second tries, but on the third cast draws out three fish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"After catching the fish, the fisherman is instantly taken from the mountain to the valley, runs home with the fish, and his wife snatches them from him, puts them in a basket, and goes to the king's palace.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"This time the guards have orders to let the fishwoman through to the king, who inspects the fish to see if they are the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l6434-l6559","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS. / THE FOOTLESS AND THE BLIND. / GO TO THE VERGE OF DESTRUCTION AND BRING BACK SHMAT-RAZUM. / MARYA MOREVNA.; lines 6434-6559","start":"6434","end":"6559","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"In a certain kingdom in a certain land lived Ivan Tsarevich. He had three sisters.\"","summary":"In this portion of the tale \"Marya Morevna,\" Ivan Tsarevich obeys his dying parents' command to give each of his three sisters in marriage to the first suitor, leading to their being carried off by storm-bringing bird suitors who transform into gallant youths. Later, during his travels, Ivan discovers that the warrior princess Marya Morevna has slain a great army; she hosts him, marries him, and takes him to her kingdom. When she departs to wage war, she forbids him to open a certain closet, but he disobeys and finds Koshchei Without-Death chained inside. After Ivan restores Koshchei's strength with water, Koshchei breaks free, escapes as a whirlwind, and abducts Marya Morevna. Ivan then sets out to find her, visiting the households of his married sisters Marya Tsarevna and Olga Tsarevna, who live with their falcon and eagle husbands near palaces and oaks and offer him hospitality and tokens as he continues his quest.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ivan Tsarevich lives in a kingdom with three sisters named Marya, Olga, and Anna Tsarevna, and their father and mother die.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"When dying, Ivan's parents instruct him that whoever first woos one of his sisters he must give her to that suitor and not keep his sisters with him long.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After burying his parents, Ivan goes with his sisters to walk in a green garden, where a black cloud and fearful storm arise so that he urges them to return home.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"As they reach the castle, thunder roars, the ceiling opens, and a bright falcon flies into the chamber, strikes the floor, and becomes a gallant youth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The transformed falcon greets Ivan Tsarevich, asks to marry Marya Tsarevna, and after Ivan leaves the choice to his sister she agrees; the falcon marries her and carries her away to his own kingdom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"About a year later, during another walk in the green garden, a cloud with whirlwind and lightning appears, and when they hurry home an eagle flies in through an opened roof, strikes the floor, and turns into a gallant youth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The eagle asks to marry Olga Tsarevna; Ivan says he will not oppose her will, she consents, and the eagle takes her in marriage and bears her to his kingdom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Another year later, a raven flies into the castle during a storm with thunder, strikes the floor, becomes a very handsome gallant youth, and asks to marry Anna Tsarevna; she agrees and he carries her to his own kingdom.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After his sisters have departed, Ivan Tsarevich lives alone for a year, grows weary, and decides to go on a journey to seek out his sisters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On his journey Ivan sees a great army lying slain on a field and calls out to ask if any living man is present and who killed the army.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A surviving man among the slain host answers Ivan that Marya Morevna, the fair Korolyevna, killed the great army.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ivan comes to white tents where Marya Morevna, the fair Korolyevna, comes out to meet him, asks whether God bears him of his own will or against his will, and invites him to be her guest if he is not in haste.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ivan spends two nights as a guest in Marya Morevna's tents, pleases her, marries her, and she takes him with her to her own kingdom where they live together for some time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Marya Morevna decides to make war, leaves her household to Ivan Tsarevich, and tells him to go everywhere and look after everything but explicitly forbids him to look into a certain closet.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After Marya Morevna has gone to war, Ivan cannot endure the prohibition, rushes to the closet, opens the door, and finds Koshchei Without-Death hanging inside fastened with twelve chains.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Koshchei tells Ivan that he has sat there in torment for twelve years without eating or drinking and begs him to take pity and give him water because his throat is parched.","category":"speech

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l1615-l1737","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"LI. THE HASTY WORD                                            370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 1615-1737","start":"1615","end":"1737","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Petrusha's father disappears without trace, so Petrusha mourns him, has a religious service performed for his soul, and begins to act as head of the family. On a Sunday walk to church, he rebukes a woman who stumbles over a stone and curses the Devil for it, telling her she should not think about the Evil One while going to pray. After church, a fine-looking man suddenly appears, thanks Petrusha for his \"good word,\" reveals that he is the Devil, and invites Petrusha to visit him, promising rich rewards and describing the road. The next day Petrusha travels for three days to a great dark forest where a rich palace stands, inhabited by devils. Inside he meets a fair maiden stolen from a village by an evil spirit, who warns him of the danger and advises him to refuse the Devil's offers of silver and gold and instead request a very wretched horse which evil spirits use for fetching wood and water; she explains that this horse is Petrusha's father, whom the devils seized after he came out of a tavern drunk and fell into water. The Devil feasts Petrusha and offers him money and a fine horse, but Petrusha insists on taking only the sorry jade. As he leads it away, the maiden instructs him that near his village he must remove his copper cross, trace a circle three times around the horse, and hang the cross around its neck. Petrusha does so, and the horse disappears; in its place stands his father, who remains speechless for three days before living happily and prosperously with his son, having entirely given up drinking. A closing commentary remarks that Russian peasants are humorous, that the jokes in their facetious tales are largely common to many countries, and that \"merry jests\" in Russian Skazkas belong to an international stock shared by rustic wags from various parts of Europe, the Near East, and He finds a seemingly empty castle with a table laid with food and wine. After he eats, a bear appears and reveals she is an enchanted princess who will be freed, and then marry him, if he endures three nights in the castle. Though overwhelmed by growing sorrow and unable to escape, he survives the three nights; the bear becomes a beautiful princess, and they marry and live care-free. Later, the soldier wishes to visit his native place despite the princess’s pleas for him to stay. She gives him a sack of magic seeds that create trees bearing precious fruit, with singing birds and tale-telling tom-cats, whenever they are scattered along the road. After three months she sets out along the road marked by the magic forests, and at the place where the trees stop she finds a lone magic tree and her husband sleeping beneath it. Unable to wake him despite pricking and pinching him, she angrily curses that a whirlwind carry the \"good-for-nothing sleepy head\" to unknown places. A stormy wind immediately snatches him away. The Tsar permits her, and she descends from her lofty chamber into the meadow before a steep mountain with curly trees. As she plucks blue flowers and wanders a little away from her attendants with her face uncovered, a mighty whirlwind arises, seizes her, and carries her through the air over many lands, across deep rivers, through three kingdoms into the fourth, the dominions of the Savage Serpent. The nurses, distraught, report the event to the Tsar, who is sad and angry but pardons them. Workers at a nearby brewery discuss the offer. One of them, Nikita Koltoma, boasts that the Tsar cannot obtain such a bride without his help and that he can secure her. His companions call him a fool and warn that the Tsar kills people for empty boasting, but Nikita insists. Their words are reported to the Tsar, who has soldiers seize Nikita and bring him to the palace. The Tsar repeats the conditions: if Nikita succeeds, he will receive countless treasure and be made first minister; if he fails, the Tsar will behead him with his sword. Nikita agrees but requests a month-long holiday. The Tsar consents and gives him an open order, signed by himself, commanding all inns to provide Nikita free food and drink. Nikita spends the month carousing in the capital, then returns to the Tsar and asks for twelve brave youths identical in stature, hair, and voice, and for thirteen white woven tents with gold embroidery. The Tsar promptly supplies these. They saddle horses, pack the tents, pray in church, take leave of the townspeople, and ride away in a cloud of dust. Traveling for several days, they come upon a forge in an open field where fifteen blacksmiths are hammering iron. Nikita greets them and asks for an iron staff weighing fifteen poods, offering to turn the iron himself while they strike. When the staff is made, he throws it ninety feet into the air; it lands on his hand and snaps in two under the impact, proving too weak for his strength. He pays the blacksmiths and rejoins his comrades. After more days they reach another forge with twenty-five blacksmiths. Nikita again greets them and requests a staff of twenty-five poods, turning the red-hot iron himself as they hammer. He throws this heavier staff one hundred and fifty feet; it also breaks when it strikes his hand. Dissatisfied, he pays and rides on. An unclean spirit abducts the Tsaritsa. The eldest and second sons each receive the Tsar’s blessing to search for their mother but disappear and are not heard from. The youngest son, Ivan Tsarevich, also receives a blessing and travels to a strange distant region, reaching the blue sea. There, thirty-three spoonbills land, transform into beautiful maidens, and bathe. Ivan secretly takes the girdle of the most beautiful maiden. She pleads for its return; he demands first to know where his mother is. The maiden says his mother is in the house of her father, Raven son of Raven (Voron Voronovich), and tells him to follow a silver bird with a golden crest along the sea. Ivan returns the girdle, meets his brothers, and together they pursue the silver bird until it darts beneath an iron plate into an opening. Ivan asks his brothers for their blessing, then descends alone on a rope swing through the deep opening for three years. Below, he finds the Copper Kingdom, where a castle holds thirty-three spoonbill maidens embroidering towels. The Tsaritsa of the Copper Kingdom greets Ivan, learns he seeks his mother, and warns that her father, Raven son of Raven, is cunning and wise, has flown over mountains, valleys, caves, and clouds, and will kill him. She gives Ivan a ball to roll and follow to her second sister. Ivan reaches the Silver Kingdom, where its Tsaritsa remarks on the sudden appearance of \"Russian odor,\" questions whether he flees from or seeks work, and hears that he searches for his mother. She repeats the warning about Raven, gives him another ball, and sends him to her youngest sister. {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l4719-l4839","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE FOOTLESS AND BLIND CHAMPIONS. / THE THREE KINGDOMS. / VASSILISSA GOLDEN TRESS, BAREHEADED BEAUTY. / THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS.; lines 4719-4839","start":"4719","end":"4839","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The Tsar visits Ivan the Fool’s castle, meets him, and later hosts him at the palace, where the Tsar’s beautiful daughter (Tsarevna) serves Ivan. Ivan immediately asks to marry her. The Tsar agrees on condition that Ivan create a golden road between their residences, a gold-and-silver bridge over the river with rare birds on the water, and a wax church surrounded by wax apple-trees bearing ripe fruit. Ivan uses a ring with twelve screws to summon twelve thousand men, who fulfill these demands overnight. The Tsar sees the bridge, river birds, and wax church with bare apple-trees, then prepares his daughter for the wedding. As the bridal procession moves from palace to church, the apple-trees progress from buds to leaves to blossoms, and after the ceremony servants present ripe apples on a golden salver; the wedding feast lasts three days and nights.

Later, the Tsarevna presses Ivan to reveal how he performs such wonders; he finally confides that he has a ring with twelve screws and explains how it is used. A fine-looking servant pleases the Tsarevna, and she conspires with him to steal the ring and go live beyond the sea. One evening she secretly uses the ring, summons twelve thousand men, and orders them to carry the castle with all its contents beyond the sea, leaving an old cabin with her ragged husband in its place. The men obey. Ivan wakes in the cabin on a bark mat under a ragged coat, with no castle in sight. Weeping, he goes to the Tsar, but the Tsar rejects him, mocks his poverty, and orders him walled up in a stone pillar.

Ivan’s cat and dog remain with him, dig a hole, and feed him through it. They decide to go beyond the sea to recover the ring. Swimming across the sea, they reach the relocated castle, where the Tsarevna walks in the garden with the servant, laughing at her husband. The cat enters the castle, is welcomed and fed, and searches the rooms until she finds the ring in a glass box on the stove. At night she breaks the box, catches the ring in her mouth, hides, and is eventually driven out when the Tsarevna discovers the broken box and blames "that scoundrel’s cat." The cat rejoins the dog, announcing she has the ring and wishes they could get home quickly.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Tsar content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l5715-l5961","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"APPENDIX: EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA. / PART OF THE SECOND LAY OF HELGI HUNDINGS-BANE (1) / PART OF THE LAY OF SIGRDRIFA (1) / THE LAY CALLED THE SHORT LAY OF SIGURD.; lines 5715-5961","start":"5715","end":"5961","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Sigurd of yore, / Sought the dwelling of Giuki,","summary":"Sigurd, after winning a battle, comes to the hall of Giuki, swears oaths of brotherhood with Giuki’s sons, and is given their sister Gudrun in marriage along with great wealth. Later he rides with them to woo Brynhild; although the poem says he would have wed her if fate had permitted, he instead gains her as a bride for Gunnar and lies chastely beside her with a naked sword between them. Brynhild, married to Gunnar but in love with Sigurd, is tormented by jealousy and fate; she wanders over icy wastes at night while Sigurd lies in bed with Gudrun, and she finally threatens to leave Gunnar and surrender her lands unless he kills Sigurd and their young son, whom she calls a ‘young wolf’ who would one day seek vengeance. Gunnar, torn between his sworn oaths to Sigurd and Brynhild’s demands, consults his brother Hogni. Although Hogni calls it unseemly to break oaths, he suggests that their unsworn and reckless younger brother Guttorm, who is outside the oaths, should kill Sigurd, tempted by the prospect of ruling over the Rhine-gold. Guttorm stabs Sigurd in the heart as he lies in the hall; the dying Sigurd hurls his sword Gram and cuts Guttorm in pieces. Gudrun, sleeping peacefully beside Sigurd, wakes to find herself swimming in the blood of ‘Frey’s beloved.’ She strikes her hands together in grief, rousing Sigurd enough to speak. In his last words he tells her not to weep, reminds her she still has her brothers, mentions their young child who is too small to escape hostile kin, condemns her brothers’ evil counsel, predicts estrangement between them and their sister’s son, and declares that Brynhild alone brought about this disaster.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigurd travels to the dwelling of Giuki after winning a fight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"At Giuki’s hall, Sigurd takes troth from two brethren and they swear oaths between them.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Giuki’s household gives Sigurd a maiden, Gudrun the young, Giuki’s daughter, together with great wealth, and she becomes his wife.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sigurd, Gudrun, and the sons of Giuki drink together and ‘give doom’ for many days.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The group later sets out for Brynhild’s wooing, with Sigurd riding in their company.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"

It argues that both Snorre Sturleson and Olaf Hvitaskald contributed: Snorre compiled the main mythological sections (such as Gylfaginning, Brage’s Speech, Skaldskaparmal, and Hattatal) from much older Odinic traditions also found in the Elder Edda’s ‘Vala’s Prophecy,’ while Olaf wrote the grammatical and rhetorical parts. An anonymous scholar wrote the alphabet treatise, another anonymous author wrote the forewords and afterwords, and the whole work was finally edited in the early fourteenth century, though the mythological material itself is said to be as old as the Teutonic people.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Olaf Thordsson Hvitaskald, Iceland.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"It is proposed that the Odinic religious system may have taken a permanent prose form in popular memory long before {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l8040-l8285","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE SONG OF ATLI. / THE WHETTING OF GUDRUN. / THE LAY OF HAMDIR / THE LAMENT OF ODDRUN.; lines 8040-8285","start":"8040","end":"8285","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""Mightily sang Oddrun,
Sharp piercing songs
By Borgny's side:

Till a maid and a boy
Might tread on the world's ways..."","summary":"King Heidrik's daughter Borgny suffers a severe, protracted childbirth that no one can ease until Oddrun, sister of Atli and former lover of Gunnar, rides to her hall and sings powerful songs that enable Borgny to bear a boy and a girl. Borgny thanks Oddrun, invoking Frey and Freyia and the gods, while Oddrun says she helped only because of an old vow to aid every soul, despite resentment toward Borgny. In her ensuing lament, Oddrun recounts her upbringing in a royal hall, her father's dying arrangements of her marriage to a son of Grimhild and of Brynhild's fate as a "Death-chooser," Brynhild's later vengeance and self-chosen death for Sigurd, and Oddrun's own illicit love for Gunnar. Attempts by the sons of Giuki to win Oddrun for Gunnar with rich gifts are rejected by Atli; Oddrun and Gunnar continue their secret affair, are spied upon in the murkwood by Atli's servants, and betrayed despite bribing the spies with gold. The fragment ends with the noisy arrival of the sons of Giuki riding into Atli's garth on gold-shod Hamdir answers by recounting Gudrun’s past tragedies involving Sigurd, Atli, and the deaths of Erp and Eitil, warning that the sword’s edge often turns back on its wielder. Sorli advises their mother to weep for her dead kinsmen and foretells that she will also mourn them as they ride "fey" to die in distant lands. Hamdir and Sorli depart in fury to seek vengeance, riding over the fells on Hunnish steeds. On the way they meet their younger kinsman Erp, described as "wise in all wiles" and "of alien womb"; after a cryptic exchange about mutual help, they take offense at his mockery, kill him, and thereby diminish their own strength by a third. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l4457-l4579","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH. / THE FOOTLESS AND BLIND CHAMPIONS. / THE THREE KINGDOMS. / VASSILISSA GOLDEN TRESS, BAREHEADED BEAUTY.; lines 4457-4579","start":"4457","end":"4579","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ivan Goroh goes to the palace where his sister Vassilissa Golden Tress waits and watches for the Savage Serpent. He proves his strength and identity by drinking great quantities of mead and breaking the serpent’s chair, then orders the serpent’s blacksmith to forge a nine-ton iron club, which he tests by throwing into the sky and catching when it returns. When the Savage Serpent arrives on his fire‑breathing steed Whirlwind, Ivan confronts and kills him with one blow of the club. The people hail Ivan as Tsar, and he rewards the wise blacksmith by appointing him as their new head. Ivan obtains the water of life and the water of death to revive his brothers and uses the serpent’s water to rejuvenate an old woman, then builds a ship and sails with Vassilissa on the Swan’s river through three kingdoms into a fourth back to their homeland. Their parents rejoice, messengers spread news of Vassilissa’s return, great celebrations and two weddings are held, and after his father’s death Ivan receives the crown and rules with lasting renown.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ivan Goroh goes to the palace knowing that his sister Vassilissa Golden Tress is there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Vassilissa looks out of the window to see if the Savage Serpent is coming.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Seeing Ivan from afar, Vassilissa sends quietly to learn from what land he has come, of what stock he is, and whether he was sent by her father or mother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Vassilissa hears that Ivan, her youngest brother whom she does not know by sight, has come, runs to him, and wets him with tears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Vassilissa urges Ivan to run quickly, warning that the serpent will soon arrive and will destroy him if he sees him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ivan replies that he has no fear of the serpent or his strength and asks first for a drink because he is tired from traveling in the heat.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ivan asks for three gallons of sweet mead and drinks a three‑gallon measure at one breath, then asks for another.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Vassilissa orders mead to be brought, watches Ivan drink, and concludes that he must indeed be Ivan Goroh.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Vassilissa commands that a strong chair be brought, but it breaks under Ivan and flies into bits; a second chair bound with iron cracks and bends under his weight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Vassilissa cries out that the iron chair is the chair of the Savage Serpent.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l2822-l2879","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XII. / LIFE IN VALHAL. / CHAPTER XIII. / CHAPTER XIV.; lines 2822-2879","start":"2822","end":"2879","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ganglere remarks that Utgard-Loke is powerful and works by delusions, and asks whether Thor has avenged himself. Har replies that, though it is little told, Thor made amends by setting out quickly on a new journey alone, disguised as a young man. Thor leaves Midgard and comes in the evening to the giant Hymer, where he stays as a guest. In the morning Hymer prepares to row out to sea to fish; Thor asks to join him. Hymer doubts Thor’s size and strength and warns about the cold and distance, but Thor insists and restrains his anger. When Hymer tells him to find his own bait, Thor kills Hymer’s largest ox, Himinbrjot, taking its head as bait. They row far out; Thor rows so strongly that Hymer admits the boat speeds fast. Hymer warns they are in dangerous waters because of the Midgard-serpent, but Thor rows still farther. Thor prepares an immense line and hook, baits it with the ox-head, and casts it to the bottom. The Midgard-serpent bites the bait and is hooked; it pulls so hard that Thor’s hands strike the gunwale. Thor assumes his divine strength, braces his feet through the boat onto the sea floor, and hauls the serpent up to the gunwale. Thor and the serpent stare at each other; the serpent spews venom, and Hymer turns pale with fear as water comes into the boat. Just as Thor raises his hammer to strike, Hymer cuts the line so the serpent sinks back into the sea. Thor throws his hammer after it; some say he struck off its head, though the narrator believes the serpent still lives in the ocean. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l7645-l7690","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VARIANT OF THE RESCUE OF IVAN TSAREVICH AND THE WINNING OF THE COLT. / YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS.; lines 7645-7690","start":"7645","end":"7690","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A mighty whirlwind created by South Wind carries a soldier through the air over mountains and seas to the clouds, bringing him in three hours to the new kingdom where a beautiful princess lives. Hermod reaches Hel’s gate and has his horse leap over it, then enters Hel’s hall, where he sees his brother Balder on the foremost seat and spends the night. Hel answers that Balder may go back only if all things, living and dead, weep for him; if anything refuses, he must remain. Learning that Fedot has been sent by the king to the verge of destruction to bring back the wonder Shmat-Razum, the old woman tries to help. She summons all beasts and birds, and later all fish and sea creatures from above an abyss in the middle of the ocean, but none know the way until an old limping frog, long out of service, steps forward claiming to know. The old woman returns home with Fedot and the frog, who explains that the place lies at the rim of the world but that she is too old to go herself. The old woman places the frog in a bowl of fresh milk and gives it to Fedot to carry as a guide. Led by the frog, Fedot travels until he reaches a flaming river and a lofty mountain with a door. At the frog's instruction, he rides on her back as she swells to enormous size and leaps across the flaming river, then she sends him alone into the mountain. Inside a pitch-dark cave, Fedot hides in a cupboard and observes two old men enter and command Shmat-Razum to feed them. Instantly lights, a table, and abundant food and wine appear; after they eat, they order Shmat-Razum to remove everything, which vanishes. When they depart, Fedot calls Shmat-Razum, is similarly served, and invites the unseen being to sit with him, noting it is unpleasant to eat alone. Shmat-Razum replies that he has served the old men faithfully for nearly thirty years without ever being seated with them. Fedot, who cannot see Shmat-Razum but witnesses food and drink being consumed and bottles pouring themselves, asks the spirit to serve him instead and promises a pleasant life. Shmat-Razum, tired of his current service, agrees and follows Fedot out of the cave as an invisible The king is angry at the early return but, seeing the deer, lets Fedot go and grants the sailors a six-year holiday. Wanting Fedot’s death, the king orders the mayor to find a way, and the mayor consults the witch Baba-Yaga. She suggests sending Fedot to the \"verge of destruction\" to bring back Shmat-Razum, a task she says he will never complete. The king commands Fedot to undertake this quest under threat of beheading. Fedot’s wise and beautiful wife calculates the journey as nine years each way, tells him to pray and sleep, then uses a magic book to consult two youths who do not know the route. She instructs Fedot to ask the king for travel money and, when he returns, gives him a magic ball that will roll ahead and a towel to use wherever he is. Fedot departs, following the rolling ball. After a month, the king assumes Fedot will not survive the eighteen-year journey, sends for Fedot’s wife, and offers to marry her and make her queen. She refuses because her husband is still alive; when the king threatens force, she laughs, strikes the floor, turns into a blue dove, and flies out the window. Meanwhile, Fedot travels through many lands and kingdoms, the ball turning into a bridge at a river and into a soft couch for rest, until he reaches a splendid palace where the ball disappears at the gate and three beautiful maidens greet him and ask where he comes from and for what purpose.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l1147-l1280","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER III. / OF THE HIGHEST GOD. / CHAPTER IV. / THE CREATION OF THE WORLD.; lines 1147-1280","start":"1147","end":"1280","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In dialogue form, Ganglere asks Har (with Jafnhar and Thride) how the world and the races originated. Har cites a prophecy describing the beginning of time when nothing existed—no earth, sea, or heaven—only the yawning gap Ginnungagap. Jafnhar explains that Niflheim, with the central well Hvergelmer and many rivers including Gjoll near Hel’s gate, existed long before the earth. Thride adds that to the south lay Muspelheim, a blazing, bright world guarded by the fire-giant Surt, who will one day come with a flaming sword to conquer the gods and burn the world, as described in a prophetic verse. 

Har then explains that venomous streams called Elivogs flowed from their source, hardened into ice, and accumulated as rime in the northern part of Ginnungagap, while sparks from Muspelheim lit the southern part. As cold from Niflheim met heat from Muspelheim, Ginnungagap became mild; when the warm blasts melted the rime, drops quickened into life by a higher power and formed a manlike being, Ymir (Aurgelmer), from whom all giants descend, as confirmed by verses from the Lay of Hyndla and Vafthrudnir’s Lay. Ymir and his offspring are said to be evil frost giants. While Ymir sleeps, a man and woman grow from his left arm and a son is generated between his feet, producing the frost-giant race. 

From further melting rime a cow, Audhumla, comes into being. Four streams of milk from her teats feed Ymir. Audhumla survives by licking rime-covered salt-stones; over three days her licking produces a man: first his hair, then his head, then his whole body. This man, Buri, fathers a son Bor, who marries the giant’s daughter Bestla. Their sons Odin, Vile, and Ve are presented as rulers of heaven and earth, with Odin regarded as the greatest and most famous. 

Finally, Har recounts that Bor’s sons kill the giant Ymir. So much blood flows from Ymir’s wounds that almost all frost giants drown. Only one, Bergelmir, escapes with his household; he and his wife board an ark and survive. From them a renewed race of frost giants descends, as a verse recalls Bergelmir lying safe in his ark long before the earth was made.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"At the beginning of time there was no sand, sea, cooling waves, earth, or heaven; only Ginnungagap existed and there was no grass anywhere.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Niflheim had existed many ages before the earth was made, with the well Hvergelmer in its midst, from which numerous streams flow, including Gjoll near the gate of Hel.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"To the south there was another world, Muspelheim, described as light, hot, and so dazzling that no non-native can endure it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Surt stands on the border of Muspelheim guarding it and holds a flaming sword in his hand.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At the end of the world Surt will come from the south, attack and conquer all the gods, and burn the whole world with fire; a prophetic verse describes blazing flames, rocks crashing together, witches collapsing, men going to Hel, and the heavens splitting apart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Streams called the Elivogs carry venomous matter that, as they flow far from their source, hardens like slag from the fire and turns into ice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the ice from the Elivogs ceased to flow, drizzle arising from the venom froze into rime, and layers of ice and rime accumulated across Ginnungagap.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The northern part of Ginnungagap is filled with thick, heavy ice and rime, with pervasive drizzle and gusts, while the southern part is lit by glowing sparks from Muspelheim.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Cold and all grim things proceed from Niflheim, while the region bordering Muspelheim is hot and bright, making Ginnungagap warm and mild like windless air.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"When heated blasts from Muspelheim meet the rime, it melts into drops that, by the might of the one who sent the heat, quicken into life and take the shape of a man named Ymer (Aurgelmer to the frost giants).","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The Lay of Hyndla states that all völvas descend from Vidolf, all wizards from Vilmeide, all enchanters from Svarthofde, and that all giants come from Ymer.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In Vafthrudnir’s Lay, the wise giant says that Aurgelmer originated from venomous drops from the Elivogs that grew until a giant was formed, and that the giants’ race descends from him and is therefore fierce.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Har states that Ymer and all his offspring are evil and are called frost giants, and that he is not regarded as a god.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"While Ymer slept, he sweated; from They invite him on a sea journey, then while he sleeps they place him in a boat and set him adrift. A storm carries him to a desolate island. After exploring and thanking God for his survival, Ivan discovers an underground passage leading to an underground kingdom ruled by a six-headed serpent. In the serpent’s white-walled castle, Ivan finds an enormous book stating that a Tsar never has sons, only a Tsaritsa does; he scratches out the words and reverses them, so that when the serpent wakes and consults the book he believes Ivan is his son. The serpent adopts him, shows him vast treasures, and they live together. Later the serpent gives Ivan keys to all chambers but forbids him to enter one locked with gold and silver locks. After months alone, Ivan grows weary, opens the forbidden chamber, and finds two chained maidens: Tsarevna Yelena the Wise with golden wings and her maid with silver wings. At Yelena’s request, he gives them spring water to drink; their chains break and they fly out the window. Ivan despairs over how to face the serpent. A storm announces the serpent’s return; upon learning what Ivan has done, he beats him with a heated iron rod but spares him because he is his son. Once healed, Ivan begs to go into the world to seek Yelena the Wise. The serpent, who claims it took thirty-three years to capture her, doubts Ivan’s chances but gives him a magical flying carpet and warns that Yelena is terribly cunning and will deceive content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l3255-l3351","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XVI. / RAGNAROK. / CHAPTER XVII. / REGENERATION.; lines 3255-3351","start":"3255","end":"3351","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ganglere asks Har what happens after heaven, earth, gods, warriors, and humans are destroyed by fire. Har replies that there are many good and bad abodes: blessed halls like Gimle, Brimer, and the golden hall Sindre, and dreadful places like Nastrand, a serpent-woven hall where perjurers and murderers wade through venom, and Hvergelmir, where Nidhug tortures the dead. Har then describes the regeneration after Ragnarok: the earth rises green from the sea; unsown fields bear crops; Vidar, Vale, and Thor’s sons Mode and Magne survive Surtr’s fire and dwell on Ida plain, recovering Mjolner and the golden tables once owned by the gods. Balder and Hoder return from Hel and join them. A human pair, Lif and Lifthraser, having hidden in Hodmimer’s grove and lived on morning dew during Surtr’s fire, repopulate the world. The sun has a daughter who will follow her mother’s course after the sun is taken by Fenrer and the gods are dead. Har says he knows nothing beyond this about the world’s fate. Then Ganglere hears a great noise, finds himself standing outside on a plain with the hall gone, returns to his kingdom, and transmits what he has learned, which is then handed down among humans.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ganglere asks what happens when heaven, earth, and all the world are consumed in flames and all gods, einherjar, and humans are dead, noting that Har has said all men will live in some world forever.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Har replies that there are many good and bad abodes after this destruction, and that the best is to be in Gimle in heaven.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Har describes the hall Brimer, also in heaven, where there is plenty of good drink for those who enjoy it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Har describes an excellent hall called Sindre, built of red gold on the Nida mountains, where good and well-minded men shall dwell.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Har describes Nastrand as a large and terrible hall far from the sun, whose doors open to the north, built of serpents wattled together so that venom drips through openings and flows in streams where perjurers and murderers must wade.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The verse cited about Nastrand describes a hall on a strand of dead bodies, made from serpents’ backs, with drops of venom At night they find a huge hall and sleep inside. The building shakes violently with noise in the night, so they move into a smaller side room while Thor keeps watch with his hammer. At dawn Thor discovers that the hall was actually the glove of a very large man, who names himself Skrymer, and the side room was the glove’s thumb. Skrymer, whose snoring caused the noise, joins their company, proposes that they pool their provisions, ties everything into one bag, carries it, and leads them through the wilderness. In the evening they rest under a large oak. Skrymer sleeps and snores, while Thor finds he cannot loosen a single knot of the provision-sack. Angered, Thor strikes Skrymer’s head with his hammer three times during the night, believing he has hit hard enough to kill him, but Skrymer wakes each time and casually attributes the impacts to falling leaves, an acorn, or moss from the tree. At dawn Skrymer tells them they are near Utgard, warns them not to boast when they come before Utgard-Loke’s thanes, and advises them to turn back or continue straight east if they insist on going. Skrymer then departs north toward the mountains with the provision-sack, and the narrator remarks that it is not known whether the gods wished to meet him again in A new story begins about a king with three sons. Hoping to make them worthy heirs, the king sends them to school, but they abandon their studies and return home. Furious, the king forbids them to appear before him and withdraws to a chamber by the rising sun, where he constantly looks eastward, one eye weeping and the other laughing. When, as adults, the sons seek to know the reason, the king twice responds to the question by hurling a sword at the eldest and second sons, who dodge and escape. The youngest, Mirko, remains in place, pulls the sword from the stone wall, and lays it before his father, who then explains himself. He says one eye weeps because his sons are insignificant and unfit to rule, and the other laughs in remembrance of his youthful comrade, the Hero of the Plain, who promised to share his old age but is endlessly beset by enemies in a silken meadow and cannot yet come. The brothers then decide to ask leave to try their fortune. The eldest and second sons each obtain permission, choose good horses, and after a year return carrying the tops of a copper and a silver bridge, but their father dismisses their feats as soft compared to his own youth. Mirko likewise asks leave, but finds no steed to his liking in the royal stables or stud. An old witch advises him to request from the king a horn that once summoned the king's golden-haired steeds, to sound it, and to choose not one of the golden horses but a shabby, crooked-legged old mare whose tail strike will shake the palace. As she grows marriageable, many suitors seek her, but none want the stepmother’s daughters. The stepmother angrily refuses to let the younger girl marry before her elders and beats Vasilissa. After the merchant father departs on a long journey, the stepmother moves the household to a house near a dense forest where, in a clearing, stands Baba Yaga’s hut. Baba Yaga eats people and lets no one approach. The stepmother repeatedly sends Vasilissa into the forest, but the doll guides her home and keeps her away from the hut. In autumn the stepmother assigns evening tasks: lace-making, sock-knitting, and weaving, with a single candle lit. A stepsister, following her mother’s orders, pretends to snuff the wick but extinguishes the candle, leaving the house without fire. The girls say they must go to Baba Yaga for a light; the two stepsisters claim their pins or knitting needles give enough light and refuse to go, forcing Vasilissa out. Vasilissa feeds the doll and tells it she has been sent to Baba Yaga for a light and fears being eaten; the doll’s eyes glow like candles and it tells her not to fear, promising that no harm will come as long as she keeps it with her. Vasilissa prepares, puts the doll in her pocket, crosses herself, and trembles as she walks into the thick forest. A white rider on a white horse passes and day begins to break; later a red rider on a red horse passes and the sun rises. After walking all night and the next day, Vasilissa reaches the clearing containing Baba Yaga’s hut, surrounded by a fence made of dead men’s bones, with skulls bearing eyes on top, men’s legs as gateposts, arms as bolts, and a mouth with sharp teeth as a lock. Terrified, she stands motionless. A black rider on a black horse gallops to the gate and disappears into the ground; night falls, but the skulls’ eyes shine and illuminate the clearing. A terrible roar sounds, the trees crack and leaves rustle as Baba Yaga emerges from the forest, riding in a mortar, urging it on with a pestle, and sweeping away her tracks with a broom. She stops at the gate, sniffs the air, and declares she smells Russian flesh. Vasilissa approaches, bows, and says her stepsisters have sent her for a light. These enchantresses are typically old, hideous, hateful, magically powerful yet dull-witted, hostile to humanity, and generally resemble European monstrous female figures like giantesses, lamias, trolls, ogresses, and dragonesses. The most prominent example, Baba Yaga, is described as a tall, gaunt hag with disheveled hair who sometimes lies across a miserable hut supported on fowl’s legs at the forest’s edge; the hut can turn on command. In other tales she inhabits a mansion with a fence of dead men’s bones. She rides in a mortar, uses a pestle as a goad, and sweeps away her traces with a broom. She is closely associated with the Snake, commands Day and Night as servants, and has all animals at her disposal.\n\nThe text then presents a specific tale. An old man’s first wife dies, leaving a daughter. He remarries an evil stepmother who beats the girl and plots her death. While the father is away, the stepmother sends the girl to visit “your aunt, my sister” to borrow a needle and thread, but this aunt is actually Baba Yaga. The girl first goes to a real aunt, who warns her about dangerous beings at Baba Yaga’s place—a birch-tree, creaking doors, savage dogs, and a cat—and tells her how to appease each with gifts. The girl reaches Baba Yaga’s hut, greets her as aunt, and is told to sit at the loom and weave. Outside, Baba Yaga orders her servant-maid to heat the bath and wash the girl, intending to eat her for breakfast. Terrified, the girl persuades the servant to delay by wetting the firewood and fetching water in a sieve, bribing her with a handkerchief. Baba Yaga calls through the window to ask if her niece is weaving; the girl answers that she is. The girl then feeds bacon to the cat and asks how to escape. The cat gives her a towel and a comb, explaining that if Baba Yaga pursues her she must throw down the towel to form a wide river and, if necessary, the comb to create a dense forest to block pursuit. The girl flees, pacifies the dogs with rolls, the doors with oil, and the birch-tree with a ribbon, and so escapes. Following the horse’s magical instructions, Jalmir makes a long rope and a net from the steed’s hairs, ties them at the cellar entrance, and descends three hundred steps into a brightly lit underground cellar full of vessels with precious hoops that he must ignore. At the far end he seizes a small wooden-hooped vessel that proves extraordinarily heavy; when he accidentally strikes another vessel, a blow shakes the whole castle. He races back up, jumps into the net, and is hauled up by the steed. The sorceress flies out and attacks the horse, but he knocks her down, tramples her, and pulls Jalmir up; Jalmir mounts with the vessel, and they flee through the air, pursued by the sorceress until they cross the boundary of her land and are safe. Returning home exhausted, Jalmir deposits the cask at the king’s chamber and sleeps. In the morning the king discovers that the little cask contains an inexhaustible supply of wine that can change type (red or yellow) at his spoken command. Overjoyed, he adopts Jalmir as his son and appoints him viceroy, and a seven-day celebration is held, with the people embracing the new viceroy. Jalmir’s jealous brothers, however, shun the festivities and pore over books until they find mention of a golden castle in the sea containing an extraordinarily beautiful princess whose marriage would restore the king’s youth and prolong his life. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l7651-l7798","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL. / FOOTNOTES:; lines 7651-7798","start":"7651","end":"7798","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage consists of scholarly footnotes to Ralston’s chapter on mythological themes in Russian fairy tales. a detailed discussion of possible etymologies for the name Yaga/Baba Yaga, including connections to Sanskrit \"ahi\" (snake), roots meaning \"to brawl\" and \"to eat\", and South Asian demon terms \"yaka\"/\"yaksha\"; a summary of a Vishnu Purana legend about Brahma creating hungry Yakshas; an observation that Yaga often resembles an Indian Rakshasi; a note on a variant story in which the hero Martin and his comrades confront a small bearded gnome resembling German dwarf figures; a comment on a Gaelic torture motif traced to Scandinavian influence and absent from Russian skazkas; glosses of Russian words such as \"krasavitsa\" (beauty), \"prigovarivaya\" (uttering a charm with a gesture), \"nevyesta\" (marriageable maiden/bride), \"ishbushka\" (little cottage), \"luchina\" (splinter-candle), and an exclamation about a \"Russian smell\" compared to \"Fee, faw, fum\" in English tales; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l12650-l12786","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MAGYAR MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE POOR MAN, AND THE KING OF THE CROWS. / THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON.; lines 12650-12786","start":"12650","end":"12786","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mirko learns from his father that an old horn lies hidden in the wall of the seventh cellar. He has a mason open the wall, retrieves the horn, and blows it to the four directions in the square before the palace. The ringing of golden horse bells fills the city and many splendid steeds appear, among them a shabby, shaggy-haired, crooked-legged mare whose tail strike shakes the palace. Mirko chooses this mare, leads her to the stable, and declares he has taken her to try his fortune. The mare speaks, insisting she must be fed before the long road. Mirko, offering whatever his father has, follows her instructions: he feeds her peas, then beans, then half a measure of glowing coals. After eating the coals she transforms into a golden-haired steed \"as the Star of Dawn\" and instructs Mirko to obtain from the king the old saddle, sword, weapons, and bridle once used when the king rode her in his youth. Mirko finds the saddle filthy in the carriage-house, and the weapons on a shelf. Each item the mare has him place before her, she blows on, and it becomes a magnificent golden saddle, gold-mounted sword and weapons, and a golden bridle. Mirko arms himself, bridles and saddles the mare. She tells him not to mount until they are outside the city. Once beyond the city he mounts, and the mare asks how swiftly to carry him, offering the speed of the whirlwind or of thought. Mirko lets her choose, asking only to endure the flight. She tells him to close his eyes and hold fast, then races forward. After a time she stops, has him open his eyes, and he sees a great river with a copper bridge. She explains it is the bridge from which his eldest brother brought home the top, pointing him to the gap. She again bids him close his eyes and carries him to another great river with a silver bridge, missing the top taken by his second brother. A third time she speeds on to an enormously wide and deep river spanned by a golden bridge guarded at both ends by four immense lions, which she crosses safely while Mirko’s eyes are shut. Beyond this, Mirko sees a summitless, very steep glass mountain which they must cross. Mirko doubts it is possible, but the mare tells him she wears shoes fixed by his father with diamond nails seven hundred years ago. With Mirko’s eyes closed she springs up, and in an instant they are on the glass mountain. Looking back, Mirko sees something dark as large as a great plate, which the mare identifies as the round of the earth, and asks what he sees About them many stories are current, generally having reference to their alleged jealousies and disputes."","summary":"The passage first recounts a tale in which a priest's daughter wanders into the forest without permission and disappears for three years. A bold hunter from the same village, who habitually roams the woods with his dog and gun, encounters a young-looking but grey-haired moujik sitting on a log, plaiting a bast shoe, and menacingly addressing the moon. The moujik identifies himself as the devil's grandfather, revealing that he is the forest spirit Leshy. The hunter shoots him and, following his wounded trail with the aid of his dog, reaches a hill with a fissure containing a hut. Inside, the Leshy lies dead and a young woman weeps that she has lost the one who fed and watered her. Questioned by the hunter, she says she does not know her parents or the light of day. The hunter promises to take her back to Holy Russia, marking trees along their route. The narrator explains that she had been carried off by the Leshy and kept naked in his hut for three years, without shame. Back in the village, the hunter asks if anyone has lost a girl; a priest and his wife claim the maiden as their long-lost daughter. At first she understands nothing, but gradually regains her senses. Her parents marry her to the hunter and reward him richly, but their attempts to relocate the Leshy’s hut in the forest fail.

The text then turns to another group of mythological personifications: the rivers. It notes that many tales about them focus on jealousies and disputes. One story tells how, when God was allotting shares to the rivers, the Desna arrived late and lost precedence over the Dnieper. God told her to try to get ahead on her own; she repeatedly attempted to overtake Dnieper but he always remained before her until he reached the sea, where Desna was obliged to join him. Another story concerns Volga and her tributary Vazuza, who argued about which was wiser, stronger, and more worthy of respect. They agreed that the one who first rose from sleep and reached the Caspian Sea would be superior. Vazuza secretly rose in the night, fled along the shortest and straightest path, and flowed away. Volga woke later, travelled at fitting speed, caught up with Vazuza at Zubtsof, and so frightened her that Vazuza declared herself Volga's younger sister and begged to be carried to the Caspian Sea. The tale adds that Vazuza is still the first to awaken in Spring and then rouses Volga from winter sleep.

A similar tradition from the Government of Tula is told about the rivers Don and Shat, both flowing from Lake Ivan. Lake Ivan is described as their father. Shat, contrary to his father's wishes, roams abroad but cannot gain acceptance anywhere and returns home. Don, rewarded for his quietness, receives his father's blessing and sets out on a long journey. On the way he meets a raven flying to the blue sea; they go together. Don plans to dive through the sea and carry it away with him, instructing the raven to croak when it reaches the opposite shore. THE HASTY WORD                                            370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 474-564","start":"474","end":"564","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston’s introduction compares Cinderella’s rise from a despised younger sister sitting by the hearth to a position of honor with the changing status of the popular tale, which moved from the peasant hearth and social neglect to scholarly recognition as part of a noble, even divine, mythic family. He outlines how modern scholars value folk-tales and debate their origins, viewing them variously as distorted nature-myths, moral apologues, relics of primeval wisdom, or blurred pages of medieval history, and often as very ancient compositions rooted in prehistoric mythic philosophy. He then describes two competing hypotheses about European popular tales: one that they are part of a common Indo-European inheritance shared across Europe and India, and another that many are Oriental imports brought by translators, pilgrims, merchants, sectarians, Crusaders, Arab rulers in Spain, and Tartar rulers in Russia. He concludes that instead of resolving this debate he will focus on describing the distinctive characteristics of Russian folk-tales.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Cinderella is described as a despised and flouted younger sister who long sits unnoticed beside the hearth, furtively visits glittering halls, and is eventually transferred from her obscure nook to a place of honor that matches her merits.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Cinderella is singled out as one of the best-known inhabitants of Fairy-land mentioned in popular tales.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The fortunes of the popular tale are explicitly compared to those of Cinderella.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Popular tales are said to have long dwelt beside the hearths of the common people and to have been utterly ignored by their social superiors.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At a later period, the cultured world recognized the existence of popular tales but treated them merely as nursery stories or old wives’ tales, occasionally adapted by condescending scholars.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Eventually popular tales were transferred from the dusk of the peasant’s hut into public daylight, stripped of disfiguring additions, and recognized as the scions of a royal family whose members sometimes trace their origin to old gods.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In modern times folk-tales are carefully tended and highly honored by leading scholars instead of being left to the care of youth and ignorance.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Scholars hold differing views of folk-tale origins, describing them variously as distorted nature-myths, demoralized apologues or parables, relics of primeval wisdom, or blurred transcripts of medieval history.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Critics generally agree that folk-tales are not casual creations of popular fancy but were composed centuries ago, and some may be traced back to prehistoric myths in which early philosophers expressed ideas about the material or spiritual world.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The text notes that not every popular tale has such an ancient or noble lineage, and that mythologists struggle to decide which tales are truly antique and worth deep analysis.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"It is considered difficult to determine, for the tales of any particular country, which are native property and which are borrowed or adapted from elsewhere.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"One hypothesis holds that most European stories were already common in germ to the Aryan tribes before their migrations, forming part of the common inheritance of the Indo-European peoples along with their language.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Under this first hypothesis, similar Märchen told in the Thuringian forest, Norwegian villages, and under the pippal trees of India are viewed as a shared heirloom of the Indo-European race.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A second hypothesis regards many European popular tales as foreign, Oriental fancies introduced into Europe through translations and through the activity of pilgrims, merchants, emissaries of heretical sects, Crusaders, Arab rulers in Spain, and Tartar rulers in Russia.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"According to the second view, European tales are naturalized aliens rather than true inheritances, comparable to stories transmitted from India to authors such as Boccaccio or La Fontaine.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The author states that he will not dwell on the dispute about origin but will instead examine Russian folk-tales as they exist, focusing on their main characteristics and differences from other countries’ stories.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Children are said to listen to Märchen not only in European locales like the Thuringian forest and Norwegian villages but also under the pippal trees of India.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Cinderella","description":"A despised and flouted younger sister The mare instructs him to close his eyes and trust her as she carries him safely across, through a region of total darkness, to snow-covered mountains surrounding a silken meadow with a black silk tent belonging to the Hero of the Plain. Inside the tent, Mirko finds the hero asleep, guarded by a self-moving sword, and honorably refuses to kill him in his sleep; he sets his own sword to guard him in the same way. When the Hero of the Plain awakens, he recognizes Mirko as his old friend’s son, befriends him, and explains that the silken meadow is daily filled with enemies whom he cuts down. After feasting, the two heroes ride out and, with their autonomous swords, slaughter the invading horde, pursuing twelve fleeing warriors to a glass mountain. The fugitives vanish into a breach at the summit, and Mirko, following them down winding steps, reaches a lower world lit by a shining diamond castle in place of the sun, where he kills the twelve. Inside the castle an old witch weaves endless armed men from her loom; Mirko’s sword cuts them down, then dismembers the witch, but a rib from her burned body re-forms her. She begs for mercy, offering four diamond horse-shoe nails and knowledge of how to escape; Mirko takes the nails but kills and burns her completely so she cannot rise again, then searches the underground world and finds it empty of living beings.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mirko sees a narrow glass road rising like a darkness and again instructs him to shut his eyes and hold on firmly.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Emerging from the darkness, Mirko sees glorious snow-covered Mirko regrets leaving her seven-story diamond castle, so she uses a diamond rod to shrink it to the size of a booth, enters it, and transforms it into a golden apple that he can carry in his pocket, keeping the rod as well. Mirko returns home with the princess, the golden apple, and the magic steed.
