THE HASTY WORD                                            370 / RUSSIAN FOLK-TALES. / CHAPTER I. / INTRODUCTORY.; lines 1993-2150","start":"1993","end":"2150","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A poor orphan-lad works for a rich peasant for three years at a copeck a year, each time throwing his wage into a well to test his faithful service; after the third year all three copecks float and he recovers them. He spends them to rescue a kitten from cruel boys and then serves a merchant whose business prospers; the merchant takes the cat on a sea voyage to a distant land plagued by rats and unknown to cats, where the animal saves him and is sold to a landlord for a heap of gold. On the return voyage the merchant decides to keep the gold instead of paying the orphan, but a fierce storm nearly sinks the ship until he repents and promises to give every copeck, after which the sea calms and he pays the orphan a sack of gold. The orphan buys a shipload of incense, burns it along the shore in honor of God, and is visited by an old man who offers him a choice between riches and a good wife; after consulting three ploughing brothers and their strangely infant ‘elder brother’, who counsels him to choose a good wife, the orphan receives a beautiful woman who appears as his divinely granted spouse. Editorial commentary then notes that folk-tales strongly condemn avarice, that stories about misers are widespread and often of Eastern origin, and introduces a new tale about a miserly merchant named Marko and a beggar asking alms.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A poor little orphan-lad, having nothing to live on, hires himself to a rich moujik for one copeck a year.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After his first year of work the orphan throws his copeck into a well, saying that if it does not sink he will keep it as proof he served faithfully, but it sinks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The orphan repeats the same wage test after the second year with the same result, and after the third year insists on receiving a copeck instead of a rouble from his master.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When he throws the third copeck into the well, all three copecks are seen floating on the water, and he takes them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the town, small boys are tormenting a kitten, and the orphan pities it and buys it from them for his three copecks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The orphan hires himself to a merchant to sit in his shop, taking the kitten with him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The merchant’s business begins to prosper remarkably, with goods being bought up very quickly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Preparing for a sea voyage, the merchant asks to take the cat with him to catch mice and amuse him, and the orphan warns he will hold him responsible if the cat is lost.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In a distant country where people know nothing of cats and rats and mice have the upper hand, a landlord lodges the wealthy merchant in a room swarming with rodents, hoping they will eat him so he can seize the money.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The merchant spends the night in the infested room with the cat; in the morning the landlord finds the merchant safe, the cat purring in his arms, and a heap of dead rats and mice on the floor.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The landlord asks to buy the cat, and the merchant agrees on the condition that gold pieces be piled around the cat standing on its hind legs until it is hidden from sight; the landlord pays this price.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"While sailing home with a sackful of gold, the merchant thinks it would be too much to give the money to the orphan for a mere cat and decides to keep it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"As soon as the merchant resolves to keep what does not belong to him, a tremendous storm arises and the ship nearly sinks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The merchant prays to the Lord, confesses his sinful longing, and promises not to keep back even a single copeck; immediately the winds cease, the sea becomes calm, and the ship proceeds safely.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Upon arrival at the quay, the orphan greets the merchant and asks for his cat; the merchant says he has sold it and gives the orphan a sack of gold as payment.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The orphan exchanges his gold with shipmen for a shipload of incense, which he strews along the strand and burns in honor of God, filling the land with a sweet smell.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"An old man suddenly appears and asks the orphan whether he desires riches or a good wife, and the orphan says he does not know.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The old man tells the orphan to go to a field where three brothers are ploughing and ask them for advice.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The orphan finds peasants tilling the soil, greets them, and they direct him to their elder brother, a little boy about three years old sitting in a cart.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The orphan asks the child which to choose, riches or a good wife, and the child tells him to choose the good wife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The orphan returns to the old man and reports that he is to ask for the wife; the old man approves this choice and disappears.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"After the old man vanishes, a beautiful woman stands beside the orphan, greets him as her husband, and invites him to go and seek a place where they may live.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Editorial commentary states that popular tales strongly oppose the sin of avarice, delighting in depicting misers’ sufferings in life and in a troubled ghostly existence.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The commentary content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l13435-l13540","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE POOR MAN, AND THE KING OF THE CROWS. / THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN.; lines 13435-13540","start":"13435","end":"13540","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of the Reed Maiden tale, the king's son splits reeds that contain maidens. The first two maidens who emerge beg for water, but the prince has none; each withers, dies in his arms, and is buried by him with a split reed as grave-mark, from which black roses of mourning grow. The remaining unsplit reed wails as if in grief, while the prince is tormented by sorrow and curiosity described as the 'devil's boring.' When he is about to split the third reed, his magic steed prevents him and only returns the reed when they reach a lake. There the prince splits it, and an incomparable maiden appears, asks for a tiny swallow-beakful of water, which he gives her so she recovers. They embrace and pledge themselves as lovers. The prince tells her to hide in a willow tree and keep absolute silence while he rides home to fetch a glass and golden carriage. While she is hidden in the willow, a crawfish-gathering gypsy girl comes by, sees the maiden's reflection in the water, mistakes it for her own, and is corrected by a golden bird in the tree, which reveals the princess above. The gypsy drags the maiden down by her foot, strips off her purple velvet robe, throws her into the water, where she becomes a golden-feathered duck, then clumsily puts on the stolen robe and sits in the willow. She throws stones at the golden duck but cannot hit her, as the duck always dives in time. When the king's son returns with the glass and gold carriage, the gypsy refuses to come down until he shoots the golden duck so she may drink its blood and eat its flesh. The prince shoots all his arrows, but each turns so that the feathered end points toward the gypsy instead of striking the duck. At nightfall he gives up, takes the gypsy as his bride, and returns home, where the wedding guests are astonished that the promised world-beautiful Reed Maiden has been replaced by a leather-cheeked gypsy girl.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"When the first reed is split, a beautiful maiden emerges, begs for water, receives none, withers, grows pale, dies on the king's son's breast, and is buried by him with a reed planted as a grave-mark from which a black rose blooms in mourning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After the first maiden's burial, a bitter wail is heard from the two unsplit reeds, as if someone were mourning a brother, and the king's son feels deep sadness and guilt for causing her death.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Curiosity, compared to the 'devil's boring' that bores his side like an iron auger, drives the king's son to split the second reed despite his remorse.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"From the second reed up as mourning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The remaining unsplit reed, containing the world-beautiful maiden herself, utters a bitter wail of pain as the bosom.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The magic steed prevents the king's son from immediately splitting the third reed by reaching back and taking it from him, Alenka prepares the oven and invites Ivashko to sit on a shovel, but he feigns ignorance, gets her to demonstrate, and pushes her into the oven, then escapes, climbs a very tall oak-tree near the hut, and hides there. The witch returns with her guests, finds Alenka's baked body in the oven, serves it, and they unknowingly eat her. Outside, the witch rolls on the grass chanting that she has fed on Ivashko's flesh; from the top of the oak Ivashko replies that she has eaten Alenka. Eventually she notices him, gnaws the oak in rage, breaks her teeth, twice visits the smith to have iron teeth forged, and repeatedly gnaws through trees as Ivashko jumps from one to another. In distress, Ivashko calls to passing flocks of swans and geese to carry him to his parents' cottage; the first two flocks refuse, but the third bears him on their wings and drops him in the upper room at home. The next morning his mother bakes pancakes and longs to see her son, while his father recounts a dream in which swans and geese brought Ivashko back. As the parents divide the cakes between themselves, Ivashko twice calls out that none are for him. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l13759-l13860","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING.; lines 13759-13860","start":"13759","end":"13860","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Kiss Miklos tells his two brothers to hide under a bridge and explains that the twenty‑four‑headed dragon will arrive on the steed of the sun, with the shining sun hanging from its saddle‑bow. He predicts that in battle he and the dragon will be equal in strength, eventually turning into a blue and a red flame respectively, and instructs his brothers to strike a sulphur stone against the red flame when it surges upward. The steed of the sun soon arrives on the golden bridge, carrying the dragon and the sun. The dragon curses the horse for stumbling and boasts that if Kiss Miklos were present he would fight him. Miklos springs out, orders his sword to cut off the dragon’s twenty‑four heads, but new heads grow instantly and the monster remains unharmed. The dragon then proposes that they both turn into flames and that the one who extinguishes the other will win the steed of the sun and the shining sun. They transform into blue and red flames that struggle without decision until the two brothers throw the sulphur stone on the red flame, allowing the blue flame to extinguish it and killing the dragon. Miklos gives the steed of the sun to his elder brother, sends his brothers home, and goes his own way. He shakes himself and changes into a little gray cat, runs along the road, and slips into a cabin where the dragons’ mother and the two dragon wives live. The younger dragon’s wife declares that, if she knew Miklos had killed her lord, she would turn into a spring whose water would kill Miklos and his brothers if they drank even a drop. The elder dragon’s wife says she would become a pear‑tree whose pears would kill them if they ate even a morsel. Their mother has them prop open her heavy eyelids with a twelve‑hundred‑pound iron bar so she can see, then threatens that, if Miklos has killed her sons, she will turn into a gigantic mouth with one jaw on earth and the other in the sky, to catch and grind Miklos and his brothers. Several anecdotes are summarized: a husband kills his contradictious wife over a dispute about how something was cut, and she signals her opinion while drowning; a widower looks for his contrary drowned wife by going upstream; a husband who has found a treasure makes his wife appear foolish so her accusation before the seigneur fails, leading to their divorce and his remarriage and prosperity; and a capricious, Western-educated wife is cured by being swaddled and rocked in a traditional Russian cradle. The narrator then introduces the tale \"The Bad Wife,\" describing a woman who always does the opposite of her husband's wishes and a husband who discovers a bottomless pit beneath a currant bush and plans to exploit her contrariness. This tale is said to belong to an old international cycle traced by Benfey from its Indian origin in the Panchatantra through Persia into Europe. The section repeatedly cites Russian proverbs that depict women as contrary or foolish.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The narrator states that many Russian jests deal with themes like the incorrigible folly of man and the inflexible obstinacy of woman, and that such jokes often resemble those found in other countries.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"One anecdote describes a husband and wife disputing whether a rope was cut with a knife or with scissors; the husband throws the scissors-defending wife into a river, and as she is drowning she moves her fingers above the water to indicate scissors.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A Russian variant from Astrakhan features a quarrel about whether a man’s beard was shaved or merely cut off; he throws his contradicting wife into a deep pool, and she raises her hand from the water, making a two-finger sign to indicate that it was cut.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The rope-and-beard anecdotes are associated with a proverb about a contrary woman: \"If you say 'shaved' she'll say 'cut.'\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Another joke tells of a widower whose wife was very antagonistic; when searching for her drowned body he goes up the river rather than down, explaining that she always did everything contrary-wise and must have gone against the stream.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In a further story, a husband who has secretly found a treasure and fears his wife will reveal it tells her various absurd stories that she eagerly repeats, thereby making her testimony in general seem unreliable.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In one variant, the wife accuses her husband before the village seigneur of hiding a treasure, but she talks such nonsense and the husband complains so bitterly that the seigneur pities the husband, frees him, grants a divorce, and marries him to another, young and good-looking wife; the husband then digs up his treasure and lives in great comfort.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The punchline of the treasure story invokes a proverb: \"Women have long hair and short wits.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Another tale describes a man whose wife is so capricious that life with her is impossible; he learns she was raised almost entirely with German and French education, with little Russian influence, and that she was neither swaddled nor swung in a Russian liulka as a baby.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"To remedy her upbringing, the husband has his wife swaddled and placed in a liulka whenever she is capricious or squalls, swinging her to and fro until, after half a year, she becomes gentle and loses her caprices.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the tale \"The Bad Wife,\" the wife lives on the worst of terms with her husband and always does the opposite of what he says: staying in bed when told to get up, refusing to sleep when told to sleep, denying him pancakes when asked, and cooking an enormous pot when he tells her not to bother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In the same tale, when the husband urges his wife not to toil or go out to cut hay, she insists she will go and orders him to follow her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Tormented by his bad wife, the husband goes into the forest to pick berries, finds a currant bush with a bottomless pit in the middle, and considers throwing his wife into it to end his suffering and teach her a lesson.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After returning home, the husband tells his wife not to go into the woods for berries and not to pick the currant bush, prompting her to declare that she will go, pick it clean, and give him no currants.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The narrator remarks that such comic stories can travel great distances with very little change and that Russian skits against women match time-honored quips found in English facetiae collections.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The narrator notes that one of the bad-wife tales has a long family tree traced by Dr. Benfey from an original Indian version in the Panchatantra, through a Persian phase, into numerous European lands.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Russian peasants are said to use the cited proverbs about contrary or foolish women in everyday speech as characterizations of such women.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Narrator / collector","description":"Unspecified narrator who comments on Russian jests, their international parallels, and introduces the bad-wife tales, citing Benfey’s research.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Knife-advocating husband","description":"Husband who insists a rope was cut with a knife, throws his scissors-defending wife into a river, and causes her death.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Scissors-upholding wife","description":"Wife who maintains stream.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Contrary drowned wife (widower story)","description":"The widower’s deceased wife, characterized as very antagonistic and expected to behave contrary-wise even after death.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Treasure-finding moujik (husband)","description":"Peasant husband who finds and hides a treasure, fears his wife will reveal it, and manipulates events so he keeps the treasure and gains a new wife.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"First wife of the moujik","description":"Wife who is prone to repeating absurd stories, accuses her husband of instructions.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:16","name_or_label":"Dr. Benfey","description":"Scholar mentioned as having traced the bad-wife tale from its original content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l14464-l14570","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE USELESS WAGONER. / MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING.; lines 14464-14570","start":"14464","end":"14570","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"The Green Daughter of the Green King lay there neither dead nor alive, like a lifeless block of wood, for she was a magic woman who could leap out of her skin and let a devil endure the blows meant for her.","summary":"Kiss Miklos and the Green Daughter of the Green King arrive at the Lead Friend's lead mansion after travelling across forty-nine kingdoms. While the Lead Friend works at his furnace with Kiss Miklos, the princess explores the house with a lamp, reaches a cellar locked by seven iron doors that open before her magic, and discovers seven leaden vats filled with gold and silver. She repeatedly fills her apron with the treasure, summons a goldsmith, and has the lead thresholds of the house gilded to a hand's thickness. The Lead Friend, an extreme miser, reacts with furious rage, tearing out his lead beard and hair, roaring until the house trembles, and violently dragging the princess by her long golden hair, intending to beat her with a lead flail. Kiss Miklos prevents him from killing her and lays her on a silken bed, where she lies as if lifeless. The narrator explains that she is a powerful magic woman who can suddenly leap out of her skin so that a devil enters it; the devil feels no pain and even laughs when beaten. Distressed by her apparent lifelessness, the Lead Friend begs her to wake and promises to please her if she will stop gilding the house, but she only offers to stop if he reveals where his strength lies, which he refuses to do. The next day the pattern repeats: the Lead Friend takes Kiss Miklos to the furnace, suspecting a plot; the bride again opens the seven iron doors, takes gold from the vats three times, and has three thresholds gilded. On seeing this, the Lead Friend again flies into a rage, abuses her by her golden hair, and is again prevented from killing her by Kiss Miklos, while she escapes injury through her witchcraft and the devil that inhabits her discarded skin.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Kiss Miklos and the princess arrive at the Lead Friend's mansion after travelling across forty-nine kingdoms, and Kiss Miklos declares that they are at home there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Lead Friend runs panting out of his mansion to meet the beautiful princess, but she turns away from him, and he silently brings her into his lead house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At sunrise the Lead Friend goes to his furnace, taking Kiss Miklos with him and leaving the young woman alone in the house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The princess takes a lamp and searches through the lead house from chamber to chamber until she reaches a cellar closed with seven iron doors that open of themselves before her magic.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Inside the cellar the princess sees seven leaden vats in a row, each filled to the brim with gold and silver.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The princess fills her apron with gold from the vats, summons a goldsmith, and has the lead threshold gilded to the thickness of a hand.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Lead Friend is described as so miserly that he scarcely has enough bread to eat and turns every coin seven times between his teeth before parting with it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When the Lead Friend returns in the evening and sees the gilded threshold and the housekeeping, he tears out his own lead beard and hair, tramples them like tow, and roars until the lead house trembles.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Lead Friend seizes the princess by her golden hair, which reaches to her heels, drags her twelve times along the lead floor, and intends to beat her with a lead flail.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kiss Miklos prevents the Lead Friend from beating the princess with the lead flail, takes her from his grasp, and lays her on a silken bed, where she lies neither dead nor alive, like a lifeless block of wood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The narrator explains that the Green Daughter of the Green King is a magic woman who feels no pain and has much power.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"When the Lead Friend winds the princess's golden hair around his hand, she suddenly jumps out of her skin and a devil enters it, so that the more the devil is beaten the more he laughs and feels no trouble.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Distressed and ragged, with torn hair, the Lead Friend goes into the white chamber where the princess lies without life, pushes and talks to her, and finally promises to do all that may please her if she will stop gilding the house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The princess replies that she will stop gilding only if the Lead Friend tells her where his strength lies, but he refuses, saying he would rather part with his life than reveal it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The next day at sunrise the Lead Friend again goes to his furnace, taking Kiss Miklos with him because he suspects Miklos and the Green Daughter of the Green King of plotting his destruction.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Left alone, the bride again goes with a lamp to the cellar; the great iron doors open before her and close behind her; she fills her silk apron with gold three times and has the thresholds of three chambers gilded to the thickness of a hand.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"On seeing that now three thresholds are gilded a hand's thickness, the Lead Friend again tears out his lead beard and hair, tramples them, and roars so terribly that the lead house quivers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"After the second gilding, the Lead Friend seizes the princess's golden hair, drags her twelve times up and down the lead floor, hurls her twelve times against it, and runs for the lead flail to kill her, but Kiss Miklos again rescues her and lays her on the silken bed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The princess again lies as a soulless block of wood but feels no pain, because she knows witchcraft and each time the Lead Friend twists her golden hair she jumps out of her skin so that a devil occupies it and takes the beating as if it were They then offer mythological commentary on several stories: interpreting the name of Tsar Bail Bailyanyin in 'The Three Kingdoms' and connecting it with a White God and color symbolism of light vs darkness; mentioning a sea maiden Nastasya whose beauty affects the sun; describing a variant of 'Ivan Tsarevich, the Fire-Bird, and the Gray Wolf' where Ivan uses his own craft to abduct Yelena the Beautiful and a golden-maned steed and to secure the Fire-Bird; noting extraordinary helpers Freezer and Great Eater and a magical picture-boat in 'Ivan the Peasant's Son'; highlighting a sleeping maiden and slumbering host in 'Water of Youth, Water of Life, and Water of Death' and comparing them to the Irish Queen of Tubber Tintye; remarking that 'The Footless and Blind Champions' resembles the Brünhilde and Gunter episode in the Nibelungenlied; and pointing out that in another 'Three Kingdoms' tale Raven, a great power, becomes a common raven after defeat and surrender of his feather staff.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The editor explains that the name of Tsar Bail Bailyanyin is best translated as 'White of White Bailyanyin, 'White of White Land,' may be identical with Bail Bog, the White God of pre-Christian Russians.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The note states that in tales of Indians and other peoples preserving 'primitive thought,' the people of the myth-tellers are on the side of light and goodness and their enemies on that of darkness and harm, paralleling the antithesis of day and night.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Russian expressions translated as 'white day' and 'white world' and the title content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l9686-l9765","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL. / SOZH AND DNIEPER.; lines 9686-9765","start":"9686","end":"9765","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives brief summaries of three folkloric episodes used as examples in a mythological discussion. First, Prince Vasily climbs a steep hill to the palace where his mother lives with Vikhor. His mother hides him and instructs him to seize Vikhor’s right little finger if Vikhor is in a friendly mood. When Vikhor flies in angrily, Vasily waits for his mother’s signal, then grasps Vikhor’s little finger and clings to him as Vikhor flies about and into the sky. Vikhor finally crashes to the ground and crumbles into fine yellow sand; Vasily keeps the little finger, gathers the sand, and burns it in the stove. Next, the author mentions two other strange beings. The first is Morfei, a supernatural cook in a variant of a well-known tale. A king requires a general, who loves the king’s daughter, to go where none have been and bring back what none have seen. The general travels over swamps, hills, and rivers, reaches a forest hut with an old crone, and is fed by an invisible cook named Morfei. The crone gives Morfei to the general as his servant. On the way home the general twice meets shipwrecked crews by a river; each time Morfei miraculously provides food. In return, the crews successively give the general a magic book, then a magic sabre and towel, although Morfei secretly follows his master instead of remaining with the crews. Using these magical possessions, the general proves himself worthy to marry the princess. The second being is a mysterious magician called Oh, who appears in a story known in many countries and in many Russian versions. A father takes his son to the bazaar to find a teacher who can instruct him in a science that allows people to work little and live well. After a long walk the father exclaims, “Oh! I’m so tired!” and an old magician instantly appears, saying he was called by name. He reveals his name is Oh and offers to educate the boy for a small fee. The commentator notes that in other Russian versions this teacher is explicitly demonic or a devil, so Oh belongs to the supernatural order. The passage concludes by observing that magicians and fiends in stories often wield the same powers for similar purposes, making them hard to distinguish.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Prince Vasily, the youngest of three, is the only one who succeeds in climbing the steep hill where a palace stands in which his mother and Vikhor live.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Prince Vasily enters the palace during Vikhor’s absence and makes himself known to his mother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Vasily’s mother gives him food and hides him in a distant apartment behind cushions so that Vikhor may not easily discover him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Vasily’s mother instructs him that if Vikhor quarrels he must not come out, but if Vikhor chats he should emerge, greet him as father, and seize the little finger of Vikhor’s right hand and go wherever Vikhor flies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Vikhor flies into the house and angrily addresses the queen; Vasily stays hidden until his mother signals him to come out, then he greets Vikhor and grabs Vikhor’s right little finger.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"While Vasily holds his finger, Vikhor flies first about the house and then outside, trying unsuccessfully to shake him off.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After soaring high, Vikhor strikes the ground, falls to pieces, and becomes fine yellow sand; Vasily retains the little finger, gathers the sand, and burns it in the stove.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The author introduces two other singular beings from the Skazkas, the first being Morfei, who appears in a variant of a well-known tale.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In Morfei’s tale, a king has a daughter, and a general who lives opposite falls in love with her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The king will not allow the general to marry his daughter unless the general goes where none have been and brings back what none have seen.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After much thought, the general sets out and travels over swamps, hill, and rivers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The general reaches a wood with a hut in which an old crone lives, and he tells her his story.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The crone calls out to Morfei to dish up the meal, and a dinner immediately appears, which she shares with the general.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The next day the crone presents Morfei, described as a cook, to the general and orders Morfei to serve the general as he has served her; the general then departs with the cook.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"By a river, a shipwrecked crew begs the general for food; he calls on Morfei to give them food and excellent viands appear.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The grateful mariners give the general a magic volume in exchange for his cook, but Morfei does not remain with them and secretly follows his master.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Later, the general meets another shipwrecked crew who, in exchange for Morfei, give him a sabre and a towel, each having magic power.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The general returns to his city and uses his magic properties to convince the king that he is a suitable suitor for the princess.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The second singular being is a mysterious person named Oh, who appears in a story familiar in many countries and found in numerous Russian versions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"In Oh’s story, a father sets out with his boy for the bazaar to find a teacher who can teach a science that allows people to work little, eat delicately, and dress well.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"After a long walk the father grows tired and exclaims, “Oh! I’m so tired!”, whereupon an old magician immediately appears and asks why he was called.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The father replies that he did not call the magician and does not know who he is; the magician explains that his name is Oh and the father had cried “Oh!”.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The magician asks where the boy is being taken, hears that a teacher is sought, and undertakes to educate the boy for one assignat rouble for a year’s tuition.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The commentator notes that in this story the teacher is merely called a magician, but in other Russian versions his counterpart is described as demoniacal and often openly styled a devil.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The commentator concludes that Oh belongs to the supernatural order of beings and remarks that in stories magicians and fiends often wield the same powers for the same purposes, making them hard to distinguish.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Prince Vasily","description":"Youngest prince who climbs the steep hill to the palace, hides at content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l612-l664","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"WITH EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA / SELECTED BIBLIOGRAPHY: / RECOMMENDED READING-- / INTRODUCTION; lines 612-664","start":"612","end":"664","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Introductory prose describes how the poems in the volume are surviving fragments of ancient Scandinavian poetry, collected by Vigfusson and Powell. It outlines a long tradition of poets preserving old tales, the impact of Christianity and calmer social conditions in Iceland, and the shift from verse to prose storytelling influenced slightly by Irish models. The emergence of the saga is described as the Icelanders’ preferred medium: the life of a hero told in prose with simple plot, chronological order, formulaic phrases, avoidance of digression, and an effaced narrator. The perfection of the saga is linked to long winter evenings and communal gatherings where households worked (spinning, weaving, net-making) while listening to one member retell stories of adventure and heroic deeds. Sagas arose while the deeds of dead heroes were fresh, often recited before those who shared in the events, and in pure form remained truthful to the teller. Even sagas based on old poetic debris about mythological heroes are said to be deeply entwined with racial tradition and the storyteller’s thought-life. Repeated communal retelling at feasts and firesides made these tales more coherent and structurally organic, helped fix their sequence, eased reciters’ memory, and encouraged decorative devices that aided remembrance and preservation. After generations of polishing, sagas were written down mainly between 1141 and 1220, and their form influenced later learned works, including histories and hagiography, which adopted saga style. The editor notes that only a small portion of existing sagas has appeared in English.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poems in the volume are described as surviving fragments of ancient Scandinavian poetry, all that remain of a larger tradition.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Vigfusson and Powell collected the surviving pieces of this poetry into volumes of a \"Corpus\".","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A long and illustrious line of poets preserved old traditions over centuries, though the earlier great harvest of song was never equalled later.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After Christianity entered Iceland and other causes quieted people’s lives, poetry continued but lost its exclusive hold over people’s minds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In a less He hears a wolf-like cry and sees four bears, Deer Raiser's named pets, advancing in single file with aggressive posture, apparently sent to kill him. Nati'nesthani proclaims himself by the names of powerful gods, including Nayénezgani, Hastséyalti, and Sasnalkáhi, and as the bears pass he shoots each with arrows, killing them so their bodies tumble out of sight over a ledge. Deer Raiser approaches, calling out to his \"pets\" by name and asking them to save him a portion, then feigns anger that Nati'nesthani has let them pass. Nati'nesthani reveals he has slain them; Deer Raiser looks over the ledge, is shocked and sorrowful at the death of his bears, and sits in silence, not thanking his son-in-law. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 10909-11006","start":"10909","end":"11006","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes explain several ritual figures, objects, and practices in Navaho tradition. The Dsahadoldzá or Fringe-mouths are divine beings of land and water, represented in the klédzi hatál rite by sand-paintings and elaborately costumed masqueraders whose body paint and basket crown symbolize clouds, lightning, and sunlight. Tielin are ferocious, blue-horned pets guarding the door of Tiéholtsodi the water monster's dwelling. Na-tsi-li't a-kó-di is a short or fragmentary rainbow. Black Hastsé (Black God) is a reserved deity dwelling at Tsení`hodilyil; he owns all fire, first made fire, and invented the fire-drill. He appears rarely in an elaborate \"scene of succor\" with three other gods, impersonated by a black-clad actor carrying a fire-drill and cedar bark. The fire-drill, though largely replaced by matches and flint-and-steel, remains prominent in myths and ceremonies and is considered a rudimentary apparatus among aboriginal fire-drills. One note suggests that peculiar acts in a preceding paragraph likely refer to agricultural rites. Another note outlines historical changes in smoking: Navahoes now smoke cigarettes but formerly used terra-cotta pipes; pipes occur archaeologically and are still ceremonially used by Mokis. In ceremonies, tobacco is sacrificed as cigarettes, which also appear in ancient caves. The expression Ni-no-ká-di-ne` (People up on the Earth) may denote mountain dwellers or the whole Indian race in contrast to whites; in the myth it likely refers to supernatural people Nati'nesthani meets. A final note lists several plants mixed with tobacco, whose exact botanical identities remain uncertain.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Dsahadoldzá or Fringe-mouths are described as a class of divine beings represented in the rite of klédzi hatál by sand-paintings and by masqueraders.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"There are two kinds of Fringe-mouths: Fringe-mouths of the land and Fringe-mouths of the water (Thastlátsi Dsahadoldzá), the latter being those referred to in the story.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Zigzag lines on the bodies of the Fringe-mouths in the pictures represent crooked lightning, which they used as ropes to lift a log.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"On the mask shown in the dry-painting, the mouth is surrounded by white radiating lines, giving the name Fringe-mouths.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The actor representing Fringe-mouths of the land has one half of his body and mask painted black and the other half red.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The actor representing Fringe-mouths of the water has his body painted half blue and half yellow, and wears a similar mask and crown or headdress.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The crown consists of a basket without a bottom fitted on the head; its lower surface is painted black to represent a dark cloud and streaked with white for lightning, while the upper surface is colored red to represent sunlight on the back of the cloud; feathers of the red-shafted woodpecker attached to the edge represent sunbeams.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"This basket crown is said to be similar to that worn by Gánaskidi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ascending from the basket crown is a tripod of aromatic sumac twigs painted white, with finely combed red wool laid between the limbs and a downy eagle-feather tipping each stick.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The actor carries a bow in his left hand adorned with three eagle-plumes and two tufts of turkey feathers and a white gourd rattle in his right hand, sometimes decorated with two whorls of feathers.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The actor’s torso, arms, and legs are naked but painted; he wears a shirt around his loins, rich necklaces, ear pendants, and a fox-skin collar that is vaguely indicated in the painting.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The angles of the white lightning painted on the actor’s chest and limbs are fewer than those shown in the sand-paintings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Tielin are described as ferocious pets belonging to Tiéholtsodi, the water monster, guarding the door of his dwelling and having blue horns.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Na-tsi-li't a-kó-di (short rainbow) is defined as a fragmentary or incomplete rainbow.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Has-tsé-zin-i means Black Hastsé or Black God; several such beings are said to dwell at Tsení`hodilyil near Tse`gíhi.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Black God is described as a reserved and exclusive individual whom other yéi do not visit whenever they wish.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Black God is said to own all fire, to have been the first to make fire, and to be the inventor of the fire-drill.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Black God is rarely represented by a masquerader; when a night chant is given without the public dance of the last night, he appears in a scene of succor on the evening of the ninth day with Nayénezgani, To`badzistsíni, and Hastséoltoi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The personator of Black God is described as wearing black clothes, a black mask with white marks and red hair, a fox-skin collar, and carrying a fire-drill and a bundle of cedar-bark.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The author notes that he has never seen Black God represented in a dry-painting or masquerade, and has not witnessed the described scene of succor; the ceremony was described to him by medicine-men.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The ceremony involving Black God is said to be very elaborate; the actor must be well paid for services that occupy the whole day from sunrise to sunset, although the act of succor itself lasts only a few minutes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The fire-drill is now little used by the Navahoes, having been largely replaced by matches and flint-and-steel, but it is frequently mentioned in myths and used in ceremonies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Among many aboriginal fire-drills described by Dr. Walter Hough, the Navaho fire-drill is characterized as the rudest, looking like something made to order.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Tsin-tli'-zi is glossed as signifying hard, brittle wood.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The author suggests that various peculiar acts described in an earlier paragraph probably refer to agricultural rites still or recently practised by the Navahoes, but notes he has never witnessed such rites.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Navahoes are said now to universally smoke cigarettes, while in ancient days they smoked terra-cotta pipes; fragments of such pipes are often found in New Mexico and Arizona.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Cliff-dwellers also had pipes, and such pipes are still ceremonially used by the Mokis.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"In ceremonies, Navahoes sacrifice tobacco in the form of cigarettes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"Cigarettes have been found in ancient caves and other neglected places in New Mexico and Arizona, indicating that cigarettes are not new to the Southwest.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"Ni-no-ká-di-ne` (People up on the Earth) may refer to people living up on the mountains as opposed to those in canyons and valleys, or to the whole Indian race contrasted with whites; JOHN COMFORT FILLMORE. / TEXTS AND INTERLINEAR TRANSLATIONS.; lines 12282-12489","start":"12282","end":"12489","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents several Navajo songs and explanatory notes. In an initial song, figures called "Reared under the Earth" and "Changing Grandchild" arrive from houses made of knives, where knives hang high, while a refrain addresses a holy one whose treasures are said not to be for the singer's sake. The singer explains that the song refers to Nayénezgani speaking with his mother Estsánatlehi; they exchange compliments about who is truly divine, and Nayénezgani declares that weapons and other treasures given by the Sun belong to his mother. The "houses of knives" are identified as chambers in the Sun's house.

"Song of the Sun" (281) then gives four verses in which Nayénezgani ("Slayer of the Alien Gods"), Child of the Water, Reared Beneath the Earth, and Changing Grandchild each proclaim that they come with various knives (dark, serrate, of all kinds, yellow) from houses made of knives and from where these knives hang high, bearing an implement of the rites called alíli. A note glosses alíli as a show or dance of the rites and as a wand or sacred implement, possibly colored hoops used to raise a storm.

Another "Song of the Sun" (282) depicts the singer's mind, the Sun God, the border of the earth, and Estsánatlehi's house approaching the hearth area of a lodge, together with "walking in old age" and a "beautiful trail." A parallel verse describes the Moon God and Yolkaí Estsán in the same pattern. Notes explain that yúni is a specific part of the lodge floor toward which the house approaches, and that the phrases "in old age walking" and "his trail beautiful" function in prayers as a request for long life and happiness.

Finally, the "Significant Words of Songs of the Log" briefly describe a beautiful tree or log which falls, is prepared or trimmed for the singer, has been prepared, and is carried with the Over four consecutive mornings, the young woman brings him stewed venison and a basket of mush made from wild seeds, the basket being of a type used in Navaho rites. Her father has secretly placed poison first at the point of finish of the basket, then around the edge, then throughout the mush, and finally in all the food, intending to kill the visitor. The Wind People repeatedly whisper to Nati'nesthani, telling him where the poison lies and which food is safe. Each morning he adopts or cites a personal \"custom\" in how he eats: first, he turns the basket and eats from the side opposite the point of finish; second, he eats only from the middle of the basket near sunrise; third, he refuses mush entirely, claiming he has sworn that the sun shall never see him eat mush; and fourth, he fasts completely, saying he always eats nothing one day in every four. The old man, who usually kills visitors with poisoned tobacco or baskets, becomes increasingly frustrated and suspicious, wondering if his daughter is warning her husband, but she denies this. Sigi is declared a \"wolf in holy places\" (outlaw) and leaves the land with Odin, later becoming a successful warrior-king over the Huns and fathering Rerir. Sigi is eventually killed by his wife’s brothers, but Rerir returns, avenges his father by destroying the kin-slayers, and becomes an even mightier king; he and his wife remain childless and pray to the gods. Odin and Freyia hear their prayer, and Freyia sends her giant-born maid in crow gear with a special apple, which the king and queen receive; the queen conceives after eating part of it, though her pregnancy is prolonged. Rerir goes to war, falls sick, dies on campaign, and is said to be minded to \"go home to Odin,\" a fate greatly desired in those days.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigi is introduced as the son of Odin and is said to be mightier and higher of kin than Skadi, according to the speech of men of that time.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Skadi has a thrall named Bredi, who is praised for prowess and might of hand equal to free men considered more worthy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Sigi and Bredi go deer hunting for a whole day, and when they gather their prey, Bredi has slain far more deer than Sigi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sigi resents being outdone by his thrall, falls upon Bredi, kills him, and buries his body in a snow-drift.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Upon returning home, Sigi tells Skadi that Bredi has ridden away from him into the wild-wood and that he quickly went out of sight, pretending ignorance of what happened.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Skadi mistrusts Sigi’s tale, sends men to seek Bredi, and they eventually find his body in a certain snow-drift.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Skadi declares that the snow-drift should be called \"Bredi’s Drift\" and notes that people later call any very great drift by that name.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Because Sigi has murdered the thrall, he is declared a \"wolf in holy places\" and may no longer remain in the land with his father.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Odin gives Sigi fellowship, leads him away from the land to certain war-ships, and provides him strength for warfare before they part.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Sigi is successful in war, gains land and lordship, marries a noble wife, becomes a great and mighty king ruling over the land of the Huns, and has a son named Rerir who grows tall and shapely.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"As Sigi grows old, his wife’s brothers, whom he trusted, turn against him, fall on him when he is unwary and poorly banesmen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After avenging his father, Rerir acquires land, lordship, and wealth through war, becomes mightier than his father, THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 10689-10782","start":"10689","end":"10782","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes explain a version of the Deer Spring People story, interpreting it as evidence for former totemism and local origins of Navaho gentile names. Additional notes analyze the etymology of Ho-na-gá`-ni (People of the Walking Place), Na-nas-te'-zin (Navaho name for Zuñi Indians), and Kin-a-á`-ni (People of the High Pueblo House), relating them to places, ruins, and a high stone wall passed by immigrants. The passage then describes the ritual depiction and dance of the female yéi or goddess yébaad, including her mask, costume, color symbolism, and masquerade performers. Finally, it explains the meaning of the hero name Na-ti'n-es-tha-ni (Nati'nesthani) as ‘he who teaches himself’ and notes that storytellers continue to use this name or call him ‘the man’ or ‘the Navaho.’","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"During a march, one woman lingers behind at Deer Spring for a while, as if reluctant to leave.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Because she loiters at Deer Spring, she is called Deer Spring, and her descendants become a gens bearing that name.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The same version of the legend explains names at magic fountains by saying women loitered at the springs rather than calling out their names.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The story of the Deer Spring People is treated as strong evidence for the former existence of totemism in the legend.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Immigrants from the west are assumed to have once had totemic clan names such as the Deer gens.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"People of the Deer gens are said to have stayed behind at a spring and given their clan name to that spring.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Over time the group becomes known as People of the Deer Spring, retaining their old name in a changed form.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Because the clan keeps its altered name, the storyteller states that the fate of the original deer totem is unknown.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The name Maitó`dine` is suggested to have a similar explanatory origin to that of the Deer Spring People.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ho-na-gá`-ni is interpreted as meaning People of the Walking Place, derived from ho (locative), nága (to walk), and ni (people).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Navaho gentile names are said to generally have local meanings, and origin stories explaining them may be entirely mythical.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"An episode in the legend is interpreted as showing that kindness and pity exist among Navahoes, and that although there are many thieves, there are also honest men and women.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Na-nas-te'-zin is the Navaho term for the Zuñi Indians and is analyzed into aná (alien or enemy), naste (horizontal stripe), and zin (black).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Some say Na-nas-te'-zin refers to the way Zuñi people cut their hair straight across the forehead like bangs, while others say it is the name of a locality.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Kin-a-á`-ni or Kin-ya-á`-ni is glossed as People of the High Pueblo House or of the high wall of stone or adobe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The term kinaá` could apply to many ruins in Navaho country, but it is actually known for a massive ruin six or seven stories high in Bernalillo County near Chaves Station.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"This ruin consists of unusually large stone fragments and looks more like a ruined European castle than other old Indian dwellings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The ruin near Chaves Station is considered too far from the San Juan settlements, where the western immigrants ended their journey, to plausibly be the origin place of the Kinaá`ni gens name.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A high stone wall passed en route by the immigrants is proposed as the place originally associated with the Kinaá`ni name.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"There are many pueblo remains around San Francisco Mountain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Plate I, fig. 1 shows a yébaad, a female yéi or goddess, typically represented in dry paintings wearing a square mask that covers only the face and is painted blue with a yellow lower margin representing evening light.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The yébaad mask has red and black lines for hair and ears and is topped with downy eagle-feathers tied on with white strings.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The goddess wears a white robe from armpits to near the knees, decorated with red and blue designs representing sunbeams and a fringe at the bottom.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Her costume also includes white leggings with colored woven garters, embroidered moccasins, an ornamental sash, a wand of spruce twigs in each hand or spruce in one hand and a seed-basket in the other, turquoise and coral jewelry, and long fox-skin strips hanging from wrists and elbows.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"In the nahikáï dance there are ideally six yébaad in masquerade, though sometimes fewer are used because it is hard to find enough suitable performers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Yébaad actors are usually low-sized men and boys whose appearance must contrast with those playing male gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"Each male yébaad dancer wears only moccasins and a skirt held by a silver-studded belt, has body and limbs painted white, hair unbound over the shoulders, wears the square female mask, and carries bundles of spruce twigs in both hands secured with strings so they cannot be dropped.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"Occasionally females dance as yébaad; they wear ordinary women’s clothing but also the mask and spruce wands like the young men.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"In the referenced plate, male gods except Dsahadoldzá are shown with white arms, while the female deity is depicted with yellow arms.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"The exact etymology of Na-ti'n-es-tha-ni is undetermined, but the name conveys the idea of one who teaches himself, discovers things for himself, or thinks out problems independently.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"The verb nasinítin means 'Teach me how to do it,' and in it the second and third syllables function as pronouns.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"Although the hero later has his name changed, storytellers usually continue to call him Nati'nesthani throughout the story.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"Storytellers often refer to the hero as 'the man' or 'the Navaho.'","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Loitering woman at Deer Spring","description":"A woman who, during a march, lingers at Deer Spring and is named after that spring.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Deer Spring People","description":"Descendants of the woman named Deer Spring who form a gens bearing the Deer Spring name.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Women at the magic content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l8813-l8880","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 8813-8880","start":"8813","end":"8880","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic description of how reed cigarettes and wooden kethawns are prepared and used as sacrifices in Navaho ritual. Reed segments are cut from root toward tip, notched to mark precedence, and kept oriented with the butt near the operator and the tip pointing east in the medicine-lodge. Cigarettes are painted, fitted with sacred feathers, filled with tobacco, sealed with pollen, symbolically lighted with rock crystal, placed on a patient, and finally sacrificed, all in a strict order of precedence. Sacrifices are laid out according to cardinal directions in rows and circles, matching the ranked gods to whom they are offered. Additional items are bundled in corn-husks oriented east, sprinkled or daubed with pollen from butt to tip. Only hollow reed internodes are used; nodes and other debris are discarded in a way that prevents divine misunderstanding and are deposited north of the lodge. Commercial tobacco is forbidden; feathers and pollen help keep the tobacco in place. Kethawns have established sizes measured by body-based units, and the text notes that this sacrificial system is common among pueblo tribes of the Southwest and seen elsewhere. Specific forms of kethawns are described: a talking kethawn made of a male black stick and female blue stick, a set of a dozen kethawns for the night chant without gender distinction, and a set of fifty-two kethawns for the night chant comprising four central cigarettes on meal and forty-eight surrounding sticks of different woods arranged by cardinal direction.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Reeds for cigarettes are cut in pieces starting from the end nearest the root and continuing toward the point, with each piece notched near the butt using a stone knife.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Notches and handling of the pieces ensure that the relations of butt and tip ends of each cigarette and their order of precedence from butt to tip are not forgotten.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"During painting and other manipulations, the butt end of each cigarette must remain nearer to the operator and the tip end farther away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The cigarette-maker sits in the west of the medicine-lodge facing east, and while there the cigarettes lie east and west with their tips to the east.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When several cigarettes are made for one act of sacrifice, the first piece cut off is marked with one notch, the second with two, the third with three, and the fourth with four near the butt ends to keep them distinguishable and ordered.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When cigarettes are painted, given sacred feathers of the bluebird and yellowbird, filled with tobacco, sealed with moistened pollen, and symbolically lighted with rock crystal, the segment cut nearest the butt is handled first and that nearest the tip last.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Cigarettes are collected, placed in the patient’s hands, applied to the patient’s body, and then taken out and sacrificed, always maintaining the established order of precedence.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When sacrifices are laid out in a straight row, the order of precedence runs from north to south with the senior sacrifice at the northern extremity and the junior at the southern extremity.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When sacrifices are laid out in a circle, the order runs from east back to east by way of the south, west, and north.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The gods to whom sacrifices are made commonly have an order of precedence; the senior sacrifice is dedicated to the higher god and the junior sacrifice to the lower god.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Other articles to be sacrificed, such as feathers, beads, and powdered vegetable and mineral substances, are placed together with cigarettes in corn-husks.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Corn-husks are laid on a clean cloth with their tips to the east, and the cigarettes and sacred feathers placed in them are also oriented with their tip ends to the east.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Dry pollen is sprinkled on cigarettes from butt to tip, and moist pollen is daubed on their sides from butt to tip.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Only the hollow internode of the reed is used for cigarettes; the part containing the solid node is discarded and split so the gods will not mistake it for a true cigarette and be disappointed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"All debris from cigarette manufacture is carefully collected and deposited to the north of the medicine-lodge.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Tobacco of commerce must not be employed in making the cigarettes.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A plug of feathers is shoved into the reed tube from tip to butt with an owl’s feather to keep tobacco from falling out at the butt, while moistened pollen keeps the tobacco in at the tip end.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Rules for measuring kethawns use units such as one or more finger joints, the span, the width of the outstretched hand from tip of thumb to tip of little finger, and the width of three or four joined fingertips.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Each kethawn has its established size determined by these measurements.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The system of sacrifice described is said to be common among pueblo tribes of the Southwest, and traces of it have been found elsewhere.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The talking kethawn (ketán yaltí) consists of a male stick painted black and a female stick painted blue.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"A kethawn used in the ceremony of the night chant is made in sets of a dozen for one occasion, and in this case male and female are not distinguished.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"A set of fifty-two kethawns used in the night chant includes four cigarettes lying on meal at the center and forty-eight surrounding sticks of wood.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"In this set of fifty-two, sticks in the east are made of mountain mahogany, those in the south of Forestiera neo-mexicana, those in the west of juniper, and those in the north of cherry.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"cigarette-maker","description":"Person who sits in the west of the medicine-lodge facing east and performs the cutting, notching, painting, and assembling of sacrificial cigarettes.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"patient","description":"Person whose hands and body the cigarettes are applied to before the cigarettes are taken out and sacrificed.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"gods","description":"Deities to whom the sacrifices of cigarettes and kethawns are made and who may be ranked as higher or lower recipients.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4","role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"pueblo tribes of the Southwest","description":"Neighboring cultural groups among whom the described system of sacrifice is said to be common.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"ritual cigarette-maker","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Described as sitting in the west of the
