{
  "record_id": "batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l9668-l9765",
  "source_text_path": "texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md",
  "passage_locator": {
    "label": "III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9668-9765",
    "start": "9668",
    "end": "9765",
    "translation": "Navaho Legends",
    "notes": "Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."
  },
  "canonical_text": {
    "quote": "",
    "summary": "Ethnographic notes 76–85 discuss a Navaho hoop-and-pole game (nánzoz) compared to the Mandan chungkee game, possible identification of shells in the myths, the vague and contested characterization of the deity Békotsidi (linked to animal creation, moon-bearing, and prayers for horses), imported bayeta cloth used for red blanket designs, the linguistic role of coyote as a naming standard for other canids, a divine family of twelve brothers and one sister who die and become immortal, the structure and use of Navaho sweat-houses, a Coyote trickster episode involving emesis and food theft, the ritual command word tóhe used to make objects stand, and the convention of representing the gods’ hair as yellow or reddish in masks and dry-paintings.",
    "language": "English",
    "quote_policy": "summarized"
  },
  "literal_observations": [
    {
      "id": "obs:1",
      "text": "The game of nánzoz uses a hoop rolled along the ground while long poles are thrown after it.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:2",
      "text": "Nánzoz is said to be much the same as the Mandan game of chungkee described by Catlin.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:3",
      "text": "The Navaho pole for nánzoz is made of two overlapping alder pieces, each a natural fathom long, bound by a long branching hide strap called thágibike or turkey-claw.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:1"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:4",
      "text": "Certain shells mentioned in the myths may correspond to actual shells, possibly the same as those in the story of \"The Great Shell of Kintyél.\"",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:2"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:5",
      "text": "Békotsidi is only vaguely described, not represented by masked characters or dry-paintings, and is said to look like an old man.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:6",
      "text": "There is a myth and four songs of sequence about Békotsidi, and a Navaho who wants a fine horse may sing the second and third songs while praying to him, specifying the desired horse’s color and appearance.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:3"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:7",
      "text": "Some traditions say Békotsidi made all animals not otherwise accounted for in the myths, others that he and the Sun made the animals, and others that he created only large game and modern domestic animals.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:8",
      "text": "In one part of the text Békotsidi is called the god who carries the moon, in another Kléhanoai is named as moon-bearer, and some informants say Békotsidi is the same as the God of the Americans.",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:4"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:9",
      "text": "Bayeta, a crimson baize with a long nap and Spanish-labeled bales, replaced scarlet strouding in the Southwest and provided bright red threads for Navaho blankets, especially in older finer pieces.",
      "category": "object",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:5"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:10",
      "text": "The coyote (mai) is treated as the type for wild canids: the great wolf is maítso (“great coyote”) and the kit fox is maidotli'z (“blue or gray coyote”).",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:6"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:11",
      "text": "One version describes a divine family of twelve brothers and one sister, collectively called Diné Nakidáta (“Twelve People”).",
      "category": "relationship",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:12",
      "text": "Estsánatlehi creates another brother to replace Léyaneyani, who left the brotherhood.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:13",
      "text": "These brothers once died, came to life again, and are now immortal and endowed with superhuman powers.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:7"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:14",
      "text": "The Navaho sweat-house is usually not more than three feet high and uses stones heated in an external fire, placed on the floor and covered with blankets to create intense heat.",
      "category": "setting",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:15",
      "text": "In a nonceremonial sweat, the occupant emerges to roll in the sand, dries, brushes the sand away, and may return to the sweat-house repeatedly in an afternoon.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:8"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:16",
      "text": "In a ceremonial sweat, a bath of yucca suds usually follows, and the subject is dried with corn meal.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:9"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:17",
      "text": "One version relates that before entering the sudatory, Coyote suggests producing emesis by tickling their throats, using large pieces of pine bark as dishes for the vomit.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:18",
      "text": "In the story, Coyote, who has eaten only bugs and worms, secretly exchanges bark dishes after emesis so that Yélapahi’s dish appears to contain bugs and worms, while the other dish holds fat venison.",
      "category": "action",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:19",
      "text": "Coyote tells Yélapahi to open his eyes and see the bad things in his stomach, and the giant believes that bugs and worms made him sick and slow.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:10"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:20",
      "text": "The word tóhe (thóhay), interpreted as \"stand, stick, or stay,\" is shouted in an authoritative tone during rites when it is desired that an object obey the conjurer’s will.",
      "category": "speech",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:21",
      "text": "In the Mountain Chant’s dance of the standing arcs, the cry \"tóhe\" is repeatedly used when arcs are placed on performers’ heads so that they stand without apparent support.",
      "category": "sequence",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:11"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:22",
      "text": "The hair of the gods, both friendly and alien, is said to be yellow; ceremonial masks have reddish or yellowish hair, and in dry-pictures the gods’ hair is represented by red.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:12"]
    },
    {
      "id": "obs:23",
      "text": "Navahoes often refer to dull tints of red as yellow.",
      "category": "attribute",
      "evidence_refs": ["ev:12"]
    }
  ],

GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 8454-8537","start":"8454","end":"8537","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Navaho hero, later called Sadáni, demonstrates two young bumblebees to the Eagle People, gradually reducing their fear, then lays the bees and tumbleweed seeds on the ground as tokens showing he has slain their enemies. The people rejoice, and chiefs including Great Wolf of the white pueblo and Fox of the blue pueblo promise him eight beautiful maidens in marriage. Great Wolf leads him to a fine apartment in his house, richly furnished, and grants it to him as his son-in-law. Principal men from all the pueblos visit and thank him, while maidens from yellow, black, white, and later blue houses perform a structured bathing, drying, feeding, and bedding service for him using soap-weed suds, corn meal, and various foods.

The next morning the Navaho goes to the sky-hole with the bees and tumbleweed seeds, commands them to go down to the land of the Navahoes, multiply, and serve his people without causing sorrow, and throws them down to earth. The narrative explains that bees’ honey and tumbleweed seeds are now used in the rites of yói hatál, the bead chant. The Navaho remains in the pueblos of the Eagle People for twenty-four days, during which he is taught their songs, prayers, ceremonies, and sacrifices, corresponding to the rites of yói hatál, until they tell him to return to earth.

The Eagles put a robe of eagle plumage on him, lead him to the sky-hole, and promise that he will now be light and able to move through the air by his own power. He spreads his wings, and with the Eagles’ powerful breath descends through the sky-hole, gliding on outstretched wings until he lands on the summit of Tsótsil. Returning to his Navaho relations, he finds their lodge’s smell intolerable, so they build a medicine-lodge for him. They bathe and reclothe his younger brother and send him into the lodge, where the two stay twelve days while the elder brother recounts his story and instructs the younger in all the rites and songs learned among the Eagles.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Navaho hero takes two young bumblebees from his blanket and swings them around his head, frightening the surrounding people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The people initially run behind their houses in terror, but with repeated swinging of the bees they run shorter distances and become progressively less frightened.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After the people regain courage, the Navaho lays the two bees on the ground, places tumbleweed seeds beside them, and declares these are the children of the Eagle People’s enemies, showing that he has slain the enemies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Eagle People rejoice at the news that their enemies are slain, and individuals speak of brothers, fathers, and sons who were killed by those enemies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Great Wolf, chief of the white pueblo, offers two beautiful maiden daughters to the Navaho, while Fox, chief of the blue pueblo in the south, and other chiefs promise additional maidens, totaling eight promised wives.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The chief of the white pueblo conducts the Navaho to his house and into a large, beautiful apartment with smooth white earth-coated walls, a fireplace, mealing-stones, pots, and water-jars.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The white pueblo chief addresses the Navaho as Sadáni and as his son-in-law, declaring that the apartment is head, maidens of the black house wash his limbs and feet, and maidens of the yellow house dry him with corn meal.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After the bath, the maidens leave and then return at dark with maidens from the blue house; each of the eight maidens carries a bowl of food of a different kind, which they set before the Navaho, who eats until he is satisfied.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The maidens bring beautiful robes and blankets and spread them on the floor to serve as the Navaho’s bed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The next morning the Navaho goes to the sky-hole carrying the young bees and tumbleweed seeds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"He tells the bees to go down to the land of the Navahoes, multiply there, and be used by his people, warning them not to cause sorrow and trouble or he will destroy them again, then throws them down to the earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"He similarly addresses the tumbleweed seeds and throws them down through the sky-hole to the earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The narrator explains that bees’ honey and tumbleweed seeds are now used in the rites of yói hatál, or the bead chant.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Navaho remains in the pueblos of the Eagle People for twenty-four days, during which he is taught their songs, prayers, ceremonies, and sacrifices, identified with rites now known in yói hatál.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"When the Navaho has learned all the rites, the people tell him it is time for him to return to the earth from which he came.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Eagles outside.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The Navaho’s relations build a medicine-lodge where he may sit by content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l9963-l10063","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9963-10063","start":"9963","end":"10063","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes 107–116 supplement the Navaho War Gods myth, explaining life-feathers and pollen symbolism, Spider Woman’s hardening of the twin heroes, their journey to the Sun’s house through personified cosmic obstacles, the colored sentinels and Thunder brothers in the Sun’s house, and the stone armor and elemental weapons given to the War Gods, with comments on possible cultural influences.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A life-feather or breath-feather is a feather taken from a live bird, especially from a live eagle.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Life-feathers are believed to preserve life, possess other magic powers, and are used in all the rites.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Pueblo Indians catch eaglets and rear them in captivity to obtain life-feathers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Navahoes catch full-grown eagles in traps and pluck them while alive to obtain life-feathers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Pollen is described as an emblem of peace and underlies expressions such as “Put your feet down in peace.”","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Spider Woman’s ladder has only four rungs, and she has many seats in her house; the elder brother sits on an obsidian seat and the younger on a turquoise seat.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Spider Woman offers the brothers food of four kinds, but they accept only one kind.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"An obsidian image emerges from an eastern apartment and stands on a serrated platform; the elder brother stands beside it while Spider Woman blows a strong breath four times on the image toward him, giving him the hard nature of obsidian to preserve him in future trials.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A turquoise image comes from the south room and stands on a serrated platform; the younger brother stands beside it while Spider Woman blows on the turquoise image toward him, giving him the hard nature of turquoise.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Modern rites of hozóni hatál include a prayer about these incidents that begins, “Now I stand on pésdolgas,” referring to the serrated platform.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"On their journey to the Sun’s house, the War Gods reach Tó`sato or Hot Spring and encounter Tiéholtsodi, a water monster who threatens them but is appeased with prayer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The War Gods meet Old Age People who treat them kindly but warn them not to follow the trail leading to the house of Old Age.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"They come to Hayolkál (Daylight), which rises like a great range of mountains in front of them; Daylight later rises from the ground and lets them pass under after songs are sung.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"They come to Tsalyél (Darkness); Wind whispers songs into their ears, they sing them, and Darkness rises to let them pass under.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"They come to water, walk over it, and on the other side meet their sister, the daughter of the Sun, who silently turns around and leads them to the Sun’s house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"According to version A, groups of sentinels lie in the entrance passageway to the Sun’s house; each group of four lies behind a curtain, and within each group the first sentinel is black, the second blue, the third yellow, and the fourth white.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The brothers sing songs to the guardians and sprinkle pollen on them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Version A gives the names of two young men as Black Thunder and Blue Thunder.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Other storytellers report that when the brothers enter the Sun’s house they declare they came to seek their father, though this teller omitted the detail.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Each War God receives four articles of armor: knife moccasins (peské), knife leggings (pesistlê'), knife shirt (pesê'), and knife hat (pestsá).","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The term ‘pes’ originally applied to flint knives and their flakes, later expanded to iron knives and to all kinds of metal, such as copper (peslitsí, red metal) and silver (peslakaí, white metal).","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Many Navahoes now think their gods’ mythic armor was of iron; the author once thought the idea of armored heroes was borrowed from Spanish invaders but later concluded the armor was imagined as stone flakes; Mokis believe their gods and heroes wore armor of flint.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Weapons given to the War Gods include chain-lightning arrows, sheet-lightning arrows, sunbeam arrows, rainbow arrows, a stone knife-club, and hatsoilhál, described by some as a thunderbolt and by others as a broad stone knife.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Some say only one stone knife was given, for Nayénezgani, and only two thunderbolts were given, both for To`badzistsíni.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"In current rites, the personator of Nayénezgani carries a stone knife of unusual size, and the personator of To`badzistsíni carries two wooden cylinders, one black and one red, to represent thunderbolts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"Version A adds that when the War Gods were equipped they were dressed exactly like their brothers Black Thunder and Blue Thunder, who dwell in the Sun’s house.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Nayénezgani (War God)","description":"One of the two War Gods; receives armor and weapons and is associated with a large stone knife in ritual impersonation.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"To`badzistsíni (War God)","description":"One of the two War Gods; receives armor and weapons and is associated with thunderbolts represented by wooden cylinders in ritual impersonation.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Spider Woman","description":"Female figure who hosts the two brothers, seats them on stone seats, offers them food, and uses breath on stone images to give them a hard nature for future trials.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Black Thunder","description":"Thunder-associated brother who dwells in the house of the Sun and serves as a model for the War Gods’ equipment and dress.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Blue Thunder","description":"Thunder-associated brother who dwells in the house of the Sun and serves as a model for the War Gods’ equipment and dress.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:8","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Tiéholtsodi","description":"Water monster encountered by the War Gods at Hot Spring; threatens them and is appeased with prayer.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l10275-l10391","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 10275-10391","start":"10275","end":"10391","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes to the Navaho war gods legend explain the meanings of several names, variant episodes in different versions, and the locations associated with the hero Nayénezgani. They mention a cliff monster whose hair is cut so it falls, the Navaho Mountain, transformations of an enemy's young into animals, the birthplace of the Bináye Aháni monsters, a Salt Woman who supplies a bag of salt, bird helpers, and differing trophies. The notes discuss two principal war gods, Nayénezgani and To`badzistsíni, and additional heroes Léyaneyani (Reared Beneath the Earth) and Tsówenatlehi (Changing Grandchild), as well as their mother Estsánatlehi hiding her children underground from the monster Yéitso. A list of place names marks where a stone was chased and chipped, places said to have constant springs and water gods (Tiéholtsodi). Other notes mention a wicked woman killed by Nayénezgani, vicious swallows, possible reference to Pueblo legends, a ritual talisman against a destructive storm, common rock pillars, Nayénezgani’s claim to have visited the ends of earth, waters, sky, and mountains, a valued mineral (Pás-zin-i) used for beads and sacrifices to gods of the north, large fossil bones, and personified optical phenomena called Mirage People and Ground-heat People.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The name Tse`-ta-ho-tsil-tá`-li is said to mean \"He (Who) Kicks (People) Down the Cliff,\" with an alternate pronunciation Tse`-ta-yi-tsil-tá`-li.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In versions A and B, the hero simply cuts the hair of the monster and allows the latter to fall down the cliff.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Na-tsis-a-án is identified as the Navaho Mountain, an elevation 10,416 feet high, located about ten miles south of the junction of the Colorado and San Juan rivers in Utah.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Navaho story-teller uses the legend to try to score a point against the hereditary enemy Pah Ute, although the Pah Ute are said usually to have been more than a match for the Navaho; in Version A, the enemy young are transformed into Rocky Mountain sheep, and in Version B they are changed into birds of prey.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A particular place is noted as where the Bináye Aháni were born, while the other monsters mentioned in Part II were not found by Nayénezgani at the places where they were said to be born.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Other versions of the legend mention a Salt Woman or goddess of salt, Ásihi Estsán; the version of Hatáli Nez does not mention her, but Version A states that she supplied the bag of salt which Nayénezgani carried on his expedition.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Tsi-dil-tó-i means \"shooting\" or \"exploding bird,\" perhaps named from a peculiarity of this bird, which gives warning of the approach of an enemy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hos-tó-di is probably an onomatopoetic name for a bird that is said to be sleepy in the daytime and to come out at night.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Version B says that scalps were the trophies.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In all versions of the legend, two hero gods or war gods, Nayénezgani and To`badzistsíni, are prominently mentioned, but in these songs four names are given to satisfy Navaho reverence for the number four and the poetic requirement of four stanzas in a song.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Léyaneyani, or Reared Beneath the Earth, is described as an obscure hero whose only deed of valor in this version is killing his witch sister; the deeds of Tsówenatlehi, or the Changing Grandchild, are not known to the writer. Some say that Léyaneyani and Tsówenatlehi are other names for Nayénezgani and To`badzistsíni, but the best tribal authorities think otherwise.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"One version says that Estsánatlehi hid her children under the ground when Yéitso came seeking to devour them, and this may have given rise to the idea that one of these children was also called Reared Beneath the Earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"A list of place names is given where pieces were knocked off a stone as Nayénezgani chased it four times in a circle, and the chips he knocked off are said to remain there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"These named places are all said to be locations of constant springs of water, rare in Navaho land, and the note suggests that probably every constant spring or watercourse has its water god Tiéholtsodi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Version A adds an account of a wicked woman at Ki'ndotliz who slew her suitors until Nayénezgani killed her, and of vicious swallows who cut people with their wings; Version B omits the encounter with Sasnalkáhi and Tsé`nagahi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"A note states that one element \"possibly\" refers to Pueblo legends.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Version B, which gives only a meagre account of a destructive storm, mentions only one talisman but says that songs were sung and dances performed over this talisman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The kind of pillars referred to in the myth are said to be common throughout Navaho land.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Version A makes Nayénezgani say that he has been to the end of the earth, the end of the waters, the end of the sky, and the end of the mountains, and found none that were not his friends.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Pás-zin-i is the name given by the Navahoes to a hard mineral substance used to make black beads and other sacrifices to the gods of the north; it is identified by a geologist as a fine bituminous coal similar to cannel coal.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Pás-zin-i is described as scarce in Navaho land and valued by the Indians.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"One note refers to large fossil bones found in many parts of Arizona and New Mexico.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Names are given for Mirage People and Ground-heat People; ground-heat refers to the wavering appearance of objects in hot weather, common in the arid region and due to varying refraction near the ground.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Tse`-ta-ho-tsil-tá`-li","description":"A monster whose name means \"He (Who) Kicks (People) Down the Cliff\" and who in some versions falls down the cliff after the hero cuts its hair.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id

JOHN COMFORT FILLMORE.; lines 11492-11573","start":"11492","end":"11573","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Prof. John Comfort Fillmore introduces his transcription of twenty-eight Navaho songs from phonographic records made by Dr. Washington Matthews, emphasizing their scientific value as examples of natural folk-song forms and \"primitive\" emotional expression in music unaffected by contact with civilized traditions. He argues that such music allows the study of natural psychical laws expressed through the voice. The Navaho songs are said to carry listeners back toward the beginnings of music-making, with tones resembling howling more than singing but clearly musical due to strong rhythm and harmonic relations, leading him to analyze them under the headings of Rhythm and Harmonic Melody. Drawing on Richard Wallascheck, he stresses the primacy of sonant rhythm, which precedes other musical elements, incites tone-production, and, through a natural law of pulsation, organizes vocal sounds into metrical groups usually in twos or threes across both \"savage\" folk-music and advanced culture-music; groupings into fives or sevens are rare and more common in \"savage\" music than in civilized music. Fillmore then describes the metrical character of the Navaho songs: singers freely alternate between metres based on twos and threes, intermixing compound metres so that few songs fit a single time signature, and many measures deviate from the fundamental metre. He gives specific examples from different recording cylinders, noting songs with 9/8 and 6/8 time, 2/4 and 3/4 metre, rich and monotonous rhythmic structures, irregular measures with varying numbers of eighth notes, and an 8/8-based song varied by 4/8. He concludes that, in terms of metrical grouping, Navaho songs are essentially similar to the songs of various other tribes (Omahas, Kwakiutls, Pawnees, Otoes, Sioux), other aboriginal music, and music of other nations including his own, although he finds that some tribes, especially the Omahas and Kwakiutls, display greater metrical complexity. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9576-9666","start":"9576","end":"9666","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes describe the Navaho deities Hastséyalti (Talking God, Yébitsai) and Hastséhogan (House God), their multiple localized forms, beneficent character, ritual representations in the night chant (klédzi hatál), and associated mask and costume symbols. Hastséyalti is a chief among local divinities, a dawn god, and principal figure in the Yébitsai dance, while Hastséhogan is a leading yéi, a farm and house god, and a god of evening dwelling in caves, cliff-dwellings, and sacred mountains. A further note explains that wind gods—Ni'ltsi, Ni'ltsi-diné` (Wind People), and Niltsiázi-diné` (Little Wind People)—whisper friendly warnings and advice into humans' ears in Navaho tales.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Hastséyalti (Has-tsé-yal-ti) is translated as Talking God or Talking Elder of the Gods and is also called Yébitsai, the Maternal Grandfather of the Gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Hastséyalti is described as a chief or leader among several groups of local divinities who dwell at Kininaékai in Chelly Canyon, Tse'nitse, Tsé`híhi, and other sacred places, and Navaho myths and prayers indicate belief in many gods of this name.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In rites, the man who personates Hastséyalti never speaks while in character but utters a peculiar whoop and makes signs, whereas myths depict the god speaking after whooping and making signs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Hastséyalti is described as a beneficent character who is always ready to help humans and rescue them from peril, and he is frequently mentioned in songs and prayers as the principal character in the night chant (klédzi hatál).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In dry-paintings, Hastséyalti is shown carrying a tobacco bag made from the skin of Abert's squirrel, with the black tips of toes, nose, and ears and a reddish spot on the back carefully indicated, and wearing a mask with eagle-plumes, owl-feathers, and symbols at the mouth and eyes.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The symbol surrounding each hole for the eyes and mouth on Hastséyalti's mask is said to represent a storm cloud hanging above and mist rising from below to meet it, corresponding to clouds and mist that often appear in the Navaho mountains during the rainy season; a cornstalk symbol over the nose is also mentioned although not shown in the dry-painting.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The personator of Hastséyalti wears a collar of fresh spruce boughs and has his whole person clothed, traditionally with multiple finely dressed deerskins tied together, though in recent times an ordinary calico shirt may be used.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hastséhogan (Has-tsé-ho-gan), freely translated House God, is a leading personage in each local group of yéi (divine beings) who dwell in caves, old cliff-dwellings, and sacred mountains at places such as Tse`gíhi, Tsé`nihogan, Tsé`nitse, and Kininaékai.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Navaho myths show belief in many gods called Hastséhogan, who are commonly treated as a single deity but differ by locality, and in most myths he appears as second in authority to Hastséyalti while occasionally being equal or superior.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hastséhogan is both a farm god and a house god, to whom farm-songs sung during the night chant and many other songs and prayers are attributed, and he is characterized as beneficent and a friend to humans.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the night chant (klédzi hatál), Hastséhogan is represented by a man wearing a collar of spruce, a blue mask with eagle-plumes and owl-feathers, moccasins, a shirt and leggings ideally made of buckskin, and various quill-embroidered garments and ornaments, including an otter-skin with colored quill-wrapped strings.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Hastséhogan's representation includes a staff painted black with charcoal of four sacred plants, streaked transversely with white and adorned with a whorl of turkey tail-feathers and eagle plumes tipped with downy feathers, as well as a yellow stripe at the chin symbolizing the yellow light of evening and a blue neck crossed with four red stripes whose meaning is debated.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Some informants say that the four red stripes across the blue neck in the dry-paintings represent the larynx with its cartilaginous rings, while others say they represent the collar of spruce-twigs, and others remain uncertain.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The note states that Hastséyalti is also a dawn god, whereas Hastséhogan is a god of evening.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Navaho tales frequently portray men receiving friendly warnings or advice from wind gods who whisper into their ears.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Some storytellers mention a single wind god called Ni'ltsi (Wind), while others distinguish Ni'ltsi-diné` (Wind People) and Niltsiázi-diné` (Little Wind People) as friendly prompters.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Hastséyalti (Has-tsé-yal-ti / Talking God / Yébitsai)","description":"A Navaho deity translated as Talking God or Maternal Grandfather of the Gods, portrayed as a chief among several groups of local divinities dwelling at specific sacred places. JOHN COMFORT FILLMORE. / TEXTS AND INTERLINEAR TRANSLATIONS.; lines 11710-11870","start":"11710","end":"11870","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Water with Hill Central water flowed from in different directions; to the east one flowed, at the south one flowed, one to the west flowed... To the east extended ocean... within Tiéholtsodi lay... Chief of the people they say.\"","summary":"The passage presents, first, a short ritual asseveration attributed to Torlino in which he repeatedly says he is ashamed before various cosmic elements such as Earth (Woman Horizontal), Sky, Dawn, Evening, Blue Sky, Darkness, and the Sun, concluding that something stands in him and speaks with him, for which he is ashamed. The text then begins an origin legend: from a place called Water with Hill Central, lights of different colors rise in the four cardinal directions, marking day, evening, and darkness before the beings lie down and sleep. Water then flows from this central place toward the east, south, and west, forming border regions where inhabitants dwell, with multiple named places associated with corn, reeds, pots, water, mountains, earth, aromatic sumac, and rock. Various ants, beetles, bugs, bats, and locusts live there, and twelve people start their lives. The land is surrounded on all sides by oceans, within which lie four beings—Tiéholtsodi in the eastern ocean, Blue Heron in the southern, Frog in the western, and Thunder Mountain White in the northern—each described as a chief of the people. The beings in this world quarrel and commit adultery and other crimes, several women being mentioned as offenders, and they fail to banish these misdeeds. Tiéholtsodi asks how they should act, noting that the people dislike their land. Blue Heron and Frog say the people should not dwell there, and Thunder Mountain White says they must quickly depart elsewhere, just before the text breaks off as Tiéholtsodi is mentioned again when adultery is committed once more.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The section is titled \"ASSEVERATION OF TORLINO (IN PART),\" indicating that Torlino is the speaker of the following lines.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker addresses Earth (called \"Woman Horizontal\"), Sky (\"dark above\"), Dawn, Evening (\"Land of Horizontal Yellow\"), Blue sky (\"Land or Place of Horizontal Blue\"), Darkness, and Sun, saying of each \"for it I am ashamed.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker concludes, \"In me it stands, with me it talks, for it I am ashamed,\" suggesting that something within him that communicates with him is the cause of his shame before these cosmic elements.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An origin legend begins at a place called \"Water with Hill Central,\" from which to the east a white light rose up; to the south a blue light rose up; to the west a yellow light rose up; then to the north a dark light rose up, after which they lay down and slept.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"From Water with Hill Central, water flowed out in different directions: one stream to the east, one to the south, and one to the west, and at the borders where the water flowed the beings dwelt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Specific place names are given along the borders: to the east Corn, Pot One, Earth under House; to the south Nahodoóla, Water They Come for Often, Aromatic Sumac among; to the west Reed Great Standing, Mountain Red Made of House, Rock Red Made of House.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Various insects and animals are said to live there: Dark Ants, Red Ants, Dragon-flies, Yellow beetles, hard beetles (Wointli'zi), stone-carrier beetles, black bugs, coyote-dung beetles, Bats, White-faced beetles, Locusts, and White Locusts.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Among these inhabitants, twelve people (Nakidátago diné` aísi) \"started (in life).\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"To the east, south, west, and north there are extended oceans surrounding the land.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Within the eastern ocean lies Tiéholtsodi, within the southern ocean lies Blue Heron (Thaltláhale), within the western ocean lies Frog (Tsal), and within the northern ocean lies Thunder Mountain White (Idní`dsilkai).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Each of these four beings in the oceans is described as a chief and specifically as \"chief of the people.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The beings in this world quarrel around where they live and commit adultery with one another; several women are specifically said to commit crime, and those present fail to banish these offenses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Tiéholtsodi in the east asks, \"In what way shall we act? Their land the place they dislike,\" indicating concern about how to respond to the situation and the people's dissatisfaction with their land.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In the south, Blue Heron speaks; in the west, Frog says, \"Now I (say) not here shall they dwell\"; and it is noted that Frog is a chief.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In the north, Thunder Mountain White says, \"Quickly elsewhere they must depart,\" indicating a decision that the people should leave their current land.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"After this, the text says, \"To the east Tiéholtsodi when again they committed adultery,\" suggesting that adultery is committed again and Tiéholtsodi is involved in some way, though the sentence is incomplete in the excerpt.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Torlino","description":"Named in the heading as the person whose asseveration is partially given, GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9866-9961","start":"9866","end":"9961","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This passage consists of numbered ethnographic and mythological notes related to the Navajo War Gods myth and associated traditions. It explains the name and non-ritual representation of White Shell Woman; describes Water Sprinkler (Tó`-ne-ni-li) as a rain-god and his portrayal as a clownish masked dancer in a ritual; outlines contemporary Navajo obstetric customs and the role of medicine-men as birth attendants; presents two versions of the conception and birth of the War Gods Nayénezgani and To`badzistsíni involving the Sun, ritual bathing, mountain yuccas, cornmeal, a brush shelter, and in one version conception from water; describes the elder War God's baby basket made from clouds, rainbow, stars, lightning, and sunbeams; identifies certain plants botanically; discusses Yé-i-tso as the greatest of the alien gods with ambiguous parentage (stone or sun); and notes that part of the myth alludes to the behavior of trap-door spiders living in ground nests.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Yol-kaí Es-tsán, meaning White Shell Woman, is named and noted as not being represented by a character in ceremonies nor depicted in dry-paintings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Tó`-ne-ni-li or Tó-ne-ni-li, Water Sprinkler, is described as an important character in Navajo mythology and explicitly called a rain-god.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In dry-paintings of Navajo rites, Water Sprinkler is shown wearing a blue mask bordered with red, trimmed on top with life-feathers, and sometimes carrying a water-pot.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In the klédzi hatál rite, during the public dance of the last night, Water Sprinkler is represented by a masked man who behaves as a clown, disrupting the line of dancers, dancing out of order and time, peering foolishly, sitting and rocking on the ground, and sometimes continuing to dance alone after others retire.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The clown representing Water Sprinkler sometimes carries a fox-skin, drops it, pretends to lose it, searches for it although it is visible, then jumps on and beats it as if alive, and afterward shoulders it as if it were a heavy burden.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Although Water Sprinkler is portrayed as a fool in ceremonial rites, the note states that he is not depicted as a fool in the myths.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A described Navajo custom for childbirth involves manipulating the abdominal parietes in the belief that this will ensure a favorable presentation; the note adds that this practice exists among the Navahoes in the present day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Among the Navahoes, medicine-men serve as accoucheurs, acting as birth attendants.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"One version (A) of the myth presents Estsánatlehi as a maiden who goes out to gather wood, feels a foot pressed on her back several times while kneeling to lift a bundle, and eventually sees a man who questions her about where she lives.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In Version A, the man identified as the Sun instructs Estsánatlehi to find four yuccas of different kinds on a nearby mountain, marked by cuts on their north sides, to dig their roots for a bath, obtain meal of tohonoti'ni corn (yellow from her mother, white from her father), build a brush shelter away from her hut, and sleep there four nights.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Estsánatlehi tells her foster parents of the Sun’s instructions, and they follow these directions, recognizing the visitor as the Sun.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"During three nights in the brush shelter in Version A nothing occurs that Estsánatlehi is aware of; on the morning after the fourth night she is awakened by departing footsteps and sees the sun rising in the direction of the sound.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In Version A, four days (or twelve days in some accounts) after the fourth night in the shelter, Nayénezgani is born to Estsánatlehi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In Version A, four days after Nayénezgani’s birth, Estsánatlehi goes to cleanse herself at a spring, conceives from the water there, and four days later To`badzistsíni, the second War God, is born.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Version B states that the Sun or bearer of the sun meets Estsánatlehi in the woods and designates a trysting place where First Man builds a corral of branches.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In Version B, the Sun visits Estsánatlehi in the corral in the form of an ordinary man for four nights in succession; four days after the last visit she gives birth to twins, Nayénezgani and To`badzistsíni, who are identified as the War Gods.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Version A describes the elder brother’s baby basket: the child is wrapped in black cloud; a rainbow forms the hood studded with stars; the back of the frame is a parhelion; zigzag lightning is laid on each side and straight lightning down the middle in front; Niltsátlol (sunbeams shining on a distant rainstorm) make the fringe; and sunbeams form the carrying-straps.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Mountain mahogany of New Mexico and Arizona is identified botanically as Cercocarpus parvifolius (Nutt.), and its Navajo name Tsé`estagi is glossed as meaning \"hard as stone.\"","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Round cactus is noted as one or more species of Mammilaria, while sitting cactus is identified as Cereus phoeniceus and possibly other Cereus species.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Yé-i-tso is defined from Navajo terms yéi (a god or genius) and tso (great) as the greatest and fiercest of the anáye or alien gods, with accounts of him said to be substantially the same.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"According to some accounts, Yé-i-tso’s father is a stone, while in another passage and in Version B the sun declares that Yé-i-tso is his child; the note suggests this may mean he is the child of the sun in a metaphysical sense.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The note states that a part of the myth alludes to trap-door spiders or tarantulas of the Southwest, which live in carefully prepared nests in the ground.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Yol-kaí Es-tsán (White Shell Woman)","description":"A mythic female figure whose name means White Shell Woman; birth.","figure_refs":["fig:9","fig:10"],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Version A of Estsánatlehi and the births of the War Gods","summary":"In Version A, the maiden Estsánatlehi encounters a mysterious man while gathering wood who presses his foot on her back; after repeated occurrences she finally sees him. He, identified by her foster parents as the Sun, instructs her to obtain roots from four marked yucca plants on a nearby mountain, make a bath, get colored cornmeal from her parents, build a brush shelter, and sleep there four nights. After four nights she hears departing footsteps and sees the rising sun; four days later she gives birth to Nayénezgani. It reports differing accounts of his parentage: some say his father is a stone, while other passages and Version B portray the sun as claiming Yé-i-tso as his child, which the author suggests may be intended in a metaphysical sense.","figure_refs":["fig:11","fig:4"],"symbol_refs":["sym:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"scene:9","label":"Mythic allusion to trap-door spiders","summary":"The final note states that part of the myth alludes to trap-door spiders or tarantulas of the Southwest, which live in carefully prepared nests in the ground.","figure_refs":["fig:12"],"symbol_refs":["sym:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"candidate_motifs":[{"id":"motif:1","label":"Rain-god depicted as ceremonial clown and boundary-breaker","taxonomy_refs":["trickster_boundary"],"basis":"Water Sprinkler, a rain-god, is personated in the klédzi hatál rite by a masked clown who disrupts the dancers, dances out of time and order, performs foolish antics, and plays with a fox-skin, explicitly to vary the monotony of the long night’s performance, while the note distinguishes this comic portrayal from his mythic character.","evidence_refs":["ev:2"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"The trickster-like behavior is confined to ceremonial representation; the note states that he is not portrayed as a fool in the myths, so the motif applies specifically to ritual enactment rather than mythic narrative."

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l10393-l10489","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 10393-10489","start":"10393","end":"10489","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes (161–168) explain details of Navajo myths and customs: Estsánatlehi’s nubility ceremonies at Tsinlí and San Francisco Mountain and their role as models for modern maiden puberty rites; geographic identifications of Black Mountain, Meeting Waters, and canyon sites associated with the yéi gods; a scientific explanation (Circle of Ulloa) for reported reflections of war gods on the San Juan River; and ethnographic comments on the nuclear gens Tse`dzinki'ni, the phrase “seven times old age has killed,” and the etymology and local origin of related place and clan names.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A ceremony at Tsinlí (Chinlee Valley) celebrated the nubility of Estsánatlehi, who was already a mother in a miraculous way but had not previously shown signs of nubility.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"A nubility ceremony of the type described for Estsánatlehi is now performed for every Navaho maiden, with a second ceremony held four days after the first.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the second ceremony for Estsánatlehi at San Francisco Mountain, she was laid on top of the mountain with her head to the west because she was to go to the west to dwell there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"During the second ceremony, Estsánatlehi’s body was manipulated and her limbs stretched, and in the present-day fourth-day ceremony Navahoes try to mould the maiden’s body to resemble Estsánatlehi’s perfect form.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Estsánatlehi instructed the people to perform the described body-moulding rites for all Navaho maidens in future, and this practice is said to continue today.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A variant of the story (Version A) places Estsánatlehi’s nubility ceremony before the birth of her child.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Dsil-li-zi'n or Dsillizi'ni (Black Mountain) is an extensive mesa in Apache County, Arizona, and the pass mentioned in the myth is believed to correspond to Marsh Pass, about 60 miles north of the Moki villages; the mesa name is spelled “Zilh-le-jini” on the map.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"To`-ye't-li (Meeting Waters) is described as the junction of two important rivers somewhere in the valley of the San Juan River in Colorado or Utah, with its precise location undetermined but frequently mentioned in Navaho myths.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Matthews reports that warriors offered sacrifices at the sacred shrine of Thoyetli in the San Juan Valley and that the Navajos have a tradition that the gods of war, or sacred brothers, still dwell there and that their reflection is sometimes seen on the San Juan River.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Matthews considers the reported reflections of the war gods on the San Juan River to be due to some natural phenomenon.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Brennan recounts that a clergyman travelling in the San Juan Valley observed mists rising over the San Juan River and saw shadows of himself and his companions reflected near the river’s surface, surrounded by a circular rainbow called the “Circle of Ulloa,” which moved in response to their motions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Brennan suggests that similar reflections could have led local Indians to interpret such figures as reflections of their deities.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Tse`-gí-hi is the name of a canyon north of the San Juan River, probably McElmo or Mancos Canyon, that abounds in cliff-dwellings.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Navahoes regard Tse`-gí-hi canyon and its cliff-houses as a favorite home of the yéi or gods, and the ruined cliff-houses are believed to have been inhabited by divine beings.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The cliff ruins in Chelly Canyon, Arizona, are also supposed to have been homes of the gods, who are still thought to dwell there unseen.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Chelly is a Spanish orthography of the Navaho name Tsé`gi, Tséyi, or Tséyi; when a Navaho says “in the Chelly Canyon” he says Tséyigi, an expression resembling Tse`gíhi but referring to a different locality, and both names have the meaning “Among the Cliffs” or “Among the Rocks.”","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The storyteller used the expression “seven times old age has killed,” which Navaho-speaking whites freely translate as “seven ages of old men.”","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Navahoes variously estimate an “age of an old man”: some as a definite cycle of 102 years (the same number as the counters used in the game of kesitsé), others as threescore years and ten, and others as an indefinite period marked by the death of some very old man in the tribe.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Using these estimates, the existence of the nuclear gens of the Navaho nation is calculated at between five hundred and seven hundred years.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Hodge’s study on the “Early Navajo and Apache” computes dates given in the legend and compares them with Spanish-American history, arriving at a later date for the creation or first mention of the Tse`dzinki'ni but finding many of the legend’s dates approximately correct.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"In the legend, Tse`dzinki'ni is described as the nuclear gens of the Navahoes, yet the diné`digíni or holy people are supposed to have existed before this gens was created.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The name Tse`-dzin-ki'n-i is derived from tse` (rock, here rendered “cliffs”), dzin (black, dark), and kin (a straight-walled stone or adobe house) and, like other Navaho gentile names, appears to be of local origin based on the described dark cliffs and houses.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The author remarks that the rock formations of Arizona and New Mexico are often so fantastic that the condition described in the associated myth could easily occur.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Estsánatlehi","description":"Female figure whose nubility ceremony at Tsinlí and San Francisco Mountain is described; she is already a mother in a miraculous way and serves as the physical model for Navaho maiden ceremonies.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Navaho maidens","description":"Collective figure of Navaho girls for whom nubility ceremonies are now performed, including a second ceremony on the fourth day in which their bodies are moulded to resemble Estsánatlehi’s form.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Navahoes (people)","description":"The Navaho people as a community who perform maiden nubility ceremonies, hold shrines and myths at places like Meeting Waters and canyon cliff-dwellings, and trace their history to the nuclear gens Tse`dzinki'ni.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"War gods or sacred brothers at Thoyetli","description":"Deities of war, described as sacred brothers, who are believed to dwell at the shrine of Thoyetli and whose reflections are sometimes seen on the San Juan River.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Warriors at Thoyetli","description":"Warriors who are said to offer sacrifices at the sacred shrine of Thoyetli in the San Juan Valley.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Yéi or gods of the canyon","description":"Divine beings (yéi or gods) believed by Navahoes to have inhabited the cliff-dwellings of Tse`-gí-hi canyon and the cliff ruins of Chelly Canyon and to continue dwelling there unseen.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"Diné`digíni (holy people)","description":"Holy people who, according to Navaho belief, existed before the creation of the nuclear gens Tse`dzinki'ni.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Tse`dzinki'ni gens","description":"The nuclear gens of the Navahoes, associated with an estimated existence of 500–700 years and with the place-name Tse`-dzin-ki'n-i derived from dark cliffs and straight-walled houses.","role_refs":["role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Unnamed clergyman","description":"A clergyman travelling in the San Juan Valley who observed his and his companions’ shadows reflected on the river, surrounded by the Circle of Ulloa.","role_refs":["role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:10","name_or_label":"G. A. Brennan","description":"Author of a note in the American Naturalist who reports the clergyman’s experience of the Circle of Ulloa and offers it as an explanation for Navajo accounts of war gods’ reflections.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:11","name_or_label":"Dr. W. Matthews","description":"Ethnographer who previously wrote on Navajo deities and demons and reported the tradition of war gods dwelling at Thoyetli and appearing as reflections on the San Juan River.","role_refs":["role:11"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"Ritual exemplar","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"Estsánatlehi’s body is ceremonially arranged and moulded, and Navahoes are instructed to model the bodies of maidens on her perfect form in future ceremonies.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"Ritual participants (maidens)","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"Navaho maidens undergo a first and fourth-day ceremony, during which their bodies are manipulated to resemble Estsánatlehi’s ideal form.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"Community / nation","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The Navahoes are described collectively as maintaining nubility ceremonies, venerating shrine","assigned_to":["fig:4"],"basis":"The deities at Thoyetli are explicitly called “gods of war, or sacred brothers,” said to dwell at the shrine and to appear as reflections on the and are homes of the yéi or gods, who still dwell there unseen.","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"role:7","label":"Holy beings predating the gens","assigned_to":["fig:7"],"basis":"The diné`digíni are nation","assigned_to":["fig:8"],"basis":"The legend identifies Tse`dzinki'ni as the nuclear gens of the Navahoes and uses cycles of “ages of old men” to estimate its the source of the description of Thoyetli and the war gods’ reflections.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"Mountains as ritual and mythic sites","literal_form":"San Francisco Mountain, where Estsánatlehi’s second nubility ceremony took place, and Black Mountain (Dsil-li-zi'n / Dsillizi'ni), an extensive mesa referenced in the myth.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":["mountain"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"Waters and river junction","literal_form":"Meeting Waters (junction of two body is manipulated and limbs stretched. She instructs that future Navaho maidens undergo similar ceremonies, and their bodies are moulded on the fourth day to resemble her perfect form.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3"],"symbol_refs":["sym:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"scene:2","label":"Thoyetli shrine, Meeting Waters, and reflections of war gods on the San Juan River","summary":"At the sacred shrine of Thoyetli, situated in the San Juan Valley near Meeting Waters, warriors offer sacrifices and the gods of war or sacred brothers are believed to dwell. Their reflections are said to appear on the San Juan River. Brennan recounts a clergyman’s experience of the Circle of Ulloa—reflected shadows surrounded by a circular rainbow—and proposes this as the natural basis for the reported divine reflections.","figure_refs":["fig:4","fig:5","fig:9","fig:10","fig:11"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"scene:3","label":"Gods dwelling in canyon cliff-houses and ruins","summary":"Tse`-gí-hi canyon, rich in cliff-dwellings north of the San Juan River, and Chelly Canyon in Arizona are regarded by Navahoes as favorite homes of the yéi or gods. The cliff-houses and ruins are thought to have been inhabited by divine beings who still dwell there unseen. Similar-sounding place-names referring to cliffs and rocks are distinguished by the author.","figure_refs":["fig:3","fig:6"],"symbol_refs":["sym:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Ages of old men and the antiquity of Tse`dzinki'ni","summary":"The storyteller’s phrase “seven times old age has killed” is interpreted as seven ages of old men, with varying estimates of an old man’s age used by Navahoes. These cycles are employed to estimate the age of the nuclear gens Tse`dzinki'ni, yielding 500–700 years. Hodge’s historical analysis suggests a later creation date but affirms that many of the legend’s dates are approximately accurate, and the diné`digíni holy people are believed to predate the gens.","figure_refs":["fig:3","fig:7","fig:8"],"symbol_refs":["sym:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"scene:5","label":"Fantastic rock formations and mythic descriptions","summary":"The author notes that rock formations in Arizona and New Mexico are often so fantastic that unusual configurations described in associated myths could easily occur in reality.","figure_refs":[],"symbol_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"candidate_motifs":[{"id":"motif:1","label":"Supernatural woman’s nubility ceremony as origin of female initiation rite","taxonomy_refs":["initiation","culture_hero"],"basis":"Estsánatlehi’s nubility is marked by ceremonies at Tsinlí and San Francisco Mountain in which her body is ritually positioned and moulded. She explicitly commands that similar practices be applied to all Navaho maidens, and present-day fourth-day ceremonies aim to shape the maiden’s body to match her perfect form, making her ceremony an origin story for an ongoing female initiation rite.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The passage summarizes the ceremony without detailing all ritual meanings; identifying Estsánatlehi as a culture-heroine who institutes initiation rites is inferred from her instructions rather than explicitly stated."},{"id":"motif:2","label":"Miraculous motherhood occurring before or apart from puberty","taxonomy_refs":["miraculous_child","sacred_birth"],"basis":"Estsánatlehi is described

It then provides ethnographic notes describing, in detail, how human actors personate the deities Nayénezgani (Slayer of the Alien Gods) and To`badzistsíni (War God, Child of the Water) during a Night Chant healing scene. Their body paints, masks, symbolic designs (bows and queues/scalps), costumes, and ritual actions toward a patient are described, including sacrificial cigarettes deposited under piñon and cedar trees. A brief aside mentions differing population counts for Navajos in an 1869 census versus the Eleventh Census.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Thirteen named male characters are listed and numbered 1 to 13 under the heading \"MALE.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"For the first seven male characters, each wears a different mask, while the last six wear masks of one pattern called that of yébaka.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"One female character, Hastséoltoi, is listed as number 14, and characters 15 to 21 are collectively called Hastsébaad or goddesses under the heading \"FEMALE.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"All the female characters wear masks of one kind.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"An ethnographic note states that Plate IV shows a man dressed to personate Nayénezgani, or Slayer of the Alien Gods, during an act of succor in the Night Chant on the afternoon of the ninth day, together with personators of To`badzistsíni and Hastséoltoi.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The personator of Nayénezgani has his body painted black with charcoal made from four sacred plants and his hands painted white.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Nayénezgani mask is black with a fringe of yellow or reddish hair across the crown, a turkey and eagle feather ornament on top, lightning designs of five parallel lines with five angles on one cheek, and diamond-shaped eye and mouth holes edged with small white shells.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Eight bow figures are drawn in white clay on the personator of Nayénezgani: six shown as complete or strung, and two on the left leg and left side of the back shown open or unstrung; the left leg symbol is drawn first and the left shoulder symbol last, with all component lines drawn from above downward and all symbols turning in one direction.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The personator of Nayénezgani wears a fox-skin collar, rich necklaces of shell, turquoise, and coral, a fine skirt or sash around his loins, a silver-decorated belt, and moccasins.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The personator of Nayénezgani carries a great stone knife and, in the act of succor, makes motions with it at the patient and the medicine-lodge to draw out disease; the patient prays to him and gives him a black-painted cigarette decorated with bow symbols, which is then deposited under a piñon-tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The author notes that no dry-painting of the god Nayénezgani has been seen and that informants say none is ever made.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"An ethnographic note states that Plate VII shows a man personating the War God To`badzistsíni, or Child of the Water, in the same act of succor described for Nayénezgani.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The personator of To`badzistsíni has his body and limbs painted with native red ochre, his hands smeared with white earth, and eight white symbols on his body (two on the chest, two on the arms, two on the legs, and two on the back), with the symbol on the left leg painted first and that over the left shoulder-blade painted last; these two are left open or unfinished, which some say indicates that the god's labors are not yet done.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The white symbols on To`badzistsíni’s body are said to represent a queue such as Navahos wear; some say they depict his mother's queue, while others say they represent the scalps of conquered enemies.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The mask of To`badzistsíni is painted red with a small triangular area over the face colored black and bordered with white, is decorated with multiple queue symbols in numbers that are always multiples of four, and has a fringe of red or yellow hair, a turkey-tail and downy eagle-feather cockade, and diamond-shaped eye and mouth holes with white shells attached.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The personator of To`badzistsíni wears a fox-skin collar, rich necklaces of shell, turquoise, and coral, a skirt or sash of bayeta or other rich material, a silver-plaque belt, and moccasins, and carries a small red-painted cedar-wood cylinder in his left hand and a black-painted piñon cylinder in his right, which he uses to make motions at the patient and the lodge in the succor scene.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The sacrificial cigarette for To`badzistsíni is painted red and marked with queue symbols and is deposited under a cedar-tree.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The author notes that no dry-painting of To`badzistsíni has been seen and that informants say none is made.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A note quotes language from the Eleventh Census regarding Navajo population and mentions that Captain Frank T. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 7472-7563","start":"7472","end":"7563","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Nati'nesthani returns to his farm and finds only the tracks of his pet turkey. Making four widening circuits around his hut, he discovers that the trail leads to a mountain to the north. Over four days he ascends the mountain in a sunwise spiral, finds many turkey tracks at the summit but no bird, and finally sees where it has flown off from the eastern edge toward the east. Grieving, he laments the loss of his pet, describing it as embodying clouds, mist, rains, lightning, rainbow, four types of corn, and beans, and declares that its feathers and beard will be used in future human rites. The narrator adds that he never sees the turkey again, that it is regarded as the ancestor of white men’s tame turkeys, and that the bird’s plumage and features still display the colors of corn, storm, and rainbow.

Nati'nesthani dries his tears, descends the mountain, and returns to his brush hut and farm, where his corn has already formed ears and other plants are nearly mature. He plucks one ear from each of four varieties—white, blue, yellow, and multicolored—wraps them in his wood-rat-skin mantle, and brings them to his wife, who has never seen corn. Laying the ears in a row with their tips pointing east, he names corn (natán) and each color variety, and explains that when green it can be eaten in four ways: roasted in coals with the husk, roasted in ashes without the husk, boiled whole, or cut off the cob and made into mush.

His wife carries the four ears to her parents’ lodge. The old couple are astonished; she repeats her husband’s explanations and cooks each ear by a different method. During cooking the corn increases so that it provides a hearty meal for all, and the old people delight in its taste and fragrance. At their request she brings a large dish of the corn to her husband, and they eat together; he is now unafraid of poison because the food does not belong to his father-in-law.

That night she questions Nati'nesthani about the corn’s origin. After evasive answers, he admits that he plants it and that it grows where he sows it, and offers to show her his field. With her father’s permission the next morning, she prepares for the journey. She brings Nati'nesthani pemmican and mush; the Wind People whisper that he need not fear this food, and he eats freely. After breakfast he tells her to dress for travel, she informs her parents she is going with her husband, and they permit her to accompany him to see the
