content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l7996-l8093","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"II. EARLY EVENTS IN THE FIFTH WORLD. / III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 7996-8093","start":"7996","end":"8093","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Nati'nesthani is honored by a host who is chief of five totemic gentes for having slain the bears that tormented them. The chief’s daughter feeds him and the chief gives him two animal-based medicines as an antidote to Deer Raiser’s poison and as protection against witchcraft. Returning home, Nati'nesthani is scolded by his father-in-law Deer Raiser for having gone east, a place he calls bad, and is warned not to go south. Nati'nesthani secretly decides to disobey and over successive days travels south, west, and north, crossing colored ridges. In each direction he meets a small Tsidastói man in deer or antelope costume with a distinct face color, who teaches him how to make a short painted cigarette associated with that direction and to place it in a cedar or piñon tree, and sends him to two lodges where events resemble those of his earlier eastern journey. After the fourth journey, Deer Raiser again confronts him angrily, but Nati'nesthani now reveals where he has been, what he has learned—cigarettes, medicines, charms, and rites that protect against a wizard’s power—and exposes Deer Raiser’s attempts to kill him and others. Deer Raiser admits his guilt, promises to abandon his evil ways, and asks to be treated with the newly learned rituals. Nati'nesthani complies, performing the first atsósi hatál ceremony. He then returns to his people, teaches them all he has learned, establishing the atsósi hatál rite among the Navaho, and finally goes back to the whirling lake of Tó`nihilin, where he continues to dwell.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The host thanks Nati'nesthani for killing the bears, gathers his people into his tent, tells them the story of the Navaho, and they rejoice and recount how Deer Raiser and the bears killed their relatives.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The people present are organized into five gentes—the Puma People, Blue Fox People, Yellow Fox People, Wolf People, and Lynx People—and the host is chief of all of them.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The chief orders one of his daughters to prepare food; she brings in deer pemmican for Nati'nesthani to eat.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The chief gives Nati'nesthani two medicines: a small object made from the gall of birds of prey and a small quantity of substance made from material vomited by each of the five totem animals, saying these will kill Deer Raiser’s poison and are potent against witchcraft.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Deer Raiser is Nati'nesthani’s father-in-law, has been trying to kill him with poison, and has killed others as well.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Upon returning from his first forbidden journey to the east, Nati'nesthani is rebuked by Deer Raiser, who calls the east a bad place and warns him not to go south; Nati'nesthani nevertheless plans to disobey.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Traveling south across a blue ridge, Nati'nesthani meets a small bluish-faced man dressed as an antelope, wearing an antelope hunting-mask with horns and carrying a haliotis wand, a special bow, and arrows with red-tailed buzzard feathers; this man, one of the Tsidastói People, teaches him to make a blue cigarette with yellow spots and place it in the fork of a cedar-tree, and directs him to two lodges where people are playing nánzoz.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On later journeys west and north, Nati'nesthani crosses yellow and black ridges and meets other small Tsidastói men with yellowish and very dark faces, in deer or antelope masks without horns, who similarly instruct him in making painted cigarettes (yellow with blue spots, black with white spots) and depositing them in piñon or cedar trees, with events at nearby lodges resembling his earlier eastern experience.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Each of the small men Nati'nesthani meets is described as being like a similar little man he had previously met in the east, and all belong to the Tsidastói People.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After returning from his fourth journey, Nati'nesthani confronts Deer Raiser, recounts his journeys and the people he has met, and declares that he has learned cigarettes, medicines, charms, and rites that protect him against a wizard’s power, including Deer Raiser’s attempts on his life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Deer Raiser admits the truth of Nati'nesthani’s accusations, promises to abandon his evil ways, and asks to be treated with the powerful sacrifices, rites, and medicines his son-in-law has learned.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Nati'nesthani treats Deer Raiser with the newly learned rites, performing the first atsósi hatál ceremony, then returns to his people, teaches them all he has learned, thus establishing atsósi hatál among the Navaho, and finally goes back to dwell at the whirling lake of Tó`nihilin.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Nati'nesthani","description":"Navaho protagonist who kills the bears, receives medicines from the chief of the five gentes, disobeys his father-in-law’s prohibitions to travel to the four directions, learns cigarettes, medicines, charms, and rites from small Tsidastói men, confronts and treats Deer Raiser with the first atsósi hatál, teaches the rite to his people, and then returns to dwell at the whirling lake of Tó`nihilin.","role_refs":["role:1","role:7","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Host, chief of the five gentes","description":"Unnamed piñon-tree.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Little man of the north","description":"A small, very dark-faced man dressed and armed like the man of the THE GOLDEN AGE.; lines 1460-1542","start":"1460","end":"1542","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ganglere asks what Alfather did after Asgard was built. Har replies that Alfather appointed rulers in Idavold, a place in the middle of the burg, to sit with him in judgment over human disputes and the affairs of Asgard. Their first work was to erect a great court-house, Gladsheim, with twelve seats and a high-seat for Alfather, described as the best and largest house on earth, shining like solid gold. They then built a beautiful hall, Vingolf, as a home for the goddesses. The gods built a forge, made tools such as hammer, tongs, and anvil, and worked in iron, stone, wood, and especially gold; all their household wares were of gold, and this period was called the golden age until it ended with the arrival of certain women from Jotunheim. The gods then sat in their high-seats and took counsel. They remembered that dwarfs had quickened in the mould of the earth and in Ymer’s flesh like maggots. By the gods’ decision the dwarfs received understanding and the likeness of men but were required to dwell in earth and rocks. Modsogner and Durin are named as dwarfs. A quotation from the Vala’s Prophecy describes all the gods going to their judgment seats to take counsel on who should create the race of dwarfs from the bloody sea and Blain’s bones, making many dwarfs in the earth in the likeness of men, as Durin says. The text then lists numerous dwarf names, distinguishing some that dwell in the mould, some that dwell in rocks, and others that come from Svarin’s How to Aurvang on Joruvold, from whom Lovar is sprung, with a footnote identifying the verses as drawn from the Elder Edda’s Vala’s Prophecy.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Alfather content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-navaho-legends-matthews-gutenberg-l11115-l11214","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","passage_locator":{"label":"III. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 11115-11214","start":"11115","end":"11214","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes on the Navaho tale of Nati'nesthani describe ritual cigarettes marked with animal tracks and unusual color symbolism possibly linked to a wizard; explain hunting practice of imitating a wolf's cry and its deceptive use by an old man to trick Nati'nesthani; give etymologies for bear names; note that the bear is sacred so the hero will not skin or eat it, though the old man, as a wizard, might. The notes discuss a jocose recognition phrase used among relatives, narrative structure of Deer Raiser's repeated devices to kill his son-in-law (including an episode with twelve bears and the burnt moccasins incident), and the convention of adding -ni/ini to the names of the dead. They compare the burnt moccasins episode to a Coyote tale in the Origin Legend. Further comments describe directional color symbolism applied to ridges and to the faces of symbolic people of the four directions, the behavior of a bird called tsi-das-tó-i, the concept of Bi-za as a personal treasure or magical charm used by both humans and divinities, medicines made from eagle gall and totemic animals that vomit, used against witchcraft and indigestion, and Navaho classification of the red-tailed hawk's tail as yellow, reflected in its name atsé-litsói ('yellow-tail').","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In certain Navaho ceremonies, series of cigarettes made from specific plants (mountain mahogany, cliff rose, sunflower, and strong-smelling sunflower) are placed over the east, south, and west doors and at the bottom of steps, each painted in particular colors and marked with four symbols of deer-, antelope-, or fawn-tracks, with separate cigarettes designated for male and female.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In this series of ceremonial cigarettes the colors are not in the usual Navaho order; the narrator suggests this may indicate special symbolism for the animals, or that the cigarettes belong to a wizard and are therefore unholy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Navaho hunters often imitate the cry of the wolf when driving game to a party in ambush; in the Nati'nesthani myth the old man gives the cry not to drive bears but to make Nati'nesthani think deer are being driven.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The bear characters include one named Tsa-na-naí, derived from tsan meaning dung, and another named Tse'-sko-di, meaning Spread-foot; other bear names existed but were forgotten by the narrator.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The comment that the old man \"did not even thank his son-in-law\" is identified by the editor as an instance of sarcasm within the tale.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The bear is described as a sacred animal for the Navahoes, which explains why the hero did not skin the slain bears or eat their flesh, though the old man, being a wizard, might do both.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The expression Há-la-dzi-ni? means \"What are you doing?\" but is a jocose phrase used only among intimate relatives or relations by marriage, and its use in the tale signals that the Navaho recognizes the old man.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The episode of the twelve bears is assessed by the editor as the weakest and least artistic part of the tale and as a fifth device by Deer Raiser to kill his son-in-law, whereas four devices would normally be expected; it is considered a later interpolation to get the two men out together again so the burnt moccasins incident can occur.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Among the Navahoes, when a person dies, the suffix ni or ini is added to that person's name, and this modified name is used thereafter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The burnt moccasins incident from the Nati'nesthani story had previously been recorded in a version of the Origin Legend as a Coyote tale, where Coyote tries the same trick on his father-in-law but the father-in-law is warned and foils him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A ridge that the hero crosses in the east, and other ridges he crosses in the south, west, and north, are described as colored according to the regular order of Navaho symbolism.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The bird called tsi-das-tó-i is described as about the size of a screech-owl and is said not to fly away when a man passes but to sit and look at him, moving its head in every direction.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"References to pale-faced people in the east are explained as symbolic rather than as allusions to Caucasians; white is the color of the east in Navaho symbolism, and similarly a man in the south is said to have a blue face, in the west a yellow face, and in the north a dark face.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The term Bi-za ('his treasure') denotes something a person specially values and extends to meanings such as charm, The author notes that Greek religion, like others, mixes primitive animal rites with noble ideas, and insists that the Norse gave their gods a distinctive, high-minded character. The text then summarizes a Prose Edda account of Norse cosmology: Allfather is the first god, eternal creator of heaven and earth, who made humans and gave them immortal souls; the righteous dwell with him in Vingolf, while the wicked go to Hel and then Niflhel beneath the ninth world. Before creation there was only a \"Yawning-gap\" between Niflheim, a cold realm of ice and rime, and Muspell, a blazing southern land guarded by Surtr, who will one day destroy the gods and burn the world. When heat from Muspell met the rime from Niflheim, melting drops \"quickened\" into the giant Ymir, whose sweat generated further beings and from whose foot-born offspring came the frost-giants (Hrimthursar). As the rime continued to drip it formed the cow Audhumla, whose four rivers of milk nourished Ymir; by licking salty rime-stones she gradually freed a man, Turi, from the ice. Turi fathered Bor, who married the giantess Besla, daughter of Bolthorn; their sons Odin, Vili, and Ve killed Ymir. His blood drowned almost all the frost-giants except Hvergelmir and his household, who escaped in a boat. Bor’s sons carried Ymir’s body into the middle of the Yawning-gap and made the world from it: seas and waters from his blood, earth from his flesh, rocks from his bones, stones and pebbles from his teeth and broken bones, encircling the earth with sea; the passage ends as they take his skull for further shaping.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The settlers who colonized Iceland brought with them the ethnic religion of the Norsefolk, which is described as having fought its last great battle at Sticklestead, where Olaf Haraldsson died and was later regarded as a saint.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Norse religion is characterized as a compound of myths, some surviving from savage times and others expressing a more developed understanding of life and nature.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Some historians and commentators claim that apparent similarities between Norse religion and later Christianity were borrowed from Christian teachings, dismissing the remaining elements as crude survivals.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The commentator argues that every people, from the lowest savage to more advanced cultures, develops its own philosophy to explain nature and the mysteries of life and to reconcile behavior with its view of reality.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Northmen are described as a mighty, imaginative, and literary folk, far advanced in the arts of life, whose religion corresponded to their stage of cultural development rather than remaining totemistic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The author concedes that some religious elements may have been influenced by contact with Greeks and Irish, but warns against scholars who force facts to fit preconceived theories of religious borrowing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Modern investigation is said to show that the main period of myth-transmission occurs before recorded history, and that Greek religion, like all religions, mixes primitive practices with exalted ideas; cited primitive Greek practices include snake-dances, bear-dances, swimming with sacred pigs, imitating wolves, dog-feasts, and dog-flesh offerings to the gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Despite any borrowed material, the Norse are said to have given their gods a giving them souls that live forever.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Right-minded men are described as living with Allfather in Vingolf after death, whereas wicked men go to Hell and then into Niflhel beneath, in the ninth world.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Before the earth existed, there was a time when nothing existed: no sand, sea, cooling streams, earth, or heaven, but only a Yawning-gap with no grass.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Many ages before the earth was shaped, Niflheim was made; the first land in the southern sphere was called Muspell, a burning and blazing region that cannot be trodden by outsiders without hereditary rights there.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Surtr is said to sit on the border of Muspell guarding the land, and at the end of the world he will go forth, overcome all the gods, and burn the world with fire.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Before races mixed or humans arose, the north-facing side of Yawning-gap was filled with thick ice, rime, fog, and gusts from Niflheim, while the south side was lit by sparks and embers from Muspellheim.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When heat from Muspell met the rime from Niflheim in Yawning-gap, the rime melted and dripped; from these life-drops the likeness of a man was formed, named {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l1282-l1339","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER III. / OF THE HIGHEST GOD. / CHAPTER IV. / THE CREATION OF THE WORLD.; lines 1282-1339","start":"1282","end":"1339","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Of Ymer’s flesh the earth was made,
And of his sweat the seas;
Rocks of his bones,
Trees of his hair,
And the sky of his skull;","summary":"Ganglere asks Har what the sons of Bor did, and Har explains that they carried the giant Ymer’s body into Ginnungagap and fashioned the world from it: earth from his flesh, seas and lakes from his blood and sweat, rocks and stones from his bones and teeth. Jafnhar adds that Ymer’s freely flowing blood became the encircling ocean ring around the earth. Thride says they made the sky from Ymer’s skull, raised it with four sides supported by dwarfs named Austre, Vestre, Nordre, and Sudre, and that they placed glowing sparks from Muspelheim in heaven as fires (including sun, moon, and stars) with fixed resting-places and courses, from which days and years were reckoned, as confirmed by a verse from the Vala’s Prophecy. Ganglere marvels and asks how the earth was shaped. Har replies that the earth is round and surrounded by a deep ocean; lands along the outer strand are given to giant races, and to defend against restless giants the gods build the burg Midgard within the sea and around the earth from Ymer’s eyebrows. Ymer’s brains are cast into the air to make clouds. Wondering whether their abilities come from their own nature or from the gods they worship, he secretly undertakes a journey to Asgard in the guise of an old man. The asas, who can see the future, foresee his coming and receive him with an eye-deceit. In the burg he sees an immense hall whose roof is thatched with golden shields, likened in a quoted verse by Thjodolf of Hvin to Valhal. At the hall door he meets a man juggling seven swords, who questions him. Gylfe gives the name Ganglere, says he has come far seeking lodging, and is led inside to the king. The doors close behind him, and he sees many rooms and many people playing, drinking, and fighting. He recites a verse about carefully examining gates and houses, which a footnote attributes to Havamal. He then sees three high-seats, one above another, occupied by three men identified as Har, Jafnhar, and Thride, with Har as king. The bondwoman answers from drinking habits, while Hjordis explains that a gold ring given by her father grows cold at daybreak, revealing her high birth. Alf rebukes her for hiding her status, promises to marry her and give jointure once she bears him a child, and she is thereafter honoured.

Hjordis later gives birth to a son who is brought before King Hjalprek; the king, struck by the child’s keen eyes, predicts that few will equal him. The boy is sprinkled with water and named Sigurd, and he grows up in Hjalprek’s household beloved and famed above all northern men for strength, beauty, and courage; through him Hjordis is betrothed to King Alf and receives jointure. Sigurd’s foster-father Regin, son of Hreidmar, teaches him chess, runes, and many tongues but also questions him about his father’s wealth and urges him not to remain a mere horse-boy. Sigurd asks the king for a horse and is allowed to choose freely.

In the woods, Sigurd meets a long-bearded old man who tells him to drive the horses into the deep river Busil-tarn; all swim back except one grey, young, powerful horse. Sigurd chooses this horse, and the old man declares it to be of Sleipnir’s kin and the best of horses before vanishing; Sigurd names the horse Grani and understands that the stranger was Odin. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l1722-l1852","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER VII. / ON THE WONDERFUL THINGS IN HEAVEN. / CHAPTER VIII. / THE ASAS.; lines 1722-1852","start":"1722","end":"1852","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Dialogues between Ganglere and Har (with interjections from Jafnhar and Thride) explain cosmological and theological points: the wind comes from the wing-beats of the giant Hrasvelg sitting at the northern end of heaven; summer and winter are attributed to personified ancestors Svasud and Vindlone/Vindsval, whose traits determine the seasons. Ganglere then asks which Asas people must believe in. Har, Jafnhar, and Thride describe the divine Asas and Asynjes, focusing on Odin as highest and oldest, ruling all things, father of the gods and of the warriors killed in battle. Odin is called Alfather and Valfather and prepares Valhal and Vingolf for his chosen warriors, the einherjes. Frigg, Odin’s wife, knows the fate of men but does not reveal it. A verse and footnote link this depiction to Loke’s Quarrel in the Elder Edda. The text lists many of Odin’s names in a verse cited to Grimner’s Lay and explains that his many names arise from different languages and journeys. Ganglere then asks about other Asas, and Har describes Thor as foremost among them, strongest of gods and men, ruling Thrudvang and dwelling in the vast hall Bilskirner, whose floors are numbered in a verse from Grimner’s Lay. Thor travels in a goat-drawn chariot and owns three key treasures: the hammer Mjolner, a belt of strength that doubles his power, and iron gloves needed to wield the hammer, used especially against frost-giants and mountain-giants. Translator footnotes link Thor’s epithet Oku-Thor to the Finnish thunder-god Ukko and remark on an error in the Younger Edda’s explanation of this name.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ganglere asks Har where the wind comes from, noting that it moves great seas, fans fires to He finds many of the pueblo people sick with a new disease attributed to feathers from eaglets they had attacked. He tells them his brother is a powerful shaman who can cure them. They agree to employ the brother, and the Navaho insists he must serve as one of the atsá`lei (first dancers) and must be elaborately dressed in shells and turquoise, including the very largest shell basins in the pueblos, as the Wind has instructed him. People from surrounding pueblos in Chaco Canyon and along the San Juan gather for the rite and collect shells and beads. The Navaho tests and rejects many large shells until the great shell of Kintyél and the great shell of Ki'ndotliz are produced, which match the sizes the Wind described. Before the final dance, messengers invite nearby Navaho camps to attend and perform their dances. One messenger recruits Gánaskidi with his son and daughter; another meets an akáninili from Tsótsil who is inviting the Chaco people to a different Navaho ceremony. After the messengers exchange bows and quivers, the Kintyél messenger returns without additional Navaho dancers. The narrator states this explains why the last night of the yói hatál ceremony has few dances. On the final evening, a large circle of branches like those used in the mountain chant is built, fires are lit, and the atsá`lei is dressed in all the shells and beads, with the great shell of Kintyél on his back, the great shell of Ki'ndotliz on his chest, and another shell on his forehead. As the wolf grows, prophecies say he will be fatal to the gods, so they forge strong fetters. The wolf breaks the first chain, Lading, and the second stronger chain, Drome, which become proverbial for great difficulty. Fearing they cannot bind him, Alfather sends the youth Skirner, Frey’s messenger, to dwarfs in Svartalfaheim to make a new fetter, Gleipner, from six subtle, seemingly nonexistent things such as a cat’s footfall and a woman’s beard. Har explains that the materials’ absence shows the story’s truth and that Gleipner is smooth and soft like a silken string yet very strong. The gods thank Skirner, go to the lake Amsvartner and the rocky island Lyngve with the wolf, and challenge him to break the band. The wolf suspects deceit and demands that one of the gods place a hand in his mouth as a pledge they will release him. Tyr offers his right hand; when the wolf strains against Gleipner, the band only tightens and he is securely bound, while Tyr loses his hand and the gods laugh. They further secure the wolf by drawing the chain Gelgja through the rock Gjol, fastening it with the stone Tvite deep in the earth, and gagging him with a sword whose hilt rests in his lower jaw and point in his upper jaw. The wolf howls, and his saliva becomes the river Von; he will lie there until Ragnarok. Ganglere remarks that Loke’s children are very bad but strong and asks why the gods did not simply kill the wolf despite the evil expected from him. Har answers that the gods respect the holiness of their peace-stead and will not stain it with the wolf’s blood, even though prophecies say he will be the bane of THE GOLDEN AGE. / CHAPTER VII. / ON THE WONDERFUL THINGS IN HEAVEN.; lines 1545-1680","start":"1545","end":"1680","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes the cosmic ash tree Yggdrasil as the greatest tree, whose branches extend over the world and above heaven and whose three roots reach the realms of the gods, the frost-giants near the former Ginungagap, and Niflheim. Under these roots lie springs: Hvergelmer in Niflheim, associated with the dragon Nidhug; and Mimer's well among the frost-giants, where knowledge and wisdom are concealed. Mimer, owner of the well, drinks from it with the Gjallarhorn. Odin once sought a drink there and had to pledge one of his eyes. The third root in heaven stands over the sacred fountain of Urd, at which the gods hold their doomstead. The gods ride daily over the rainbow bridge Bifrost (Asa-bridge) to reach this place, while Thor travels on foot, wading several named rivers when he goes to judge near Yggdrasil. Bifrost is said to burn with fire, and its red color is burning flame; it would allow frost- and mountain-giants to reach heaven if it were fully passable.

Near Urd's fountain under the ash is a beautiful hall from which three maidens—Urd, Verdande, and Skuld—come; these norns shape the lives of men. Additional norns of different races (gods, elves, and dwarfs, including daughters of Dvalin) attend each person at birth to shape his life. A verse and Har's explanation underline that good norns of good descent give good lives, while evil norns cause misfortune and uneven fortunes among men.

Various beings inhabit and affect Yggdrasil: an eagle knowing many things sits on a bough, with the hawk Vedfolner between its eyes; the squirrel Ratatosk runs up and down carrying words of envy between the eagle and Nidhug; four stags named Dain, Dvalin, Duney, and Durathro leap in the branches and bite the leaves. In Hvergelmer with Nidhug are many serpents, including several named ones, that gnaw the tree's roots. Verses depict the ash as suffering distress from the stags above, rot at the side, and Nidhug's gnawing below. Meanwhile, the norns at Urd's fountain daily draw water and clay to sprinkle on Yggdrasil so its branches do not wither or decay. The water of Urd's fountain is so holy that anything placed in it becomes white like an eggshell film. A verse describes Yggdrasil as a high, holy ash sprinkled with white clay, from which dews fall into the dales and which stands eternally green over Urd's fountain. The dew that falls from the tree onto earth is called honey-fall and serves as food for bees. Two birds called swans live in Urd's fountain and are said to be parents of the race of swans. Thor realizes the bones were mishandled, becomes fearsome in his anger, lowering his brows over his eyes and gripping his hammer until his knuckles turn white. Its gate is closed, and Thor cannot open it, so they squeeze between the bars to enter. Inside they find a large hall filled with immense men seated on benches and approach the king, Utgard-Loke, who greets them scornfully and says that no one may stay there unless skilled in some craft or exceptional feat. Loki boasts that he can eat faster than anyone, and Utgard-Loke arranges an eating contest with a man named Loge using a trough full of meat; Loki eats all the flesh, but Loge consumes flesh, bones, and the trough, so Loki loses. Thjalfe offers to run a race; Utgard-Loke sets him against a youth named Huge on a race-course in the plain. In three heats Huge finishes so far ahead that Thjalfe is still far from the goal, and all agree the game has been sufficiently tried. Utgard-Loke then asks Thor what feat he will show; Thor chooses a drinking contest using a long sconce-horn from which local men normally empty the contents in one to three draughts. Thor drinks three times with great effort but cannot empty the horn and is mocked as less mighty than expected. The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy.; lines 1441-1551","start":"1441","end":"1551","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sigmund and Sinfjotli are imprisoned alive in a barrow by King Siggeir, separated by a stone so they can talk but not meet. Signy secretly has Sigmund’s sword smuggled in hidden inside swine’s flesh wrapped in straw. Sinfjotli discovers the sword and he and Sigmund use it to saw through the stone and break out of the barrow. At night they return to the hall, pile wood, and burn it, killing Siggeir and his men. Sigmund reveals himself, offers Signy escape and recompense, but she explains she has long plotted Siggeir’s death: she had her own children killed as unfit for revenge and once came to Sigmund in a witch-wife’s shape so that Sinfjotli would be born of both Volsung’s son and Volsung’s daughter. She declares that she worked only for vengeance and her own death, then chooses to stay in the burning hall and dies with Siggeir. Afterwards, Sigmund and Sinfjotli gather men and ships, return to Volsung’s land, drive out the king who had taken Volsung’s place, and Sigmund becomes a mighty, wise king. He marries Borghild and has two sons, Helgi and Hamund. At Helgi’s birth the Norns (fates) visit and foretell he will become the most renowned of kings. Returning from war, Sigmund names the boy Helgi, gives him various tokens, and prays he will win great fame like the Volsung kin. Helgi grows into a high-minded, beloved and exceedingly capable warrior who leads armies at age fifteen, with Sinfjotli as his companion and co-ruler in war. Endnotes explain beliefs about skin-changers or werewolves in Iceland and other cultures, define the word ‘byrny,’ and describe the Norns as three fates—Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld—who sit by the fountain of Urd beneath the world-tree Yggdrasil and nourish it with water from the fountain.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Sigmund and Sinfjotli are placed alive in a barrow on either side of a stone so they can hear each other’s speech but cannot pass from one side to the other.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"As the barrow is being closed, Signy comes carrying straw, throws it down to Sinfjotli, and orders the thralls to hide this from the king, which they agree to do.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Inside the barrow, Sinfjotli finds that the queen has cast in swine’s flesh wrapped in straw, and discovers Sigmund’s sword hidden inside the meat, recognizing it by the hilts in the darkness.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Sinfjotli pushes the point of the sword into the large stone between them and saws along it until the sword bites into the stone; Sigmund grasps the point and together they saw the stone in two, eventually cutting through both stone and iron to escape from the barrow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After escaping the barrow, Sigmund and Sinfjotli go to the hall at night while everyone sleeps, carry in wood, and set the hall on fire, waking the people inside with smoke and flames.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"As the hall burns, the king cries out asking who kindled the fire, and Sigmund answers that he is there with Sinfjotli, his sister’s son, and that not all of the Volsungs are dead.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Sigmund calls to his sister to come out of the burning hall and receive good things, great honour, and fair atonement from him for her sufferings.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Signy replies that she has kept Siggeir’s killing of King Volsung in memory, had her children slain because she thought them unfit for avenging their grandfather, went to Sigmund in a witch-wife’s shape, and that Sinfjotli is thus the son of both Sigmund and herself; Of the Slaying of the Worm Fafnir.; lines 2419-2552","start":"2419","end":"2552","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"On a heath near a high cliff where the dragon Fafnir crawls to water, Sigurd and Regin prepare an ambush. Regin tells Sigurd to dig a pit and stab Fafnir from below, then rides away in fear. As Sigurd digs, an old man with a long beard appears, criticizes the plan, and advises him to dig several pits so the dragon’s blood will drain off; the man then vanishes, and Sigurd follows this counsel. When Fafnir crawls down to drink, the earth shakes and he spouts venom, but Sigurd remains fearless. As Fafnir passes over the pits, Sigurd thrusts his sword up under the dragon’s left shoulder to the hilt, wounding him fatally; Fafnir thrashes with head and tail, breaking everything around. Mortally wounded, Fafnir questions Sigurd’s identity. Sigurd first answers in riddling fashion, then reveals his name and lineage. They argue about courage, bondsman status, and inheritance. Fafnir says Regin, his brother, has caused his death and will also cause Sigurd’s, and he warns that the gold hoard will be the death of Sigurd and of anyone who owns it. He also warns Sigurd against sea voyages. Sigurd, accepting that all men must die once, insists he will take the treasure anyway. At Sigurd’s prompting, Fafnir speaks of the Norns—some of Aesir kin, some elvish, some daughters of Dvalin—and identifies a holm called Unshapen where Surt and the Aesir mingle the ‘water of the sword.’ Fafnir describes the terror he inspired after brooding over his brother’s heritage. He advises Sigurd to flee lest a dying foe take revenge, but Sigurd refuses and rides to claim the treasure. Fafnir repeats that the gold will be his bane. Sigurd prefers to keep wealth until his last day and tells Fafnir to lie in his death-pangs until Death and Hell take him; Fafnir Balder, Odin’s second son, is praised as the best of the gods, extraordinarily beautiful and bright, with a brow compared to the whitest plant; he is wisest, mildest and most eloquent, his judgments cannot be altered, and he dwells in the heavenly place Breidablik, where nothing unclean can enter and where there is the least evil. Har then describes Njord, who lives in Noatun in heaven, rules the winds, and calms sea and fire; seafarers and fishermen invoke him, and he is so wealthy he can grant land and abundance. Fostered in Vanaheim, he was given by the Vanir as a hostage to the gods, who in turn sent Honer; Njord established peace between the gods and the Vanir. Njord marries Skade, daughter of the giant Thjasse: she wants to live in her father’s mountain home Thrymheim, while Njord prefers the sea. They try living nine nights in Thrymheim and three in Noatun, but each dislikes the other’s environment, as shown in verses complaining about wolves’ howls and sea-fowl’s cries. Skade returns to the mountains, skis with bow to hunt wild beasts, and is called a ski-goddess. Njord later fathers Frey and Freyja, who are fair and mighty. Frey rules over rain, sunshine, and the fruits of the earth, and is invoked for harvests, peace, and wealth. Freyja, the most famous goddess, lives in the heavenly dwelling Folkvang; when she rides to battle she takes half of the slain each day for the seats in her hall, while Odin takes the other half. Her hall Sesrynmer is large and beautiful, and she drives in a car drawn by two cats, hears those who call on her, lends her name to noblewomen’s title, and is invoked in love matters. Ganglere remarks on the importance of such gods, and Har then describes Tyr, a very daring and stout-hearted god who grants victory in war and is a byword for bravery and wisdom. In binding the wolf Fenrer with the chain Gleipner, Tyr places his hand in the wolf’s mouth as a pledge; when the gods refuse to release the wolf, it bites off his hand at the wrist, leaving him one-handed. mapping this onto an afterlife journey motif is therefore partial."},{"id":"motif:5","label":"Weather and harvest deity ensuring prosperity and peace","taxonomy_refs":["seasonal_cycle"],"basis":"Frey is described as ruling over rain, sunshine, and the fruits of the earth and is invoked specifically for harvests and peace, as well as for wealth, indicating a deity whose control of natural cycles underpins human prosperity and social stability.","evidence_refs":["ev:6"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The text links Frey to weather and harvest but does not narrate explicit seasonal myths or cyclical death-rebirth; Odin sees him from Hlidskjalf; when the gods arrive, Kvaser deduces from the ashes of Loke’s burned net how to make such a contrivance for catching fish, and the asas weave their own net. After several casts in the river and toward the sea, during which Loke hides between stones and leaps over the net, Thor finally seizes the salmon by its tail, explaining why salmon have slim tails. Loke is then taken to a cave, bound over three pierced rocks with the intestines of his son Narfe, who has been torn apart by his wolf-shaped brother Vale; the fetters become iron. Skade hangs a serpent above Loke so its venom drips on his face, while Sigyn stands by holding and emptying a dish to catch the drops; when venom strikes Loke’s face he writhes so violently that the whole earth shakes, which is identified as earthquakes, and he will lie bound until Ragnarok.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ganglere Atli welcomes them but demands the gold once owned by Sigurd and now Gudrun’s, claiming it as his right. Gunnar refuses, saying Atli must face them in battle before they will yield anything, and mocks Atli for arranging a feast while planning slaughter. Atli replies that he has long intended to kill them, seize the gold, and avenge the deceit they did to the best of their affinity. Hogni answers that it is useless to brood over such plans without acting, and fighting breaks out with missiles. 

News of the battle reaches Gudrun, who becomes extremely angry, casts off her mantle, runs out to greet and kiss her brothers, and gives them what proves to be a final greeting. She says she had given counsel that should have kept them from coming, but that no one can escape his shaped fate, and asks whether seeking peace would help. Her brothers stoutly refuse. Seeing the battle going badly for them, Gudrun arms herself in a mail-coat, takes a sword, and fights beside her brothers in the front ranks; all agree that no fairer defence was ever seen. Many men fall; Gunnar and Hogni fight foremost among all, the battle lasts until midday, the mead runs red with blood, and Hogni’s sons also fight stoutly. 

King Atli then notes that although he has a large and fine host with mighty champions, many of his men have fallen: nineteen of his champions are dead and only six remain, and there is a lull in the fighting. He laments that of four brothers he alone survives, recalls having gained great affinity and a noble, wise wife but having little peace with her, and accuses the brothers of killing many of his kin, cheating him of realm and riches, and slaying his sister. Of the Slaying of the Worm Fafnir.; lines 2712-2880","start":"2712","end":"2880","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Sigurd rides long roads to the mountain Hindfell and sees a great fire-like light and a shield-hung castle with a banner. Entering, he finds a fully armed, sleeping figure. Removing the helm, he discovers a woman in a mailcoat grown to her flesh; he cuts the byrny off with his sword, waking her. She asks who has broken her sleep and recognises Sigurd Sigmundson, bearer of Fafnir's helm and slayer of Fafnir. Sigurd identifies himself and notes that he has heard she is a king's daughter, lovely and full of lore. 

Brynhild sings of her long enchanted sleep and the woes of mankind, greeting day, night, gods, goddesses, and the fruitful earth, asking for fair words, wisdom, and healing. She then explains that in a battle between two kings, Helm Gunnar and Agnar (Audi's brother), Odin had promised victory to Helm Gunnar, but she struck Helm Gunnar down. As punishment, Odin drove a sleep-thorn into her, decreeing that she would never again win victory and would be given away in marriage. In response, she vowed never to marry a man who knows fear.

Sigurd asks her to teach him great lore. Brynhild replies that although he may be more skilled, she will gladly teach him runes and other fundamental matters. She invites him to drink with her, praying that the gods grant them a good day so that he may gain help and fame from her wisdom and remember their conversation. She fills a beaker, gives Sigurd a "drink of love," and describes the beer as mixed with fame, songs, and runes, full of wise and sweet words.

Brynhild then teaches various runic charms. War-runes are to be cut on a hardened sword's hilt, back, and side, with Tyr's name named twice. Sea-runes, cut on a ship's stern and rudder-blade and accompanied by fire on the oar, ensure safe return over high blue seas. Word-runes, wound and woven about oneself at assemblies, prevent others from repaying grief at the Thing. Ale-runes, carved on mead-horn and hands with an N nicked on the nail and leek laid in the liquor, protect against unfaithful wives and harmful drink. Help-runes, cut on the hollows of the hands and around the joints while calling on the Good-folk, aid in easing childbirth. Bough-runes, scored on bark and on buds of eastward-facing trees, serve for healing and wound-searching. A prolonged Fimbul-winter of three summers-less winters, preceded by three winters of war and kin-strife, is foretold in both prose and verses from the Vala’s Prophecy. Cosmic portents follow: wolves devour the sun and moon, stars fall, earth and mountains shake, bonds break, and the Fenris-wolf and Midgard-serpent are loosed. The serpent’s writhing floods the world, the ship Naglfar made from dead men’s nails is freed and steered by the giant Hrym, and fiery sons of Muspel led by Surt ride from a rent heaven across Bifrost to the vast battlefield Vigrid, joined by Loke, frost-giants, and the friends of Hel.

Heimdal blows the Gjallar-horn to awaken the gods, who hold council. Odin rides to Mimer’s well for advice as the world ash Ygdrasil trembles and all beings fear. The Asas and Einherjar arm and march out. On Vigrid, paired combats unfold: Odin against Fenris-wolf, Thor against Midgard-serpent, Frey against Surt, Tyr against the hound Garm, Vidar against the wolf after Odin’s death, and Loke against Heimdal. Thor kills the serpent but dies from its venom; Frey falls because he lacks the sword he once gave Skirner; Tyr and Garm kill each other; the wolf swallows Odin but is torn apart by Vidar using a special shoe made from discarded leather strips; Heimdal and Loke kill each other.

Finally, Surt casts fire over the earth and burns the world. Verses from the Vala’s Prophecy poetically repeat these scenes: Heimdal’s horn, Odin with Mimer’s head, Ygdrasil groaning, giants and dwarfs in turmoil, Hrym’s advance from the east, Jormungand churning the sea, an eagle feeding on corpses, Naglfar loosed and a ship of Muspel steered by Loke, Surt arriving from the south with a blazing fire-brand and sun-bright sword, mountains crashing, giant maidens terrified, heroes going to Hel, and heaven rent in two.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ganglere says he has never heard tidings of Ragnarok and asks Har about it; the stars are hurled from heaven.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The earth and mountains shake so violently that trees are torn up by their roots, mountains topple down, and all bonds and fetters are broken, allowing the Fenris-wolf to get loose.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The sea rushes over the earth because the Midgard-serpent writhes in giant rage and seeks to gain the land.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The ship Naglfar is described as made from the nails of dead men, with a warning that dying with unpared nails provides material for its construction; Naglfar becomes loose in the flood, and the giant Hrym is its steersman.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Fenris-wolf advances with mouth wide open, the upper jaw reaching to heaven and the lower jaw resting on the earth, with fire flashing from its eyes and nostrils.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Midgard-serpent vomits venom that defiles all the air and sea, is described as very terrible, and positions itself beside the wolf.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The heavens are rent in twain and the sons of Muspel come riding through the opening; Surt rides first with burning flames before and behind him, bearing a sword that shines brighter than the sun, and as they ride over Bifrost the bridge breaks to pieces.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The sons of Muspel, the Fenris-wolf, the Midgard-serpent, Loke, Hrym and all the frost-giants, and the friends of Hel repair to the plain Vigrid, where the sons of Muspel have effulgent bands by themselves; Vigrid is described as one hundred miles on each side.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"While these events occur, Heimdal stands up and blows with all his might in the Gjallar-horn, awakening all the gods, who then hold counsel.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Odin rides to Mimer’s well to ask advice of Mimer for himself and his people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The ash Ygdrasil quivers, the old tree groans, and all things in heaven and earth fear and tremble as a giant gets loose.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Asas and the Einherjes arm themselves and hasten to the battlefield.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Odin rides first to the battle against the Fenris-wolf, wearing a golden helmet and resplendent byrnie and carrying his spear Gungner, while Thor stands at his side but cannot help him because he is engaged in combat with the Midgard-serpent.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Frey encounters Surt and they exchange heavy blows until Frey falls; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l3597-l3652","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW NJORD GOT SKADE TO WIFE. / CHAPTER IV. / THE ORIGIN OF POETRY. / AFTERWORD; lines 3597-3652","start":"3597","end":"3652","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An afterword to Brage’s talk advises young skalds to study the book to learn poetic diction and understand obscure verses, while preserving traditional sagas and periphrastic expressions. It warns Christian readers not to believe in heathen gods or the literal truth of the sagas, explaining that men from Asia (Turks), called asas, falsified tales of Troy so people would think them gods. The text equates elements of Norse myth—Brime’s hall, Ragnarok, Thor’s fishing for the Midgard serpent, the serpent’s killing of Thor, Hymer’s death, the flame of Surt, Fenris-wolf, Odin’s death, and the survival of Thor’s sons—with episodes from the Trojan War: King Priam’s palace, battles involving Hektor, Volukrontes, Achilleus, Roddros, Pyrrhos, the burning of Troy, and the later deeds of Elenus/Ale/Vidar/Æneas and Hektor’s sons. Elenus and Alexander are said to have reworked these stories, with Ale/Æneas surviving after the gods perish in a world-burning fire, while Mode and Magne and the sons of Hektor claim lands and found kingdoms after Troy’s fall.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Young skalds who desire poetic diction, old names, or understanding of obscure songs are told they must master this book for instruction and pastime.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The text states that sagas should not be forgotten or disproved in a way that removes old poetic periphrases valued by great skalds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Christian men are instructed not to believe in heathen gods nor in the truth of the sagas except as explained earlier in the book about events leading people away from the true Since I intend to wade
To the gards of giants.
Know, if you wax,
Then waxes my asa-might
As high, as the heavens.","summary":"Thor tells Groa how he once carried Orvandel from Jotunheim, freezing and then throwing Orvandel’s toe into the sky to become a star, which so delights Groa that she forgets her healing songs and leaves the flint-stone lodged in Thor’s head, leading to a taboo on throwing flint-stones. Thjodolf of Hvin’s poem then recounts Thor’s fiery, world-shaking battle journey to the giant Hrungner, the flying shield, the giant’s fall, and the flint-stone striking Thor’s skull before Groa removes it. In a new episode, Æger asks Bragi about Thor’s other deeds among giants; Bragi narrates how Loki, in Frigg’s falcon-guise, is captured and starved by Geirrod and bargains to bring Thor to Geirrodsgard without hammer or belt. On the way, Thor visits the giantess Grid, who warns him about Geirrod and lends him her belt of strength, steel gloves, and staff. Thor then wades the great river Vimer, stemming its wild torrent with Gridarvol while Loki clings to his belt, and recites a verse commanding the river not to grow, asserting that his divine might The Latter End of all the Kin of the Giukings. / APPENDIX: EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA. / PART OF THE SECOND LAY OF HELGI HUNDINGS-BANE (1); lines 5301-5521","start":"5301","end":"5521","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Helgi weds Sigrun and they have sons, but Helgi is slain by his brother-in-law Dag, son of Hogni, who sacrifices to Odin and receives Odin's spear to avenge his father. Dag kills Helgi at Fetter-grove and then rides to Sevafell to tell Sigrun, speaking sorrowfully of Helgi as the best of kings. Sigrun recalls oaths Dag swore to Helgi at a bright white water and a sea-covered rock, and she curses Dag so that his ship, horse, and sword will fail him and declares that a proper price will be paid when he becomes a wolf in the wild wood eating corpses. Dag says she raves and blames Odin for casting strife-runes between kin, then offers her gold rings, lands, and half the land as compensation. Sigrun rejects happiness at Sevafell and praises Helgi’s bravery, likening his superiority to an ash-tree rising above thorns and a dew-sprinkled fawn whose horns gleam against heaven.\nA burial barrow is raised over Helgi. When he comes to Valhall, Odin appoints him lord of all things there like himself, and Helgi orders his enemy Hunding to perform menial tasks such as preparing foot-baths, kindling fires, tending hounds and horses, and washing swine. One evening Sigrun’s bondmaid passes Helgi’s mound and sees Helgi riding toward it with a great company of dead warriors, spurring their horses. She wonders if this is illusion or the end of all things and whether dead warriors can go home. The dead reply that it is no illusion or ruin, and that dead warriors may ride homeward.\nThe bondmaid tells Sigrun that Helgi has come to his uncovered mound with bleeding wounds and bids her come to stop the stream of sorrow. Sigrun goes into the mound to Helgi, joyfully comparing the meeting to hungry hawks of Odin anticipating warm quarry or seeing dawn. She kisses her king laid lifeless and describes his hair covered with death’s rime, his body dripping with the dew of the dead, and his hands cold. She asks how she can win healing for him. Helgi tells her that her gold-clad tears have made him drip with grief’s dew, each falling in blood upon his breast, cold and bitter. He says they will drink dear draughts though they have lost life and lands, that no sorrow-song will be sung despite his wounds, and that brides and kings’ daughters abide with the departed in the mound. THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9369-9472","start":"9369","end":"9472","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes explain several Navajo sacred mountains and divine figures. Do-kos-líd (San Francisco Mountain) is a sacred western boundary mountain, associated with the color yellow and haliotis shell, and poetically called \"The Wand of Haliotis.\" White Corn Boy and Yellow Corn Girl are divine corn figures whose names are analyzed; there may be more than one divine pair with these names. Depe'ntsa (San Juan Mountains) forms the northern boundary and contains the Place of Emergence, associated with the color black and objects like cannel coal and blackbirds. Pollen Boy and Grasshopper Girl are divine figures, with Grasshopper Girl depicted in corn pollen in a ceremonial dry-painting. Dsil-ná-o-til (Encircled Mountain) is said to have been encircled by Estsánatlehi and her people moving their camp around it and is associated with goods of all kinds. Boy and Girl Who Produce Goods personify the increase of goods, originally trade items like furs and textiles. Tso-lí-hi is one of seven sacred mountains, of uncertain location and meaning. A large yellow bird named Tsoz-gá-li is mentioned. Boy and Girl Who Produce Jewels personify hard, brittle materials used for jewelry, such as shells, turquoise, and cannel coal. A-ki-da-nas-tá-ni (Hosta Butte) is a prominent butte whose name means one round thing on top of another. Tse`-ha-dá-ho-ni-ge (mirage-stone) is a ritual stone kept by medicine-men, likened to a mirage and possibly a form of pyrophyllite; medicine-men will exchange but not sell it, and a shaman refuses to trade it for a Chinese idol. Finally, Tó`-la-nas-tsi is a ritually significant mixture of waters from various sources and the four quarters of the world, carried in jars by the deity Tó`nenili and imitated in present-day rites.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Do-kos-líd or Do-ko-os-li'd is the Navajo name of San Francisco Mountain, a prominent landmark in Arizona regarded as a sacred mountain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The name Do-kos-líd seems to contain the words to` (water) and kos (cloud), although its precise meaning is unknown.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Do-kos-líd is considered the sacred mountain that bounds Navajo land on the west, and yellow is the color associated with the west; various mostly yellow things symbolize the west and are sacred to this mountain.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Haliotis shell, regarded by the Navajo as yellow, is sacred to Do-kos-líd, and in sacred songs the peak is figuratively called \"The Wand of Haliotis.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"White Corn Boy (Na-tál-kai A-si-ké) and Yellow Corn Girl (Natáltsoi Atét) are named divine figures whose names derive from the Navajo words for corn, white, yellow, boy, and girl; the text notes a creation of a White Corn Boy and Yellow Corn Girl elsewhere.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"It is uncertain whether the White Corn Boy and Yellow Corn Girl mentioned here are the same as the deities associated with Do-kos-líd, and the Navajo likely believe in more than one divine pair with these names.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Depe'ntsa is the Navajo name for the San Juan Mountains in southwestern Colorado, derived from depé (Rocky Mountain sheep) and intsá (scattered all over).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The San Juan Mountains are said to bound the Navajo land on the north, and somewhere among them lies Níhoyostsátse, the Place of Emergence.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Black is the color associated with the north, and black objects such as cannel coal and blackbirds symbolically belong to the San Juan Mountains.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Pollen Boy and Grasshopper Girl are divine figures mentioned elsewhere, and in a dry-painting of klédzi hatál, Grasshopper Girl is depicted in corn pollen.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Dsil-ná-o-til is explained by Navajo informants as meaning a mountain encircled by people travelling around it, connected to a story that Estsánatlehi and her people moved their camp to various places around the base of the mountain.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The author considers the Dsil-ná-o-til account mythical, has never seen the mountain, and does not know its location; a similarly named range, the Carrizo Mountains, is not identified as containing the sacred hill.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Goods of all kinds are thought to belong to Dsil-ná-o-til, the Encircled Mountain.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Boy Who Produces Goods and Girl Who Produces Goods personify the increase of goods; the term yódi or yúdi originally referred to trade items such as furs, skins, and textiles, excluding food and jewels, and now applies to most merchandise in a trader's store.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Tso-lí-hi or Tso-lín-i is one of the seven sacred mountains of the Navajo country, of undetermined location and meaning, possibly deriving its name from tsó (spruce).","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The relation of Tso-lí-hi to jewels is unknown; the author can only conjecture about this connection.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Tsoz-gá-li is described as a large yellow bird of undetermined species.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Boy Who Produces Jewels and Girl Who Produces Jewels are associated with inkli'z, a term meaning something hard and brittle and here applied to materials such as shells, rough turquoise, cannel coal, and other stones used for Navajo jewels rather than to finished jewels.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A-ki-da-nas-tá-ni (Hosta Butte) means One-round-thing-sitting-on-top-of-another and names an 8,837-foot butte in New Mexico surrounded by lower hills, forming a prominent landmark.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Tse`-ha-dá-ho-ni-ge, or mirage-stone, is believed to resemble a mirage and is kept in the pollen bags of medicine-men, who are willing to exchange but not sell pieces of it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"A stone Chinese idol, pronounced similar to mirage-stone, was analyzed and found to be silicate of magnesia, probably pyrophyllite; the author offered this idol to a shaman in exchange for mirage-stone, but the shaman refused after learning it represented a Chinese god.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Tó`-la-nas-tsi is a mixture of all kinds of water—spring, snow, hail, and water from the four quarters of the world—and such water is supposed to have been carried by Tó`nenili in his jars; contemporary Navajo rites attempt to approximate this mixture.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The Navajo color-symbol system links yellow with the west and black with the north, assigning corresponding natural objects (e.g., haliotis shell, cannel coal, blackbirds) to the sacred mountains of those directions.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Do-kos-líd / Do-ko-os-li'd (San Francisco Mountain)","description":"A prominent Arizona THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 8882-8982","start":"8882","end":"8982","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Hatáli Nez explained that while he recounted the adventures of his ancestors in the nether world \"we were travelling in the land of the dead\" among evil and potent ghosts, and that only when the tale reached the ascent into \"this—the fifth and last world\" would the danger cease. Elsewhere the notes describe the ritual preparation of sacred buckskin, a yucca-leaf mask for the Night Chant that must be torn up after use, the meaning of hatál (sacred chant), and Navajo color symbolism for the four cardinal points.","summary":"The passage consists of ethnographic notes. One describes the carefully regulated preparation of \"sacred buckskin\": a deer is killed without being wounded, marked with pollen, skinned in a prescribed manner, oriented to the east, and its own bones are reused as tools under strict taboos. Another explains a mask woven from yucca leaves for the Night Chant that must be ritually destroyed after use, though the author was allowed to photograph it. A long note recounts the behavior of the shaman Hatáli Nez while narrating the creation myth: he hurried and avoided interruptions during the episodes set in the nether world, saying that during these they were travelling in the land of the dead among dangerous ghosts and were in danger until the story reached the people’s ascent into this fifth and last world via the Place of Emergence in the San Juan Mountains. After finishing the subterranean portion he performed a private prayer to counteract the evil effects of this symbolic journey. Additional notes define hatál as a sacred chant, hatáli as the ceremonial singer or shaman, distinguish this from a herbalist healer, and list two Navajo systems that associate specific colors with the four cardinal directions.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The deer used for \"sacred buckskin\" must not be shot or otherwise wounded; instead it is surrounded by men on foot or horseback, driven until exhausted, and then smothered with a pollen-filled bag placed over its mouth and nostrils.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After the deer is killed, lines are drawn with pollen from the center outward along the median line of the body and along the insides of the limbs before cutting the skin.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Incisions are made with a stone knife along the pollen lines from within outward to open the skin, after which the flaying may be completed with a steel knife.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Once removed, the skin is laid to the east of the carcass, with the head toward the east and the hairy side down.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The deer’s fibulae and ulnae are cut out, placed back into the appropriate leg-skins, used as scrapers for the skin, and, when masks are made, the right and left fibulae are used as awls for sewing the corresponding sides of the masks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Bones (fibulae and ulnae) from any deer other than the one that provided the skin must not be used in preparing or working that sacred buckskin.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A mask made from leaves of Yucca baccata, from which the thick dorsal portions have been torn away, is GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 10848-10907","start":"10848","end":"10907","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes the Gánaskidi, a numerous group of Navajo divinities associated with mountain sheep. Their chief home is at Depéhahatil near Tse`gíhi, though they may appear anywhere and often accompany the yéi and other gods. Belonging to the Mountain Sheep People, they sometimes appear to humans as Rocky Mountain sheep. In myths of the night chant they captured the prophet of the rites, brought him to their home, and taught him many of the chant’s mysteries. Treatments linked with them use parts of the mountain sheep for healing, and they are explicitly identified as gods of plenty and harvest gods.

The text then details a human masquerader who represents a Gánaskidi during the night chant. He appears about sundown on the last day in an act of succor after representatives of Hastséyalti and Dsahadoldzá. He wears a blue yébaka mask, a basket crown painted and feathered to represent storm cloud, lightning, sunlight, and sun rays, with horns made from Rocky Mountain sheep skin tipped with eagle feathers. On his back he carries a buckskin bag distended to look full, decorated with plumes and painted lines; it represents a heavy bag of black cloud filled with produce of the fields, forcing the god and impersonator to walk bent and leaning on a cherry-wood staff painted with charcoal from four sacred plants and marked with a lightning stripe, feather-trimmed. These items are also shown in dry-paintings. Red powder on the plumes signifies pollen; rainbows are said to tie the cloud bag to the god; and a yellow line on the chin of the mask symbolizes evening twilight. The actor wears a fox-skin collar and ordinary clothing. The name Gánaskidi is glossed as "Humpback" and also given as Nánaskidi.

A final note mentions Ki'ndoliz or Ki'ndotliz (Blue House), identified by the writer as a ruined pueblo in Chaco Canyon, but he doubts this is the Blue House named in the myth and suggests there is probably another ruin of that name on the San Juan River.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Gánaskidi are described as a numerous It then explains that ritual baths are an important part of Navaho rites, often made with yucca-root suds in a wicker basket, followed by rinsing with water and drying with corn meal, and that such baths occur in various ceremonies, including preparation for a deer hunt for both practical and religious reasons. Finally, it details the sacred use of pollen (thaditín), mainly from corn, carried in buckskin bags with small sacred stones or fetishes; pollen offerings accompany nearly all rites and prayers and are used in various ways, including placing live animals in pollen to increase its virtue, preserving pollen from dry-paintings, using special mixtures (such as with a striped lizard) for easy childbirth, and extending the term to fine powders like the misty hues of the horizon; similar pollen usages are noted among the Apache. Explains that the name, not exactly translated, contains the words for spruce (tso) and white (kai).","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","rights_note":"public_domain"},{"id":"ev:2","type":"summary","locator":"lines 8774-8789","quote_or_summary":"Explains that the bath is an important part of Navaho rites, administered on many occasions and often mentioned in tales. The bath usually consists of suds made in a water-tight wicker basket by soaking the root of a yucca species, typically Yucca baccata, in water; the subject is then rinsed with plain water and dried by rubbing on corn meal. Different ceremonies involve different observances connected with the bath. In the myth of 'The Mountain Chant,' a bath is part of the deer-hunt ceremony, given in preparation for the hunt for both practical and religious reasons, including minimizing the hunter's personal odor when pursuing game.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","rights_note":"public_domain"},{"id":"ev:3","type":"summary","locator":"lines 8790-8809","quote_or_summary":"Describes pollen (thaditín) obtained for sacred uses from various plants, chiefly Indian corn. Pollen is carried in small buckskin bags that usually also contain small sacred stones such as rock crystal and pyrophyllite or small animal fetishes. The administration or sacrifice of pollen is part of all rites witnessed and nearly always follows or accompanies prayer. Uses vary: a common method is to take a pinch, applying some to the tongue and some to the crown of the head. For some purposes, a shaman gathers pollen in a large bag, immerses a live bird, insect, or other animal, then lets it escape, which is believed to add extra virtue to the pollen; a special preparation i`yidezná includes a bluebird, a yellowbird, and a grasshopper. Another note gives a mythic account of pollen placed on the young of a sea monster and preserved. Pollen from ceremonial dry-paintings is saved for later use. Pollen in which a live striped lizard has been placed is used to favor easy childbirth. The term thaditín is also applied to impalpable powders such as the misty hues of the horizon in morning and evening, often due to dust. Captain Bourke's work on Apache medicine-men is cited for many modes of pollen use that also occur among the Navahoes.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","rights_note":"public_domain"},{"id":"ev:4","type":"summary","locator":"lines 8810-8811","quote_or_summary":"States that a few additional observances concerning kethawns will follow in the text.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/navajo/project-gutenberg/navaho-legends-matthews.md","rights_note":"public_domain"}],"confidence":{"extraction":"high","motif_candidates":"medium","comparison_claims":"high","notes":"Core ritual descriptions are straightforward, but mapping pollen uses to broader motif families like 'sacrifice' and especially 'sacred_birth' involves some interpretation; these links should be reviewed by a specialist in Diné traditions."},"reviewer_status":{"status":"needs_review","reviewer":"","reviewed_at":"","notes":""},"extracted_by":"gpt-4.1","extracted_at":"2026-07-18","notes":""}

She foretells that the male addressee will give his sister Gudrun in marriage to a powerful man, Atli, against Gudrun’s will. Atli, the speaker’s brother and son of Budli, will win Gudrun, thwart the addressee’s attempt to gain Oddrun, and later cruelly cast him into a narrow serpent-pit. The speaker says Oddrun and the addressee will nevertheless come together in secret, and Oddrun will love him as the speaker once did. She predicts that Atli will in turn be slain by Gudrun, together with his sons and wealth, when Gudrun prepares a deadly bed for him with a sword.

The speaker reflects that it would have been more fitting for Gudrun to die after her first beloved husband, Sigurd, if she had had better counsel or a heart like the speaker’s. Instead, Gudrun will survive: the sea and high waves will carry her to Jonakr’s ancestral land, where she will bear Jonakr sons who are supports of his lineage. Gudrun will send her daughter Swanhild, born of Gudrun and Sigurd, away from that land. Swanhild will be harmed by the counsel (‘rede’) of Bikki, and Jormunrek’s life will benefit nothing from these deeds. As a result, all the kin of Sigurd will be destroyed, bringing yet more grief for Gudrun.

Turning fully to her own death, the speaker offers a final prayer: that a burial mound or stronghold of the dead be built broad upon the field, with room for all who died at Sigurd’s death to lie there. She orders that the mound be hung with fine woven hangings and shields made by Gauls, and that the Hun King be burned lying beside her. On the other side of the Hun King are to be burned those who served her, strewn with treasure, with two attendants at the head, two at the feet, and also two hounds and two hawks. She commands that between her and the man who lies with her there be laid properly-prepared metal and sharp-edged steel, as had lain between them when they once shared a bed and were called husband and wife.

She adds that if this is done, the bright ring-adorned door of Valhall will not clash shut behind the man, and if she and her companions follow him there, their journey will not be wretched. She specifies that five of her bondmaids, eight bondsmen, her fosterer, and the dowry that her father Budli once gave her should accompany her in death.
