content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l7110-l7320","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE HELL-RIDE OF BRYNHILD. / FRAGMENTS OF THE LAY OF BRYNHILD / THE SECOND OR ANCIENT LAY OF GUDRUN. / THE SONG OF ATLI.; lines 7110-7320","start":"7110","end":"7320","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A prose preface states that Gudrun, Giuki's daughter and Atli's wife, avenged her brothers by killing Atli's sons and Atli himself, then burning his hall and household; the following song tells of the events leading up to this. Atli sends a crafty messenger, Knefrud, to Gunnar's richly appointed hall to invite him to Atli's court, promising shields, weapons, hosts of Huns, and rich lands such as Gnitaheath and Murkwood. Gunnar, already abundantly wealthy, consults his brother Hogni, who has received a ring from their sister Gudrun wrapped in wolf-clothing and wound with a wolf hair, which he interprets as a warning that their path will be beset by wolves. Ignoring all counsel, Gunnar orders a lavish feast, acknowledging it may be their last, and foresees wolves and bears ruling the Niblung wealth if he does not return. Gunnar and his men depart, ride through fells and dark woods, and come to Atli's fortified land and hall, where Atli drinks while warders watch for Gunnar's people. Gudrun meets her brothers, warns Gunnar that he is betrayed and that a pit of serpents (worm-close) now awaits him, saying it would have been better had he come armed so he could have reddened the fields with battle and brought Atli himself to the worm-close. Gunnar replies that her warning comes too late to summon help from the Niblungs on the Rhine. In the fighting that follows, Hogni kills seven men and thrusts an eighth into the fire, but Gunnar is overpowered, bound in fetters, and offered life in exchange for gold; he nobly declares he will first hold Hogni’s bleeding heart in his hand, cut from the brave warrior’s breast.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Gudrun, Giuki's and people are drinking merrily.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Knefrud is described as a guileful man of the Southland with a cold voice who sits on the high The witch-wife, in Signy’s likeness, sleeps with the king, while Signy goes in the witch-wife’s guise to her brother Sigmund’s underground house, claims to be a lost lone woman, and is given hospitality. Sigmund finds her attractive and shares a bed with her for three nights. Signy then returns home and changes semblances back with the witch-wife. In time she bears a son, Sinfjotli, who grows up strong, handsome, and like the Volsung kin. Signy has previously tested her other sons by sewing gloves onto their hands through flesh and skin; they cry out from the pain. She performs the same torment on Sinfjotli, who does not flinch and remarks that Volsung would have felt such pain little. Before he is ten, she sends Sinfjotli to Sigmund’s earth-house. There Sigmund has the boy knead meal; Sinfjotli suspects something living in it but kneads it in. Sigmund reveals that the dough contains deadly worms (serpents). Each mountain is composed of earth mixed with specific materials (white shell, turquoise, abalone shell, cannel coal, assorted goods, shells and precious stones). Afterward, directional gods carry four of the mountains to the four quarters of the world, leaving two in the center, and pairs of boy-and-girl deities are assigned to dwell in each mountain. Notes then identify Tsisnadzi'ni as the eastern sacred mountain, linked with white shell and the color white, and describe its deities Rock Crystal Boy and Girl, who were stone images that came to life when placed in the mountain. Another note identifies Tsó-tsil (San Mateo / Mount Taylor) as the southern sacred mountain, describes its modern geographic names and location, its role as a southern boundary of Navaho country, and its association with the color blue, femaleness, turquoise, and \"she-rain.\" Two named figures, Boy Who Carries One Turquoise and Girl Who Carries One (Grain of) Corn, are also given. Loki borrowed Ran’s net, captured Andvari, forced him to surrender his gold and last ring, and ignored Andvari’s curse that the treasure would be the bane of its owners. The gods paid the ransom, Odin using the ring to cover the last uncovered hair, and Loki foretold that the gold would doom Hreidmar and his son. Fafnir then slew Hreidmar and took the treasure, becoming a fearsome dragon who broods over the hoard, while Regin became a smith at a king’s court. One note explains that after the people emerged, the Sun and then the Moon stopped in the zenith until each received a human life as payment, establishing the rule that Sun and Moon require continual human deaths to move, with the Sun now taking Navajo lives and the Moon those of other peoples. Another note describes how the world was originally small, bounded by nearby mountains; the people prayed to the four winds, who pulled the mountains outward and widened the world over four successive days until the climate became pleasant. A third note recounts how First Man and First Woman planned the stars with fragments of mica, arranging key stars and constellations, but Coyote impatiently threw the remaining fragments into the sky, causing many stars to be scattered randomly. A further note lists various destructive beings that sprang from blood, including entities associated with colored areas under cliffs that kill people who approach; these are identified with Those Who Talk Under the Cliffs. The last note explains the meaning and ethnographic identification of Kintyél (Broad Pueblo), a ruined pueblo site in the Navajo country, possibly identical with the ruin called Pueblo Chettro Kettle When a chief’s wife dies, the Sun continues his course. That night the Moon similarly stops and, after Coyote explains that it too demands pay, the man who saw the dead woman in the nether world dies, allowing the Moon to move. This establishes an ongoing requirement that the Sun and Moon receive human lives, with the Sun now taking Navajo lives and the Moon taking lives from other peoples.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2","fig:3","fig:4","fig:5","fig:6"],"symbol_refs":["sym:1","sym:2","sym:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"scene:2","label":"Enlargement of the world by mountains and winds","summary":"The world is said to have been originally small, its bounding mountains close together so that the Sun passed near the surface, causing unbearable heat. Coyote appears, claims three red mica pieces as his own stars, and later, impatient with the slow planning, throws the remaining fragments into the sky and blows them upward. The planned stars adhere in their intended places, but the rest stick at random, producing the scattered clusters seen in the sky.","figure_refs":["fig:3","fig:8","fig:9"],"symbol_refs":["sym:5","sym:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Destroyers from blood and the deadly colors under cliffs","summary":"A list is given of destructive beings that sprang from blood, including Travelling Stone, Great Wood That Bites, Old Age Lying Down, several beings linked with different colors under cliffs, Sparkling Under Cliffs, Devouring Antelope, Brown Yéitso, and Slashing Reeds. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 8373-8452","start":"8373","end":"8452","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Spider Woman shows the Navaho hero four direction-colored hoops with ragged feathers and asks him to bring new eagle plumes from a coming battle. She explains that the Eagles' enemies are actually bumblebees and tumbleweeds, gives him a long black cane to gather and burn tumbleweeds, and instructs him to use the juice of a plant, tsildilgi'si, to protect himself from bee stings. She tells him to collect seeds and bees' nests for future use when he returns to earth. The Navaho travels on and joins Eagle warriors hiding behind a hill as they prepare for battle. When he looks for the enemy, he sees only a sandy plain with sunflowers and dead weeds. The Eagles charge, a whirlwind rises, tumbleweeds whirl into the air, and bumblebees swarm from among the sunflowers. In the ensuing battle many Eagles fall, and the survivors retreat in disorder. When the wind dies and the enemies vanish, the Navaho enters the plain, gathers seeds, piles tumbleweeds with his black wand, burns them with fire he kindles, and then, using tsildilgi'si as Spider Woman taught him, he stuns and kills many bees, digs out their nests and honey, captures two young bees, and collects eagle plumes from the fallen warriors. He returns to Spider Woman, gives her the plumes, and she thanks him for both the feathers and his service to the Eagles. He resumes his journey, sleeps on the trail, and next day reaches the Eagles' towns, where the people are mourning their dead kinsmen and also him, believing he had been killed in the She retrieves a turquoise wand and leads him to a small hill, where a large turquoise-adorned stone stands like a stopper in the ground. Touching it with the wand in the four cardinal directions makes it rise; touching it upward makes it fall aside, revealing a hole with four stone steps. They descend into a square underground apartment with four rock-crystal doors, each with a rainbow above it. With the wand she opens the eastern door onto a vast, beautiful country filled with deer, flowers, fragrant pollen, birds, gentle rain, and many rainbows, which Nati'nesthani takes to be his father-in-law Deer Raiser's farm. She also shows him three other similarly beautiful apartments: to the south with antelope, to the west with Rocky Mountain sheep, and to the north with elk. Returning to the central chamber, they find Deer Raiser, who confirms that Nati'nesthani has seen all the game. He points out sacrificial cigarettes associated with each direction and animal—deer, antelope, Rocky Mountain sheep, a single white cigarette of Hastséyalti over the north door, and fawn cigarettes at the foot of the steps—and tells his son-in-law to remember how they are painted, since such are now sacrificed in ceremonies. Nati'nesthani expresses gratitude and admiration. Deer Raiser then has his daughter catch a buck deer from the eastern game-land. They leave, closing the doors and replacing the stone stopper, bring the buck home, bind its legs with short rainbows, cut its throat with a stone arrow point, and skin it as deer are skinned in current practice. Deer Raiser resumes plotting to kill his son-in-law: since he cannot poison him, he plans to use four fierce pet bears kept in a nearby canyon with only one entrance. He spends the day making tracks with the deer hoofs to lead into the bear canyon while Nati'nesthani stays home with his wife. The next morning, while the young woman cooks in the other lodge, Deer Raiser tells Nati'nesthani that four pet deer have escaped and been tracked to the single-entrance canyon. He first proposes that Nati'nesthani stand at the entrance while Deer Raiser drives the deer out, then pretends to reconsider and insists that Nati'nesthani enter the canyon while he waits outside to kill the supposed deer. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l89-l149","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"WITH EXCERPTS FROM THE POETIC EDDA / SELECTED BIBLIOGRAPHY: / RECOMMENDED READING-- / INTRODUCTION; lines 89-149","start":"89","end":"149","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage first lists recommended readings in related Germanic and Scandinavian literature, then introduces the importance of Northern history and Icelandic tradition. The author argues that Northern peoples, whose speech, laws, and customs come largely from a Northern root, ought to regard the North almost as a holy land and to keep the faith and deeds of their forefathers in remembrance. Instead, modern education has turned attention to Greek and Roman history and literature, so that schoolboys know classical battles like Marathon and Salamis but are ignorant of Northern battles, kings, Viking kingdoms, and the settlements of Iceland and Normandy. The author claims that Iceland alone preserved the old Northern tongue and large stores of tales and poems while pagan traditions elsewhere in Europe were altered by foreign influences. Icelandic records are praised for their truth, care, literary beauty, and preservation of old speech and character. Only after Bishop Percy translated Mallet’s \"Northern Antiquities\" in 1770 did Icelandic literature become known in England, and its study remains limited. Icelandic is presented as a crucial \"word-hoard\" and \"mine\" of noble beauty and high manhood for English-speaking peoples, and the author hopes that renewed attention to it will begin a \"great new birth\" restoring to their language and literature what ignorance nearly destroyed.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage opens with a selected bibliography recommending English translations of \"Kudrun\", the \"Nibelungenlied\", and Saxo Grammaticus’s \"The First Nine Books of the Danish History\".","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The author states that a Northern folk derive the greater and better part of their speech, laws, and customs from a Northern root.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The author argues that for such a Northern folk, the North ought to be, if not a holy land, at least a place more to be regarded than any other part of the world, and that the faith and deeds of their forefathers should remain of enduring interest and in remembrance even as their knowledge of other peoples widens.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The author says that various causes have turned attention toward classic men and lands at the expense of the history of the author’s own people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"He observes that every schoolboy knows the stories of the battles of Marathon and Salamis, but that very few would recognize more than the names, if that, of the battles of Hafrsfirth or Sticklestead.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The language, history, laws, and religions of Greece and Rome are described as long having been considered essential parts of an educated man’s learning, while no comparable effort has been made to familiarize him with his own people or their tongue.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The author claims that even an Englishman well read in figures like Alfred, Bede, and Caedmon, as well as Plato, Caesar, Cicero, and Pericles, would still be poorly equipped if asked about the great peoples from whom the English sprang, such as Harold Fairhair, Saint Olaf, the Viking kingdoms in the British Western Isles, or the settlements of Iceland and Normandy.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The author states that knowledge of these Northern matters would be even smaller than it is if there were not one land where old learning found refuge and was preserved.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"He contrasts England, Germany, and the rest of Europe—where traditions of pagan times have been much altered by foreign influence and by the influx of foreign blood affecting peoples and speech—with Iceland, which held to the old tongue that was once the universal speech of northern folk and preserved great stores of tale and poem now again becoming a common heritage.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Iceland’s records are praised for their truth, care, and literary beauty, for the strong and varied life they show in in his country of Icelandic or its literature.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"He notes that Icelandic has been studied only in the latter part of the THE WAR GODS. / IV. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 11008-11113","start":"11008","end":"11113","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes 219–233 explain several ritual and ethnographic details connected with the Navaho tale of Nati'nesthani: the symbolic lighting of sacred cigarettes with sunbeams before they are offered to the gods; terms and uses for external medicines and priestly incense; identification and ritual use of wild tobacco species; a narrator’s explanation of certain diseases, their causes, and treatments in a sweat-house with emetics; the broader meaning of a Navaho adjective translated as “beautiful”; myths about the rapid growth of corn in gardens of the divine yéi and in Nati'nesthani’s farm due to divine seed; the ceremonial ordering and directional color symbolism of ears of corn and other sacred objects; descriptions of foods such as fawn-cheese, pemmican, and several green-corn dishes; and a note on how the storyteller indicated distance using a local landmark.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In Navaho ceremonies, completed sacred cigarettes are symbolically lighted with sunbeams before being deposited as offerings to the gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The hero of the tale is said to have lighted his pipe with the sun, which the commentator interprets as referring to the symbolic sunbeam-lighting of sacred cigarettes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Ke'tlo is a name for any medicine used externally by rubbing it on the body; atsósi ke'tlo is the liniment or wash of the feather ceremony, also called feather medicine or feather herbs.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Yá-di-di-nil is a composite incense used by Navaho priests; during certain healing ceremonies it is scattered on hot coals placed before the patient, who actively inhales the dense white fumes that fill the medicine-lodge.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The incense mixture yá-di-di-nil is pungent, aromatic, said to contain feathers, and its main plant components have not been botanically identified by the author.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The note states that there are certain animals the hero raises and controls, details of which are given elsewhere in the text.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Navahoes recognize four kinds of wild tobacco used in their rites; two are identified as Nicotiana attenuata (mountain tobacco) and Nicotiana palmeri (sheep tobacco), while the species called weasel tobacco and cloud tobacco are uncertain but probably belong to one or more of three Nicotiana species.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Patients with certain named diseases are described as weak, staggering, and losing appetite; they then go to a sweat-house and take an emetic as treatment.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Different diseases are distinguished by what the patients vomit and by associated signs: yellow disease involves vomiting something yellow and often yellow eyes and skin; cooked blood disease involves vomiting something like cooked blood; slime disease is said to come from drinking foul water full of green slime or small fish; worms usually come from eating worms; tapeworm is said to come from eating parched corn.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Hatáli Natlói is cited as the source of this disease classification, which emphasizes ingestion of contaminated food or water rather than demoniac causes; the editor notes that this contradicts a prevalent theory that \"savages\" regard all disease as of demoniac origin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The adjective yazóni or yasóni, translated as \"beautiful,\" is explained as meaning both good (or useful) and beautiful, and as containing elements of words that signify good and beautiful.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Navaho myths and songs state that corn and other products in the gardens of the yéi or divine ones grow and mature in a very short time.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The rapid growth of the crops in Nati'nesthani's farm is attributed to the divine origin of the seed he uses.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Nati'nesthani lays down ears of corn in a specific color order that matches the ceremonial order for colored sacrificial cigarettes, kethawns, and other sacred objects in a straight row: first white, then blue, then yellow, and then black or The woman is revealed to be Gefjun of the asa-race. Gefjun goes north to Jotunheim, takes four oxen who are the sons of a giant and herself, and harnesses them to a plow. The plow cuts so hard and deep that it tears a piece of land loose, which the oxen drag westward into the sea until it rests in a sound. Gefjun sets the land there and names it Seeland. The place in Sweden from which the land was removed later becomes the sea called Logrinn, identified with Malar Lake, whose bays correspond to the capes of Seeland. A verse by the old skald Brage is quoted, describing Gefjun drawing excellent land from Gylfe as Denmark's increase, reeking from the running beasts, and noting that the four oxen together bore four heads and eight eyes as they went before the robbed grassy isle. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI.; lines 7038-7122","start":"7038","end":"7122","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Navaho man, Nati'nesthani, is escorted out of the water by the gods Tó`nenili and Hastsézini. As they leave, the frog Tsal calls after them and explains that he and other underwater beings can inflict disease on those who enter their dwelling, but that sacred cigarettes painted specific colors for each being can remove the spell; this practice is said to underlie a current Navaho ritual for curing water sickness after near-drowning. The gods then take Nati'nesthani back to his hollow log. Tó`nenili opens a passage through the river, drains water from the log, and the man crawls inside. The gods seal the log and send it floating down the San Juan River, where it becomes stuck at a waterfall. The Fringe-mouth water beings (Dsahadoldzá) arrive, place their zigzag lightning under the butt of the log like a rope, and free it. The log drifts to a whirling lake at the end of the San Juan River called Tó`nihilin, the End of the Water, surrounded by mountains. The log circles the lake four times, moving gradually toward the center and then toward the shore, finally stranding on the south side. Four gods stand around the log at the cardinal directions—Hastséhogan in the east, Hastséyalti in the south, and a Gánaskidi on the west and on the north. They open the log with their wands, let the Navaho out, retrieve the remaining food, a leafy cedar bow, and two reed arrows from inside, and plug the log again with a black cloud. The gods tell the man they have done all he asked, brought him to the end of the river, and now give him a new name, Áhodiseli, He Who Floats. They have him sit with his back turned, then send him to a hill west of the lake. When he looks, the log is moving back the way it came, the gods have vanished, and he is alone. He feels sad and lonely, regrets insisting on coming yet recognizes it was his own choice, and weeps. The mountains around the lake are steep except on the west side, where he considers crossing. He then hears the gobbling of a turkey four times, each louder and closer, and sees his pet turkey, which he thought lost, approaching from the east. The turkey repeatedly comes near and withdraws while circling him sunwise through the south, west, and north; when it reaches the east again it allows itself to be embraced. He welcomes, pities, and thanks the turkey for following him. Night falls suddenly, forcing them to seek shelter in a nearby gulch with small cedar trees. They make a bed of dead leaves and soft debris and lie down side by side. GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9767-9864","start":"9767","end":"9864","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic notes explain several Navaho mythic and ritual elements. Rainbows can form bridges or trails created by deities like Hastséyalti, who once made a rainbow bridge for a hero; a natural stone bridge is believed to be a transformed rainbow. Spiders in Arizona are mostly ground-dwelling. Four yucca species are named with their Navaho and botanical names; they are ritually important—for games, initiation flogging, mask-making, drumsticks—and practical uses such as cleansing (due to saponin) and fiber, with one species providing edible fruit. Cane cactus is identified botanically. The title Tsiké Sas Nátlehi means Maid Who Becomes a Bear; multiple such bear-maidens are believed to exist, now dwelling at the hill of Tsúskai, with later bear-maidens seen as less malevolent and invoked by the sick. One story implies that great misfortune, not only death, can render a house haunted or evil. A note clarifies that only a particular group is being traced; other bands of Diné survived divine wrath and later joined as a holy or mystic people, diné digíni. Gods and favored men travel swiftly on miraculous ‘holy trails’ made of rainbows, sunbeams, and lightning, even using sunbeams as aerial rafts. Another note directs readers to compare this account with the creation of First Man and First Woman. Es-tsá-na-tle-hi is said not to be represented by masked performers or sand-paintings. A detailed version of her origin relates that First Man and First Woman were living around the sacred mountain Dsilnáotil when a black cloud descended on the mountain Tsolíhi for four days. First Woman circled the mountain four times and found a female infant on its summit, daughter of Earth Mother (Naestsán) and Sky Father (Yádilyil). When lifted, the infant cried until brought to Dsilnáotil, where Salt Woman wanted her. The sun is believed to have fed the infant with pollen; in twelve days she became a big girl, and in eighteen days a woman, after which a nubile ceremony with twelve songs was held. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l907-l998","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INDEX                                          291 / THE YOUNGER EDDA. / INTRODUCTION. / FOREWORD.; lines 907-998","start":"907","end":"998","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives a pseudo-historical genealogy linking the Norse gods and European royal dynasties to Trojan and Asiatic ancestors. It traces descent from Jupiter through Dardanos and other sons to Priamos and his famous son Hektor, describing the near invincibility of the Trojans and the Romans’ later adoption of Trojan titles, customs, and laws. It then narrates how, during Pompey’s eastern campaigns, Odin fled Asia to the north and claimed that Priamos had borne his name Odin and his queen Frigg, with their realm called Frigia. A further genealogy is given from a Trojan king Munon/Mennon and Priamos’ daughter Troan to their son Tror (Thor), his fosterage in Thrace, his prodigious strength, slaying of his foster-father Loricos and monsters including a dragon, and his marriage to the golden-haired prophetess Sibyl (Sif). Their descendants culminate in Vodin (Odin), noted for wisdom, and his wife Frigida (Frigg). Odin and his wife possess divination and Odin foresees his renown in the northern world, prompting him to depart from Turkey with many people and treasures. As he travels, he and his followers are regarded as godlike. He settles in Saxland, subjugates the land, and installs his three sons as rulers, whose lines produce Hengist, Svipdag, and the Volsungs, among others. Continuing north, Odin conquers Reidgotaland, establishing his son Skjold as ancestor of the Danish Skjoldung kings, and moves to Svithjod (Sweden), where King Gylfe offers him whatever he desires. Wherever the Asiamen (asas) stay, crops and peace flourish, and they are seen as superior in beauty and understanding. Odin chooses Sigtuna for his burg, sets up chiefs, appoints twelve law-judges, and shapes rights to correspond with those previously in Troy and among the Turks.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Jupiter is described as having many sons, including Dardanos, Herikon, Tros, Ilos, and Laomedon, famous of all men in the world for strength, stature, accomplishments, and knightly deeds.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The text states that Greeks and forces from the north and east could not defeat the Trojans unless they invoked the gods and that human strength alone could not conquer them without betrayal from within, which later occurred.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"It is said that later men, especially Romans, took titles from Trojan fame and that when Rome was built the Romans adapted their customs and laws as nearly as possible to those of the Trojans, considered their forefathers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"During Pompey’s campaigns harrying the eastern region, Odin is said to have fled out of Asia to the north, giving himself and his men new names and claiming that Priamos had been called Odin and his queen Frigg, with the realm named Frigia.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The narrator notes uncertainty whether Odin made this claim out of pride or through changes of language, Thrudheim.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Thor visits many lands, learns the countries of the world, and single-handedly conquers all berserks, all giants, one very big dragon, and many beasts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the north region Thor finds a prophetess named Sibyl, called Sif, described as the fairest of all women with hair like gold, and marries her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A long genealogical list traces descendants from Thor through Loride, Henrede, Vingethor, Vingener, Moda, Magi, Kesfet, Bedvig, Atra, Itrman, Heremod, Skjaldun, Bjaf, Jat, Gudolf, Fjarlaf to Vodin, called Odin, who is noted as famous for wisdom and accomplishments; his wife Frigida is identified with Frigg.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Odin and his wife are said to have the power of divination, and Odin learns that his name will be held high and honored in the north beyond that of all kings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Because of this foreknowledge, Odin is eager to begin a journey from Turkey, departing with many people of all ages and many costly things and traveling northward.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Wherever Odin’s He invents crafts, practices magic, discovers a red earth substance that yields gold, and presides over an era of abundance in Crete, where only gold money circulates and crops never fail. People come from famine-stricken lands to obtain goods, and the Cretans and Macedonians come to regard Saturn as a god, which the author calls an "error." Saturn himself claims to be God and ruler of heaven and earth.

Saturn later sails to Greece in pursuit of a king’s daughter he loves. He takes on the form of a bull with golden-colored hair to attract her, sheds this form, seizes her, and carries her to Crete. When his wife Juno discovers this, Saturn turns the king’s daughter into a heifer and sends her east to the Nile, where a thrall named Argulos guards her for twelve months before she is restored. The text notes that Saturn performs many similar or greater wonders.

Saturn has three accomplished sons: Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto. Jupiter is depicted as the greatest—a crafty warrior who wins many kingdoms, assumes the likeness of various animals to achieve superhuman feats, and is feared by all nations and "evil wights." Saturn builds seventy-two burgs in Crete and, when secure in his rule, shares his kingdom with his sons, establishing them as gods and assigning Jupiter heaven, Neptune the earth, and Pluto hell. Pluto receives Saturn’s dog Cerberos to guard hell; Greeks say that Herakles later drags Cerberos out of hell onto the earth.

Jupiter, dissatisfied with ruling only heaven, harasses his father’s kingdom, has Saturn captured and emasculated, and declares himself a god for these deeds. Macedonians assert that Saturn’s severed members were thrown into the sea and that from them arose a woman named Venus, counted among the gods and revered as goddess of love, able to turn men’s and women’s hearts toward love.

After his emasculation, Saturn flees west from Crete to Italy. The people there are described as non-working cave- and hole-dwellers living on acorns and grass. text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic and explanatory notes discuss: historical severity of adultery punishments among some Indian tribes versus relatively mild sanctions among the Navahoes and the protected position of Navaho women, as reflected in a legend from the days of Góntso; current and former Navaho ceremonial practices, including temporary and former permanent medicine-lodges, seasonal timing, and reference to a nine-day healing rite called the Mountain Chant whose secret rites culminate in a public nighttime performance inside a circular corral of evergreen branches around a central fire, featuring dancers covered in white earth who perform a sleight-of-hand trick with eagle-down in a show called nahikáï (“it becomes white again”); glosses of place-names such as Tse`-zin-di-aí (Black Rock Standing) and Háltso, discussion of Navaho slavery and its official abolition in 1883, lexical notes on terms like lin and Bi-tá`-ni, identification and description of landmarks such as Sunset Peak and Agathla Needle, and Navaho traditions about kindred northern tribes with related languages, called Diné` Nahotlóni (“Navahoes in Another Place”), whom Navaho travelers once sought out.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Many Indian tribes formerly had various severe punishments for adultery, including mutilations such as nose amputation and even capital punishment.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Among the Navahoes in the author’s time, punishment for adultery rarely exceeds a light whipping, and such punishment is seldom inflicted.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The social position of Navaho women is such that very harsh punishments for adultery would not be tolerated.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In a legend set in the days of Góntso, a husband who was a potent chief did not dare to punish his wives until he had obtained the consent of their relatives.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"For nine-day ceremonies, the Navahoes now build temporary medicine-lodges, usually using them only once.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Navaho ceremonies are rarely performed twice in the same place, have no fixed starting day tied to lunar phases, and many may be held only in the cold months.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Navaho tradition holds that when they once lived in a compact settlement on the banks of the San Juan River, they had permanent medicine-lodges and exact dates for some ceremonies.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Another Navaho ceremony, mentioned elsewhere, is said to have lasted all winter.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Mountain Chant is described as an important Navaho healing ceremony lasting nine days, with rites held secretly in the medicine-lodge until the final night.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"On the last day of the Mountain Chant, just after sunset, a large circular corral of evergreen branches called ilnásdzin (“dark circle of branches”) is built, about forty paces across and eight feet high, with an opening about ten feet wide in the east.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"From about 8 P.M. on the last night of the Mountain Chant until dawn, dances, dramatic shows, medicine rites, and sleight-of-hand tricks are performed in the corral before several hundred spectators of all ages and both sexes, and admission is not restricted.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"In the nahikáï performance, the actors march around very close to a great central fire that gives off intense heat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The performers’ skin is thickly coated with white earth, which probably protects them from being scorched by the fire’s heat.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Each performer carries a short wand with a ball of eagle-down at the tip, burns the ball off in the central fire, and then, using sleight-of-hand, appears to restore the eagle-down to the wand.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After seemingly restoring the eagle-down, the actor rushes out of the corral trumpeting like a sand-hill crane.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The term nahikáï means “it becomes white again” and refers to the The Eagles first consider clothing him in a dress of eagle plumes but abandon the idea and instead lay him face down with crooked and straight lightning, a sunbeam, and a rainbow placed under different parts of his body as supports. Twelve Eagles seize the ends of these supports and fly with him and the eaglets upward, circling as they rise above the cliff and over Tsótsil (Mt. Taylor) until they nearly touch the sky. Exhausted, they complain they can fly no farther; an unseen voice from above tells them to let go their burden. They drop him, but two Arrow-snakes coil around him in midair, carry him through a sky-hole, and set him safely on the surface of an upper world above the sky. There he sees four pueblos: white in the east ruled by Wolf, blue in the south ruled by Blue Fox, yellow in the west ruled by Puma, and black in the north ruled by Big Snake. The Wind whispers that he may visit all except the northern black pueblo, where Chicken Hawk and other bad characters dwell. He observes a war party being prepared; the warriors depart to fight enemies he does not know. In the pueblos he is well treated and fed, and he sees that the Eagles, once home, remove their feather suits, hang them up, and go about like ordinary people in white suits. He visits all pueblos except the northern one. The warriors return amid mourning, for many have been killed. Later a second war party is formed. The Navaho resolves to join them but is repeatedly mocked, warned of his helplessness against their extremely swift enemies, and told to return. Each time he lags behind only to follow again and eventually reach their camp, where he is fed but still discouraged from going. The next morning he again pretends to stay but follows after they depart. On the trail he sees smoke rising from the ground and finds a smoke-hole with a smoke-yellow ladder leading down to a subterranean chamber like those in pueblo houses. Looking down he sees a strange old woman with a large mouth and protruding, claw-like teeth, identified as Spider Woman (Nastsé Estsán). GROWTH OF THE NAVAHO NATION. / NATI'NESTHANI. / NOTES.; lines 9192-9275","start":"9192","end":"9275","translation":"Navaho Legends","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic and mythological notes describe a sacred emergence lake in the San Juan Mountains through which the people came from a former world into this one, surrounded by cliffs, a central island with a ladder-like feature, and four peaks at the cardinal directions. The lake is feared and revered by Navaho people, and several modern lakes are proposed as possible identifications. Variant myth fragments explain how supernatural figures opened surrounding cliffs with a wand or a horn-shaped knife, and how people prayed to four colored Winds corresponding to the four directions, a practice preserved in a ritual wind-song. Other notes contrast the stone-wall building Kisáni with Navaho brush shelters, describe women’s gambling games played with sticks, stones, and a blanket, and recount parts of a flood story: Coyote and Hastsézini steal the young of the water-being Tiéholtsodi, causing rising waters; their guilt is detected by First Man. In restoration variants, enormous shell offerings, shell ornaments, and sacred pollen are given back with the young to Tiéholtsodi, who descends under the earth so that the waters recede through a hole; redistributed pollen brings rain, game, and good fortune. Another note gives differing accounts of the first death: a hermaphrodite called Natliyilhátse (identified by some as the Woman Chief) or, in another version, the wife of a great chief, said to be the chief of devils in the lower world.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A small lake in the San Juan Mountains is said to be the place through which the people came from the fourth world to this world.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The sacred lake is surrounded by precipitous cliffs, has a small island near its center with something that looks like the top of a ladder rising from it, and outside the cliffs stand four mountain peaks to the east, south, west, and north that are often mentioned in Navaho songs and myths; people fear to visit the lake’s shores but climb nearby mountains to view it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The place is called Ha-dzi-naí or Ni-ho-yos-tsá-tse, translated as Place of Emergence or Land Where They Came Up.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Modern lakes such as Trout Lake (San Miguel Lake, regarded as sacred and called Spirit Lake), Island Lake (with a central rocky island), and Silver Lake (surrounded by four high peaks but without an island) are suggested by various observers as possible identifications of the Navaho Place of Emergence.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In one version, Gánaskidi strikes the cliffs with his wand, which sounds “Gong ê'” and breaks the cliffs open.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In another version, a being called He of the darkness of the east cuts the cliffs with a horn-shaped knife to open them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In Version A, people pray to four Winds—the black Wind of the east, blue Wind of the south, yellow Wind of the west, and white Wind of the north—and sing a wind-song that is still used in the rite of hozóni hatál; Version B simply states that they prayed to the four Winds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Kisáni, described as builders of stone houses, erect a stone wall, while others representing the Navahoes build a brushwood shelter, matching current Navaho custom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Tsi-di'l or tsin-di'l is a game played by Navaho women using three sticks thrown ends-down onto a flat stone around which gamblers sit; an overhead blanket prevents the rebounding sticks from flying away, and small stones in a square serve as counters with additional sticks placed between them according to the game’s progress; the rules are not recorded.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Other games named are dilkón (played with two arm-length sticks), atsá (with forked sticks and a ring), and aspi'n.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In Version A of the flood-related story, Coyote and Hastsézini are partners in the theft of the young of Tiéholtsodi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"When Coyote sees the water rising, he points with his protruded lips toward the water and glances significantly at Hastsézini; First Man notices the glance, becomes suspicious, and begins to search.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In one restoration variant, people obtain an enormous haliotis shell, fill it with other shells and precious stones, sprinkle pollen on the young sea monsters and remove some of the now-more-holy pollen, place the young and pollen in the shell, and lay it on the horns of Tiéholtsodi; he then disappears under the earth and the waters go down after him, while the pollen distributed among the people brings rain, game, and good fortune.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In another restoration variant, the young and shell ornaments (“treasures of the sea”) are thrown down to their father; the waters immediately rush down through a hole and away from the lower worlds.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Some sources name the hermaphrodite who died as Natliyilhátse and say that she is now the chief of devils in the lower world, perhaps the same as the Woman Chief mentioned elsewhere; another version says the first to die was the wife of a great chief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Navaho Indians / the people","description":"The people whose myths speak of emerging from a former The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy.; lines 1342-1439","start":"1342","end":"1439","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""Now these twain were spell-bound skin-changers, and wolf-skins were hanging up over them in the house... Sigmund and Sinfjofli do the wolf-skins on them, and then might they nowise come out of them."","summary":"Sigmund judges Sinfjotli too young to help avenge past wrongs and decides to toughen him through violent exploits. They roam the woods killing men for their wealth. Sigmund believes Sinfjotli has both the evil heart of King Siggeir and the strength and daring of the Volsung line, and Sinfjotli often urges him to seek revenge. In the forest they discover a house where two kings' sons, enchanted skin-changers, lie asleep with wolf-skins hanging nearby. Sigmund and Sinfjotli put on the wolf-skins and become unable to remove them, taking on wolf form while retaining human understanding. They agree to hunt separately and to risk fighting at most seven men, using wolf howls as signals.

Sigmund howls when he meets some men, and Sinfjotli comes and kills them. Later Sinfjotli encounters eleven men, kills them all, and rests under an oak. When Sigmund finds him and learns he did not call for help, Sigmund in wolf form bites Sinfjotli in the throat and carries the wounded youth home, cursing the wolf-gear. Sigmund witnesses two weasels: one bites the other, then retrieves a healing leaf that revives its companion. A raven brings Sigmund a similar herb, which he uses to heal Sinfjotli completely. They dwell in an earth-house until they can shed the wolf-shapes, then burn the wolf-skins with fire and pray that no further harm will come from them, having accomplished many deeds in King Siggeir's realm while in that guise.

When Sinfjotli reaches manhood and Sigmund deems him fully tested, he turns again to avenging his father. They leave their earth-house, go to King Siggeir's abode at evening, and hide in the porch among ale-tuns. Queen Signy becomes aware of them, meets them secretly, and they agree that Volsung will be avenged that night. Signy and Siggeir have two small children who play with a golden toy; a golden ring rolls from it into the porch where Sigmund and Sinfjotli are hidden. One child follows, sees the two grim, armed men, and reports this to King Siggeir, who suspects treachery. Overhearing, Signy takes the children out to the porch and tells Sigmund and Sinfjotli that the younglings have betrayed them and should be slain.

Sigmund refuses to kill the children for revealing his hiding-place, but Sinfjotli draws his sword, kills them both, and throws their bodies into the hall at Siggeir's feet. Siggeir gathers his men to seize the intruders. Sigmund and Sinfjotli fight fiercely but are overwhelmed by superior numbers, bound in fetters, and held through the night. The next morning Siggeir, plotting the longest and worst possible death for them, has a large barrow of stones and turf constructed. {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l9656-l9775","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE. / THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG. / THE KING OF THE TOADS.; lines 9656-9775","start":"9656","end":"9775","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A king is ferried by an old man to a mysterious shore; the old man gives him a green twig that will be useful, says the king must return over dry land, and disappears. The king enters a nearby palace, finds it entirely deserted, and concludes it is an enchanted castle. In the last chamber he discovers an old man, bent double on a chair, who welcomes him as the first human face he has seen. This old man reveals that he is a king who has lost his subjects and power, and that another rules in his place because of his wife's treason. He warns the visitor to flee before his wife returns from her lover, the King of the Toads, and kills him. The visiting king refuses to flee and insists on confronting and killing the traitorous queen.

The old king recounts his story: he once ruled a powerful nation, with a great city and a beautiful garden around his palace, but now the city and garden have been turned into a dark forest and a lake. The fish in the lake are his former subjects. He had been happy with his beautiful and kind wife, but the King of the Toads came to the place where the lake now is and turned her heart away from him. Despite his protests and threats, she visited the Toad daily and listened to his sweet talk. Spying on them in a summer-house, the king overheard the King of the Toads promise to find the nest of a magic bird, steal its eggs, and give them to her to eat so that she might become immortal and eternally young. The king sprang from hiding, called the Toad a deceitful serpent, and cut him in two with his sword. The queen wept over the Toad, who miraculously grew together again. The King of the Toads then cursed the king with incomprehensible words, making his blood cold and his veins stiff, froze him to his chair, and laid a spell on the land. Since then the old king has sat there for years, while his wife spends every day with her lover, catching frogs from the lake for him as he continues to promise her immortality and eternal youth.

The visiting king persists in his resolve, draws his sword, and waits for the queen despite the old king's pleas for him to escape. At sunset the queen appears and is surprised to see the stranger with her husband. The king runs at her with his sword, but when the blade touches her clothing it breaks in two. Remembering the green twig given by the boatman, he strikes her three times with it; at the third blow she falls on a seat and becomes motionless, unable even to move her eyes. The old king, encouraged by seeing his wife frozen as he is, suggests that they try to persuade the King of the Toads to free the kingdom and himself from enchantment.

The visiting king decides to impersonate the queen. He dresses in her garments, plans to go to the King of the Toads pretending to be his beloved, and says that if the Toad will not do as he wishes, he will freeze him with the twig and beat him with his sword. The old king urges him to beg first. That night, the disguised king goes in search of the King of the Toads, but cannot find him and must call out. He changes his voice to sound like the queen, deceiving the Toad, who quickly comes and tries to embrace him. The king, still pretending to be the queen, withholds the embrace and demands first that the Toad either kill her husband outright or restore him so he may die, specifically by lifting the spell so that he will fall to dust and ashes. At dawn people think the gleaming castle is on fire, but the princess claims it as her golden castle. The king, delighted, tries to embrace her, saying she is now his, but she refuses, insisting she needs the key to the castle. The king relies on Jalmir again. Guided by his talking steed, Jalmir flies to the island where the castle had stood and, using a whistle given by a fish he once helped, summons the fish. They search the sea, and a small fish finds the key and gives it to the chief fish, who delivers it to Jalmir. Jalmir returns home quickly, gives the key to the king, and then shuts himself alone in his room, distressed by his feelings for the princess.
The king, thinking all is settled, brings the key to the princess, but she now demands the water of death, the water of life, and the water of youth from her island, saying life in the castle would be worthless without them. After consulting some brothers, the king once more asks Jalmir to perform this final service. Jalmir, devoted to the princess, agrees and seeks help again from his steed. Jalmir walks slowly along the dam, constantly thinking of the princess so that the rest of the world seems nothing to him. Suddenly the sea rises and destroys the dam. Jalmir screams and disappears into the water. Hearing his cries but believing he cannot help, the steed moves slowly away. A new tale begins: an old man and his wife have three daughters, the youngest extraordinarily beautiful. When he goes to the fair, the elder daughters ask for fine clothes, but the youngest wants only a red flower. Unable to find one, the father meets an unknown old man who will give the flower only if the youngest daughter is promised to his son, Bright Finist the Falcon. Troubled but persuaded, the father agrees and brings the flower home, explaining the bargain to his youngest, who reveals she already knows and loves Bright Finist, a falcon in the sky and a heroic youth on earth. That night she places the flower in water and opens her window; Finist arrives as a falcon, transforms into a young man, spends the night talking with her, and gives her a feather from his wing that, when waved to the right, will provide any finery she desires. He departs as a falcon and thereafter comes nightly when the flower is set on the window. On Sundays, while her elder sisters go to Mass, the youngest uses the feather to conjure a crystal carriage, spirited horses, servants, and splendid robes, appearing at church as an unknown beauty whom people take for a Tsar’s daughter. After the service she vanishes home and dismisses the magic with a wave of the feather to the left. This continues for three Sundays, but on the third she forgets to remove a diamond pin from her hair, and her sisters notice it, recognizing it as the ornament worn by the mysterious church beauty and demanding to know where she got it.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Tsar rejoices, keeps the horse for himself, gives his daughter daughters.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The youngest daughter is described as so beautiful that her beauty cannot be adequately told or written.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Before going to the fair, the father asks each daughter what she wants him to buy: the eldest requests a new dress, the second a shawl kerchief, and the youngest a red flower.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The father laughs at the youngest daughter’s request for a red flower and suggests he would rather buy her clothes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Despite her father’s attempts to persuade her otherwise, the youngest insists that he buy her only a little red flower.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"At the fair the father buys a dress for the eldest and a shawl for the second daughter, but he cannot find a red flower in the whole town.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"On his way home the father meets an unknown old man holding a red flower and asks to buy daughter tells her father not to worry and describes Bright Finist as good and kind, a bright falcon in the sky and a heroic youth when he touches the earth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The youngest explains that she already knows Bright Finist; he was at Mass the previous Sunday, looked at her constantly, spoke with her, and loves her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The father questions his daughter, makes the sign of the cross over her, and sends her to her room, saying they will discuss the matter in the morning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In her room the youngest daughter puts the red flower in water, opens the window, and looks into the distance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Bright Finist appears as a falcon outside, wheels before her, flies in through the window, strikes the floor, and becomes a young man; she is frightened at first but feels joy and ease when he speaks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"They talk together until dawn, and Bright Finist tells her he will come every night whenever the bright little flower is placed on the window; he gives her a feather from his wing and instructs her that if she waves it on the right side she will instantly receive whatever robes she desires.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"At daybreak Bright Finist kisses the maiden, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l12240-l12278","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE CUIRASSIER AND THE HORNED PRINCESS. / THE TREACHEROUS BROTHERS. / MAGYAR MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE POOR MAN, AND THE KING OF THE CROWS.; lines 12240-12278","start":"12240","end":"12278","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A poor man asks the king about the contents of a great letter the king has just received. The king explains that the Turk-Tartar is advancing on the country with a cruel army that destroys property and massacres innocent, weeping people, whose blood soaks the earth and whose flesh is eaten by dogs. The poor man asks what reward will be given to whoever drives the enemy out; the king promises great honor, marriage between the rescuer’s two sons and the king’s two daughters, half the kingdom, and eventual inheritance of the whole kingdom after the king’s death. The poor man vows to drive out the enemy alone. Although the king gathers his soldiers and marches against the Turk-Tartar, the poor man goes between the two camps, commands his club to strike, and the club beats the enemy army until only one man survives to carry home the news. The poor man receives half the kingdom and the two princesses, whom he marries to his two stalwart sons, and they celebrate a wedding said to speak to the seven worlds.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The poor man stands forth before the king and asks permission to pose a question.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The poor man asks the king to tell him the contents of the great letter the king has just received.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The king replies that the poor man could not mend the affair described in the letter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The poor man responds, asking what if he can mend the affair.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The king explains that the letter says the Turk-Tartar is moving on their country with a great army, cruelly destroying man asks what reward will be given to the one who drives the enemy out of the country.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The king promises that great reward and death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The poor man declares that he will drive out the enemy all Once they have crossed the boundary of the sorceress’s lands, the steed orders Jalmir to release the bird from its cage. Jalmir obeys, and they reach home by night. At dawn, the king’s garden is filled with wonderfully singing birds, astonishing everyone. A brother reminds the king that he had sent Jalmir for the birds; the king has Jalmir brought to him, embraces him joyfully, and Jalmir becomes very dear to him, which increases his brothers’ hatred. The brothers consult books in a special chamber and discover that the king has no beasts, which cost more than birds. Maliciously, they suggest to the king that Jalmir can procure beasts as well, and the king commands Jalmir to get them. Jalmir is bewildered, but the white steed comforts him and tells him to come in the evening. That night the steed flies with him through the air back to the sorceress’s castle. Jalmir fears being caught, but the horse instructs him: in the first three chambers are magnificent chained beasts with silver, golden, and pearl hair and chains, which he must not touch or else a blow will shake the castle and the sorceress will seize and kill him; instead he must go to the fourth chamber, seize an ugly dog tied with a ragged rope, and run back. Jalmir timidly but carefully passes the first three chambers, shielding his eyes from the glitter, breaks the dog’s rope in the fourth, takes it in his arms, and escapes on the horse. The sorceress rushes out, again cursing him and shouting that he will return. After they cross the boundary of her lands, the steed tells Jalmir to release the dog, and he promptly does so. By dawn they are home. Soon there is a great noise in and around the town as if the earth were breaking; looking from his window, the king sees that his garden is full of deer, stags, rabbits, squirrels, mice, and countless other beasts. The animals thrive in the royal garden, but people in and outside the town try to kill and stone them, which displeases the king. He decrees that all beasts belong to him and must not be harmed, then goes to Jalmir, thanks him warmly, and embraces him. The whole kingdom rejoices in the beasts, but the brothers, frustrated that Jalmir is in even greater favor, again consult the books. They read that the king has no wine, which costs him money, and decide Jalmir should fetch it, remarking that he will need luck from hell to return. He carries her to a green oak in an open field where Ivan Tsarevich waits, then bears them swiftly toward the kingdom of Tsar Afron, outrunning all pursuers. During the ride Ivan and Yelena fall deeply in love, but Ivan must surrender her to Tsar Afron in exchange for the golden‑maned steed and weeps at the prospect. The Gray Wolf proposes a plan: he will transform himself into Yelena’s exact likeness so that Ivan can deliver the false princess to Afron, obtain the steed, and later recover the Wolf. Striking the damp earth, the Wolf becomes indistinguishable from Yelena; Ivan leaves the real princess outside the town, brings the disguised Wolf to Tsar Afron, and receives the golden‑maned steed. Tsar Afron rejoices in his supposed bride. The Wolf lives with him three days, then asks leave to walk in the open field to ease his sorrow. Afron agrees and sends nurses, maidens, and court ladies to accompany the ‘princess.’ Meanwhile Ivan rides with the real Yelena and forgets the Wolf until he suddenly remembers, at which point the Wolf appears, tells Ivan to mount him, and has Yelena ride the golden‑maned steed. They travel toward the kingdom of Tsar Dolmat. Near the capital, Ivan, reluctant to part with the steed he has just acquired, begs the Wolf for one more service: to transform into a golden‑maned steed so Ivan can give that steed to Tsar Dolmat. The Wolf again strikes the damp earth and becomes a golden‑maned steed. Ivan leaves Yelena in a green meadow, rides the disguised Wolf to Dolmat’s palace, and is joyfully received. After two days of feasting, Tsar Dolmat gives Ivan the Fire‑bird in its golden cage along with the golden‑maned steed. Ivan then departs, rejoins Yelena outside the town, and sets off toward his homeland. The next day Tsar Dolmat goes to ride his new steed in the open field; the horse throws him, turns back into the Gray Wolf, and runs to catch up with Ivan. On his journey he feeds various herdsmen. In a wild forest he commands the mill, and a table appears set for two; a great fat man appears, already knowing the mill's powers. The stranger offers to trade a knotty club—capable of killing any person the owner has in mind when commanded—for the mill. Fearing robbery, the poor man accepts, then quietly orders the club to strike the fat man, who dies instantly. After travelling for seven years, the poor man returns home. His wife, who has been mourning him and their two lean cows, and his now-grown sons scarcely recognize him until he sets down the mill and removes his mantle. His wife angrily dismisses the mill as useless and scolds him for his long absence, but he insists it is better than nothing and could be used to grind for others. When she complains of having nothing to eat, he commands the mill, and an overabundant feast of meat and drink appears. The wife regrets her harsh words; the family eats and drinks, and the sons feel like dancing. When the elder son wishes for a gypsy musician, a band of gypsies instantly appears by the chimney and plays lively music; the family dances. Neighbors, surprised by the music in a poor man's house, gather and see the gypsies playing, the laden table, and the family dancing. The poor man invites neighbors and kin inside, and guests keep arriving while the table continues to be spread. Seeing that his small cabin cannot contain all the guests, he remarks that it is a pity his house is not larger, and immediately the cabin becomes a magnificent palace with twelve chambers in a row. A king and his nobles, out walking nearby, notice that a poor man's cabin has been replaced by a kingly palace with music sounding, and they decide to investigate. The king leads them in; the poor man warmly receives them and seats them at the head of the table. They feast and revel like at a small wedding. While they are enjoying themselves, a sealed letter arrives to the king, reporting that the Turk-Tartar is approaching with a great army, devastating his kingdom with fire and sword, slaughtering innocent, weeping people so that the earth drinks their blood and dogs devour their flesh. Drunk, Hrungner boasted he would seize Valhalla, destroy Asgard, and abduct Freyja and Sif. Thor arrived, confronted Hrungner, and accepted his challenge to a duel at the boundary place Grjottungard. The giants, fearing Thor, created a clay giant, Mokkerkalfe, to support Hrungner, who armed himself with stone shield, stone head and heart, and a flint weapon. At the duel, Thor’s companion Thjalfe tricked Hrungner into changing his stance; Thor hurled his hammer as Hrungner threw his flint-stone. Their collision created flint-mountains, and a fragment lodged in Thor’s head, but Mjolner shattered Hrungner’s skull and he collapsed on top of Thor. Thjalfe slew Mokkerkalfe. The gods could not move Hrungner’s foot from Thor until Thor’s three-night-old son Magne lifted it and claimed he could have killed the giant himself. Thor rewarded Magne with Hrungner’s horse Goldfax, drawing Odin’s criticism. The king offers to buy the cows for double price because his army has not eaten for three days, but the poor man refuses money and instead asks that the king return a cow for a cow. The King of the Crows agrees, promising four cows for the two and telling the man to find his black castle in the north. The king then vanishes, and later the crow army appears like a black cloud, cawing as they descend to tear the two cows to pieces before flying away. The poor man watches the direction they take, then goes home sadly, says farewell to his two sons and his wife in tears, and sets out to find the black castle.\nHe journeys over forty-nine kingdoms, beyond the Operentsia Sea, the glass mountains, and further strange regions, until he reaches an immense sandy desert where there are no settlements, his provisions are exhausted, and his gourd bottle is dry. After confirming his identity, they also feed him meat stew, offer rest on a sheepskin, refill his bag and bottle, wish him well, and direct him onward. Sigurd digs a ditch in Fafner's path, spears him from below as he crawls to water, and kills him. At Regin's demand Sigurd cuts out Fafner's heart and roasts it; Regin drinks Fafner's blood and sleeps. When Sigurd tests the cooking heart, its fat burns his finger and he puts it in his mouth, so the heart-blood touches his tongue and he understands bird speech. Eagles in a tree advise him to eat the heart and warn that Regin plans to deceive and kill him. Sigurd then kills Regin, mounts his horse Grane, takes Fafner's gold from the dragon's bed, packs it on Grane, and rides away; the narrator notes that this explains poetic names for gold as Fafner's bed, the metal of Gnita-heath, or Grane's burden. Sigurd later finds a house on a mountain where an armored woman sleeps; he cuts off her mail-coat, waking her. She calls herself Hild, named Brynhild, a valkyrie. Sigurd then stays long with King Gjuke and Queen Grimhild; he marries their daughter Gudrun, and Gjuke's sons Gunnar and Hogne swear brotherhood with him. Sigurd and Gjuke's sons go to King Atle to ask for his sister Brynhild as wife for Gunnar. Brynhild sits on Hindfell, in a hall encircled by the bickering flame Vafurloge, and has vowed to wed only the man who rides through the fire. Gunnar's horse Gote refuses the flames, so Sigurd and Gunnar exchange form and weapons, since Grane will not carry any but Sigurd. In Gunnar's guise Sigurd rides Grane through the fire and that evening holds a wedding with Brynhild, but he places Gram unsheathed between them in bed. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l506-l601","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / CHEKH MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / MAGYAR MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / INTRODUCTION.; lines 506-601","start":"506","end":"601","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Curtin discusses Morning-star myths, noting that Delawares and Modocs, like Latins, see the Morning-star as a Light-bearer. He contrasts this with a myth of stars struggling with the sun, and a later combined form where the Morning-star becomes a rebel against the sun. This physical astral myth is then moralized and provides material for Milton’s Paradise Lost. Curtin remarks that the current American Morning-star myth parallels Aryan mythology as far as the non-Aryan tribes of America have developed it. He explains his view that mythic heroes were originally personified forces of nature whose human naming obscures their non-human origin and accounts for their superhuman deeds. To illustrate, he recounts an Indian myth from eastern Oregon and Washington in which two families of winds (five Northeast brothers with a cruel sister and five Southwest brothers with elderly grandparents and an in-married wife from the Southern seas) contend. The Northeast winds win a lethal wrestling match, behead the Southwest brothers, and oppress both people and the aged grandparents. Later, a posthumous son of the slain eldest Southwest brother is born in the Southern seas, grows to full strength in three weeks, and, upon learning of his fathers’ deaths, travels via the Columbia River to the ancestral land. Displaying immense strength by uprooting trees and overturning cliffs, he kills the abusive Northeast sister and defeats and beheads the five Northeast brothers. The land rejoices, suffering ceases, and the youthful hero rules happily; Curtin concludes that knowing the characters are winds confirms the story’s truth as a nature-myth.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Delawares on the Atlantic and Modocs near the Pacific share a belief that the Morning-star is the Light-bearer, as do the Latins.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"An opposite view produces a myth of the stars struggling with the sun for possession of the sky.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Combining the Light-bearer Morning-star myth with the star–sun struggle yields a third myth in which the Morning-star becomes not just an opponent but a rebel, later reinterpreted as a moral drama and used by Milton in Paradise Lost.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Curtin states that the present American Morning-star myth shows complete parallelism with Aryan mythology up to the highest point reached by non-Aryan tribes of America.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Curt

She says the hairs have wondrous power and gives them to the prince along with a latch-string, instructing him to climb a terribly high mountain that supports the heavens and, at its summit, to strike the hairs three times with the latch-string to summon a magic steed raised on a silken meadow, fed on dragon's milk, glowing coals, and fiery flames. The prince thanks her, climbs the great mountain, and performs the ritual; a fiery cloud rushes toward him with loud rumbling, triple neighing shakes the earth, and the magic steed appears. The latch-string transforms into an ornate saddle. The steed offers to travel as fast as whirlwind, thought, or bird, and explains that because dense darkness reigns on certain islands, they must first go to the bright antechamber of the Sun to take a burning ray. Rising through the airy heavens, they journey across forty-nine kingdoms to the portals of the earth, where two bearded wolves demand a toll of two pounds of flesh from the steed. To avoid weakening his mount, the prince cuts two pounds of flesh from his own body and throws it to the wolves, who then let them pass. They reach the Sun's bright antechamber; the prince ties his steed to a diamond pillar, bathes in fire and uses fire-towels, examines himself in the shining wall, and combs his hair with a golden comb. A subject-spirit serving the Sun becomes angry and, with a powerful breath, blows the prince so far that he does not feel ground under his feet for seventy-seven miles. He falls into a terribly dark opening and gropes through a cavern, stepping on serpents and toads and seeing red-eyed worms. He hears seething water and the pounding of iron hammers at the place where thunderbolts are made. Coming to a great iron gate guarded by a hundred-headed dragon who lets no one pass, the prince plays a sweet, sorrowful tune on his magic flute.
