{"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l2180-l2298","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON.; lines 2180-2298","start":"2180","end":"2298","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The youngest sister, a beautiful maiden, secretly receives visits from Bright Finist the Falcon. Her elder sisters spy on her, overhear her conversation with him, and see him leap from the window and fly away. Out of malice they place hidden knives across the window so that he will cut his wings. That night, unaware of the trap, the maiden lays a red flower on the window and falls asleep. Bright Finist flies to the window, is wounded on the knives, and departs angrily beyond the dark forest while she sleeps. In the morning she finds the crossed knives, blood dripping onto her flower, and realizes he is gone. She weeps, keeps sleepless vigils at the window, and waves his bright feather, but he no longer comes or sends servants.

Finally she seeks her father’s blessing and has three pairs of iron shoes, three iron caps, three iron staffs, and three iron Easter cakes forged. She arms herself with one set and sets out in the direction Bright Finist flew. Traveling through slumbering, darkening forests over stumps and logs, she wears out the first set of iron gear.

She comes to an iron hut on hen’s legs that turns constantly. Commanding it to stand with its back to the forest and front to her, she enters and finds a huge Baba-Yaga lying from corner to corner. Baba-Yaga smells the presence of “Russia” and asks where she is going, whether fleeing from labor or seeking it. The maiden addresses her as grandmother and says she once had Bright Finist the Falcon of Flowery Feathers, whom her sisters harmed, and now she seeks him. Baba-Yaga says the maiden must pass thrice nine lands; Bright Finist lives in the fiftieth kingdom in the eightieth land and is betrothed to a Tsar’s daughter. Baba-Yaga feeds her, lets her sleep, and at dawn gives her a small golden hammer and ten little diamond nails, instructing her that when she reaches the blue sea and Bright Finist’s bride walks on the shore, she must drive the nails with the hammer. The bride will try to buy them, but the maiden must take no payment, asking only to see Bright Finist. Baba-Yaga sends her on to a second sister.

The maiden continues through darker, deeper forest; a second set of iron shoes, cap, staff, and cake are nearly worn away. She reaches another iron hut on hen’s legs, commands it to turn its back to the trees and front to her so she may enter and eat, and finds another Baba-Yaga. After the same formula of smelling “Russia” and asking her destination, the maiden says she seeks Bright Finist the Falcon. This Baba-Yaga tells her that Bright Finist is going to marry and that the maiden’s party is that night. She likewise feeds and lodges the girl, then at daybreak gives her a golden plate with a diamond ball, instructing her to roll the ball on the plate at the blue sea, where Bright Finist’s bride will try to buy it; again, the maiden must accept no payment but only ask to see Bright Finist. She sends her on to her eldest sister.

The maiden goes farther into the dark, deep forest, wearing out her third set of iron gear, and comes to a third iron hut on hen’s legs, turning about. She commands it to stand with its back to the trees and face to her so she can enter and eat bread. Inside lies another immense Baba-Yaga, who smells “Russia” and asks where she is going. Ivan returns to the Pearl Kingdom, takes his mother, and then visits the Golden, Silver, and Copper Kingdoms, taking their Tsaritsas; each kingdom turns into a ball and rolls after him. At a rope swing he calls his brothers with a golden trumpet. The brothers haul up, in turn, the Tsaritsas of the Copper, Silver, and Golden Kingdoms, quarreling over each, then their mother. When Ivan is being raised, they cut the rope, and he falls into a great depth, lying senseless for half a year. On reviving, he strikes the earth with the feather staff; twelve youths appear and carry him back to the free world. He learns that his brothers have married the Tsaritsas of the Copper and Silver Kingdoms. His destined bride, the Tsaritsa of the Golden Kingdom, refuses to marry anyone, while his aged father the Tsar wishes to wed her. The Tsar has his own wife executed on charges of intimacy with evil spirits, then proposes to the Golden Tsaritsa. She delays by demanding shoes and then robes made to fit her without any measuring. Ivan, living incognito as a workman with an old man, secretly fulfills both tasks by producing shoes and garments from the Golden Kingdom, using leather and cloth given by the Tsar. Finally, the Tsaritsa demands that the old man’s “son” be boiled in milk. A huge cauldron of milk is prepared over a hot fire; Ivan throws himself in and emerges transformed into an indescribably beautiful youth. The Tsar, hoping for the same result, jumps into the cauldron and is boiled to death. The elder son marries the elder sister of the Reed Maiden, while the younger son refuses any ordinary bride and insists on marrying the most beautiful maiden in the world. While hunting, the younger persuades his elder brother to ask his wife whether anyone more beautiful than she exists. The wife remains silent in front of the younger brother but later, in private, reveals that she has a younger sister, the world-beautiful Reed Maiden, hidden inside the middle of three reeds on the seventy-seventh island of the Black Sea. The island is shrouded in darkness and the reeds are guarded by a witch whose life will end if the reeds are cut; whoever brings the maiden away will light the islands and gain a wife admired even by the stars. The younger prince overhears this, secretly leaves, saddles his best horse, and journeys over forty-nine kingdoms and beyond the Operentsia Sea. In a strange land where even birds do not go, he meets three old women in successive huts. Each threatens to eat him but relents when he calls her \"old mother\"; they guide him onward by sending animal servants—a mouse and a dove-white squirrel—to show the roads. {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l8048-l8172","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YELENA THE WISE. / THE SEVEN SIMEONS, FULL BROTHERS. / THE ENCHANTED PRINCESS. / VASSILISSA THE CUNNING AND THE TSAR OF THE SEA.; lines 8048-8172","start":"8048","end":"8172","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In the Tsar of the Sea’s palace, Ivan the merchant’s son serves in the kitchen. The cook Chumichka, who dislikes him, falsely claims that Ivan boasts he can in one night clear a dense forest, cultivate it, harvest wheat, and bake cakes for the Tsar’s breakfast. The Tsar orders Ivan to perform this impossible task under threat of decapitation. Grieving, Ivan is approached by the Tsar’s daughter, Vassilissa the Cunning, who advises him to pray and sleep, saying the morning is wiser than the evening. At midnight she goes onto the great porch and cries out; countless laborers appear, perform all the work from felling trees to baking cakes, and by daybreak Ivan brings the cakes to the Tsar, who praises him and orders him rewarded.

Chumichka again maligns Ivan, saying he boasts he can build in one night a ship that will fly through the air. The Tsar repeats the lethal ultimatum. Vassilissa again reassures Ivan, and at midnight her cry summons carpenters who quickly build the flying ship. The Tsar calls Ivan a hero and proposes a trip; he, Ivan, and Chumichka fly in the ship. When they pass over a place of wild beasts, Chumichka leans over the side to look down and Ivan pushes him off; the beasts tear him to pieces. Ivan calls out that Chumichka has fallen, and the Tsar replies that such a one deserves a dog’s death. On returning, the Tsar sets a third task: Ivan must break an unridden stallion, and if he succeeds he will marry the Tsar’s daughter; if not, he will be executed.

Ivan initially thinks this easy, but Vassilissa warns that the stallion will actually be the Tsar himself, who will carry Ivan through the air above the forest and below the clouds to destroy him. She instructs Ivan to have blacksmiths forge an iron hammer three poods in weight and to beat the stallion’s head while riding. The next day the grooms bring out the wild stallion, barely able to hold it. Once Ivan mounts, the horse rises above the forest and flies below the clouds. Ivan clings tightly and strikes its head with the heavy hammer until the stallion collapses to the earth. Ivan returns to the palace, where the Tsar meets him with his head bound, complaining of pain but promising that Ivan may choose a bride the next day.

The following morning, Vassilissa explains that she and her two sisters will be transformed by their father and that Ivan must recognize her. First they will appear as mares, among which her bridle will have one dim spangle. Then they will be doves: her sisters will quietly pick buckwheat, but she will flap her wings. Finally they will appear as three maidens identical in face, stature, and hair; Vassilissa will signal him by shaking her There the youngest has them hide underneath, predicting the arrival of the steed of the moon and a twelve-headed dragon from whose saddle-bow the bright moon dangles. A milk-white steed of the moon carrying the twelve-headed dragon arrives and stumbles, prompting the dragon to curse the horse and mention the famed Kiss Miklos. The youngest brother, revealed as Kiss Miklos, springs onto the silver bridge on his golden-haired magic steed, grapples with the dragon, and orders his rusty sword to cut; the sword shears off the dragon's heads until all twelve are severed and the dragon dies. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l2300-l2437","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON.; lines 2300-2437","start":"2300","end":"2437","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A maiden seeking Bright Finist the Falcon learns he has married a Tsar’s daughter. Given a swift steed, she rides through a thinning forest to the blue sea and sees the shining golden summits and white-walled chambers of Finist’s kingdom. On three successive days she sits by the shore with wondrous items: first diamond nails and a golden hammer, then a diamond ball and golden plate, and finally a steed that eats glowing coals. Each time, the Tsar’s daughter, Finist’s current wife, wishes to buy the marvels, and the maiden offers them freely in exchange for a chance to look at Finist. The Tsar’s daughter repeatedly uses a magic pin to plunge Finist into deep sleep before allowing the maiden into the palace, so the maiden can only weep over him without waking him. On the third visit, while the maiden is looking in Finist’s head, the pin falls out and he wakes, rejoices at seeing her, and hears of her sisters’ envy, her wanderings, and her bargain with the Tsar’s daughter. He convenes boyars, princes, and people of all degrees to judge whether he should remain with the wife who sold him or the one who bought him. They unanimously choose the one who bought him and condemn the seller to be hanged on the gate and shot, which Finist carries out.\n\nA new tale follows. A Tsar has a daughter, Tsarevna Priceless Beauty, whose hand and half his kingdom he offers to anyone, regardless of birth, who can kiss her through twelve windows. A merchant with three sons lives in this kingdom; the two elder are crafty and the youngest is a simpleton. The elder brothers decide to try for the Tsarevna, take the best horses, and mock the simpleton when he prepares to go as well. After they depart, the simpleton follows on a poor, mangy horse, then in a field summons a splendid steed by an incantation. Crawling into one ear of the steed and out the other, he becomes an extraordinarily handsome hero and rides to the Tsar’s palace, breaking six panes of glass with his arrival. Onlookers cry out to seize him, but he escapes, reverses the transformation in the field, and returns home to lie on the stove. His brothers tell their father about the unknown hero, and the simpleton claims it was he, but they mock him. The next day they all prepare again, and the simpleton once more goes to the field and calls the magical steed.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A maiden is told that Bright Finist the Falcon has married a Tsar’s daughter, is given a swift steed, rides through a thinning forest, and comes to a blue sea before a kingdom with golden summits and lofty white-walled chambers identified as Finist’s realm.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Sitting on the movable sand of the seashore, the maiden hammers diamond nails with a golden hammer until the Tsar’s daughter, walking with her nurses, maidens, and serving-women, stops and wants to buy the nails and hammer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The maiden offers the diamond nails and golden hammer for free if she may look at Bright Finist the Falcon; Finist wakes immediately, rejoices to see her, hears how her sisters envied her, how she wandered, and how she exchanged with the Tsar’s daughter, and he loves her more than before and kisses her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Bright Finist the Falcon summons boyars, princes, and people of every degree and asks whether he should live with the wife who sold him or the one who bought him; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l5180-l5299","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE THREE KINGDOMS. / VASSILISSA GOLDEN TRESS, BAREHEADED BEAUTY. / THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS. / THE FOOTLESS AND THE BLIND.; lines 5180-5299","start":"5180","end":"5299","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Nikita warns the terrible Tsar that his bride, Yelena the Beautiful, will test his strength on the first three wedding nights by pressing on his chest so strongly he cannot endure it. He advises the Tsar to flee the bedchamber each time so Nikita can secretly take his place and \"tame\" her. At the wedding, Yelena nearly crushes the Tsar before he makes an excuse to leave and swap places with Nikita. Yelena, thinking Nikita is the Tsar, cannot overpower him; he seizes her and hurls her to the floor so hard the castle shakes. With this trick repeated for three nights, the Tsar is then able to live peacefully with Yelena. Later Yelena discovers that the Tsar deceived her, that he is weak, and that Nikita was the one who subdued her. Enraged, she conceals thoughts of revenge. When the Tsar decides to sail home with Yelena and a ship full of valuables, Nikita falls into a twelve-day heroic sleep. Taking advantage of this, Yelena orders her servants to cut off Nikita's legs at the knee, place him in a boat, and cast him adrift at sea. He awakens on the thirteenth day, legless and surrounded by water. Meanwhile the Tsar returns to his kingdom, is welcomed with honors, and forgets Nikita. Yelena soon seizes control of the realm, forces the Tsar to herd pigs, and orders that Nikita's relatives be sought out and punished. Messengers find Nikita's brother Timoféi, whom Yelena has blinded and driven out. Wandering by touch, Timoféi reaches the seashore and hesitates at the water's edge. Nikita's boat drifts to the same shore; the footless Nikita calls for help, and the blind Timoféi explains he cannot see. They learn they are brothers and that Yelena blinded Timoféi. Nikita instructs Timoféi to find and uproot a tall oak and lay it into the water as a bridge. Despite his blindness, Timoféi tears up the oak by the roots and places it so Nikita can climb ashore. Reunited, they embrace, and Timoféi tells Nikita that the Tsar now herds pigs and daily receives only bread, water, and a beating. The brothers then agree that Timoféi will carry Nikita, who will guide him, so that together, though both maimed, they will function as one whole content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l14963-l15060","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MIRKO, THE KING'S SON. / THE REED MAIDEN. / KISS MIKLOS, AND THE GREEN DAUGHTER OF THE GREEN KING. / THE HEDGEHOG, THE MERCHANT, THE KING, AND THE POOR MAN.; lines 14963-15060","start":"14963","end":"15060","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A king's son chooses the most beautiful place in his kingdom, thinks once, and a copper-roofed marble palace turning on a cock's foot appears, filled with golden furnishings. He leads a beautiful golden bird—the fair princess—into this palace and they live in harmony. When the merchant's three daughters and the two elder princesses learn how happily the youngest princess has married, several in their despair kill themselves. The merchant's second daughter, however, resolves to ruin the youngest princess's happiness, goes to the palace disguised as an old woman, and enters service. At this time the Burkus king declares war, and while the king's son is away in the field, the Lord gives the princess two beautiful children. The old woman packs the infants in a basket, leaves them under a tree in the woods, and tells the recovering princess that the babies were monstrous and have been thrown into the river. The children sleep under the tree until a white deer bursts from the thicket, hangs the basket on his antlers, and carries it to a stream, calling three times. The Forest Maiden appears, takes the basket to her own palace, and raises the children for seven years as if they were her own. One day she sends the little girl with a green jug to a well, warning her not to break it; the girl tries to catch a little golden bird flying around the well and breaks the jug. The Forest Maiden then sends the little boy with another jug; he tries to strike the golden bird with it and also breaks it, and both children sit crying at the well. The golden bird asks why they weep, and the boy explains they fear a beating from their mother for breaking the jugs. The bird tells them that the Forest Maiden is only their foster-mother, that their true parents live far away beyond green mountains, and offers to lead them home. The children follow the bird and do not return. Journeying through the forest, they find a great heap of gold with dice nearby and each takes a handful of gold. Later they come to an inn at evening, where three lords are playing dice. The boy plays with his gold and wins all the lords’ money. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l5432-l5581","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE THREE KINGDOMS. / VASSILISSA GOLDEN TRESS, BAREHEADED BEAUTY. / THE RING WITH TWELVE SCREWS. / THE FOOTLESS AND THE BLIND.; lines 5432-5581","start":"5432","end":"5581","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"My death is in the broom which lies around at the threshold.\"","summary":"Bulat the hero uses a ruse of speaking for the silent Vassilissa and bringing her food from Ivan Tsarevich to induce her to unlock a cupboard; he then seizes her from a tower, seats her on Ivan’s steed, and they flee. Tsar Kirbít discovers his daughter’s disappearance and sends pursuers, whom Bulat twice destroys by pretending to have lost a treasured ring and a handkerchief so he can ride back and ambush them. While the three camp at night, Ivan fails to keep watch and Koshchéi Without-Death carries off Vassilissa, prompting Bulat and Ivan to search for her. They track Koshchéi’s herd, kill his shepherds, disguise themselves in their clothes, and drive the herd to his house. Using a gold ring Vassilissa had given Ivan and a vessel of milk from Vassilissa’s goat, Bulat signals their presence to her, and she secretly welcomes and feeds them. At Bulat’s urging, she hides them and then coaxes Koshchéi, on his return from hunting, to boast of his invulnerability and to state that his death lies in a broom at the threshold, a report she carries back to the hidden heroes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Vassilissa is frightened and sits in silence while Bulat the hero speaks as if answering in her voice, telling himself to take the key, open the cupboard, drink vodka, and go.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Bulat goes to Ivan Tsarevich and asks for a duck and later a goose; Ivan cuts off a wing from each bird and gives the pieces to Bulat on a plate.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Bulat carries the poultry portions to the tower, greets Vassilissa in Ivan’s name, and repeats the formula of asking about Ivan’s health and telling himself to take the key, open the cupboard, and drink vodka.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When Bulat brings the goose, Vassilissa quickly takes the key, opens the cupboard, and reaches for a glass of vodka; Bulat seizes her by the right hand, draws her out of the tower, seats her on Ivan Tsarevich’s steed, and they ride away together.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The next morning Tsar Kirbít wakes, sees the top of the tower broken and his daughter missing, becomes very angry, and orders a pursuit over all roads and ways.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"During the flight, Bulat hides his ring and claims he has lost it, saying it was a priceless gift from his mother, who told The Wooing of Brynhild.; lines 3407-3540","start":"3407","end":"3540","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Heimir says, that she must needs wed but him whom she herself chose freely; and tells them how her abode was but a little way thence, and that he deemed that him only would she have who should ride through the flaming fire that was drawn round about her hall.","summary":"Gunnar, Sigurd, and Hogni ride to King Budli to seek Brynhild in marriage. Budli replies that only the man she herself chooses may wed her. They continue to Hlymdale, where Brynhilds foster-father Heimir explains that she will accept only the man who can ride through the flaming fire encircling her hall. The men ride to the hall, a castle with a golden roof surrounded by roaring fire. Gunnars horse refuses to enter the flames, and even when he borrows Sigurds horse he still cannot pass. Grimhild has taught Gunnar and Sigurd how to change semblance; they exchange appearances, and Sigurd, now in Gunnars likeness, mounts Grani with the sword Gram in hand and rides through the intensifying fire as the earth quakes and flames reach toward the heavens. When the fire at last subsides, he dismounts and goes into Brynhilds hall.

Inside, Brynhild asks his name. He calls himself Gunnar, son of Giuki, and claims her as his wife by the will of her father and foster-father and by having ridden through her fire, according to her own condition. Brynhild, sitting in armor with sword, helm, and byrny and likened to a swan on a billow, speaks of her battle-deeds and declares that only the first and best of men should speak to her of marriage, and that he must be willing to slay her other wooers. Sigurd reminds her of the oath she swore to go with the man who rode through the flames. She accepts his words as truth, rises to greet him, and he remains three nights in her hall. They lie in one bed, but Sigurd lays the sword Gram between them and explains that he must in this way either wed his wife or meet his death. Brynhild gives him the ring Andvaris-loom, which he had earlier given to her, and he gives her another ring from Fafnirs hoard.

Sigurd then rides back through the fire, resumes his own shape as Gunnar resumes his, and they return to Hlymdale and tell how things have gone. The same day Brynhild returns to Heimir and confides that a king who named himself Gunnar rode through her fire to woo her, but she believes that such a deed could only have been done by Sigurd, with whom she had plighted troth on the mountain and who is her first and well-beloved betrothed. Heimir says events must remain as they are. Brynhild declares that Aslaug, the future daughter of herself and Sigurd, will be fostered there with Heimir.

The kings return home, and Brynhild goes to her father. Grimhild welcomes the kings and thanks Sigurd for his fellowship. A great feast is held, attended by Budli with Brynhild and his son Atli, and during this feast Gunnar is wedded to Brynhild. After the feast Sigurd remembers the oaths he has sworn to Brynhild but allows matters to stand in peace. Brynhild and Gunnar sit together in joy and drink wine. the horse leaps into the fire, the flames burn higher, the earth trembles, and the fire rises toward heaven before subsiding.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After passing through the fire, Sigurd dismounts and goes into Brynhilds hall.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Brynhild asks the visitors identity; in return, he gives her another ring from Fafnirs hoard.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Sigurd rides back through the same fire to his companions, and he and Gunnar change semblances again before returning together to Hlymdale and reporting what happened.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Brynhild goes to her foster-father Heimir and tells him that a king came who rode through her fire, said he was Gunnar, and came to woo her, but she said that only Sigurd, with whom she had plighted troth on the mountain, could have done the deed and that he is her first troth-plight and well-beloved.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Heimir says that matters must remain as they have now come to pass.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Brynhild says that Aslaug, the daughter of herself and Sigurd, shall be nourished with Heimir.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The kings go home while Brynhild goes to her father; she is described armed in helm, byrny, and with a sword, recounts her battle-deeds, demands the foremost of men as husband, had previously plighted troth with Sigurd on the mountain, lies chastely with Sigurd-as-Gunnar for three nights, exchanges rings with him, then is brought to a feast where she is wedded to Gunnar, later sitting joyfully with him and appearing again at the queens bathing.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13","ev:15","ev:16"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Budli","description":"King whose house Gunnar and his companions first visit to woo Brynhild; {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l4543-l4654","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE POETICAL DICTION. / THOR AND HRUNGNER. / IDUN. / THE NIFLUNGS AND GJUKUNGS.; lines 4543-4654","start":"4543","end":"4654","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage recounts late episodes in the Niflung/Gjukung cycle and related Volsung material. King Atle marries Gudrun, Sigurd’s widow. Atle invites Gunnar and Hogne to visit him; before traveling they hide Fafner’s gold hoard in the Rhine. Atle raises an army, defeats the brothers, has Hogne’s heart cut out alive, and throws Gunnar into a snake den. A harp is smuggled to Gunnar, and he plays it with his toes so that the snakes fall asleep except an adder, which bites him, burrows into his wound, and kills him. Gunnar and Hogne are called Niflungs/Gjukungs, and their gold is known as the Niflung treasure.
Later Gudrun kills her two sons, makes their skulls into gold-trimmed goblets, and during the funeral feast serves King Atle mead mixed with their blood and roasted hearts. After revealing this and speaking harshly, she and her son Hogne kill Atle in his sleep, burn down the hall so that all inside perish, and Gudrun attempts to drown herself in the sea. Instead she is carried across a fjord to the land of King Jonaker, who marries her. They have three sons, Sorle, Hamder, and Erp, whose hair is as black as ravens, like Gunnar, Hogne, and the other Niflungs.
Sigurd’s daughter Swanhild is fostered at Jonaker’s and is the fairest of women. King Jormunrek learns of her and sends his son Randver to ask for her as his bride. Swanhild is entrusted to Randver to bring to Jormunrek. The counselor Bikke suggests that the young Randver should marry Swanhild instead of the old king, and Randver and Swanhild like this idea. Bikke informs Jormunrek, who seizes Randver and sends him to the gallows. Randver plucks the feathers from his hawk and asks that it be sent to his father before he is hanged. Seeing the featherless hawk, Jormunrek realizes that, like the hawk, his kingdom is unprotected now that he is old and sonless.
While riding with his courtiers from the hunt, Jormunrek has them trample Queen Swanhild, who is sitting and combing her hair, and she dies beneath the horses. Hearing this, Gudrun urges her sons to avenge Swanhild. She equips Sorle, Hamder, and Erp with byrnies and helmets so strong that iron cannot injure them and instructs them to attack Jormunrek at night while he sleeps: Sorle and Hamder are to cut off his hands and feet, and Erp his head. On the journey, when asked what help he will give them, Erp says he will aid them as the hand aids the foot; they reject this answer, angry at their mother’s harsh urging, and kill Erp to spite her. Later Sorle slips while walking and saves himself with his hands, realizing too late that the metaphor was true and lamenting Erp’s death.
Sorle and Hamder reach Jormunrek at night and cut off his hands and feet while he sleeps. He awakens, calls his men, and Hamder remarks that the king’s head would have been off if Erp were alive. The courtiers attack but cannot harm the brothers with weapons because of their armor. Jormunrek orders them to be stoned, and Sorle and Hamder are killed with stones, dying as the last descendants of Gjuke.
The text notes Sigurd’s daughter Aslaug, fostered by Heimer in Hlymdaler, from whom great lineages descend. It also states that Sigmund, son of Volsung, can drink venom unharmed, and that his son Sinfjotle and Sigurd are so hard-skinned that venom on their bodies cannot hurt them. A verse by the skald Brage mentions a tortuous serpent, full of the “drink of the Volsungs,” hanging in coils on the “bait of the giant-slayer.”
Many skalds have composed lays on these sagas. Brage the Old, in a drapa about Ragnar Lodbrok, tells of Sorle and Hamder’s fall: Jormunrek wakes from an evil dream as they attack; sword-clashing is heard in Randver’s father’s house as the raven-blue brothers of Erp avenge the insult. Blood (“sword-dew”) flows from the bed; bloody hands and feet of the king are seen cut off; a ring of men surrounds the house; and Sorle and Hamder are struck down with slippery content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l3487-l3579","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER III. / HOW NJORD GOT SKADE TO WIFE. / CHAPTER IV. / THE ORIGIN OF POETRY.; lines 3487-3579","start":"3487","end":"3579","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Brage tells Æger how poetry (skaldship) began. After a war between the gods (asas) and the Vans, both sides make peace by spitting into a jar and later shape this spittle into a man named Kvaser, so wise he can answer any question and who travels the world teaching wisdom. The dwarfs Fjalar and Galar murder Kvaser, drain his blood into two jars (Son and Bodn) and a kettle (Odrarer), mix it with honey, and make a mead that turns anyone who drinks it into a skald and sage; they lie to the gods that Kvaser choked on his wisdom. The dwarfs later drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his grieving wife with a falling mill-stone. Gilling's son Suttung avenges them by stranding the dwarfs on a rocky island that floods at high tide; they ransom their lives by giving him the precious mead. Suttung stores the mead in a place called Hnitbjorg and sets his daughter Gunlad to guard it. Brage explains that, because of this, poetry is called Kvaser's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttung's mead, and similar names. Æger then asks how the gods obtained Suttung's mead. Brage relates how Odin travels, meets nine thralls mowing hay, sharpens their scythes with a whetstone, and then causes them to kill each other as they scramble for the stone. Odin, calling himself Bolverk, lodges with the giant Bauge, Suttung's brother, and offers to do the work of nine men over the summer in exchange for a drink of Suttung's mead. After Suttung refuses to share the mead, Odin and Bauge conspire to get it by trickery. Odin has Bauge bore a tunnel through the rock with an auger called Rate; after ensuring the hole truly goes through, Odin turns into a serpent, crawls into the mountain, and reaches Gunlad. He shares her couch for three nights, and she grants him three draughts from the mead; with these he empties all three vessels. Odin then becomes an eagle and flies away with the mead. Suttung sees this, turns into an eagle, and pursues him. As Odin approaches Asgard, the gods set jars in the yard; he expels the mead into them, but, nearly caught, he sends some of it out backwards and this portion is carelessly spilled, becoming available to anyone as the \"share of poetasters.\" Odin keeps Suttung's mead for the gods and for men able to compose verses, and poetry is also called Odin's prey, find, drink, and gift.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A conversation between Æger and Brage frames the account of the origin of poetry, with Æger settlement.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When the gods parted from the Vans, they shaped the spittle in the jar into a man named Kvaser, not wishing this mark of peace to perish.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Kvaser is described as so wise that no one could ask him any question he could not answer.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Kvaser traveled widely in the world to teach men wisdom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The dwarfs Fjalar and Galar called Kvaser aside, saying they wished to speak with him alone, and then slew him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The dwarfs let Kvaser’s blood run into two jars, Son and Bodn, and a kettle called Odrarer, mixed it with honey, and made a mead that makes whoever drinks it into a skald and sage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The dwarfs told the asas that Kvaser had choked in his wisdom because no her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Gilling's son Suttung seized the dwarfs, carried them out to sea, and left them on a rocky island that was flooded at high tide.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The dwarfs begged Suttung to spare their lives and offered him the precious mead as atonement for their father's blood, which he accepted.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Suttung brought the mead home, hid it in a place called Hnitbjorg, and set his daughter Gunlad to guard it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Because of this story, poetic songship is called Kvaser’s blood, the drink or fill of the dwarfs, the mead of Suttung, and the liquor of Hnitbjorg, among other names.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Odin set out from home and came to a place where nine thralls were mowing Gunnar downplays the first dream but admits no one can escape fate and that his time may be short. Despite attempts by their people to delay or dissuade them, Gunnar, Hogni, several of Hogni’s sons, and the champion Orkning prepare to travel. Gunnar orders wine for what he calls possibly their last feast and speaks of an old wolf and a bear who will seize their gold if they die. Their household follows them weeping; farewells are exchanged. Glaumvor accuses the messenger Vingi of bringing ill fortune, but he swears by the gallows that he is not lying. The company rows away with such force that the ship nearly breaks, then rides through a dark wild wood. They see a king’s army, a great host filling all the gates of a burg. Hogni breaks open the shut gates and they ride in. Vingi then reveals his treachery, saying he lured them gently but evil was hidden, and that he will find the gallows-tree on which they will hang. Hogni refuses to be intimidated, and Gunnar and his companions cast Vingi down and kill him with axe-hammers. The Death of King Siggeir and of Signy. / CHAPTER XV. Of the Welding together of the Shards of the Sword Gram. / CHAPTER XVI. The prophecy of Grifir. / CHAPTER XVIII. Of the Slaying of the Worm Fafnir.; lines 2555-2710","start":"2555","end":"2710","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial endnotes explain terms such as dragon, an onomastic taboo against giving one's name to a dying enemy, and Surt's role in destroying the world at Ragnarok. The narrative then relates how Regin greets Sigurd after the slaying of Fafnir, first praising him and then lamenting that Sigurd has killed his brother. Regin and Sigurd dispute whether courage or smithcraft deserves credit for the victory. Regin has Sigurd cut out and roast Fafnir's heart, intending to eat it himself, and drinks some of Fafnir's blood. While roasting the heart, Sigurd tests it with his finger; when he tastes the dragon's heart-blood, he suddenly understands the speech of birds, especially woodpeckers. The birds comment that Sigurd should eat the heart himself to gain wisdom, warn that Regin plans to betray him, and advise him to kill Regin, seize the gold hoard, and later ride to Hindfell, where Brynhild sleeps within a hall encircled by fire, from whom he will gain great wisdom. They add a proverb about wolves to underline the danger. Sigurd decides that Regin will not be his doom and beheads him. The text then gives bird-songs elaborating on the counsel: they speak of binding bright red rings, a fair maiden adorned with gold, the hall of King Giuki and his daughter with whom Sigurd will deal in gold and affection, the high gold-bright hall on Hindfell surrounded by red flame, and a shield-maiden sleeping on the fell within fire because Odin has pierced her with a sleep-thorn for choosing against his will in battle. They urge Sigurd to go to this helm-wearing maiden whom Vinskornir carried from battle, calling her a dear offspring of kings despite the Norns. Sigurd eats more of Fafnir's heart and keeps the rest, then follows the dragon's trail to his underground iron-beamed lair, dug deep in the earth. He finds an immense hoard of gold, the sword Rotti, the Helm of Awe, a golden byrny, and other treasures, so much that two or three horses could scarcely carry it. He loads the gold into two large chests and places them on his horse Grani, who refuses to move until Sigurd mounts; once Sigurd is on his back, Grani runs as if unladen. An endnote states that the songs of the birds were inserted from the Eddic poem Reginsmál.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An endnote gods.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Regin greets Sigurd after Fafnir's death, praising the victory as unmatched and saying the deed will be renowned as long as the world lasts.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Regin calls Fafnir his own brother and repeatedly laments that Sigurd has slain him, saying he himself is not guiltless in the deed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Sigurd rebukes Regin, saying Regin stayed far away during the fight, while Sigurd struggled with all the might of a dragon and Regin lay low in a heather-bush scarcely aware of his surroundings.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Regin insists that his forge-work on the danger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13","ev:14","ev:15","ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The birds also advise that Sigurd should go to Fafnir's lair to take the treasure and then ride content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l3683-l3807","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XXIII. Sigurd comes to Hlymdale. / CHAPTER XXIV. Sigurd sees Brynhild at Hlymdale. / CHAPTER XXVI. Sigurd comes to the Giukings and is wedded to Gudrun. / CHAPTER XXVII. The Wooing of Brynhild.; lines 3683-3807","start":"3683","end":"3807","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Brynhild confronts King Gunnar about a ring and recounts how her father King Budli forced her to choose between obedience and losing his favour, leading her to vow to marry only the man who would ride the horse Grani with Fafnir’s hoard through her flaming fire and slay certain men. She says only Sigurd had the courage to do this, slaying the Worm Fafnir, Regin, and five kings, while Gunnar failed, so Sigurd is truly the noblest man, yet she is married to Gunnar and sees her oath as broken. She denounces Gunnar as no champion and blames Grimhild for evil, vowing to bring about Gunnar’s death. After Gunnar defends Grimhild, Brynhild attempts to kill him, is fettered by Hogni, then released at Gunnar’s command. She renounces all joy and participation in Gunnar’s hall, tears her needlework, orders her bower doors opened, and fills the house with loud lamentation. Gudrun notices her maidens’ sorrow, learns from the waiting-woman Swaflod that the hall is full of lamentation, and is told that Brynhild has taken neither mead nor wine for many days and is under the wrath of the gods. Attempts by Gunnar and Hogni to speak with Brynhild fail, and they ask Sigurd to visit her. The next day Sigurd tells Gudrun he foresees great evil and that Brynhild will die; Gudrun says Brynhild has lain as if asleep seven days and nights, and Sigurd says she is not sleeping but brooding on dreadful intent against him. At Gudrun’s urging he goes to Brynhild’s chamber, finds her apparently asleep, uncovers her, and urges her to awake and be glad. She instead accuses him of being the worst traitor to her. Sigurd denies cruelty and says she has the husband she chose, but Brynhild reveals that Gunnar never rode through the fire or gave her the dower of the host of the slain. She says she recognised Sigurd’s eyes in the man who came to her hall but was blinded by a heavy veil upon her fortune. Sigurd praises the sons of Giuki for slaying great kings, while Brynhild insists she must repay them for many ill-deeds and repeats that Sigurd alone slew the Worm and rode the fire for her sake.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Brynhild asks Gunnar what he did with the ring she had given him, which King Budli had given her at their last parting when Gunnar and King Giuki came to Budli and threatened fire and sword unless they obtained her as a wife.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Brynhild recounts that King Budli led her aside, offered her the choice between marrying whom he wished or losing his wealth and friendship, after she had requested to stay to guard the land and command a third of his men, and she decided it was useless to resist him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Brynhild says she promised to wed whoever would ride the horse Grani with Fafnir’s hoard, ride through her flaming fire, and slay the men she named.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Brynhild states that only Sigurd dared ride through the fire, that he slew the Worm, Regin, and five kings, while Gunnar did nothing and turned as pale as a dead man, so she calls Gunnar no king and no champion.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Brynhild says she vowed to her father that she would love only the noblest man alive, identifies Sigurd as that man, and laments that she has broken her oath because Sigurd is not her husband; she declares she will compass Gunnar’s death and repay Grimhild with great evils, calling Grimhild the most evil and faint-hearted of women.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Gunnar replies quietly that Brynhild has spoken many vile words and is evil-hearted for reviling Grimhild; he says Grimhild would never curse her own life, has not tormented the dead or murdered anyone, and is well praised by all.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Brynhild says she has not secretly lived with evil things or done loathsome deeds but is very eager to slay Gunnar, and she attempts to kill him before Hogni intervenes and puts her in fetters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Gunnar says he does not want Brynhild to remain in fetters, and she is released.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild declares that Gunnar will never again see her glad in his hall, saying she will not drink there, play chess, speak kindly, embroider gold on fair cloths, or give him good counsel, and she laments that she could not have Sigurd as her husband.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Brynhild sits up, strikes her needlework and tears it apart, orders her bower doors opened so that her sorrowful wailing may be heard far away, and the house is filled with loud mourning and lamentation heard throughout the abode.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Gudrun notices that her bower-maidens sit joyless and downcast and asks them why they behave like witless women and what unheard-of wonders have befallen them; the waiting-lady Swaflod answers that it is an untimely, evil day and the hall is full of lamentation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Gudrun tells one of her handmaids to rise, wake Brynhild, and join her in needlework and merriment, but the handmaid refuses, saying she cannot wake or speak with Brynhild, who has drunk neither mead nor wine for many days and appears to be under the wrath of the gods.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Gudrun asks Gunnar to visit Brynhild and tell her that Gudrun is grieved by her grief; Gunnar says he is forbidden to see Brynhild or share her fortune, yet he goes to her and tries in many ways to speak, but she gives him no answer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Gunnar then asks Hogni to visit Brynhild; Hogni reluctantly goes to her but, like Gunnar, gets no response.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After Gunnar and Hogni fail, they go to Sigurd and ask him to visit Brynhild; Sigurd says nothing in reply, and the situation remains unchanged that night.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The next day, returning from hunting, Sigurd tells Gudrun that he sees matters tending toward great and evil events arising from this turmoil, and that Brynhild will surely die.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Gudrun, weeping, says that Brynhild is surrounded by great wonders, has lain as if sleeping for seven days and seven nights, and that no one has dared to wake her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Sigurd says Brynhild is not truly sleeping, but that her heart is occupied with dreadful intent against him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Gudrun laments the prospect of Sigurd’s death, urges him to see Brynhild, and suggests that he give her gold to smother her grief and anger.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Sigurd goes to Brynhild’s chamber, finds its door open, believes she is sleeping, draws the covers from her, and urges her to awake, saying the sun shines over the house, she has slept enough, and should cast off grief and take up gladness.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Brynhild asks Sigurd how he dared come to her and says that in the treason done to her, none was worse than he.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Sigurd asks why Brynhild will not speak to people and why she sorrows, saying she is as one under a spell if she thinks any cruelty is in his heart against her, and he tells her she has for husband the man she chose.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Brynhild replies that Gunnar never rode through the fire to her or gave her the dower of the host of the slain; she says she wondered at the man who came into her hall, thought she recognised Sigurd’s eyes, but could not clearly distinguish good from evil because a heavy veil lay on her fortune.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Sigurd says that no nobler men exist than the sons of Giuki, who slew the king of the Danes and the great chief who was King Budli’s brother.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Brynhild answers that she must repay the sons of Giuki for many ill-deeds and repeats that it was Sigurd, not they, who slew the Worm, rode through the fire, and did these deeds for her sake.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Brynhild","description":"Woman married into Gunnar’s household who once set a heroic trial of fire and dragon’s hoard for her suitor, identifies Sigurd as the true fulfiller of the trial and noblest man, now feels deceived, attempts to kill Gunnar, renounces joy in his hall, withdraws in grief, and accuses Sigurd of treachery.","role_refs":["role:1","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Gunnar","description":"King Gunnar, Brynhild’s husband and lord of the hall, accused by Brynhild of cowardice and of not riding through the fire, defends Grimhild, narrowly escapes Brynhild’s attack, orders her released from fetters, and unsuccessfully tries to speak with her.","role_refs":["role:2","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:5","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sigurd","description":"Hero associated with Gudrun who is credited with slaying the Worm Fafnir, Regin, and five kings, riding the horse Grani through Brynhild’s flaming fire with Fafnir’s hoard, and thus fulfilling Brynhild’s bridal condition; he foresees Brynhild’s death, is asked to visit her, and confronts her accusations of treachery.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Gudrun","description":"Woman in the same household, associated closely with Sigurd (whom she calls her lord), who oversees bower-maidens, is concerned about Brynhild’s grief, sends handmaids to wake her, asks Gunnar and then Sigurd to visit Brynhild, and weeps over the foreseen deaths and evils.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Hogni","description":"Man allied with Gunnar who restrains Brynhild by putting her in fetters when she attacks Gunnar, later visits her at Gunnar’s request but, like Gunnar, fails to get any response from her.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"King Budli","description":"King Budli, Brynhild’s father, who gave her a ring at their last parting, threatened her with loss of wealth and friendship if she did not marry as he wished, and whose brother was later slain by the sons of Giuki.","role_refs":["role:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:7","name_or_label":"King Giuki","description":"King Giuki, who came with Gunnar to King Budli and threatened fire and sword unless they obtained Brynhild as a wife.","role_refs":["role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:8","name_or_label":"Grimhild","description":"Woman whom Brynhild blames and plans to repay with great evils, calling her the most evil and faint-hearted of women, but whom Gunnar defends as better than Brynhild and as someone who has not cursed her life, tormented the dead, or murdered anyone.","role_refs":["role:8","role:9"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:9","name_or_label":"Fafnir (the Worm)","description":"The Worm, identified as Fafnir, slain by Sigurd as part

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l5061-l5161","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"NOTES. / ENEA. / HERIKON. / THE HISTORICAL ODIN.; lines 5061-5161","start":"5061","end":"5161","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Editorial notes identify the names Enea and Herikon with classical forms (Aeneas and Erichthonios) and then discuss the \"historical\" or anthropomorphized Odin as presented in the Foreword and in Heimskringla. The author stresses that, though only a myth, Odin's legend functioned as genuine history for the Teutonic ancestors, shaping their social, religious, political, and literary life. The legend is compared to Roman and Greek traditions: the story of Romulus, Remus, Mars, and the wolf is said to prophetically mirror Rome's later character and history, and detailed parallels are drawn between Odin and Aeneas as defenders of doomed causes who wander through many lands, found new kingdoms or races, and whose descendants eventually avenge themselves on former enemies (Romans or Greeks). The text claims that prophecies implicit in the Roman and Teutonic legends were fulfilled historically by Roman conquest of Greece and by Odoacer's deposition of Romulus Augustulus, and notes the name-parallels Romulus–Romulus and Odin–Odoacer. A possible comparison between Odin and Ulysses is suggested but not developed. The author laments that, unlike the Trojan cycle and Ulysses' wanderings, Odin's journeys \"driven by the norns\" to Teutondom and the Baltic have not yet been made into an epic, though this expedition could form an epic as noble as the Aeneid. Invoking William Morris' praise for the Volsung Saga, the writer presents Odin's story as the great tale of the Teutonic race, comparable in cultural role to the Iliad, Odyssey, and Aeneid, and calls for a modern skald—imagined as a descendant of Odin—who will drink from Mimer's fountain and Suttung's mead and compose a Teutonic epic. The section closes by announcing that Laing's translation of Heimskringla will provide the subsequent account of the historical Odin.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The note explains that \"Enea\" refers to the settlement of western Europe where Aeneas is said to have founded a city on the Tiber, while Bergmann instead connects it with the Thracian town Ainos.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The note states that \"Herikon\" is a mutilated form of \"Erichthonios\" and that the genealogy given corresponds to Iliad 20.215.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Odin described in the Foreword and in Heimskringla is called a \"historical or anthropomorphized\" Odin, yet the author adds that the whole story is only a myth which nevertheless served every purpose of genuine history for their ancestors, influencing their social, religious, political, and literary life.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The text says that the ancestors accepted the Odin legend in as good faith as any Christian believes in the gospel of Christ.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The author claims that in ancestral myths like the Odin story one can see reflected everything later known as reliable history of the old Teutons, and then draws an analogy to interest in the story of Romulus and Remus suckled by Mars and the wolf.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Roman myth of Mars, the wolf, and the fratricide Romulus is described as prophetic of Rome’s future career: Mars’s warlikeness, the wolf’s rapacity, and Romulus’s fratricide mirror the whole historical development of the Romans, making the story of Romulus a \"vest-pocket edition\" of Roman history.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The text asserts that there are many points of resemblance between the old story of Odin and Virgil’s account of Aeneas, that Virgil based his poem on a traditional Latin legend, and that in the comparison the Greeks correspond to Pompey and the Romans, the Trojans to Mithridates and his allies, and that Aeneas and Odin are identical.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the Teutonic legend as summarized, Odin is a heroic defender of Mithridates who, after traversing various unknown countries, reaches northern Europe, organizes various Teutonic kingdoms, settles his sons on the thrones of Germany, England, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, and instructs his people to gather strength and courage to eventually take revenge on the Romans.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the Roman legend as summarized, Aeneas is one of the most valiant defenders of Troy who, after many adventures in various lands, eventually settles in Italy and becomes the founder of a race that is destined in time to wreak vengeance upon the Greeks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The author states that the prophecy contained in the Aeneas legend was fulfilled when Metellus and Mummius conquered Greece in 147–146 BCE, and that the prophecy in the Teutonic Odin legend foreshadowed the downfall of Rome when the Teutonic commander Odoacer dethroned Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The text remarks that history repeats itself, that Roman history begins and ends with a Romulus, and notes a fancied connection between the names Odin and Odoacer, adding the proverb \"As the twig is bent the tree is inclined.\"","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The author suggests that it might be interesting to make a similar comparison between Odin and Ulysses, king of Ithaca, but says the reader must undertake this for himself.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The fall of Troy and the wanderings of Ulysses became the themes of two great Greek epics, and the wanderings and adventures of Aeneas were fashioned into a Roman epic by Virgil, whereas the \"much-traveled\" Odin, who first came to Teutondom and the Baltic shores, has not yet been sung in an epic.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Odin is described as \"driven by the norns\" when he first came to Teutondom and the Baltic shores.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Odin’s expedition, which gives a historic cause for the later hostilities and conflicts between Teutons and Romans, is said to be capable of supplying, as Gibbon suggested, the noble groundwork of an epic poem as thrilling as the Aeneid, yet it has not been woven into a song for the Teutonic race.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The editor hopes that among the readers there will be a descendant of Odin whose poetic wings are just fledged, who will drink first from Mimer’s gushing fountain and then from Suttung’s mead, which Odin brought to Asgard, and dedicate himself with ardor to this legend.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"William Morris is quoted (from memory) as saying of the Vols

Then Atli’s mother, described as a wretch, crawled out and stung Gunnar in the heart so that no help was left for him. Speaking to a gold-clad woman who has listened to her tale of many ill-fates, Oddrun laments that she loved the fallen warrior as her own self and closes by sending forth her greeting. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l4366-l4434","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE POETICAL DICTION. / THOR AND HRUNGNER. / IDUN. / THE NIFLUNGS AND GJUKUNGS.; lines 4366-4434","start":"4366","end":"4434","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Odin, Honer, and Loki travel through the world and come to a river with a waterfall, where Loki kills an otter that is actually Hreidmar’s son, Otter, who is eating a salmon. They bring the otter and salmon to Hreidmar’s farm and are seized by Hreidmar and his sons Fafnir and Regin when the dead otter is recognized as their kinsman. The gods offer to ransom their lives, and Hreidmar demands that Otter’s flayed skin be filled and covered with red gold. Odin sends Loki to the home of the dark elves, where Loki captures the dwarf Andvari, who lives as a fish, and forces him to surrender his large hoard of gold, including a small ring. Andvari begs to keep the ring, saying it will let him restore his wealth, but Loki takes it, and Andvari curses the ring so that it will bring ruin to whoever owns it. Loki is pleased by the curse and later brings the gold to Odin and Hreidmar. Odin, admiring the ring, initially keeps it back but finally uses it to cover the last uncovered hair on the otter-skin, thus completing the ransom. Loki declares that Andvari’s curse will be fulfilled and that the ring and gold will be the bane of their possessors, and the text notes that the curse later came true and that gold is called otter-ransom, forced payment of the gods, and strife-metal. Hreidmar keeps the treasure for himself, refusing to share it with his sons. Fafnir and Regin kill their father for the gold. Fafnir then denies Regin any share, arms himself with the sword Hrotti and his father’s terrifying helmet (Æger’s helmet), drives Regin away, and goes to Gnita-heath, where he takes the form of a serpent (dragon) and lies brooding over the hoard.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Three asas, Odin, Honer, and Loke, go abroad to learn to know the whole world.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The three gods come to a river, walk along the river-bank to a force (waterfall or rapids), where an otter is sitting nearby.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The otter has caught a salmon in the force and is sitting eating it with his eyes closed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Loke picks up a stone, throws it at the otter, and hits him in the head, killing him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Loke boasts that he has secured both an otter and a salmon with one throw.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The gods take the salmon and the otter with them and come to a byre belonging to a bonde named Hreidmar, described as a mighty man skilled in the black art.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Hreidmar, seeing the otter, calls his sons Fafner and Regin and tells them that Otter, their brother, has been slain by the visitors.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Hreidmar and his sons attack the gods, seize and bind them, and declare that the otter was Hreidmar’s son.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The gods offer, as a ransom for their lives, as much money as Hreidmar may demand, and this agreement is confirmed with an oath.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Otter is flayed; Hreidmar takes the otter-skin and demands that it be filled with red gold and then covered over with the same metal, promising to free the gods when this is done.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Odin sends Loke to the home of the swarthy elves to obtain the gold.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Loke comes to the dwarf Andvare, who lives as a fish in the water.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Loke catches Andvare in his hands and demands, as a ransom for his life, all the gold he has in his rock.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Inside the rock, Andvare produces all the gold he owns, which is described as a very large amount.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Andvare hides a small gold ring in his hand, but Loke sees this and demands the ring as well.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Andvare begs not to lose the ring, saying that with it he can increase his wealth again, but Loke refuses and takes the ring, declaring that the dwarf shall not keep as much as a penny.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Andvare declares that the ring will be the bane of every one who possesses it, placing a curse on it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Loke answers that he is glad of the curse and says he will see that the prophecy is fulfilled by bringing the curse to the ears of the ring’s recipient.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Loke brings the gold to Hreidmar and shows it to Odin; Odin sees the ring, thinks it fair, and keeps it aside for himself, giving Hreidmar the rest of the gold.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The otter-skin bag is filled as full of gold as it will hold, and then it is raised up when it is full.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Odin covers the otter-skin with gold and asks Hreidmar to inspect it; Near his home, Ivan and Yelena rest under a tree with the horse tied and the Fire-bird’s cage beside them, and both fall asleep. Ivan’s brothers Dmitri and Vassili, returning empty-handed from their own search for the Fire-bird, find them, envy Ivan’s success, and Dmitri kills the sleeping Ivan, cutting him to pieces. They coerce the terrified Yelena, under threat of death, to swear she will tell their father Tsar Vwislav that they captured her and won the Fire-bird and steed. After casting lots, Vassili takes Yelena, Dmitri takes the golden-maned steed and Fire-bird, and they ride home. Ivan’s dismembered body lies on the spot for thirty days until the Gray Wolf finds it by smell. Seeking a way to revive Ivan, the wolf threatens a young raven that has come with its parent to eat the corpse, then bargains with the parent raven: he will spare the chick if the raven flies beyond the thrice ninth land to the thirtieth kingdom to fetch the water of death and the water of life. On the third day the raven returns with two vials, which the wolf first uses to demonstrate their power by tearing the young raven in two and then restoring it with the waters. He then reassembles and revives Ivan with the same waters. Ivan awakes thinking he has slept; the wolf explains that his brothers killed him and carried off Yelena, the steed, and the Fire-bird, and urges him to hurry home, carrying him quickly to the edge of Tsar Vwislav’s town. Ivan arrives just as Vassili has married Yelena and is feasting with her. Yelena immediately recognizes Ivan, runs to him, kisses him, and proclaims that he, not Vassili, is her true bridegroom, denouncing Vassili as a scoundrel. Questioned by Tsar Vwislav, she recounts how Ivan won her, the steed, and the Fire-bird, how Dmitri killed Ivan while he slept, and how the brothers forced her to lie. The enraged Tsar imprisons Dmitri and Vassili; Ivan marries Yelena, and they live in perfect harmony, unable to be apart even for a minute. It then opens a new tale about Tsar Vwislav Andronovich and his three sons Dmitri, Vassili, and Ivan. The Tsar has a magnificent garden with a favorite apple-tree bearing golden apples. A wondrous Fire-bird with golden wings and crystal-like eyes comes nightly, sits on the tree, and steals the golden apples, causing the Tsar grief. He promises half his kingdom in life and all at death to whichever son captures the Fire-bird alive. On three successive nights the sons watch in the garden. Dmitri and then Vassili fall asleep, fail to see the bird, and falsely report that it did not come. On the third night Ivan keeps watch as the garden suddenly fills with light, seizes the Fire-bird by the tail, but it escapes, leaving one feather in his hand. The bird never returns. The feather shines in darkness like many candles, and the delighted Tsar stores it carefully. The Tsar then blesses his sons to seek and bring back the Fire-bird, renewing his promise of reward. Dmitri and Vassili grow hateful toward Ivan for his success, and all three depart. Though the Tsar tries to keep his youngest, needed as future ruler and defender of the realm, Ivan insists and sets out. Riding on his chosen horse, he reaches a green meadow where a pillar stands inscribed with the fates of three paths: straight ahead brings hunger and cold, right preserves the rider but kills his horse, and left kills the rider but spares the horse. Ivan chooses the right-hand road. As the drinking continues and the kings grow very drunk, Vingi emphasizes Atli’s age and the weakness of his sons and claims Atli will hand over rule of his realms to them. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l7322-l7538","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE HELL-RIDE OF BRYNHILD. / FRAGMENTS OF THE LAY OF BRYNHILD / THE SECOND OR ANCIENT LAY OF GUDRUN. / THE SONG OF ATLI.; lines 7322-7538","start":"7322","end":"7538","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Atli’s men first cut out the heart of the cowardly thrall Hjalli and present it to Gunnar, then cut out the heart of the brave Hogni, who laughs as he dies, and show this heart as well. Gunnar declares that with Hogni dead, only he knows the secret of the Niblung hoard and will never reveal it; he says the Rhine will rule over the cursed gold. Atli has the bound Gunnar led away and cast alive into a pit of venomous worms, where Gunnar plays the harp as he dies, held up as a model of a generous king who keeps his gold from foes. Gudrun, Atli’s wife and sister of Gunnar and Hogni, recalls oaths Atli swore to Gunnar by the sun, a stronghold, a bed, and the ring of Ull. After Gunnar’s death Atli returns home; Gudrun meets him with drink, and in the ensuing feast she secretly serves him the hearts of their sons, Erp and Eiril, cooked with honey. She then reveals this cannibal vengeance, describing how he will never again see his sons in the hall, and the Huns weep while she remains dry-eyed. Later Gudrun scatters gold lavishly among the house-carls, then kills the drunken, unarmed Atli in his bed, looses the dogs, and sets the hall on fire. The blaze destroys Atli’s household, treasure-houses, and shield-maidens, and the Budlung estate collapses in flames. The narrator concludes that Gudrun’s vengeance as an armored bride, who has brought death to three kings, is famed and unparalleled.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Atli’s men seize the thrall Hjalli and cut out his heart, laying it bleeding on a trencher and bringing it to Gunnar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Hjalli is described as a wailing thrall and a trembler, whose heart shakes even when laid on the trencher.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Hogni is called hardy and laughs when his heart is cut from his living body, showing no sign of fear.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Hogni’s heart is described as steady, barely quaking even when removed from his chest and laid on a dish.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Gunnar is presented first with Hjalli’s heart and then with Hogni’s heart by Atli’s followers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Gunnar states that the hoard of the Niblungs is now hidden forever in his heart, since Hogni is dead, and that Atli will not obtain it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Gunnar says the Niblung gold, called the seed of the gods and a hate-raising treasure, will lie gleaming in the waters of the Rhine unless it comes to the hands of the Huns’ children.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Atli commands that wagons be driven forth and that the bound Gunnar, called a slave, be taken away to his death.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Gunnar is described with royal and heroic epithets such as high king, Gunnar is led away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Gudrun, who is bound to Atli by wedlock and is sister to the slain Niblungs, restrains her tears and runs into the hall.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Gudrun recalls and invokes oaths Atli swore often to Gunnar, by the south-sloping sun, by the high burg of Sigry, by a worms, described as ready to dig his grave in his heart.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"While alone in the worm-pit, Gunnar strikes a harp with his hand so that its strings sound loudly.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The narration comments that in such a manner a hardy ring-scatterer should keep gold from all people when in his enemy’s enclosure.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"After Gunnar’s killing, Atli rides back across his wide land on his brazen-shod steed; the hall; beakers clash on the benches as the long-bearded men, newly arrived from Gunnar’s murder, gather and talk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Gudrun is described as sweet-faced and the delight of the shield-folk, yet also as a dreadful woman, as she bears wine and dainties to lords who are pale with fate.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Gudrun tells Atli that he has eaten the hearts of his own sons, served to him bloody from death and drenched with benches.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"Gudrun names Atli’s sons as Erp and Eiril, saying he will never again call them to his knee or see them in the high seat Atli.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Gudrun, called swan-bright, scatters the ‘seed of gold’ by giving rings of red gold to the house-carls, not sparing the wealth of the storehouses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"Atli, unaware of Gudrun’s intentions, grows weary with drink, is without a weapon, and pays no heed to
