content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l1923-l2058","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"JEREMIAH CURTIN. / RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF.; lines 1923-2058","start":"1923","end":"2058","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"I'll open my mouth from earth to sky and swallow them all.\"","summary":"Ivan the peasant's son turns into a cat to cross a bridge over a fiery river and secretly listen in the serpents' former house, where the old mother of the serpents and her three daughters-in-law plot to kill him by transforming into an apple-tree, a well, a bed, and an all-swallowing mouth. Returning to his comrades in human form, Ivan leads them on the road and overcomes successive supernatural trials of hunger, thirst, and sleep by recognizing these deceptive forms, cutting them so that blood flows, and finally leaping through the gigantic jaws with the help of his wonderful silver-haired horse marked with a bright moon. At a river-hut, a tiny but immensely strong little man with an enormous mustache beats Ivan, steals his horse, and rides away. Inside the hut, a footless, handless man explains that he was mutilated for eating bread at the little man's table and advises Ivan to ferry people on another river for three years without taking payment to win back the horse. Ivan ferries for three years, refuses money from three old men, and explains his vow; they reveal themselves as the Freezer, the Devourer, and the Wizard and offer help. The Wizard draws a boat in the sand that becomes a flying vessel, carrying them to a great stony mountain where the little man lives. The little man agrees to return the horse only if they steal the Tsar's daughter. The three old men go to the Tsar, survive his attempt to kill them in an overheated bath thanks to the Freezer, and the Devourer eats an enormous feast. That night they steal the Tsar's daughter and deliver her to the little man, receiving the horse in return. Ivan mounts the horse and departs; while he rests in a field, the Tsar's daughter appears and explains that she transformed into a pin and hid in his collar. She becomes a pin again and travels with him back to the Tsar, where she resumes her form as a fair maiden. Ivan presents her to the Tsar, who honors him and learns that his stolen daughter has been returned.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Night passes and morning comes; Ivan the peasant's son and his comrades eat, drink, and make merry.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ivan the peasant's son tells his comrades to wait, turns into a cat, and crosses a bridge over a fiery content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l1796-l1921","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"JEREMIAH CURTIN. / RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF.; lines 1796-1921","start":"1796","end":"1921","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Tsar whose courtyard contains a pillar with gold, silver, and copper rings dreams of a horse tied to the gold ring, with silver hairs and a clear moon on its forehead. He proclaims that whoever can interpret the dream and obtain the horse will receive his daughter and half his kingdom. Nobles fail, but a poor man's son, Ivan, is summoned. Ivan explains that the dream was actually a real visit by a twelve-headed serpent riding that horse, intending to steal the Tsar's daughter. Ivan says he can get the horse only after his fifteenth year, so the Tsar keeps him at court and feeds him until he turns fifteen. When Ivan tries the Tsar's horses, his hero's hand causes them to fall, so he spends three years searching the open country for a suitable horse. After rudely dismissing then apologizing to an old man, he is told to seek a mangy colt in a poor peasant's stable. The colt endures his touch; Ivan takes and feeds it, then returns to the Tsar and prepares to confront the serpent, asking only for six men as messengers. Traveling together, they reach a fiery river with a bridge and an enormous forest, pitch a tent, feast, and agree to stand nightly guard, though Ivan's comrades get drunk and fail. On his own watch, Ivan hides under the bridge and sees a three-headed serpent crossing the fiery river, boasting that only Ivan is its enemy. Ivan fights on foot against the serpent on horseback, cuts off its three heads, and takes the horse. On subsequent nights he kills six-headed and nine-headed serpents and throws them into the fiery river. On the fourth night the twelve-headed serpent appears, angry that Ivan slew its sons. Ivan gives his comrades a bowl, telling them to come when it fills with blood, then fights the serpent. In successive clashes he cuts off groups of heads while sinking progressively deeper into the earth—first to his knees, then waist, breast, and neck. Only when blood runs over the bowl's rim do his comrades act; they cut off the last head and pull Ivan out of the ground. Ivan takes the serpent's horse and leads it to the tent.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the Tsar's courtyard there is a pillar with three rings: one gold, one silver, and one copper.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Tsar dreams that a horse is tied to the gold ring; every hair of the horse is silver and a clear moon is on its forehead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Tsar proclaims that whoever can interpret his dream and obtain the horse will receive his daughter in marriage and half his kingdom.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Many princes, boyars, and lords assemble but none can explain the dream or promises to fetch the horse; they inform the Tsar that a poor man has a son, Ivan, who can do both.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Ivan is summoned to the Tsar, asks to hear the dream, and then declares that it was not a dream but a reality: a twelve-headed serpent came riding the horse and attempted to steal the Tsar's daughter.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Ivan states that it is possible to obtain the horse, but only after his fifteenth year has passed; at that time he is twelve years old.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Tsar keeps Ivan at his court, providing him food and drink until Ivan's fifteenth year is completed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When his fifteenth year has passed, Ivan asks the Tsar for a horse to ride to the place where the serpent is.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the Tsar's stables, the horses cannot withstand Ivan's strength and weight; when he lays his hero's hand on any horse, it falls to the ground.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ivan requests permission to go into the open country to seek a horse strong enough for him, and the Tsar allows him to go.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ivan spends three years travelling through the open country among many herds but cannot find a horse to suit him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"While returning in tears, Ivan meets an old man who asks why he weeps; Ivan answers rudely and chases the old man away, then reflects on his offense and returns to ask forgiveness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After Ivan explains his grief and quest, the old man advises him to go to a certain village where a poor peasant's stable contains a mare with a mangy colt that will be strong enough for him if he feeds it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ivan goes to the indicated village, finds the mare with the mangy colt, touches the colt, which does not quiver, then takes it from the peasant and feeds it for some time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Ivan returns to the Tsar, announces that he has a horse, and begins preparations to visit the serpent.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Tsar asks Ivan how many men he needs; Ivan replies that he needs no men to get the horse but asks for half a dozen to send on messages, and the Tsar gives him six men.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Ivan and his six comrades travel until they reach a fiery river with a bridge over it and an enormous forest nearby, where they pitch a tent, obtain drink, and feast.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Ivan suggests that they stand guard every night in turn to see whether anyone passes the river, but each comrade who goes on guard becomes drunk in the evening and sees nothing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"When Ivan himself stands guard, he sees at midnight a three-headed serpent crossing the fiery river and hears it say that it has no enemy or calumniator except Ivan the peasant's son, whose bones the raven has not yet brought in a bladder.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Ivan springs from under the bridge, declares his presence, and agrees to make trial with the serpent, who advances on horseback while Ivan goes forth on foot.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Ivan strikes with his sabre and cuts off the three heads of the serpent, then takes the serpent's horse and ties it to the tent.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"On the next night Ivan kills a six-headed serpent and on the third night a nine-headed serpent, throwing their bodies into As a hero, he rides into the Tsars court, breaks twelve windows, and secretly kisses Tsarevna Priceless Beauty, who marks his forehead. He then returns home, reverses the transformation, and feigns illness. Seeking to discover her unknown suitor, the Tsarevna asks her father, the Tsar, to gather men from all ranks to a feast so she can look for the mark. She eventually discovers it on the simpletons forehead and faints; the Tsar declares that she must marry him, and her sisters mock her for taking a fool as husband.

The Tsar then sends his sons-in-law to acquire wonders: first a pig with gold bristles, then a deer with golden horns and tail. The two crafty sons-in-law take the best horses, while the simpleton rides a miserable horse, calls forth a wondrous bay steed, and transforms again via its ears. Two youths appear from the horse and instantly provide a tent, bed, and the pig with gold bristles walking outside. The crafty sons-in-law, unable to find the pig elsewhere, come upon the tent and buy the pig from the disguised hero at the price of each mans middle toe. They return with the pig to the Tsar, who rejoices, unaware of the simpletons role.

The simpleton then reverts to his foolish appearance, kills his horse, wears its skin, ties birds (magpies, crows, jackdaws, sparrows) around himself, and releases them in the palace, breaking many windows. The Tsarevna weeps, her sisters laugh, and the Tsar angrily threatens the clownish fool. He again sends his sons-in-law, including the simpleton, to seek a deer with golden horns and golden tail, and the simpleton once more summons the wondrous horse, transforms through its ears, and is From this they suspect that someone must be the ruler of the heavenly bodies who can stop their course at his will, and that he must be strong and mighty and must have existed before the heavenly bodies if he rules the prime elements.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","rights_note":"Public domain; Project Gutenberg edition, Anderson translation."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"lines 755-761","quote_or_summary":"They reason that if this ruler governs the course of the heavenly bodies, he must also rule the sunshine, the dew of the heavens, the products of the earth that follow them, the winds of the air, and the storms of the sea, thus ruling all things on earth and in the air, over the heavens and heavenly bodies, the seas and the weather. {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-volsunga-saga-morris-gutenberg-l7541-l7755","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/volsunga-saga-morris-magnusson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FRAGMENTS OF THE LAY OF BRYNHILD / THE SECOND OR ANCIENT LAY OF GUDRUN. / THE SONG OF ATLI. / THE WHETTING OF GUDRUN.; lines 7541-7755","start":"7541","end":"7755","translation":"The Story of the Volsungs (Volsunga Saga); with Excerpts from the Poetic Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After Gudrun has slain Atli, she goes to the sea intending to end her life, but cannot drown; the waters carry her over the firths to the land of King Jonakr, who marries her. Their sons are Sorli, Erp, and Hamdir, and Sigurd’s daughter Swanhild is brought up there and later given to Jormunrek. Jormunrek’s man Bikki advises the king’s son Randver to take Swanhild; when Randver follows this counsel, Bikki informs the king, who has Randver hanged and orders Swanhild trampled under horses’ feet. Hearing of this, Gudrun fiercely incites her sons to avenge their sister, reproaching them by comparison with her heroic brothers Gunnar and Hogni and the kings of the Huns. Hamdir answers that she once condemned Hogni when Sigurd was slain and that she herself has wrought terrible vengeance by killing her own sons, which prevented all the brothers together from taking vengeance on Jormunrek. Nonetheless he accepts her urging, asks for war gear, and predicts that he and his brothers will not return. Gudrun laughs as she brings out helmets and mail-coats, and the heroes load their horses for the journey. 

Gudrun then sits in the forecourt and utters a long lament. She says she has known three hearths and three husbands and that Sigurd alone was better than all of them, though her brothers brought about his death. She recalls how being given to Atli increased her torment, how she sought compensation for her sorrow through her sons but finally took vengeance by cutting off the heads of the Niblungs. She describes going down to the sea in anger against the Norns, intending to free herself from their torment by drowning, but the high waves would not drown her and instead bore her to land, after which she married her third husband, the king Jonakr, and bore him sons. She recalls Swanhild, dearest of her children, sitting among bond‑maidens in the hall like a sunbeam, how she arrayed her in gold and fine clothing before giving her to the Goths, and how her hardest woe was seeing Swanhild’s bright hair trodden into the mire by horses. Gudrun further remembers Sigurd’s bloody death in bed, Gunnar being killed as serpents tore his heart, and Hogni’s heart being cut. Overwhelmed by many griefs, she questions why she should live any longer. 

Gudrun calls for Sigurd’s coal‑black horse to be bridled and sent swiftly to her, grieving that she has no more sons or daughters to receive her gifts. She recalls a former conversation with Sigurd when they lay together, in which he promised he would come to her from the hall of Hell and she to him from the fair earth. She then commands the earls to build her the highest oaken funeral pyre ever for a queen and to let the fire swiftly burn and melt her sorrow‑laden heart. The poem closes with a wish that all earls may be improved in mind and that maidens’ grief may be lessened by hearing this tale of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l2751-l2902","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON. / WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH.; lines 2751-2902","start":"2751","end":"2902","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An aged Tsar in an unnamed kingdom dreams that beyond the \"thrice ninth land\" in the distant thirtieth kingdom there is a beautiful maiden from whose hands and feet flows healing water that makes anyone who drinks it thirty years younger. His counsellors cannot explain the dream, so his three sons volunteer to seek the maiden. The eldest, Dmitri Tsarevich, takes a vast army and journeys for months into deserted regions until he reaches a towering mountain. On its summit he finds an ancient gray old man, who tells him that the road to the maiden crosses three broad rivers with ferries where the ferrymen will cut off his right hand, his left foot, and finally his head. Dmitri, unwilling to risk his life, turns back and reports failure to his father. The second son, Vassili Tsarevich, likewise takes an army, travels into forests and swamps, and encounters Baba-Yaga \"boneleg.\" She confirms the existence of the maiden with healing water and warns him of the same three ferries and their deadly prices; he too returns, saying he must spare his own head. The youngest son, Ivan Tsarevich, asks only for a good steed and the sword Kládyenets, refusing troops or treasure. He rides into regions where his horse is knee-deep in water and breast-high in grass, and he has nothing to eat, until he finds a cabin on hen's feet inhabited by Baba-Yaga. She recognizes him by name, repeats the warning about the three ferries, and urges him to turn back because he is still a \"green youth.\" Ivan replies that \"one head is not much\" and insists on continuing. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l2579-l2717","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"RUSSIAN MYTHS AND FOLK-TALES. / THE THREE KINGDOMS,--THE COPPER, THE SILVER, AND THE GOLDEN. / IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON.; lines 2579-2717","start":"2579","end":"2717","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"I want a tent here, in the tent a bed, and at the side of the tent the golden-maned steed with golden tail.\"","summary":"In this passage the simpleton, aided by a magical steed and two youths, repeatedly conjures a tent, bed, and wondrous golden animals in an open field. The Tsar’s crafty sons-in-law, travelling to obtain these beasts for their father-in-law, encounter the tent and purchase the animals from the simpleton at the cost of their own body parts: first their middle fingers for a deer with golden horns and tail, then straps cut from their backs for a golden-maned steed with golden tail. The sons-in-law bring the animals to the Tsar and receive halves of the kingdom, while the simpleton, who reverts to his usual foolish appearance by creeping through the ear of his horse or steed, appears at the palace disguised in the skin of his wretched horse and covered in birds that he releases, causing chaos. Mocked and threatened by the Tsar, he finally declares that he obtained the pig with gold bristles, the golden deer, and the golden-maned steed for the Tsar and asks that the sons-in-law be ordered to remove their boots, which they resist, hinting at concealed bodily marks from their bargains.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"After the the tent.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The deer is described as having golden horns and a golden tail.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The crafty brothers, identified as sons-in-law, travel with the aim of finding such a deer to please their father-in-law, the Tsar.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The sons-in-law come upon the tent, see the deer, salute the simpleton, and ask him to sell them the deer with golden horns and a golden tail.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The simpleton refuses to sell the deer, saying he wants it himself, and does not accept offers of one, two, three thousand rubles and more.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The simpleton agrees to sell the deer only on condition that he receives the middle finger of each man’s hand as payment.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The sons-in-law remove their gloves, allow the simpleton to cut off their middle fingers, after which he puts the fingers away and gives them the deer.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The sons-in-law return home with the deer with golden horns and a golden tail, and the Tsar is so joyful that he does not know how to address, seat, or entertain them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When the Tsar asks whether directions.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"At the palace, the Tsarevna, the simpleton’s wife, sobs while her sisters laugh, saying that their husbands brought land.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The crafty sons-in-law saddle the very best horses and depart on their journey, while the Tsar also sends the fool, who takes the very last wretched horse from the stable and follows them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In the open field, the simpleton cries out to a wishes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The simpleton asks for a tent with a bed inside and for the golden-maned steed with golden tail at the side of the tent, and immediately the tent with bed and the golden-maned steed with golden tail appear.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The crafty sons-in-law travel without {"record_id":"batch.motif.norse-prose-edda-anderson-gutenberg-l763-l838","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/norse/project-gutenberg/younger-edda-anderson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INDEX                                          291 / THE YOUNGER EDDA. / INTRODUCTION. / FOREWORD.; lines 763-838","start":"763","end":"838","translation":"The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents a universal history segment: in his old age Noah divides the world among his three sons. As their descendants grow skilled and proud, Africans descended from Ham conquer the offspring of Shem and, finding the world too small, begin building a tower of tile and stone on the plain of Sennar to reach heaven. God, seeing their pride, frustrates the project not by destroying them but by confounding their speech so they cannot understand one another, causing strife and the abandonment of the tower. Their leader, Zoroaster, who laughed before he wept at birth, oversees seventy-two master-smiths, and from this event seventy-two languages spread over the world as giants and nations disperse. On the same spot the famous city Babylon is built, taking its name from the tower. After the confusion of tongues, the number of names for people and things multiplies, and Zoroaster himself has many names. Though his pride was humbled, he gains great worldly power, becomes king over many Assyrian peoples, and is described as the originator of idolatry; when worshiped he is called Baal or Bel. As names multiply, truth is lost and people across the world begin to worship their leaders, animals, birds, the air, heavenly bodies, and inanimate things. Only speakers of Hebrew—the language that existed before the tower—still know their maker, though they lack spiritual wisdom and judge with merely earthly understanding, thinking everything is made from a single material.

The narrator then outlines a tripartite geography: the world is divided into Africa (from the south westward to the Mediterranean, with a scorched southern zone), Europe or Enea (from west to north and to the sea, with an uninhabitable cold northern part), and Asia (from the north around the east to the south). Asia is said to contain all beauty, splendor, and material wealth, including gold and precious stones, and within it lies the "mid-world," where the land is fairest and the inhabitants are most richly endowed with gifts, including wisdom, strength, beauty, and knowledge.

Near the middle of the world, in the land called Turkey, stands Troy, described as the most famous house and inn ever built. The city is larger and more skillfully constructed than others, built at great expense. It encompasses twelve kingdoms under one over-king; many lands and nations belong to each kingdom, and there are twelve chief languages in the city. The chiefs of Troy are said to surpass all other men in heroic deeds, and rulers of the northern regions trace their ancestry back to them, counting all rulers of Troy among the gods. In particular, Priamos is placed in the stead of Odin, and is said to descend from Saturn, whom northern people once believed to be God On learning of the raid and his daughter’s abduction, Hogne gathers his army and pursues Hedin by land and sea to Norway and then to the Orkneys, where Hedin is found at the island Ha. Hild goes to meet her father there, offering him a necklace from Hedin as a gesture of reconciliation and warning that Hedin will give no quarter if peace is refused; Hogne responds harshly and rejects the offer. Hild reports this to Hedin and urges him to prepare for battle. Both sides land on the island and marshal their forces. Hedin replies proudly about the sword, and the battle called Hjadninga-vig begins; they fight all day before returning to their ships at night. That night Hild goes to the battlefield and, by sorcery, awakens all the fallen warriors. The next day the kings and all who had fallen the day before fight again. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l3286-l3418","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"IVAN TSAREVICH, THE FIRE-BIRD, AND THE GRAY WOLF. / THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON. / WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH. / THE FOOTLESS AND BLIND CHAMPIONS.; lines 3286-3418","start":"3286","end":"3418","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two maimed heroes discuss how Anna the Beautiful blinded one of them and cut off the other's feet. Living together in a forest, they cooperate by having the blind man carry his footless companion, who directs the way, and they hunt for game. The footless hero proposes abducting a charitable merchant's daughter to be their housekeeper. The blind man brings his companion to town in a wagon; the merchant's daughter comes out to give alms and is seized and carried to the heroes' forest hut. They ask her to be like a sister and keep house, and she agrees, cooking and washing while they hunt. A Baba-Yaga (boneleg) secretly visits the hut whenever the heroes are away, making the maiden search her head and then sucking her blood, so that she grows thin and wasted. Uncle Katoma notices something wrong, and after questioning, the maiden confesses the visits of the blood-sucking old woman, whom the blind hero identifies as Baba-Yaga. They plan a trap: the footless hero hides under a bench, the blind waits outside, and the maiden sits in the window, passes the witch's hair outside, and the blind man seizes Baba-Yaga by her gray locks. Katoma throws himself on her \"like a stone mountain\" and smothers her. Instead of immediately burning her, they accept her plea for mercy and compel her to show them a well of \"living and healing\" water. She leads them deep into the forest to a well, but when Katoma tests it by throwing in a green branch, the branch bursts into flame before touching the water, revealing a fiery, destructive well. After renewed threats, Baba-Yaga swears not to deceive and guides them to another well. This time a dry branch thrown in buds, becomes green, and blossoms. The blind hero moistens his eyes with the water and regains sight; the footless is lowered into the well and his feet grow back. The heroes rejoice, then return to the fiery well and throw Baba-Yaga into it so she dies. Uncle Katoma marries the merchant's daughter, and together with the blind hero they travel to the kingdom of Anna the Beautiful to liberate Ivan Tsarevich, whom they see near the capital driving a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l1984-l2085","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTION / THE TRIAL OF LOVERS: / THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE / THE POOR TURKEY GIRL; lines 1984-2085","start":"1984","end":"2085","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A flock of Turkeys invite the poor \"Turkey girl\" into their house and magically renew each of her ragged garments into beautiful clothing, then cleanse and beautify her. An old Turkey produces rich ornaments, explaining the birds have gathered small valuables lost by people. They warn the maiden to remember them, leave their wicket open, and not tarry too long at the dance when her fortunes change. She gratefully promises and hurries along the river path to Zuñi, where her beauty and fine dress astonish the people. Chiefs invite her into the ceremonial dance, and the finest youths compete to dance with her. Delighted, she keeps dancing, deciding to stay longer so no one discovers who she is, intending to return just before sunset. But she dances through multiple rounds until after sunset, then suddenly runs back toward the Turkeys. Meanwhile the Turkeys, concluding she has forgotten them and is unworthy, decide to leave captivity. Led by a gray old Gobbler, they troop out, calling to each other as they run toward the Cañon of the Cottonwoods, behind Thunder Mountain, through the Gateway of Zuñi, and up the valley.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Turkeys, after returning home of their own accord, invite the maiden to enter their house and sit down, asking her to give them her articles of clothing so they can try to renew them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The maiden removes her ragged mantle, and an old Gobbler spreads it out, picks at it, tramps and struts over it, then lays it down transformed into a beautiful white embroidered cotton mantle.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Other Gobblers in turn receive each of the maiden’s garments and similarly renew them until all her clothing is as beautiful as that of wealthy women of Mátsaki.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Before she puts on the renewed garments, the Turkeys circle around the maiden, singing, clucking, and brushing her with their wings until she becomes clean, with smooth bright skin, soft wavy hair, full dimpled cheeks, and dancing eyes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Seeing her transformation, the maiden realizes that the Turkeys’ previous assurances about improving her state were true, and she feels joyful.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"An old Turkey tells her that only rich ornaments are lacking, claiming the Turkeys have keen eyes and have gathered many small precious things that men and maidens lose.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The old Turkey coughs up a beautiful necklace, and other Turkeys produce earrings and additional ornaments from their beaks, laying them at the maiden’s feet until she has all the adornments of a well-clad maiden of old.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Turkeys address her as \"maiden mother\" and warn her to leave the wicket open, to remember them when her fortunes change, not to be ashamed of having been their caretaker, and not to tarry too long away from them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The maiden thanks the Turkeys Ralston then summarizes a widely known European story about a soldier who, for a term of years, refrains from washing, shaving, or combing his hair while serving or obeying the devil, and is rewarded with great wealth. Because of his filthy appearance he has trouble finding a bride: elder sisters in a family refuse him, but the youngest accepts, after which he allows himself to be cleaned and lives happily. A Russian version is then described in more detail. An unwashed soldier lends a large sum to an impoverished king who cannot pay his troops, and in return asks for one of the king’s daughters in marriage. The king, torn between his daughters and his need for the money, has the soldier’s portrait painted exactly as he looks and shows it to his three daughters. The eldest calls the monstrous figure in the picture so repulsive that she would rather marry the devil; an actual devil standing behind her records her soul. The second daughter also declares she would rather have the devil and remain an old maid than marry the soldier; her soul is recorded as well. The youngest daughter, compared to Cordelia, agrees to marry the man who helped her father, resigning herself to fate and God’s will.

While preparations for the marriage proceed, the soldier’s term of service to a "little devil" ends. At his request, the little devil cuts the soldier into pieces, boils them in a cauldron, reassembles his body bone by bone and vein by vein, sprinkles him with the Waters of Life and Death, and the soldier arises as an exceptionally handsome young man. The little devil returns to the lake from which he came, where his "grandfather" among the demons angrily rebukes him for failing to ensnare the soldier’s soul and for wasting money, and orders him thrown into boiling pitch. The imp protests that he has booked two souls instead—the elder princesses who preferred the devil to the soldier. On hearing this explanation, the grandfather concedes he is right and releases him, praising his competence.

In a footnote, Ralston cites the Grimm tales "Des Teufels russiger Bruder" and "Der Bärenhäuter" as German versions of this story. He also summarizes an Indian tale transmitted to China by Hiouen-Thsang: a Rishi spends tens of thousands of years in religious ecstasy until his body becomes like a withered tree. On awakening, he wishes to marry and asks a king for one of his daughters. The embarrassed king gathers his hundred daughters and asks who will accept the dreaded, unkempt suitor. Ninety-nine refuse, but the youngest agrees to sacrifice herself for her father’s sake. He performs the prescribed actions and the youths revive, turning the community’s grief into rejoicing. The soldier then orders the village headman (Starosta) to gather the peasants and collect a hundred loads of aspen wood. They carry the wood to the graveyard, drag the warlock’s corpse from its grave, place it on a pyre, and set it alight while standing in a circle armed with tools. As the corpse burns it bursts open, releasing snakes, worms, other reptiles, and flying birds (crows, magpies, jackdaws). The peasants kill these creatures and throw them into the fire, allowing nothing, not even a maggot, to escape. The warlock is completely consumed; the soldier gathers the ashes and scatters them to the wind, after which the village remains at peace. The grateful community rewards and thanks the soldier. He enjoys a period at home, then returns to the Tsar’s service with money, and finally retires from the army to live comfortably. \n\nRalston then comments that such stories are numerous and rest on a belief that, in some cases, the dead in bodily form leave their graves to destroy and prey upon the living. Drawing on Hertz, he contrasts peoples who burn their dead—among whom only vague ghostly apparitions are thought to emerge from graves containing ashes—with peoples who bury the corpse, among whom a kind of ‘half-life’ is attributed to the body, sometimes thought to be driven by murderous impulses or by possession by an evil spirit. He states that belief in vampires is the specifically Slavonic form of a universal belief in spectres and notes that vampire tales flourish especially among Slavonic-speaking peoples (in Russia, Poland, Servia, Bohemia, Slovakia, etc.) and in regions influenced by them, including parts of Germany, Albania, and modern Greece. He summarizes scholarly debate over whether Greek vampire beliefs and terminology derive from Slavonic influence or from continuities with ancient Greek traditions of blood-loving or destructive spectres (such as Homeric shades, Gello, or the spectres of Medea’s murdered children). Finally, he notes that within the Russian Empire belief in vampires is strongest in White Russia and the Ukraine, where the blood-sucking Upir is especially feared, though related beliefs are The maiden supports them by tending small gardens of beans, squashes, melons, and corn, but they have barely enough food to subsist and cannot barter for meat. In winter snow falls, and she watches town youths go out well-equipped with deerskin stockings, stone axes, and rabbit-sticks, returning with strings of rabbits. Wishing she were a man so she could hunt for her parents, she resolves to go hunting herself despite being a woman. The young men are unfriendly because she has rejected their offers of marriage. That evening she tells her parents her plan to use the old rabbit-sticks and axes stored in the house to hunt rabbits in the snow. Her mother and father object, fearing cold, exhaustion, and that she may lose her way, but the father finally agrees to help since she will not be dissuaded. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-archive-l982-l1225","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/bird-parliament-attar-fitzgerald.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Bird Parliament; lines 982-1225","start":"982","end":"1225","translation":"Bird Parliament","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Shah returns to his capital amid festival, ignoring rich gifts from his subjects but stopping at the public prison where prisoners greet him by rolling severed heads over the wall; he rewards them and explains that the grisly sight proves his law has been carried out, whereas jewel-strewn welcomes are hypocritical display. An unseen ring-dove repeatedly coos the name \"Yusuf\" until a voice rebukes her, recalling how Jacob’s excessive mourning for Yusuf drew divine displeasure: a Bird of Heaven tells Jacob that God is weary of Yusuf’s name, a later vision of Yusuf in a distant field elicits only a suppressed sigh, yet a stern angel declares even that sigh contained the forbidden word, and Jacob’s over-passionate grief blinds his eyes. Other birds appear with many excuses, their souls fixed on earthly food rather than heavenly fasting. A small, modest bird addresses Tajidar, acknowledging his wisdom and vision of the Presence behind the veil but confessing the flock’s weakness and fear that they cannot reach the Mountain or be noticed by the glorious Symurgh, enthroned like Sulayman while they are but pismires. Tajidar compassionately teaches that all beings are shadows of a single divine Light and Fount of Being from which they cannot be separated and to which they must return, warns against confusing created forms with the Creator, contrasts the seeker straining beyond outward life with the worldling clinging to matter, and urges purification of the breast as a mysterious mirror able to bear and reflect God’s image without distortion or sin.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A Shah returning to his capital finds it dressed in festival, with subjects thronging streets and squares in acclamation.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Shah’s subjects kneel and fling jewels and gold before his horse as a welcome.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Shah rides past the costly offerings with scarcely a glance.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At the public prison, prisoners who lack pearls or gold roll severed heads and carcasses over the wall as a grim welcome, gold among the prisoners, and then rides on.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"One of the Shah’s train wonders why he ignored those who sued with costly gifts but smiled at the ghastly welcome from the prisoners.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Shah answers that pearls and gold only display ostentatious welcome from hypocrites with more stored at home, whereas the severed heads and trunks show his law strictly executed and his will done rather than talked about.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"From a wood an unseen ring-dove continually coos the broken name \"Yusuf\" over and over until she becomes blinds his aged eyes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After this, others come with endless arguments, enquiries, and excuses—ultimately sloth, folly, or deceit—with souls cast in the common figure of earthly food rather than heavenly fasting.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A small, rare bird of modest plumage food.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The small bird asks how such weak birds can reach the Mountain and, if they arrive, how the Symurgh, dwelling alone in glory like Sulayman on his throne, could stoop to hear or see them, calling themselves pismires at his feet and unlike him in folly, woe, death, and sin.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Tajidar, whose voice rises in compassion for the bewildered birds, tells them they are long lost in exile yet cannot be parted from the Fount of Being from which they came and to which they must, for good or evil, flow back.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Tajidar describes the the flood, and all that walk between, from lion to the least pismire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Tajidar calls all such beings authentic shadows of God and prayer.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"He warns against confounding the copy with the divine Type or drowning deity in deity, likening union to pure content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l13320-l13455","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER V. / GHOST STORIES.; lines 13320-13455","start":"13320","end":"13455","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A series of vampire and ghost legends is presented. In the first, an animated corpse instructs a moujik to cut off part of its shroud and burn it on live coals in the house where two lads have been murdered so that the smoke will revive them; after the moujik succeeds and is briefly suspected, the villagers open the grave and stake the corpse so it cannot rise again. A narrator notes that such vampires, or animated corpses, also lurk at crossroads and near cemeteries to attack travelers. In the tale of “The Two Corpses,” a soldier returning home at night is chased by a corpse to a chapel where another corpse lies on a table; the two corpses argue over which will eat the soldier and fight until cockcrow, when they fall lifeless and the soldier goes home praising God. In “The Dog and the Corpse,” a moujik hunting with his dog meets a hovering corpse in a white shroud at a crossroads by a graveyard; the dog fights the corpse while the master flees, the corpse collapses at cockcrow, and later the resentful dog attacks its master until his mother explains it is angry at being abandoned.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A corpse tells a moujik to cut off the left skirt of its shroud, burn it on live coals in a pot in the house where some youngsters were killed, and says the lads will be revived by the smoke.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The moujik cuts off the left skirt of the corpse’s shroud, returns the coffin-lid, and sees the grave open; as the dead man descends, the cocks begin to crow, and the corpse does not get fully covered, leaving one end of the coffin-lid sticking out of the ground.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At dawn the moujik drives into a village, hears cries in a house, and finds two dead lads inside; he tells their relatives he can bring them to life, and they promise him half of all they possess if he does so.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The moujik performs the ritual as instructed by the corpse, burning the shroud piece on live coals, and the lads come back to life.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the lads revive, their delighted relatives seize the moujik, bind him with cords, and plan to hand him over to the authorities, reasoning that if he knew how to bring them back to life he might also have killed them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The moujik explains what happened with the corpse during the night; the villagers assemble, go to the graveyard, identify the grave the dead man came from, open it, and drive an aspen stake through the corpse’s heart so it may no more rise up and slay, then reward the moujik richly and honor him.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The narrator states that a vampire, described as an animated corpse, is dangerous not only during sleep but also lurks at cross-roads or near cemeteries watching for unwary wayfarers to slay and eat.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A soldier obtains leave to go home on furlough to pray to holy images and bow down before his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l476-l600","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"A HOPI (MOKI) MAIDEN                                   184 / THE PINNACLES OF THUNDER MOUNTAIN                      344 / INTRODUCTION / THE TRIAL OF LOVERS:; lines 476-600","start":"476","end":"600","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In ancient times at Mátsaki, or Salt City, founded where the Goddess of Salt made a white lake, a priest-chief has a very beautiful daughter whom many young men desire. A young man from the distant Pueblo of the Winds falls in love with her, gathers fine gifts, and travels at sunset to her father’s house. Climbing the decorated ladder to the roof opening, he calls down and is brought inside by the girl’s mother. Seated by the fire, he greets the family formally. Following custom, the maiden serves him delicate corn-wafer bread, and he eats only a little out of politeness. The girl’s father then asks his purpose, and the youth states that he has come because of their daughter. After the older sons depart, the father asks the girl’s opinion; she answers that it may be well if her parents think so. When the parents lie down to sleep, the maiden quietly tells the suitor that before she accepts his gifts and lives with him he must prove his love by going to her corn-field, within her father’s lands by the river, and hoeing all the corn in a single morning. She shows him a room with soft bedding, places her father’s hoe by the door, and bids him wait till morning. Confident, he rises at dawn, takes the wooden hoe, and runs to the corn-fields. As the sun comes up, the girl watches from the roof, sees that he is working, but thinks skeptically that she and her future children will later see how well he has done and doubts that he loves her as much as he believes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The story is set 'in the days of the ancients' in the town of Mátsaki, called Salt City because the Goddess of Salt made a white lake there when the world was new.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In Mátsaki there is a very beautiful maiden, described as 'passing beautiful,' who is the daughter of the priest-chief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The priest-chief owns many buckskins and blankets, has house port-holes covered with turquoises and ocean shells, and offers many sacrifices to the gods.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The priest-chief’s house is the largest in Mátsaki, with tall ladder-poles decorated with carved wooden slabs, emphasizing his status.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Because of the maiden’s beauty and her father’s status, all the young men in the surrounding towns are in love with her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A young man living across the western plains in the Pueblo of the Winds is filled with thoughts of the maiden of Mátsaki and does not favor any girl of his own pueblo.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The young man labors to gather presents—mantles and necklaces—which he rolls up in his best, whitest buckskin.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"At sunset the young man starts toward Mátsaki, reaches the house of the maiden’s father as people are gathering to smoke and talk, climbs the house ladder, and calls down through the roof opening.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The young man asks to be pulled down and shows his bundle through the sky-hole; the maiden’s mother helps him descend the ladder into the house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Inside the house, in the fire-light, the young man lays down his bundle and greets the household respectfully as 'my fathers and mothers, my sisters and friends,' asking after their well-being.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The family replies that they are happy and invites the young man to sit on a stool placed for him in the fire-light.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The old man (priest-chief) reminds his daughter that when a stranger enters the house, the girl should place food and cooked things before him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The maiden brings fresh rolls of thin paper-like corn-flour bread (héwe) from a large vessel and sets them in a tray before the visitor where the light falls on them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The maiden tells the visitor to eat; he replies 'It is well,' sits straight, places his left hand on his breast, and eats only a very small amount with his right hand.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The narrator explains that it is considered impolite to eat much when visiting a strange girl, especially if one intends to ask to live in the same house with her.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When the elders urge him to eat more, the young man declines, saying he is 'past the naming of want,' and the family concludes he has eaten; the maiden removes the tray and sweeps away the crumbs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After a short time, the old man remarks that a stranger does not enter another’s house without a purpose and asks the young man why he has come.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The young man says he has heard of and seen their daughter and that thoughts of her are the reason he came.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The grown-up sons who had come to smoke and chat decide it is time to go home, comment that the stars must be out, bid the elders a happy night, shake the young man’s hand, and go to the homes of their wives’ mothers.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"After the sons leave, the old man addresses his daughter, asks if she has heard what the young man said, and asks for her thoughts.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The daughter replies that she does not know what else to say but 'Be it well' if that is how her elders think.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The old man responds 'As you may,' then smokes a cigarette with the young man and later asks the mother if it is time to lie down to sleep; the old couple lie down in a corner of the room.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"After the parents are asleep, the girl quietly tells the Unable to reach their food and with their granaries empty, the prairie-dogs grow lean and desperate. Their grandfathers call a council at the base of the Burrowing-owl’s mountain; the chief spokesman laments the ‘wretched rainers’ who flood their fields, and after futile plans a wise gray-cheeked elder suggests appealing to their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl. Chosen as messenger, he climbs the mound and respectfully calls to the owl, who emerges in bad humor but listens. The prairie-dog explains their trouble, and the owl, identifying himself as a priest, promises four days of fasting, meditation, and sacred labors to help stop the rain. The next morning he directs his wife to cook a large quantity of small ill-smelling beans, then hunts and captures an ill-smelling beetle. As the unceasing rain keeps them from leaving their holes, they grow very hungry and lean and can hardly get about.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:5","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (council called)","quote_or_summary":"The old prairie-dogs, or grandfathers, call a great council by coming out of their houses, standing on the mounds before their sky-holes, and crying “Wek wek” so that the women and children exclaim that the old ones are calling a council, and everyone gathers round the base of the Burrowing-owl’s mountain.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (chief spokesman’s speech and failed plans)","quote_or_summary":"At the council, the chief spokesman complains that the ‘wretched rainers’ keep dropping water until the mitäliko fields are flooded, reminds the prairie-dogs that they are short of leg and cannot go into lakes to gather food, and describes their women dying and children crying. He asks how they can stop the rain. The council talks and devises many plans, but these are considered futile and some have already been tried.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (elder’s suggestion and messenger appointment)","quote_or_summary":"A wise old gray-cheeked prairie-dog suggests that they apply to their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl, who lives in the top of the mountain. The council cries “Hear! hear!” and the elder who spoke is chosen as messenger to the Burrowing-owl.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:8","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (messenger climbs and calls)","quote_or_summary":"The chosen elder climbs to the top of the mountain with many rests, sits down at a respectful distance from the owl’s doorway, raises himself on his haunches, folds his hands across his breast, and calls out “Wek wek.”","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:9","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (Burrowing-owl’s response as priest)","quote_or_summary":"The old Burrowing-owl, not in good humor, steps out blinking and says it is not the prairie-dogs’ custom to come to his house making such a racket, then asks their message. The elder explains that the council has sought to stop the irrepressible rainers but all efforts have failed, so they turn to him. The owl replies that he is a priest, tells the elder to go home, and says he will see what he can do, setting aside four days for fasting, meditation, and sacred labors and asking them to await the result.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:10","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (owl instructs wife to cook beans)","quote_or_summary":"The next morning, the Burrowing-owl tells his wife to put on a large quantity of beans of the small, unpleasant-smelling kind and cook them well, then bids her good morning and leaves the house.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:11","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (owl finds ill-smelling beetle)","quote_or_summary":"The Burrowing-owl spends a long time hunting at the roots of bushes and eventually finds an ill-smelling beetle with its head stuck down among the roots. He grabs the beetle, despite the creature’s remonstrances, and takes him home.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:12","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (owl reassures beetle)","quote_or_summary":"At home, the Burrowing-owl tells the beetle he is making a great fuss but will not be harmed except by being presented with all the food he can eat. The beetle, called Tip-beetle, exclaims “Bless me!” and sits down, relieved and contented.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:13","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (first bowls of beans for beetle)","quote_or_summary":"The Burrowing-owl tells his wife to lay out a dish of beans on the floor; she complies. He invites the Tip-beetle to fall to and satisfy himself. The beetle eats, swallows, and gulps until he empties the dish and begins to grow quite large. The owl then orders another large bowl of bean soup, which the beetle likewise gulps until it is gone.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."},{"id":"ev:14","type":"summary","locator":"lines 7890-8004 (beetle still wants more food)","quote_or_summary":"After eating two large bowls of beans and looking like a well-blown-up paunch, the Tip-beetle responds to the owl’s question about his capacity by saying he still has somewhat left and, with a little more, believes he will be satisfied. The owl asks his wife for a little more.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain text from Project Gutenberg."}],"confidence":{"extraction":"medium","motif_candidates":"medium","comparison_claims":"uncertain","notes":"Motif and symbol extraction is based on a single passage that ends before the outcome of the Burrowing-owl’s sacred labors is revealed; some motif alignments (such as world_center or sacred_exchange) are inferential and may need confirmation from the broader narrative context."},"reviewer_status":{"status":"needs_review","reviewer":"","reviewed_at":"","notes":"Automated initial extraction; requires human expert review for cultural and contextual accuracy."},"extracted_by":"atlas-llm-gpt4.1","extracted_at":"2026-07-18","notes":"This record covers only the portion of the tale up to the beetle being repeatedly fed beans; later developments in the story may introduce additional motifs or clarify the function of the owl’s actions that are not visible in this excerpt."}

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-archive-l786-l980","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/bird-parliament-attar-fitzgerald.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Bird Parliament; lines 786-980","start":"786","end":"980","translation":"Bird Parliament","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this section of the poem, a jewel-loving bird boasts of digging and swallowing rubies from the mountain that inflame his desire. The Tajidar (Leader) rebukes him, calling jewels and gold dead, enslaving, and treacherous, and illustrates his point with the story of Sulayman (Solomon), whose tiny signet jewel gave him power over sea, land, winds, angels, and fiends until God removed it and gave it to a demon, humiliating the king. Next, the Shah-Falcon boasts of being the king’s hooded companion on the ring-bearing fist and refuses to leave royal company; the Leader warns that mortal kings are changeable and dangerous like fire and tells of a Shah’s beloved slave who, despite lavish treatment, lives in terror because the king daily proves his archery by splitting an apple on her head. The Phoenix then declares he will not serve kings whose crowns are only the shadow of his wings; this leads into a story of a dead Sultan appearing in a dream to his vizier, rejecting royal titles, acknowledging one true Shah above who lends and recalls glory, regretting his kingship, and wishing he had lived as a poor laborer. Finally, a dapper Duck prides himself on ritual ablutions and spotless feathers, claiming superior religious purity, but the Leader angrily denounces his pride and hypocrisy, insisting that despite outer cleanliness his inner ‘maw’ is unclean and that the Maker of maw and feather sees through all and will take account.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A bird describes himself as crimson with rubies and says he stabs the ground with his spurs for rubies, which he swallows even though the sparks burn his beak and eyes, because the rubies burn with inward light and make their owners lords of their desire.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The rubies are described as having ‘blood within’ and as growing and being nourished in the ‘Mountain Heart of Stone.’","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Tajidar replies that both pebbles and gold are equally dead while they lie in their mountain mine and become dangerous to those who make them shine.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Tajidar says jewels slavishly obey their lord’s commands yet are prone to escape his hands and then serve a second master, working their wonders for the worst.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sulayman is said to have worn a signet jewel, a ruby scarcely a grain in weight, by which he constrained sea and land and all that is in them.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"With his jewel and ring, Sulayman made the fierce east wind bear his vast pavilion, held a good angel subject, and compelled a lower fiend.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In his pride Sulayman prays that after him no ‘Son of Clay’ should ever touch his glory, thereby overtaxing the fountain that supplied his power.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Almighty God takes Sulayman’s jewel and gives it to a Div, who, wearing the ring and the king’s resemblance, rules for forty days in a way that shames Sulayman’s forty He persuades the old Bear, Broadfoot (his grandfather), to jump into the pit to share the feast, then laughs and reveals that they are stuck. To avoid being eaten by the angry Bear, Coyote whispers a plan: they will sing and feast loudly to attract other creatures. Their revelry draws almost every corn-pest from the fields to the pit. Coyote feigns reluctance while Bear urges the pests to join them, and the animals rush into the hole until it is packed with scrambling, snarling creatures. Coyote then climbs over Bear and the other pests, escapes from the pit, and runs off laughing. The next morning, a young man comes to the maiden’s corn-field, hears a racket, and discovers the pit half full of exhausted and struggling pests that have been destroying her corn. He ironically addresses them as friends, throws dry wood into the hole, lights it, and burns them, noting that Coyote is not among them and observing that one kind of pest can be fought, but not many. The young man reports his success to the girl, who is delighted and asks whether all the pests were trapped. He truthfully admits that all were there except Coyote. She replies that she does not care about Coyote and would rather marry a man with ingenuity than see all coyotes killed, and she accepts the ugly but clever young man as her husband. The narrator adds that ever since then pretty girls care little about their husbands’ looks, preferring resourceful men, and that rich girls tend to marry poor young men while rich young men favor poor girls. That night the boys share one robe \"like a man and his wife,\" giggling and quarrelling until the grandmother threatens them with her pudding-stick and they finally fall asleep. By morning the sun is already high when the grandmother finishes watering her garden and sits on the rooftop watching the trail for them. Discovering them still asleep and snoring indoors, she shakes them awake, calling them lazy and sarcastically addressing them as fine sprouters and warriors. The boys pretend drowsy ignorance though they know the time; they are described as very dirty yet actually the handsomest of children, simply fooling their grandmother. She tells them they should wash at the spring at sunrise. They feign surprise that the sun is out, but then abruptly seize bows and quivers, rush out half-dressed without eating, and leap down the crags like mountain goats. Assuming they are merely playing among the rocks, the grandmother goes back to her cooking. He enters their house politely, is initially slighted by the father, but the girl herself serves him rich food. He shares his bread with her, which pleases her and leads the father to treat him more favorably than past visitors. After the parents fall asleep, the maiden tells him she has a corn-field on the priest-chief's land by the river and sets a trial of love and manhood: he must hoe the entire field in a single morning, after which they may live happily together. That night, under the stars, the youth prays to the gods of woodlands and waters for strength and for the power of his prayer-medicine, scattering a meal of seeds and waters to the night-wind as an offering before sleeping. At dawn he takes the father's hoe, goes to the field, and hoes so vigorously where previous workers left off that the soil flies like from gopher burrows. The maiden sees his progress but waits. As he sweats in the heat, he strips off his clothing, then rubs his entire body with the bark of finger-root from tall yellow-tops by the field. Meanwhile, the doubtful yet hopeful maiden opens a jar holding her \"strange children\"—stinging insects hungry for blood—and commands them to test him as they did earlier suitors. The insects swarm over the field like a sandstorm and buzz around the young man, who keeps working and imagines they are biting. In fact, the first may-fly to bite finds the taste of his skin disgusting because of the finger-root and warns the others, who refuse to bite and only hum around his ears. The narrator concludes that this is why may-flies still dance in the air before deciding whom to Whenever it rains or the dew falls, he comes to her, and in due time she bears a son, to the surprise of the townspeople who cannot see her divine husband. The boy, child of the gods, grows with miraculous speed, speaking and running within days and soon behaving like a much older child. He climbs to rooftops, runs through the plaza, and hunts birds and small animals using only his hands and stones, always successful, so that his mother’s house has more plumes for sacrifice than any other. Observing that older men of the tribe use bows and arrows, whose arrows fly faster and straighter and can kill larger animals, he repeatedly asks his mother where such wood and arrow-shafts are found. Afraid something will happen to him, she resists but finally tells him of a hollow in the rocks on the eastern side of Thunder Mountain, with a great cave at its bottom. Around that shelter grow yellow-wood and oak trees for bows and shrubs with straight sprouts for arrows, enough to supply the whole town, but a great savage Bear lives in the cave and has devoured many people, so no one dares go there. {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l14147-l14259","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 14147-14259","start":"14147","end":"14259","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":""The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. Holy is His will!"","summary":"Ralston describes a class of Russian legends in which Christ and his Apostles, especially between Easter and Ascension, visit human homes in the guise of poor wayfarers, testing people’s hospitality. Russian peasants are said to fear refusing any stranger, lest they turn away angels unawares. Such tales are common throughout Christian Europe and may preserve memories of pre-Christian gods who walked the earth dispensing justice; Russian versions resemble German and Scandinavian stories and often portray St. Peter unfavorably.

An abridged legend, "The Poor Widow," tells how Christ and his twelve Apostles, wandering the world, are refused lodging by a rich moujik, who sends them to a very poor widow owning only a crust of bread, a little flour, and a cow that has not yet calved. She gives them all her food and shelter, and her bread and flour are miraculously multiplied. Later a wolf prostrates itself before the Lord and begs for food; Christ sends it to kill the widow’s cow despite the Apostles’ protests. The widow accepts the loss as God’s will. A barrel full of money then rolls up; Christ directs it to the rich moujik, who greedily stores it away complaining it is too little. The Apostles are then sent to drink at a foul well swarming with snakes, frogs, and toads, and later at a beautiful well of pure water, surrounded by wondrous trees and heavenly birds. Though they think they drank only three minutes at the second well, Christ reveals they spent three years there, and explains that the first well foreshadows the state of the rich moujik in the other world, and the second that of the poor widow.

Another story, "Christ’s Brother," tells of a young man commanded by his dying father not to forget the poor. On Easter Day he brings red eggs to church to give to beggars with the Paschal greeting. After he has none left, he invites one wretched beggar home to dinner. After the meal they exchange crosses; the beggar gives a cross blazing like fire and invites the youth to visit him the following Tuesday, telling him to follow a path while saying, "Grant thy blessing, O Lord!" On his journey the youth hears the voices of suffering children begging "Christ’s brother" to ask Christ how long they must suffer, and sees girls endlessly ladling water from one well into another, who make the same request. At the journey’s end he finds the aged mendicant and recognizes him as the Lord Jesus Christ. Christ explains that the children’s mothers cursed them before birth, barring them from Paradise, and that the girls are punished for watering the milk they once sold. Finally, Christ leads the youth into Paradise and shows him the place prepared for him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Russian legends lodging.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Russian peasants are described as unwilling to refuse hospitality to any man, fearing they might unknowingly repulse especially where folklore preserves traces of belief in heathen gods who once walked the earth and dispensed justice among men.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Many light.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"In the legend "The Poor Widow," Christ and his twelve Apostles are wandering the world, enter a village one evening, and ask a rich moujik for lodging, but he refuses and directs them to a widow who takes in beggars.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The poor widow owns only a crust of bread, a handful of flour, and a cow that has not yet calved and gives no milk, yet she sets all her food before the wayfarers and lets them sleep under her roof.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"During the widow’s hospitality, her store of bread and flour is wonderfully increased so that the guests eat and are obeys.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"When the widow learns the wolf has killed her cow, she responds, "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. Holy is His will!" accepting the loss as God’s doing.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Later a barrel full of money rolls toward Christ and the Apostles; Christ orders it to roll into the farmyard of the rich moujik, again despite the Apostles’ protests, and the moujik hides the money away, grumbling that the Lord might have sent twice as much.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Following Christ’s instructions, the thirsty Apostles go to a first well whose water is foul and impure, swarming with snakes, frogs, and toads, so that they cannot drink from it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Sent to another well, the Apostles find pure, cool water in a place surrounded by wondrous trees with heavenly birds singing; they drink there and then return to Christ.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Christ tells the Apostles that, contrary to their sense of having spent only about three minutes at the second well, they were actually there three whole years, and explains that the state of the first well will be that of the rich moujik in the next world, while the second well represents the poor widow’s condition there.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The narrator notes that in some stories Christ wanders alone, under the guise of a beggar.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"In the story "Christ’s Brother," a dying father charges his son not to forget the poor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"On Easter Day the young man goes to church with red eggs to give to beggars in exchange for the Paschal greeting; the beggar gives him a cross that blazes like fire and invites him to visit on the following Tuesday, saying he need only follow a certain path while saying, "Grant thy blessing, O Lord," to reach him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"On Tuesday the young man follows the indicated path and hears voices like those of children crying, "O Christ’s brother, ask Christ for us—have we to suffer long?"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"Further along, he sees a group of girls endlessly ladling water from one well into another, who also ask him as Christ’s brother to intercede with Christ for them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"At the end of his journey the young man finds the aged mendicant who had adopted him as his brother and recognizes him as the Lord Jesus Christ.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs
