{"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l6343-l6476","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"OR THE ORIGIN OF THE SOCIETY OF RATTLESNAKES / THE WARRIOR SUITOR OF MOKI / HOW THE COYOTE JOINED THE DANCE OF THE BURROWING-OWLS / OR WHY COYOTES RUN THEIR NOSES INTO DEADFALLS; lines 6343-6476","start":"6343","end":"6476","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In ancient times a village in a canyon south of Thunder Mountain houses the Gods of Prey—the Mountain Lion, great Black Bear, Wildcat, Gray Wolf, Eagle, Mole—and their mothers and sisters, who live together and hunt daily. On the edge of Thunder Mountain a spotted demon named Síuiuki lies in wait for human hunters from nearby towns, destroying and eating them, so the Gods of Prey receive no sacrifices from humans. The gods discuss what to do and say that if anyone kills Síuiuki they will give him their sister to marry.

Below the demon’s house in Wolf Canyon lives a Coyote who scavenges the bones discarded by the Gods of Prey. While gnawing a bone near their doorway he overhears their conversation and the promise of marriage and quickly runs home.

Early the next morning the Coyote digs a hollow in the side of the canyon below the demon’s home, rolls a heavy stone into it with another stone beside, brings many deer and antelope leg-bones, and places a large bowl of yellow medicine-fluid by the rock. He sits cracking the leg-bones between the stones and pretends to bathe his lips with the medicine.

The demon, who usually rises late, comes out, sees the Coyote below, arms himself with his war-badge, bow, and arrows, and descends as if to hunt. The Coyote greets him and, when asked what he is doing, claims he is training himself for running so he can catch deer, boasting that with his medicine he can take the swiftness out of the bones and run faster than any deer. The demon, who has difficulty catching deer and antelope, eagerly asks to be shown so they can hunt together.

The Coyote tells the demon to watch as he demonstrates. He lays his left leg over the rock, secretly places an antelope bone beside it, then strikes the bone hard with a stone so it splits, pretending the broken bone is his own leg. Crying out as if in pain, he then splashes and rubs his leg with medicine-water, claims it is healed, and runs swiftly around the plain. He repeats the demonstration with his other leg and then with his paws, each time pretending great pain, "curing" himself with the medicine-water, and running even faster. The demon marvels at the Coyote’s speed and wants to try the method himself.

The Coyote warns that the procedure hurts terribly and taunts the demon’s courage, suggesting only a baby or a woman would be afraid. The demon insists he is not afraid and asks what to do. The Coyote tells him to sit down, lay his leg over the stone, strike it as hard as he can with the other rock, then bathe it in the medicine-water and do the same with the other leg, setting up the W. Powell describes Amerindian religion as an organized system for inducing ancestral gods to take part in human affairs. Worship centers on dance and song festivals held at appointed times and seasons—such as rain-invoking days, harvest thanksgivings, grasshopper, green-corn, buffalo, bear, and elk festivals—regulated by zodiac signs and tribal calendars. Shamans practice medicine as an invocation to the gods to expel evil spirits from the sick, using music, dancing, scarifying, searing, and a doctrine of signatures to select charms. Another key form of worship is altar ritual in kivas, where priests and acolytes gather around a cleared or raised space, pray, and use altar-pieces (representations of desired foods, water, and qualities, plus picture-writing and modeled or carved images). Powell links the origins of tribal graphic art and drama to such altar practices. He then describes a more developed sacrificial worship in which offerings are thought to supply the gods themselves with food, drink, and pleasures; among Amerinds, first portions of food and drink are commonly dedicated to the gods, with human sacrifice especially noted in Mexico among the Nahua/Aztec. Powell notes that some pagan religions in America are partially affiliated in doctrine and worship with Christian-origin religions. As an example of syncretism, he recounts how the Seneca shaman Handsome Lake, influenced by Bible stories brought back by his nephew (educated as a priest in Europe by Spaniards), combined these with Seneca folk-tales to found a new cult that split the Seneca into \"Christians\" and \"Pagans\" on the same reservation. Powell also observes that collectors like Cushing include hybrid tales—such as \"The Cock and the Mouse\"—that blend Bible stories with native tales, which has misled some people into believing Amerinds descend from the lost tribes of Israel.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Amerindian primitive religion is described as an content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l8119-l8209","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE TURTLE OUT HUNTING DUPED THE COYOTE / THE COYOTE AND THE LOCUST / THE COYOTE AND THE RAVENS WHO RACED THEIR EYES / THE PRAIRIE-DOGS AND THEIR PRIEST, THE BURROWING-OWL; lines 8119-8209","start":"8119","end":"8209","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An old Gopher, busy digging his cellars, is approached by a young man with an important message from the people of Shíwina and Mátsaki, who are in difficulties and seek help for a kicked-stick race against the runners of K’iákime. The Gopher agrees to run for them if their opponents allow him to follow his own underground road, and he asks that they wager for him only red paint and sacred yellow pollen, which he prizes above all possessions. The people send a challenge to K’iákime, staking all they have against what has been won from them, and specifying that the Gopher may run underground. The runners of K’iákime gladly accept, but stipulate that the Gopher must occasionally appear at the surface so they can see where he is. That night, the Gopher visits a series of younger brother gophers living at different points along the race-course and instructs each to dig two holes, wear a red plume like his, and briefly emerge when the racers’ footsteps thunder past before diving into the second hole, so that he will seem to appear at multiple places along the course. After these arrangements, the Gopher returns to his nest. On the fourth day, the runners of K’iákime come forth from sacred houses where they have been fasting and training, stripped and girded for the race and carrying their stick. The people of Mátsaki and Shíwina gather on the plain, and the old Gopher pops up among them with a red plume on his head and places his stick on the ground so he can carry it in his teeth. He explains that he cannot kick the stick because his feet are too short, and argues that he and the runners are evenly matched because they need not dig their way as he does. The runners of K’iákime laugh contemptuously and ask why he does not ask for a privilege instead of talking about matters that mean nothing to them.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An old Gopher is sunning himself and finishing a cellar when a young man approaches him, and the Coyote then cuts open the Demon, removes his heart and windpipe, and takes his war-badge as proof of the killing before fleeing to the house of the Prey-gods. He weeps over her body until the people return from the fields, miss the maiden, and see him grieving by the priest-chief’s lands near the river. When they tell the maiden’s father, the priest-chief, he accepts the event as ordained by the gods and orders that she be brought to the plaza of Mátsaki and buried before the House of the Sun. The people wrap her in mantles and bury her there at sunset. The young man refuses to leave her grave, lamenting repeatedly that he loved her even though he killed her unknowingly. After a storyteller’s break, it is explained that he killed her because he did not know his wife from another woman. The young man continues his night-long vigil at the grave. Around midnight, after the moon has set and a ‘great snowdrift’ stretches across the sky, he sees a faint ember-like light in the grave-sands that grows until it illuminates the grave. The bride tears off her mantles, rises in her grave-bed, and looks at him coldly and sadly, reproaching him that he did not know or love her and therefore killed her, though she had hoped for love. He insists he does love her and mourns again. As a great star rises from the sky-land, she tells him she is now another being, only a spirit, and that the light by which he sees her will fade with the morning light. At dawn the light disappears and the grave appears unchanged, so he goes away sorrowing, silent all day, but returns at night to the grave. On the next night, an even brighter light appears in the grave-sands; her spirit again rises in the grave-bed, repeats her reproach, and bids him go. The narrator then explains that newborn children initially live on \"wind-stuff\" through a cord of unseen sustenance and later with difficulty begin to suck milk or soft food. Similarly, very aged people are childlike, toothless, and liable to die of diarrhea if they eat anything but soft parts and broths of cooked food. Babies are said to have just come from the hazy, steam-growing Shi-u-na world, and the aged are about to enter the mist-enshrouded Shi-po-lo-a world, where the fully dead pay no heed to cooked food. Amiwili boasts of being a warrior made to \"use up life\" and agrees to attend a council on their behalf. The boys then visit another grandfather, the turtle Etawa, prank him by shooting an arrow at his shell, and, after his angry reaction, explain their loss and seek his advice. Etawa, a self-proclaimed great warrior despite having no bow or arrows, promises to help and to come to the council. The boys travel to Oak-wood Canyon, cut branches and oak sticks, gather obsidian, return home feigning exhaustion so that their grandmother hastily prepares food for them, and afterward they strip and straighten the wooden sprouts, dry them by the fire, shape obsidian arrowheads, fletch them with eagle feathers, and make bows from the oak sticks, preparing multiple bundles of weapons.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The boys say they had a big drove of turkeys, let them out to feed, and people of Háwikuh killed many of them, leading the boys to plan to get back their winnings and even the game.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Old Amiwili responds \"Ah ha! Very well!\" lies on his belly with his head lifted and declares he will show the Háwikuh people they are not to treat his grandchildren like that, boasting that he is a warrior in every direction of himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Amiwili further emphasizes his nature by saying he is \"just made to use up life\" and repeating that using up life is what he is for.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boys ask Amiwili if he will come to the council, and he answers \"Shuathla,\" glossed as an old-fashioned word meaning \"Go ye but before me.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The boys go to a pool at the wood border where their old grandfather the Turtle is paddling around in the scum, squinting his eyes and stretching his long neck up to bite off the heads of the water-rushes.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Mátsailéma proposes to have fun with the Turtle, fits an arrow to his bowstring, draws it to the point, and shoots the arrow onto the Turtle’s back, causing the Turtle to duck under the scum, then reemerge with slimy eyes, spittle in his mouth, and legs flailing too fast to be counted.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Turtle, described as as big as the turtles in the big Waters of the World, curses the boys and calls them troublesome little beasts who never knew shame or dignity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The boys tell the Turtle not to be angry, saying they called to him while he paddled around eating rushes, and since they could not get at him otherwise, they fired an arrow at him to attract his attention.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The boys explain that they have started out \"sprouting\" and have come to their grandfather for advice.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The boys mention their flock of turkeys, and the Turtle replies that he knows about them because they came down to drink at the pool and broke his morning nap with their \"quit quit quittings.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The boys recount that the people of Háwikuh killed very nearly all of their turkeys and state that they are going to even matters with them, which is why they are out sprouting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Turtle praises the boys for coming to him, calls them wise, declares he is a great warrior although he has neither bow nor arrow, and boasts that the more weapons his enemies have, the worse it is for them; he tells them to wait until tomorrow and promises to help and come to the council.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The boys say that the council to Oak-wood Canyon, cut down a large bundle of branches with their big flint knives and four stout dry oak sticks, shoulder their \"sprouts\" despite their size, and collect obsidian on their way home.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Near home the boys act very tired, so their old grandmother pities them and quickly prepares food by stirring mush, burying content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l9664-l9783","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 9664-9783","start":"9664","end":"9783","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this segment, the boys Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma are prepared for battle by their grandmother, who fills cane tubes with a special fluid, fastens them to arrows, chants over them, and leaves food by the boys. In the morning the boys arm themselves with bows, arrows, war-clubs, knives, and a water-shield and depart. They pass the house of their grandfather Amiwili, an old Worm who is glutted with lizard plants and brusquely tells them to get out, and then visit their other grandfather, the old Turtle Etawa, who instructs them to return at midday and says he will wait by the pond bank. Near the town of Háwikuh at twilight, with the morning star high, the boys sit and sing an incantation that the narrator says is the same chant used by the Ápithlan Shíwani in the present. The younger brother scouts the pueblo and sees people sleeping on the warm roofs. He then cries out loudly and shoots a cane arrow high into the plaza; as it falls, it splits and scatters \"medicine-water\" so that the people think it is raining though the sky is clear and that someone has cried \"Murder.\" Áhaiyúta’s arrow scatters more medicine-water while Mátsailéma calls \"Murder\" again, prompting the townspeople to grab their weapons. The younger brother rejoins his sibling hiding in grass along the northern trail, and the people of Háwikuh rush out, thinking they have located their enemies, but find no one. As they mill about, the boys’ arrows strike the nearest warriors from concealment; they rarely miss, and many are killed or wounded before the survivors flee. When the younger brother runs out of arrows he urges Áhaiyúta to put on the water-shield and escape. As the people gain on them, Áhaiyúta uses the shield strapped to his back to throw water like thick rain onto their pursuers, repeatedly loosening the attackers’ sinew bowstrings so they must stop to tighten them. This allows the boys to draw near the pond where their Turtle grandfather waits, while still shooting at the leaders with war arrows. As the enemy closes in, Mátsailéma hastily takes the big Turtle onto his back. Etawa clings to him and directs him to run ahead, while the younger boy complains about his grandfather’s rock-like weight. Áhaiyúta, running in front, warns that the enemy is close and urges his younger brother to hurry, but the burden slows him. Seeing the warriors draw their bows, Etawa tells Mátsailéma to duck his head and withdraws into his shell. The enemy arrows rattle against the Turtle’s shell; the warriors shout a victory cry but then their arrows glance off the shell and strike themselves, causing them to fall. They exclaim about how hard the beings can shoot while their own glancing arrows wound one another. One leading warrior cries out that they are only shooting themselves against \"that black shield\" and that the other shield weakens their bowstrings. Meanwhile Áhaiyúta reaches the house of his other grandfather, Amiwili, who is swollen from food and almost unable to move, only wagging his head.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The boys’ grandmother fills cane tubes with fluid, fastens them to the ends of two arrows, chants an incantation over the canes, sets food near the boys, and quietly leaves the room to sleep.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The boys sleep soundly until daybreak, then rise, take bows, quivers, knives, war-clubs, arrows, and a water-shield, and quietly steal away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At Amiwili’s house, the old Worm is gorging on the leaves of lizard plants, looks so swollen that he seems like a ball, and is too busy chewing to pay attention to the boys.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boys ask Amiwili, \"How did our grandfather come unto the morning?\" and he replies \"Thluathlá!\" translated as \"Get out!\", after which they hurry on.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When the boys reach the home of the old Turtle, he tells them they will return at the height of the sun, reminds them to mind what he told them the previous night, and says he will wait on the bank for them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"As they near Háwikuh it is twilight and the morning star is high; hiding-place in the grass along the trail toward the wood border just as some residents run out to see him and shout that the enemy is on the northern trail, causing the Háwikuhkwe to pour down toward that trail but find no visible foe.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"While the people look and run about, the arrows of Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma strike the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10411-l10517","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10411-10517","start":"10411","end":"10517","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A praying figure calls his \"children\"—the Deer and Antelope—to aid him against Old Tarantula, who has stolen his sacred fine apparel, sending them toward Tarantula’s home as bait. A young man in a nearby valley loudly announces the passing deer and antelope, and Old Tarantula, living in an inner room under rocky columns, hears the calls, arms himself with bow and arrows, and goes out to hunt. He proudly kills the approaching deer and antelope, but when he tries to carry them away, each carcass becomes a crushing mass of white rock. As people converge on his den, they seize him, tear off his stolen garments and earrings, and maim him despite his pleas for mercy. Old priests decide he is too powerful and crafty to be allowed to live and command that he be roasted. The people build a great fire, cast Tarantula into the flames, and he swells until he bursts, his fragments scattering to the ends of the earth and becoming beings like him. The narrator explains that this is why tarantulas are now small, with crooked legs and backward movement, distributed throughout the world, unlike the Great Tarantula who lived below the rocky columns of Thunder Mountain. A new story begins: in ancient times, the children of the forefathers lived in Héshokta, the Town of the Cliffs, including two beautiful sisters, daughters of a master-chief. One bright summer morning the elder proposes they go to a pool to wash clothes for an upcoming dance; the younger agrees but warns that in these days the shadows of rocks and sage-bushes harbor \"unthinkable things\" that frighten solitary walkers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A praying figure addresses \"my children\" and tells them that Old Tarantula has wickedly stolen his sacred fine apparel, calling them to follow his instructions and go toward Tarantula’s home to tempt him forth.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Deer and Antelope obediently descend the sloping sides of the foothills toward Old Tarantula’s den.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A youth in a nearby valley repeatedly calls out loudly that deer and antelope are passing, urging any nearby to hasten.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Old Tarantula, alone in his inner room, hears the humming of the youth’s call, goes to his doorway, interprets the words as announcing approaching deer, and resolves to hunt them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Old Tarantula arms himself with bow and arrows, briefly hesitates about He coughs until almost all his substance is gone, leaving only a small worm. The boys finish off the weakened enemies, who either are killed and scalped or flee toward Háwikuh. They joke that the scalps, which they call caps, are better than a flock of turkeys and wonder who will proclaim their victory, though they live only with their grandmother in a lone house atop Twin Mountain. The old Turtle volunteers and goes toward Twin Mountain. On a hill south of Master Cañon he plants a stick and shouts the victory cry, then repeatedly shouts a cry meaning “Murder! Murder!” which frightens the old woman. She throws on a robe, seizes the fire poker, and limps toward him to punish the “shameless Turkey killers.” Turtle then pretends not to see her and loudly proclaims victory. In a long, formulaic dialogue, the old woman asks who has renewed himself (her grandchildren) and systematically inquires who will perform every role in the victory ceremony—purifying and bathing the scalps, swinging them around the pueblo, adopting them, preparing feasts, serving as priest of initiation, song-master, dancer, sacrificer of arrows and contester for them, recruiting women to dance, presiding at in-laws’ feasts, and being priests of their Father Society. Turtle repeatedly answers “I will” or “you will,” effectively assigning nearly all male roles to himself and most female and hosting roles to her. As they might have gone on all day, they are interrupted by the singing voices of the boys, who arrive with two large strings of scalps. The old woman groans that she cannot swing so many scalps around the pueblo, but Turtle insists she must. He strings the scalps thickly on a long pole. Day after day they dance and sing to add strands to the boys’ victory badges. Turtle must simultaneously act as master-priest of ceremonies and people, low priest, song-master, dancer, sacrificer of arrows, and striver for the arrows. The old woman must at once be mother and sister, represent clans, and serve as matron and maiden of ceremonials. Because the two of them take on so many offices, the labor is very hard and the rites do not go well. The story concludes that this is why, in the present Ceremony of Victory, there are many distinct song-masters, dancers, priests, common people, father clans, and mother content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l10957-l11063","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES / THE UGLY WILD BOY WHO DROVE THE BEAR AWAY FROM SOUTHEASTERN MESA; lines 10957-11063","start":"10957","end":"11063","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma rig an effigy of the demon Átahsaia with lion skins, a bow, and strings so it seems to move, then stage a mock attack below Twin Mountain to frighten their grandmother. Hearing cries for help, the old woman rushes from her house, finds Mátsailéma apparently fleeing and Áhaiyúta struggling with Átahsaia, and fiercely beats the stuffed demon with a piñon poker until she is exhausted, while the boys laugh and manipulate the effigy to rise again. When she realizes she has been tricked, she curses the boys, vows never to help them or let them live with her, and leaves; the brothers remark that their purpose is accomplished. The narrator adds that since then the grandmother has vanished, while Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma are the bright morning and evening stars flanking the Sun-father, their spirits hovering over shrines on Thunder Mountain, the Mount of the Beloved, or the Middle of the World to guide games and guard Zuñi warriors. A new tale then begins, explaining that in the earliest times many gods existed, some good and some evil, and that evil beings were excluded from the beloved company of the Kâkâ. Mítsina the Hermit, of evil understanding, is condemned by the gods to live alone in the Cañon of the Pines southeast of Zuñi until he becomes worthy; he dwells there in solitude, passing his time by playing the game of sacred arrows or cane-cards, whose sounds hunters sometimes hear as they pass through the canyon.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Áhaiyúta manipulates an effigy from behind, pulling strings so that, covered with lion skins and holding a bow, it looks like the living Átahsaia setting out to hunt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The boys drag the demon skin along and run as fast as they can down to the plain below Twin Mountain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Sun is described as climbing down the western ladder while the grandmother looks for the two boys from her house.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The grandmother climbs a ladder, gazes over the mountains and valleys, frets about the boys as terrible pests, and says she fears something has happened to them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A frightened voice cries \"Ho-o-o-ta! Come quick! Help! Help!\" from below, and the grandmother in her excitement tumbles through the trap-door, then grabs a piñon poker and rushes out of the house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Mátsailéma is seen running and calling for the grandmother to hurry, while Áhaiyúta appears to be struggling to get away from Átahsaia when she comes around the crags.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Mátsailéma has lost his war-club, and the grandmother, telling the boys to stiffen their feet, rushes at the effigy and beats it with her poker until dust smokes from the dry grass and the skin doubles up as if in pain.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Mátsailéma rolls and kicks in the grass, Áhaiyúta drops the stuffed demon because of his laughter, and the grandmother continues to belabor and curse the demon’s cannibal heart until she thinks it must be dead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The boys pull the strings so that the demon effigy suddenly springs up again, and the grandmother again attacks it, her blows becoming weaker until her breath fails and she falls to the ground.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The grandmother moans that her day-light is cut off and her wind of life is going, covers her head with a tattered mantle, then looks out to see her grandsons rolling and kicking in the grass with swollen eyes and red faces from laughter, while the demon skin lies torn and battered out of shape.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The grandmother angrily calls the boys \"pesky wretches,\" declares she will never help them or let them live with her again, and hobbles away.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The brothers continue laughing until the grandmother is far away and then say to one another, \"It is done!\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"It is stated that since that time the grandmother has gone and no one knows where, while Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma are the bright stars of the morning and evening, just in front of and behind the Sun-father.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma’s spirits are said to hover over their shrines on Thunder Mountain and the Mount of the Beloved, or to linger over the Middle of the World, guiding games and guarding the warriors of the Land of Zuñi.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The narrator notes that these events occurred in the days of the ancients and concludes, \"Thus shortens my story.\"","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In a time when all was new and the gods dwelt in ancient places, many gods existed, some destined for good and some for evil or for doing things beyond understanding, and those of evil intent became so bad they could not be retained in the company and council of the beloved of the Kâkâ, the Order of the Sacred Drama.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Mítsina the Hermit is described as dwelling all alone in the Cañon of the Pines southeast of Zuñi and as being of evil understanding.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The gods tell Mítsina that he must dwell alone, being unwise and evil in his ways, until through much happening The people at the council then decide to send for their grandfather, Great Eagle, praised as swiftest of wing, keenest of sight, and strong of grasp. Eagle accepts the task, noting Tarantula’s cunning, and goes before sunrise to the peak of the Mountain of the Badgers to watch the entrance of Tarantula’s den. When Old Tarantula emerges and begins to shout at him, Eagle swoops like a stone from a sling, but his attack misses, and he only clutches one plume from Tarantula’s head-dress without carrying it away. Tarantula tumbles into his lower room, exclaims that Eagle did not get him, and dances and sings a repetitive song while admiring his fine clothing. Crestfallen, Eagle returns to the council and reports his failure. The people and their old ones decide to send Hatchutsanona (Lesser Falcon), a small bird with hard, smooth, speckled gray-brown plumage like rocks and sagebrush, swift and strong enough to penetrate thickets. Lesser Falcon modestly agrees to try even though his elder brothers Kingfisher and Eagle have failed, and repeats that Old Tarantula is cunning and keen-sighted. The next morning he lies close on the edge of a high cliff above Tarantula’s den, nearly invisible against the rocks and dry grass, like an autumn leaf. At sunrise Old Tarantula thrusts out his rugged face, scans in all directions, and initially sees nothing. When he has pushed his head and shoulders out farther, he finally sees Lesser Falcon, but too late to avoid him; the falcon sweeps like a swirl of snowdrift into the mouth of the den, grabs at Tarantula’s head, and flies off with the macaw plumes of the youth’s head-dress. Tarantula falls back inside, bends double with fright and chagrin, laments the loss of his beautiful head-dress, calls the falcon a skulking wretch, then disparages macaw feathers as fragile and changeable. One day the two little brothers Áhaiyúta (elder) and Mátsailéma (younger), \"War-gods of peace times\" who lived with their grandmother at a shrine on Face Mountain, went hunting rabbits and prairie-dogs. Following their game along canyon cliffs, they entered the Cañon of the Pines near the house of the hermit Mítsina and heard him playing cane-cards. Curious, they climbed a ladder and peered through the roof opening. Mítsina gladly invited them in, seated them on blankets, and proposed a gambling game. The brothers, who carried cane-cards in their girdles, agreed. Mítsina’s basket-drum was fringed with turquoise earrings he had won, and under the robe he played on lay a pile of fine necklaces taken from players he had defeated and slain. He urged the War-gods to bet their bows, arrows, and clothing against a poleful of goods, and they did so, but lost everything they wore. Seeking to regain their losses, they accepted Mítsina’s suggestions to wager their left thighs, then the other thighs, then their sides and bodies up to their necks, and finally their heads, ears, and eyes. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l13451-l13554","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 13451-13554","start":"13451","end":"13554","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The community cannot discover who secretly married the priest-chief’s daughter, so a council decides that she, her unknown husband, and their two small children must die for deceiving their people. War-priests proclaim the sentence from the housetops and order everyone to prepare weapons. The priest-chief’s daughter learns of the decree from her younger sister. Her husband, a young man, tells the old priest (the priest-chief) that he knows what will happen; the old priest resigns himself to the gods’ will and calls his people fools. While the people arm themselves and prepare for a victory feast, the young man tells his wife that he must go to meet his father. At midday he has her open the sky-hole, then transforms into a cloud of mist that whirls upward in the sunlight toward the Sun. Reaching the Sun, he waits in shame until the Sun-father calls him, mildly rebukes him for earlier disobedience to a command given to him and his younger brother, and then consoles him. The Sun-father says he himself caused the young man’s forgetfulness so events would unfold as they did. He promises to make the young man a god seated at his left hand, a beneficent being whom humans will see and worship in the evening, and through whose will rain will fall upon their lands. The Sun-father explains that he had intended the young man to stay among humans, enriching them with precious shells and stones, knowledge, and good fortune, but calls the people unwise and ungrateful and decides instead to remove the young man, his wife, and children from earthly life to sit beside him. He instructs the young man to descend, make four sacred hoops wrapped with cotton and four sacred racing wands, and use them with an unembroidered cotton mantle spread on the floor, with all their valuables placed upon it. When the people storm the priest-chief’s house and then assault it again, the family is to sit at the four corners, grasp the hoops and wands, and lift, causing them to rise higher each time as the attackers draw nearer and begin to climb the ladders, until they reach the Sun’s country. The young man returns; the priest-chief calmly continues preparations for a festival, and the young man tells him that on the morrow they will go dwell forever with the Sun-father. At dawn the war-priests again call the armed people to gather, and a large war party assembles, shields glittering, lances dark with paint, and war-clubs clashing like thunder. In the priest-chief’s house, the young man has placed all their belongings on the mantle. Husband and wife sit at two corners and their children at the other two; they lift the corners and slowly rise toward the ceiling, then nearer the sky-hole, and finally above the roof. Outside, the warriors see the family’s shadows on the ground and shout that they are escaping.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l10187-l10307","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BOYISLAV, YOUNGEST OF TWELVE. / THE TABLE, THE PACK, AND THE BAG. / THE KING OF THE TOADS. / THE MOUSE-HOLE, AND THE UNDERGROUND KINGDOM.; lines 10187-10307","start":"10187","end":"10307","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Yarmil and the princess he has liberated return from a castle by carriage, pass a white castle where a white lady lives (the princess’s mother), and exit through a great gate that from outside appears only as a mouse-hole. They arrive at Yarmil’s father the king’s castle at the same time as his elder brothers and their brides, but all attention and glory go to Yarmil’s bride, to the secret anger of the queen and elder princes. During the weddings the queen flatters Yarmil, presses him to reveal his bride’s origin and former form, and, by naming animals, tricks him into betraying that she was once a toad and how many skins she had. The next day, while the king, princes, and some guests are hunting, the queen steals twelve shirts and tapers from Yarmil’s bride’s room and burns them in the garden. The bride feels faint, goes out, and tells Yarmil he has spoken what she forbade him to tell and that she must now go to the glass mountain, from which there is no liberation; she then vanishes. Yarmil is inconsolable, while the queen pretends horror and insists the bride was a witch; the king ends the festivities, and the elder brothers depart with their brides. Refusing consolation or another wife, Yarmil resolves to seek his bride on the glass mountain. Though his father says no one has ever heard of such a place, Yarmil rides out, at first letting his horse choose its way, then asking people everywhere, but no one knows of the glass {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l7102-l7228","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 7102-7228","start":"7102","end":"7228","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Prince Ivan, journeying far from home, first meets two old women who are sewing and whose lives are bound to finishing a trunkful of needles and thread; they refuse to take him in because they will soon die. He then meets the giant Vertodub, tasked with uprooting trees, and the giant Vertogor, tasked with leveling mountains; each predicts his own imminent death once his work is finished and so cannot shelter the prince. Eventually Ivan reaches the dwelling of the Sun's Sister, who welcomes him, feeds him, and treats him like a son. Though his life there is easy, he often climbs a high mountain to look toward his former palace, now ruined, and weeps for his home. Questioned about his red eyes, he twice blames the wind, which the Sun's Sister then orders to stop; the third time he admits the truth and begs to return. She reluctantly lets him go and equips him with a magic brush, a comb, and two apples that restore youth.

On his way back, Ivan visits Vertogor, who has only one mountain left to level. Ivan throws down the brush, causing innumerable very high mountains to spring up, and Vertogor joyfully resumes his work. Ivan then visits Vertodub, who has only three trees left; Ivan throws the comb, and dense oak forests with huge trunks arise, giving Vertodub more to uproot. Reaching the old women again, Ivan gives them the youth-giving apples; they immediately become young and gift him a handkerchief that creates a lake behind the bearer when waved.

Ivan finally returns home. His sister runs out, fondles him, and asks him to sit and play the lute while she prepares dinner. As he plays, a mouse emerges and, speaking with a human voice, warns him to flee because his sister has gone to sharpen her teeth. Ivan escapes on his horse while the mouse runs over the lute strings to mimic his playing. When the sister returns, she finds him gone, is revealed as a witch, and rushes in pursuit. Hearing a loud noise, Ivan sees her chasing him and waves the handkerchief, which produces a deep lake that delays her while she swims across. She continues the chase, but Vertodub, realizing Ivan is fleeing from his sister, tears up oaks and piles them into a mountain-like barrier; the witch gnaws through it with difficulty. As she nears Ivan again, Vertogor hurls down enormous mountains onto the road, forcing her to climb and clamber while Ivan rides far ahead. After finally surmounting these obstacles, the witch again catches sight of her brother and cries out, but the passage breaks off at her {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l8817-l8921","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MYTHOLOGICAL. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 8817-8921","start":"8817","end":"8921","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage presents several related folkloric and mythological notes. First, a Russian skazka is summarized in which the personified weekday Wednesday sends a young woman out at night to fetch water so she can "buck" her linen, apparently intending to harm her. The frightened woman consults a wise old neighbor, who reveals Wednesday's lethal intentions and instructs her to trick the spirit: she must bang her pails and cry that Wednesday's children have been burnt at sea, slip into the house while Wednesday runs out, slam the door, mark it with crosses, pray, and refuse to let Wednesday back in. Wednesday, described as an "Unclean Spirit," pleads at the door until cock-crow, when she screams and disappears, while the linen remains. 

The author then notes Russian peasant legends in which St. Petka (Friday) and St. Nedelya (Sunday) appear as saints, with St. Sunday resembling both Friday and Wednesday in disapproving of spinning and weaving at inappropriate times. In Little Russia, Sunday is said to tell women who spin at unfitting seasons that they are spinning her hair and shows them her dishevelled back plait. 

From Wallachian tales, the author cites stories where three supernatural women—"holy Mothers" Friday, Wednesday, and Sunday—help a hero searching for a dragon-stolen heroine, replacing the three benevolent Baba Yagas in similar Russian stories. In another Wallachian story, the same three assist a "Wallachian Psyche" on a quest for her lost husband. Mother Sunday is further described as ruler of the animal world, who can summon all birds and beasts with a magic flute and bestows a magic horse in a Slovak tale. In that Slovak story, a hero whose mother has been mentally corrupted by a dragon is repeatedly sent on perilous quests, but is aided by St. Nedelka (Sunday), who gives him magical implements and her steed Tatoschik, enabling him to escape danger four times.

After the hero returns home safely, his unnatural mother binds him as if in play, and the dragon cuts off his head and dismembers his body. She keeps his heart but bundles the rest of his body onto Tatoschik, who carries the pieces to St. Nedelka. The saint reanimates the youth, who lives as a man "without a heart." She then sends him, disguised as a begging piper, to his mother's castle to retrieve his heart. After succeeding, he brings the heart back to St. Nedelka, who gives it to a magic bird called Pelekan. The bird puts its long neck down the youth's throat and replaces the heart in its proper place, restoring him fully.

The author reflects that St. Friday and St. Wednesday belong to a broader class of elemental spirits, sometimes demonic, such as the Domovoy (house-spirit), Rusalka (naiad), and Vodyany (water-sprite). As an example of the related story type, he introduces (but does not yet quote) a skazka about the Leshy, a wood-sprite or Slavonic Satyr believed to haunt forests. He interprets this Leshy tale as a "vulgar" peasant form of an older myth underlying many stories about the theft and recovery of queens and princesses: in it, the traditional Snake or Koshchei abductor is reduced to a mere wood-demon, the hero becomes a simple hunter, and the royal heroine is lowered in rank to a priest's daughter, although the leading idea of the story remains the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l8696-l8815","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MYTHOLOGICAL. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 8696-8815","start":"8696","end":"8815","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston explains Russian folk beliefs and stories about the personified days Friday and Wednesday. Friday (Pyatnitsa) is said to have been consecrated in pagan times to a goddess akin to Venus, Freyja, or Siva/Seewa (a Ceres-like figure), whose personality later merged with that of the Christian St. Prascovia, producing the figure of \"Mother Pyatnitsa-Prascovia\" or \"St. Pyatinka.\" Peasants believe she visits their cottages on Fridays, so they avoid spinning, weaving, and similar work, fearing she will punish them with eye and hand ailments; some also adjust bedtime and house-cleaning to please her. A tale then narrates how Mother Friday punishes a woman who spins flax on Friday by filling her eyes with dust, and later heals her when the woman repents and offers a taper. A similar introductory note on Wednesday links it to Odin, the Thundergod, and Christian remembrance of Christ's passion, and suggests some Friday customs shifted to Wednesday. In the accompanying tale, a young housewife, spinning late at night between Tuesday and Wednesday, casually calls on \"Mother Wednesday\" for help. Before dawn, Mother Wednesday appears as an older woman, has already spun and woven the linen, directs the housewife to help bleach it and fetch water, and looks at her angrily with sparkling eyes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Friday, called Pyatnitsa in Russian, was consecrated by the old Slavonians to a goddess described as akin to Venus or Freyja.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Carinthian name for Friday, Sibne dan, is cited as evidence that the day was once holy to Siva or Seewa, a Slavonic goddess corresponding to Ceres.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In Christian times the personality of the Friday goddess became merged with that of St. Prascovia, who is addressed as \"Mother Pyatnitsa-Prascovia\" and also called \"St. Pyatinka.\"","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Mother Friday is believed to wander about peasants' houses on Fridays, and people suspend certain kinds of work so as not to offend her.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A tradition states it is a sin for women to sew, spin, weave, or buck linen on Friday, and for men to plait bast shoes, twine cord, and similar tasks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Spinning and weaving are considered especially offensive to Mother Friday because the dust and refuse from flax are believed to injure her eyes, leading her to punish offenders with sore eyes, whitlows, and agnails.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In some villages people go to bed early on Friday evening, fearing that St. Pyatinka will punish anyone found awake when she roams through the cottage.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In other places floors are swept on Thursday evening so that Mother Friday will not be annoyed by dust when she comes the next day.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Popular reports describe Mother Friday as sometimes appearing \"all pricked with needles and pierced by the spindles\" of careless women who worked on her holy day.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Any work begun on a Friday is believed to be sure to go wrong.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the tale \"Friday\", a woman who does not revere Mother Friday spends Friday combing, whirling, and spinning flax on her distaff until dinner-time, when she falls into a deep sleep.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"While the woman sleeps, Mother Friday, wearing a white dress and in a rage, enters the house, scoops up flax dust from the floor, and stuffs it into the woman's eyes before leaving without speaking.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"When the woman wakes with severe eye pain, the other women, who saw Mother Friday's visit, tell her she has brought a terrible punishment on herself from Mother Friday.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The punished woman begs Mother Friday for forgiveness, promises to offer her a taper, and vows never to let anyone dishonor her.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"During the following night Mother Friday returns, removes the dust from the woman's eyes, and restores her ability to move about normally.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Wednesday is described as the day consecrated to Odin and the eve of the day sacred to the Thundergod, and some scholars think heathen Slavonians may also have held it holy.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Other commentators consider it more likely that Russian Wednesday traditions were transferred from Friday because the Church associated Wednesday and Friday as days sacred to the memory of Christ's passion and death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The Russian name for Wednesday, Sereda or Sreda, means \"the middle,\" referring to Wednesday as the middle of the working week.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"In the tale \"Wednesday\", a young housewife spins late at night between Tuesday and Wednesday, alone for a long time, and after the first cock-crow decides she would like to sleep but also to finish her spinning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Before going to sleep, the housewife lays down her hatchel without crossing herself and prays, \"Mother Wednesday, lend me thy aid, that I may get up early in the morning and finish my spinning,\" then falls asleep.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Very early in the morning, before it is light, the housewife hears someone bustling about; she sees the room lit by a burning splinter of fir in a cresset and a fire in the stove, and an older woman with a white towel as a head-dress moving around and preparing the stove.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The stranger wakes the housewife, identifies herself as Wednesday, says she has spun the linen and woven the web, and instructs her to help bleach it and set it in the heated oven, telling her to fetch water from the brook.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"The young woman is frightened and confused by the apparition, while Wednesday looks at her angrily and her eyes sparkle.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Mother Friday / Mother Pyatnitsa-Prascovia / St. Pyatinka","description":"Personified Friday in Russian folk belief, a female figure who wanders cottages on her holy day, is offended by certain kinds of work, and can punish or heal those who honor or dishonor her.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Unreverent spinner woman (Friday tale)","description":"An unnamed woman who spins flax on Friday without due reverence to Mother Friday and is punished with painful eyes before being healed after repentance.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Other women in cottage (Friday tale)","description":"A group of women who witness Mother Friday's visit, are frightened, and explain to the offender that her suffering is punishment from Mother content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l12891-l13036","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER V. / GHOST STORIES.; lines 12891-13036","start":"12891","end":"13036","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A fiddler among fiends repeatedly snaps his instrument strings when he pronounces a Christian blessing. The fiends provide new strings, but they also break, so they send an escorting fiend when he asks to fetch his own. Returning to his village, he and the fiend stop at a wedding, where people say he has been missing three years; he explains he has been in the other world. After he delays departure by playing for the guests until cockcrow, the fiend disappears. The fiddler then tells the sons of a deceased rich peasant that their father orders them to dig up two buried pots of money and give it all to the poor. As they distribute alms, the money miraculously increases, so they set the pots at a crossroads where passersby take freely, yet the contents remain inexhaustible. On petition, the Emperor decrees that a straight bridge should be built to a nearby town using this treasure, and the long bridge finally empties the pots. Around the same time, a maid bears a son, abandons him, and the child miraculously lives three years without food or drink, always accompanied by an angel. When he reaches the bridge, he exclaims that God should grant heaven to the one who paid for it; God hears and orders the rich peasant to be released from hell. Ralston compares this bridge-building motif with another Russian tale in which a wealthy but childless merchant and his wife pray for a child, give alms, and build a bridge over swamps for the good of the faithful. The merchant sends his manager Fedor to sit under the bridge and listen to what people say; three Holy Elders cross and decide that the builder should be rewarded with a fortunate son whose every word and desire will be fulfilled. Ralston notes that this story then closely resembles the German tale ‘The Pink,’ and that a Bohemian story, ‘The Treacherous Servant,’ preserves the bridge-building incident. He then turns from the fiddler story to discuss Slavic ideas about the dead and introduces a milder ghost story titled ‘The Ride on the Gravestone.’ In it, an artisan returning at night from a feast meets an old friend who has been dead ten years. Forgetting this, he greets the man, goes to his house, and drinks with him, while the dead host urges him to stay the A ladder of flags rises from the lake and she descends beneath the waters into the Land of Spirits, from which light, glad voices, and music briefly emerge. Her young husband arrives too late, sees only the smooth lake and the old couple, and laments that he killed his beautiful bride. Around midnight a doorway opens in the dark green waters, a ladder ascends, and he sees the bright forms of the dead in white embroidered cotton with shell and turquoise ornaments moving in and out, while the Kâkâ dance for the gods. He attempts to reach the entrance, but the water becomes deep and cold; looking in, he sees his adorned bride sitting happily at the head of the dancers, seeming to forget him. In despair he collapses on the shore. A great Owl appears, speaks to him, learns his trouble, and invites him to its mountain house. In a cave that expands into a bright room, Owl-men and Owl-women greet him. The old Owl removes its owl-coat, brings a bag of medicine, and explains that instead of giving the medicine directly it will make the young man sleep. Upon waking he will see the morning star and his dead wife on the trail toward the Middle Ant Hill, and with sunrise she will awaken. The Owl warns him not to approach or kiss her until they reach the home of their fathers, or the restoration will be undone; if he obeys, they may live happily together. The Owl blows sleep medicine in his face and he sleeps; the owl-beings put on their owl-coats, fly with him to a trail near Mátsaki and the Middle Ant Hill, then fly over the lake. They cast sleep medicine through the windows of the Land of Spirits, take the plumed prayer-sticks he had brought, select some red plumes, enter the home of the Kâkâ, lay prayer-plumes before the great altar, and carry off the sleeping maiden to where the young man lies. As a great star appears, he wakes and finds his wife beside him, turns his face away to resist temptation, and waits for the sun. With the first sunray on her face she awakens, looks around, smiles at her lonely lover, and acknowledges his love. They rise and travel with physical distance between them toward their fathers’ home; the young man follows the Owl’s counsel. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l9057-l9174","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL. / SOZH AND DNIEPER.; lines 9057-9174","start":"9057","end":"9174","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage collects several legends about personified rivers and streams. In a White-Russian tale, a blind old man Dvina has two sons, the elder Sozh and younger Dnieper. While Sozh is away, Dvina's wife deceives him so that he gives the elder son's blessing to Dnieper, blessing him to become a wide, prosperous river whose brother will serve him; Dnieper immediately turns into such a river. When Sozh returns and complains, his father tells him that if he can outstrip Dnieper by racing through hidden forests, he will become superior. Sozh violently carves a path across the land and schemes, with the help of a Raven, to leap ahead from underground, but a Vulture who sides with Dnieper attacks the Raven, whose premature croaking causes Sozh to burst up and fall into Dnieper's waves. A second legend, titled the metamorphosis of the Dnieper, Volga, and Dvina, says that these rivers were once orphaned human siblings who suffered grinding poverty. They decide to wander the world seeking good fortune and the best places to become great rivers that will free them from toil while feeding others. After years of wandering they agree on their sources, but while Dnieper sleeps in a swamp, his more cunning sisters Volga and Dvina secretly choose the best sloping courses and begin to flow away. Dnieper wakes, grows angry, and, realizing he cannot outrun a river, strikes the ground and becomes a stream rushing through gullies and ravines between steep banks toward the sea. Near the shore his anger subsides and he vanishes into the sea, while his sisters separate and flee to the sea bottom; this explains the Dnieper's speed, rapids, and many mouths. A third story concerns the small stream Chorny Ruchei (Black Brook), which flows into Lake Ilmen. After a man builds a mill on its bank and diverts water, the fish complain to the stream that they have lost space. Later, a Novgorod angler in the brook meets a stranger in black who offers to show him where fish swarm if he will perform a service. The stranger instructs him that in Novgorod he will meet a tall moujik in blue garments, to be addressed as 'Uncle Ilmen'; the angler must convey that the Black Brook petitions him about the mill obstructing its flow, leaving the decision to this personified Lake Ilmen. An editorial note observes that the beginning of the Sozh and Dnieper legend appears to be taken from the biblical story of Jacob and Esau.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A blind old man named Dvina has two sons, the elder Sozh and the younger waves.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Another tale says that the Dnieper, Volga, and Dvina were once living people: an orphan boy Dnieper and his two orphan sisters Volga and Dvina, who had to labor beyond their strength, lived in rags, and suffered from hunger and cold.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After eating they can live without toiling while supplying others with meat and drink.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The three siblings walk for almost three years, choose away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"When Dnieper wakes and finds his sisters gone, he becomes angry, starts to pursue them on foot, then smites the ground and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l6718-l6851","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"INTRODUCTORY. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER II. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 6718-6851","start":"6718","end":"6851","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage closes a discussion of a tale in which an incantation—\"Split open, O Earth! disappear, O sister!\"—repeated three times causes the earth to open and a girl to sink \"into that world.\" It notes variant Russian versions where the endangered sister escapes by hiding in a hollow oak or by persuading a fisherman to ferry her across a sea or lake, and a Polish version where she descends in a magic car while the spot she has spat on answers when she is summoned. The text then outlines a South Russian story of Verlioka, a grotesque male monster described as a male counterpart to Baba Yaga, who emerges from a roaring forest to kill two orphan granddaughters and their grandmother before the surviving grandfather takes revenge with the help of a drake and other helpers. The author next explains that the supernatural Witch (Vyed'ma) of Russian tales, closely resembling Baba Yaga, is a powerful female embodiment of evil comparable to figures called Lamia, Striga, Troll-Wife, Ogress, or Dragoness in other lands, and is likened to Grendel's mother. Finally, the opening of the tale \"The Witch\" is given: an old couple dote on their only son Ivashko, who goes fishing in a canoe that moves in response to his spoken commands; his parents call him to shore with rhymed verses to feed him and collect his catch, and a witch overhears the formula, tries unsuccessfully to lure him with a hoarse imitation of his mother's call, and then goes to a smith to obtain a voice like the mother's.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A third formula in a story says, \"Split open, O Earth! disappear, O sister!\" and when this has been said three times the earth opens and a girl sinks \"into that world.\"","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In one Russian version of the same story, the sister escapes by running away and hiding in the hollow of an oak.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In another Russian version, the sister escapes by persuading a fisherman to take her across a sea or lake.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In a Polish version, the sister obtains a magic car that sinks underground with her, while the spot on which she has spat replies to every summons addressed to her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Verlioka is introduced as a malevolent monster who appears to be a male counterpart of Baba Yaga, and is known only in South Russia from a single story.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"In Verlioka's story, two old people live with two orphan granddaughters, described as charming little girls.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The younger granddaughter is sent to drive sparrows away from her grandfather's peas when the forest begins to roar and Verlioka emerges.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Verlioka is described as of vast stature, one-eyed, crook-nosed, bristly-headed, with tangled beard and moustaches half an ell long, wearing a wooden boot on his one foot, supporting himself on a crutch, and laughing terribly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Verlioka kills the younger girl with his crutch, then kills her sister and their grandmother; the grandfather escapes and later, with the help of a drake and other helpers, takes vengeance on Verlioka.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Witch (Vyed'ma) is introduced as another female embodiment of evil in Russian tales, closely resembling the Baba Yaga in disposition and behavior, and sometimes interchangeable with her between story versions.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The term Vyed'ma properly refers to a wise woman or prophetess of old, or to a modern wise-woman credited with witch-like faculties, and is considered inadequate for the vast, vaguely outlined supernatural being who sways the elements and preys on mankind in folk-tales.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The same supernatural female being is said to figure in various lands under titles such as Baba Yaga, Lamia, Striga, Troll-Wife, Ogress, or Dragoness, and is compared to the terrible female form known as Grendel's mother in an Anglo-Saxon poem.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"In the tale \"The Witch,\" an old couple have one son named Ivashko and are described as being extremely fond of him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Ivashko asks his parents to allow him to go fishing, they initially refuse out of fear he will drown, but eventually consent.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Ivashko's mother dresses him in a white shirt and red girdle and sends him out in a boat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Sitting in the boat, Ivashko chants, \"Canoe, canoe, float a little farther,\" and the canoe moves farther away while he begins to fish.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"After some time, Ivashko's mother hobbles to the riverside and calls to him with a rhymed verse promising food and drink; he recognizes her voice, commands the canoe to float to the waterside, and comes ashore where she takes his fish, feeds him, changes his shirt and girdle, and sends him back to fish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Later, Ivashko's father comes to the bank, calls him with a similar verse, and Ivashko again commands the canoe to the shore, where the father repeats the exchange of taking fish, feeding him, and changing his clothes before sending him back to fish.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"A certain witch hears what Ivashko's parents have called out to him and desires to get hold of the boy.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The witch goes to the bank and calls Ivashko with the same words his parents used, but in a hoarse voice; Ivashko notices the voice is not his mother's, identifies it as a witch's, and orders the canoe to float farther away.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"Realizing she must call Ivashko with a voice like his mother's, the witch hastens to a smith and asks for assistance (the passage breaks off at this
