content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l2684-l2789","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE TRIAL OF LOVERS: / THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE / THE POOR TURKEY GIRL / HOW THE SUMMER BIRDS CAME; lines 2684-2789","start":"2684","end":"2789","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Gopher cautiously verifies that a great heap of flesh—the four-fold Bison—is dead and reassures a boy hiding in a hole. The boy emerges, skins the beast, takes part of the hide, its heart, and a large intestine he fills with blood, and carries these home, hanging the heart on the ladder and dropping the heavy pelt through the roof sky-hole, startling his mother. She scolds him and recalls warning him about the four-fold Bison. That evening the boy presses his mother to reveal any other such dangerous beings. Reluctantly, she tells him of terrible Eagles living on Shuntekia: in the middle of an enormous cliff is a hollow place where they have a nest with their young; day after day they snatch children, young men, and women, who are never seen again. She begs him not to go, but expects he will. After she sleeps, the boy secretly cuts the Bison rawhide into an almost skin-tight green suit, scrapes off the hair, greases it, and stores it so it will not dry. Early the next morning he takes his weapons, the suit, and the blood-filled intestine and travels across an inlet and up a mesa near the Shuntekia cliff. Near the Eagles’ nest he puts on the slick rawhide suit and ties the intestine around his neck like a sausage. He cries loudly and acts terrified; the father Eagle, far up in the sky, hears and descends, circling the boy. The boy rolls up like a porcupine and lies in the trail as if helpless. The Eagle tries to seize him, but its claws slip on the greased hide. The claws tear the intestine, spilling blood over the suit and making it even more slippery. Smelling blood, the Eagle grows fiercer and finally hooks one talon through a stitch in the suit, carries the boy upward, circles over the nest, and drops him into it, where a heap of brush breaks his fall. The boy lies still while the Eagle perches on a crag and calls to his awkward, long-legged young Eagles, telling them he has brought food for them to feast on. The eaglets limp up intending to tear the boy, but when they approach he softly says \"Shhsht!\" and they tumble back, staring at him. The father Eagle urges them again to eat and complains that he must leave to hunt to feed them, then flies away. The two young Eagles walk around the boy, examining him and approaching his hands and feet.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Gopher emerges from a hole, examines a large heap of flesh, tests it by scratching out an eye, finds no sign of life, and runs back to tell the boy that the creature no longer breathes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After hearing the Gopher’s report, the boy thanks him, climbs out of his hiding place, skins the beast, removes its thick skin, takes its great heart, and cuts off a large intestine which he fills with blood.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The boy carries the heavy load home slowly, hangs the heart on the ladder beside others, drags the pelt to the sky-hole, and drops it into the room, frightening his mother.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The mother exclaims in alarm when the boy arrives, saying she had warned him about where the four-fold Bison was and expressing wonder that he returned home alive.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The boy refers to the dead creature as a \"poor\" one and comments that it is no longer handsome, strong, or large, while his mother calls him wretched and predicts he will cause both their deaths.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"That evening the boy asks his mother if there is anything else of this kind left and insists that she not disappoint him by refusing to tell.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The mother reluctantly describes terrible, great, fearful Eagles living on Shuntekia; their nest is in a hollow place in the middle of an enormous cliff, where their young live, and they catch children and young men and women and carry them away, never seen again.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The mother hopes and trusts that her son will not go to face the Eagles, calls him a foolish boy, and remarks that she can see he will go anyway; the boy tells her to go to sleep and says not to mind it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After his mother sleeps, the boy cuts the piece of rawhide from the four-fold Bison into an almost skin-tight green suit, scrapes off the hair, greases the suit, and stores it inside a blanket so it will not dry.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Early the next morning the boy takes his weapons, the rawhide suit, and the section of intestine filled with blood, runs into and across an inlet, climbs a mesa near the Shuntekia cliff, and near the Eagles’ nest puts on the suit and ties the blood-filled intestine around his neck like a sausage.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The boy begins to cry loudly and shake his head, then rolls himself up like a porcupine and throws himself down into the trail, appearing terrified; the father Eagle high in the sky hears and sees him, descends in circles, and attempts to grasp him, but the claws repeatedly slip on the smooth rawhide coat.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"During the struggle, the Eagle’s claws tear a rent in the intestine around the boy’s neck, causing blood to stream over the coat and make it more slippery; smelling the blood, the Eagle becomes fiercer and finally gets one talon through a stitch in the coat, lifts the boy, circles above the nest, and drops him into it, where he lands on a heap of brush that breaks his fall.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After dropping the boy into the nest, the old Eagle perches on a nearby crag, tells his children he has brought them food to feast on, and urges them to eat.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The awkward, long-legged, short-winged young Eagles limp up to the boy with claws and open beaks ready to strike his face, but when he says \"Shhsht!\" they tumble back and stretch their necks to look at him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The old Eagle demands to know why his children do not eat the boy, complains that he must hunt to feed them, then rises into the air and flies away northward; afterwards, the two young Eagles walk around the boy, examining him and approaching his feet and hands.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12","ev:13"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Boy / youth","description":"A young male, referred to as a boy and as the woman’s son, who relies on the Gopher’s report, skins the four-fold Bison and takes its heart and intestine, questions his mother about other dangerous beings, secretly makes and later uses a greased rawhide suit and blood-filled intestine to reach the Eagles’ nest, and interacts with the young Eagles there.","role_refs":["role:1","role:6","role:7"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12","ev:13"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Mother of the boy","description":"An adult woman living in the house with ladder and sky-hole, addressed as the boy’s mother, who scolds him for risking himself against the four-fold Bison, expresses fear that his actions will cause their deaths, and reluctantly tells him about the terrible Eagles of Shuntekia.","role_refs":["role:2","role:8"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Gopher","description":"A Gopher who hides in a hole, emerges to examine the heap of flesh, tests it by scratching out an eye, and returns to inform the boy that the creature no longer breathes, thereby reassuring him.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Four-fold Bison (dead creature)","description":"A large creature referred to as the four-fold Bison, now a dead heap of flesh whose eye the Gopher scratches out to confirm death and whose thick skin, great heart, and large intestine are removed by the boy for carrying home and later use.","role_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:7","ev:8","ev:9"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Father Eagle / old Eagle","description":"A great Eagle described as terrible, living at Shuntekia; he hears the boy’s crying from high in the sky, descends and struggles to grasp him, finally carries him to the nest in the cliff and drops him there, perches on a crag, and addresses his young Eagles, saying he has brought them food to feast upon before flying away to hunt.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:9","ev:10","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Young Eagles (two awkward offspring)","description":"Two young Eagles, described as awkward, long-legged and short-winged, living in the nest in a hollow place in the cliff of Shuntekia;     "summary": "A hunter, uncle of a maiden who cast away her child, goes out from Háwikuh toward the southern mesas near Póshaan, lair of the Deer-mother and her foster-child. He discovers a large herd of Deer gathered quietly as if in council around a splendid nude youth, their foster-brother. When the youth sees the hunter, he flees with the herd. The hunter returns to Háwikuh and reports what he saw to the maiden’s father, an old priest, and to the people. Some claim the figure was an evil apparition, but the hunter insists he was a mortal youth. The priest and council decide on a grand hunt, ordering that on the fourth day the southern mesa be surrounded so the herd and youth cannot escape. \n\nMeanwhile, the Deer slow their pace and speak with the youth. The Deer-mother tells him that he is the child of mortals and recounts how she found and raised him. He declares he will be faithful only to her because mortals rejected him, but she explains that as a mortal he cannot live through winter on roots alone, for her milk and the fruits and nuts will be gone. The older Deer explain that once their herd has been discovered they are customarily hunted on the fourth day, and that they willingly yield their lives to brave hunters who are sacred of thought and heart and make proper sacrifices to them, so that the animals’ lives in other form continue. \n\nA splendid Deer emerges, lovingly touches cheeks with the boy, says they must part despite their love, and proposes that to make the youth like other mortals, only surpassing them, he should accompany him to the Land of the Souls of Men, where the Gods of the Sacred Dance and Drama sit in council. That same day the Deer and the swift youth run toward the Lake of the Dead. By nightfall they reach its shores, where lights shine over the lake’s middle and the Gardens of the Sacred Dance, and where the old Drama-woman and Drama-man walk along the shore, calling to each other. \n\nAt the lake, the Deer instructs the youth to step boldly into the water with him. Ladders of rushes rise from the lake to receive them and bear them down beneath the waters into great, splendid halls of the Dead and of the Sacred Dance, illuminated by many lights and fires. In the largest chamber, Páutiwa, Sun-priest of the Sacred Drama, Shúlawitsi, God of Fire with his ever-living torch, and many other gods sit silently in council by a central fire and greet the newcomers. Through doors opening to the four directions, long rows of sacred dancers—spirits who have passed through the Lake of the Dead—enter, dressed in white embroidered cotton mantles adorned with shells and turquoise, and perform sacred rites to the delight of the gods and the wonder of the Deer and the youth.",

Going out hunting, he uses his ingenuity to kill a large deer but lacks a flint-knife to skin it. He goes to a place of old buildings and sings an old magic song addressed to a \"fire-striking flint-stone\" so that it will make itself known. A Coyote running through the woods hears the song, deduces that the singer has killed a deer and is seeking a flint-knife, and returns to question the Turtle. Despite the Turtle’s evasive answers, the Coyote presses him until the Turtle admits he has killed a deer lying nearby. The Coyote insists on helping to skin the deer, saying he is hungry and wants to lap up the blood. After finding a knife, they go to the deer; the Coyote holds the hind legs apart while they skin it. When the work is finished, the Coyote asks what share he will receive. The Turtle offers him the \"usual parts\" given to someone who comes along while a hunter is skinning a deer, specifically the stomach and liver, later adding some fat and intestines. The Coyote rejects this, demands half of the deer, shows his teeth, and threatens to murder the Turtle if he does not comply. The Turtle draws his flippers, then his head, feet, and tail into his hard shell and refuses to give more. The Coyote attempts to kill him by biting and gnawing the shell, but his teeth repeatedly slip off with a \"kopo\" sound. The Coyote cuts up the deer, wraps the meat in its skin, washes the stomach in a nearby brook, and stuffs it with chopped liver, kidneys, fat from the intestines, clots of blood, and sprigs of herbs. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l11169-l11310","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SOZH AND DNIEPER. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER IV. / MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT.; lines 11169-11310","start":"11169","end":"11310","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage first discusses the \"wife-gaining leap\" motif, noting that in some Eastern stories a princess will marry only the man who can leap across or into spaces protected by walls, rivers, hedges of weapons, or ditches, and that many royal suitors die attempting these feats. The commentator suggests that the secluded princess in such tales may originally have been akin to the heroine of \"Sleeping Beauty\" and argues that the motif's original idea is best preserved in Norse legends of Brynhild and Sigurd, where Sigurd awakens Brynhild from magic sleep and rides his horse through a ring of fire around her hall to win her hand for Gunnar. The text then turns to the Russian tale \"Emilian the Fool\": two clever elder brothers leave their foolish youngest brother at home with instructions to obey their wives. The fool idles on the stove until the wives force him to fetch water, where he catches a talking pike that begs to be spared and grants him the power to make spoken commands effective via a special formula. Using this power, he sends pails home by themselves, rides a horseless sledge, makes axes cut wood on their own, and animates a cudgel that beats the townspeople when they try to stop him. The townspeople, unable to capture him, petition the king and suggest luring the fool with promises of red clothing.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The commentator refers to a recurring \"wife-gaining leap\" motif in which a leap connected with marriage is often vaguely described in many stories.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"In one modern Eastern collection, the wife-gaining leap motif occurs four times.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In one Eastern story, a princess loves her marble bath, described as \"like a little sea\" with high spiked walls, and vows to marry no one who cannot jump across it on horseback.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Another princess, dwelling in a glass palace surrounded by a wide river, resolves to marry only the man who can leap into the palace, and many kings and princes perish trying to do so.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A third king's daughter lives in a garden hedged round with seven hedges made of bayonets, which generally transfix her suitors.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A fourth princess vows to marry no man who cannot jump on foot over seven hedges made of spears and across seven great ditches around her house, and hundreds of thousands of Rajahs have died attempting this leap.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The commentator suggests that the secluded princess figure in these stories may originally have been akin to the heroine of the \"Sleeping Beauty\" tales, while noting that no special significance now attaches to her isolation.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The original idea of the motif is said to be best preserved in two legends of Brynhild’s wooing by Sigurd: in one, Sigurd awakens Brynhild from magic sleep; in the other, he gains her hand for Gunnar by a daring ride.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Brynhild will only have the man who can ride through the flaming fire drawn about her hall; Gunnar fails, but Sigurd rides his horse into the fire, which roars, shakes the earth, and sends flames up to the heavens, a feat no one else has dared.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The narrator introduces the Russian story \"Emilian the Fool\" as a favorite tale illustrating the use of magical \"properties\" in the skazkas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In the story, there are three brothers, two sharp-witted and one a fool; the elder brothers go downstream to sell goods, tell the fool to obey their wives as mothers, and promise him red boots, a red caftan, and a red shirt.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After his brothers leave, the fool lies on top of the stove until the brothers' wives scold him and order him to fetch water; he takes two pails to the water and a pike ends up in one of them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Angry with his sisters-in-law, the fool intends to cook and eat the pike himself, but the pike speaks with a human voice, asks him not to eat it, and promises him good luck if he returns it to the water.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The pike explains that the promised good luck means whatever the fool says will be done if he uses the formula, \"By the Pike's command, at my request,\" before giving an order.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The fool tests the formula by commanding the pails to go home and set themselves in their places; they do so, to the astonishment of his sisters-in-law.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When the wives complain of having no firewood, the fool takes two axes and sits in a sledge without harnessing a horse, then uses the pike’s formula to command the sledge to drive into the forest, causing it to rush through a town and jam people into corners while they shout for him to be stopped.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"In the forest, the fool orders one axe to fell trees and the other to cut them into billets, and the wood is cut and loaded on the sledge without human labor.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The fool then orders one axe to cut him a cudgel as heavy as he can lift; the axe does so and the cudgel lies on top of the load.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"On his return past the town, the waiting townspeople stop the sledge and grab the fool, but at his command the cudgel jumps out and beats many of them, knocking them down like sheaves of corn so that he can escape home, where he stacks the wood and lies again on the stove.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"Afterward, the townspeople petition the king, explaining that they cannot catch the fool by direct means and proposing to entice him with the promise of a red shirt, red caftan, and red boots.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Princess with the marble content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l14261-l14318","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"GHOST STORIES. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER VI. / LEGENDS.; lines 14261-14318","start":"14261","end":"14318","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage first recounts the tale \"Beer and Corn,\" in which a very poor peasant, unable to prepare for an upcoming Church feast or even light the lamp before his sacred painting, prays in distress. An old man arrives seeking lodging, learns the cause of his sadness, and tells him to borrow malt from a rich neighbor and throw it into his well. By morning the well yields extraordinarily good beer, which the peasant shares with the villagers. When the rich, usurious neighbor imitates the act with his own well, he gets only malt and water. The text then turns to legends about saints like the Prophet Elijah and St. Nicholas, explaining that pre-Christian Slavonians once worshipped the thunder-god Perun, functionally analogous to Teutonic Donar or Thor, who drove a flaming car across the sky and hurled lightning at demons. With Christianization, Perun’s worship ceased and his attributes were transferred to Christian holy figures, especially the Prophet Ilya/Elijah.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"In the story \"Beer and Corn,\" a certain man is so poor before a Church feast that, while content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l5155-l5267","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE MAIDEN OF THE YELLOW ROCKS / THE FOSTER-CHILD OF THE DEER / THE BOY HUNTER WHO NEVER SACRIFICED TO THE DEER HE HAD SLAIN: / OR THE ORIGIN OF THE SOCIETY OF RATTLESNAKES; lines 5155-5267","start":"5155","end":"5267","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Elders instruct a young hunter and a rattlesnake maiden how to use the lightning-shaft to return upriver in a hollow log, warning him not to embrace her. The maiden places her rattlesnake skin on the log’s fangs; after they arrive and the youth throws the log into the river, its fangs turn into living rattlesnakes, explaining the origin of rattlesnakes in the world. The young man journeys south with the maiden, hunting with a bow and arrows given by Sun-father. She fears fire and cannot at first eat cooked food, but he shelters her, and they eventually reach his town under the mountains of Shíwina, where his father, sister, relatives, and the old priest-chief welcome and bless them. Living with his younger sister, the youth continues as a mighty hunter while the maiden becomes accustomed to mortals’ food and ways. In time she bears twins, who grow quickly and wander so widely that they appear suddenly on housetops and plazas, causing people to call them strange; other children beat and quarrel with them. Saddened, the rattlesnake woman declares that she must return to the country of her fathers with the children despite her husband’s pleas. For four days she teaches him her people’s prayers, chants, and medicines for rattlesnake bites, and then has him escort her only as far as the great river, where she says her fathers will take her home and that one day their fathers will come for him so he will follow them and never return, as he eats cooked food and is mortal. She departs with the children and is seen no more. Later, when young men of the tribe are bitten by rattlesnakes, the hunter uses the medicines, sacred breath, and chants to heal them and initiates eight disciples into the secret rituals. Eventually he is bitten by his rattlesnake fathers while gathering wood in the mountains; his disciples cannot cure him, and he dies, telling them to cherish the knowledge from his beloved wife. His fathers then meet his breath and being and take them to the home of the Maiden of the Rattlesnakes and their lost children. He then gives several etiological legends: (1) After God creates Adam and Eve, he sets a clean dog to guard Paradise against the Evil One; the Devil bribes the dog with bread, enters, spits on the first humans making spittle impure, and Adam and Eve are expelled. God curses the dog, now called an unclean hound barred from houses and churches, though clean within. (2) Early humans, instead of asking God, ask the Devil how to build warm houses; he teaches them to build door-only wooden huts (izbas) that are warm but utterly dark. When he cannot solve the darkness, people turn to God, who commands them to hew windows, bringing light. (3) Schismatic Dukhobortsy teach that man’s body is made from various earthly materials (earth, stone, roots, water, grass, wind, cloud) into which God breathes life; Ralston remarks that some Russian creation traditions are close to Teutonic myths. (4) A tale of rye says that once it bore ears from top to bottom, but lazy harvest-women cursed \"God's corn\" so God stripped off the ears, leaving only a single ear after they repented; similar stories occur in Western Europe. (5) A Little-Russian variant has Ilya (Elijah) enraged at a woman’s base use of \"God's corn\"; he begins to destroy all corn, but a dog begs and receives a few ears. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l7652-l7721","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE COYOTE AND THE BEETLE / HOW THE COYOTE DANCED WITH THE BLACKBIRDS / HOW THE TURTLE OUT HUNTING DUPED THE COYOTE / THE COYOTE AND THE LOCUST; lines 7652-7721","start":"7652","end":"7721","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A Locust, disliking the Coyote and warned that coyotes are unfriendly to insects, decides to play a trick and teach him to mind his own affairs. The Locust splits his back, sheds his skin, finds a light quartz stone, places it inside the empty skin, seals it with pitch, and leaves the counterfeit skin on the tree while he flies to a neighboring tree. Coyote, having lost the song the Locust taught him after being startled by ground-pigeons, returns to the tree and repeatedly asks the apparent Locust to sing again. Receiving no reply, he grows angry, threatens to eat the Locust, then bites the skin, crushing the hidden stone and badly breaking his teeth. In pain, Coyote rolls in the sand, runs away, and at a brook sees his damaged teeth. The narrator explains that because ancient Coyote failed to mind his business and restrain his anger, he bit the stone-filled skin and all his descendants inherited his broken teeth, and that locusts still protect themselves by skinning themselves and leaving their counterparts on trees when they sing on sunny mornings.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Locust does not like the Coyote, having been told that members of Coyote's tribe are sometimes unfriendly to locusts and other insects.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Locust decides to play a trick on the Coyote and teach him a lesson in minding his own affairs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Locust grasps the tree bark, swells up, strains until his back splits open, and skins himself out of his old skin.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Locust crawls down the tree, finds a suitable light-colored, clear quartz stone, carries it back up, places it inside the empty skin, and cements the back together with pitch.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Locust leaves his exact counterfeit skin sticking to the bark and flies away to a neighboring tree.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After regaining some composure, the Coyote realizes he has lost his song and runs back tusks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Coyote drops the stone, rolls in the sand, howls, snarls, wriggles with pain, then runs away with his tail between his legs.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At the first brook the Coyote stoops to lap water to alleviate his pain and there sees that the teeth behind his canines are driven down so only their points are visible and look broken up.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The narrator states that in the days of the ancients the Coyote did not mind his own business or restrain his anger and bit a locust that was only a skin with a stone inside.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The narrator claims that all of the Coyote's descendants have inherited his broken teeth.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The narrator says that to this day, when locusts venture out on sunny mornings to sing, they often protect themselves by skinning themselves and leaving their counterparts on the trees.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The storyteller closes the tale with the phrase 'Thus shortens The gods gather, breathe on him, and touch his lips and ears with moisture and oil, granting him speech and understanding. They bring a bundle of fine garments and jewelry, place it at his feet, and declare him child of the Sun. Páutiwa instructs the youth and Deer about a coming hunt in which some deer must voluntarily die for the youth's sake, foretells that the youth will be treasured among men, and directs him to lead his uncle, a hunt leader with priest-youths, so the uncle may guide him home. The youth and Deer depart. On the morning of the hunt, the deer herd gathers on the southern mesa, circles the youth, teaches him to open the bundle, purifies him with steaming breath, and helps him dress in sacred costume with macaw feathers and a shell knee band. The deer chief calls for volunteers to die, and many deer offer themselves. During the hunt, the devoted deer are shot with arrows by hunters of Háwikuh. Only the old Deer-mother and her two children remain with the youth, who leads them while the fleetest hunters pursue. The youth's deer foster-brother and foster-sister are killed; the faithful Deer-mother is spared and turned back by the uncle and his sons. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l6749-l6842","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE WARRIOR SUITOR OF MOKI / HOW THE COYOTE JOINED THE DANCE OF THE BURROWING-OWLS / OR WHY COYOTES RUN THEIR NOSES INTO DEADFALLS / HOW THE COYOTES TRIED TO STEAL THE CHILDREN OF THE SACRED DANCE; lines 6749-6842","start":"6749","end":"6842","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mountain Lion crushes Coyote’s head with a great stone, providing an etiological explanation for why coyotes stick their noses into baited stone deadfalls and get them crushed. The next tale begins: in ancient times near the valley of Zuni, an old Coyote lives with his family in Cedar Canyon while the god K’yámakwe dwells with his many similar children on the crest of Thunder Mountain. A detailed ethnographic note describes the Sacred Drama Dance (Kâkâ), its masked and costumed Zuñi dancers, and the demi-god K’yámakwe beings who control weather and herbivorous animals and are spiritually linked to initiated performers through breath and ceremony. The K’yámakwe are represented by distinctive masks and robes, and in the dance a file of these figures comes from the south bearing slain game and decorated packages with toys for children. Later, as the old Coyote hunts below Thunder Mountain, he hears the clanging rattles and cries of the K’yámakwe, sees their children running on the mountain’s edge, admires their beauty, and resolves to capture them and raise them as coyotes.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Mountain Lion growls \"Good enough for you\" and throws a great stone down with all his strength upon the head of the Coyote.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The narrator says this event happened a great while ago and explains that for this reason, whenever a Coyote sees meat inside a stone deadfall, he sticks his nose in and gets his head mashed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the times of the ancients, the Zuñi people lived in various places around the valley of Zuñi where ruins now stand.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An old Coyote lived in Cedar Cañon with his family, including a fine litter of pups.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"On the crest of Thunder Mountain, behind a broad rock column guarding its western portion, lived one of the gods of the Sacred Drama Dance (Kâkâ), named K’yámakwe, with many children altogether like himself.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Kâkâ, or Sacred Drama Dance, is performed by Zuñi dancers wearing a great variety of masks and costumes representing traditional characters.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Many characters of content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l5269-l5378","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE MAIDEN OF THE YELLOW ROCKS / THE FOSTER-CHILD OF THE DEER / THE BOY HUNTER WHO NEVER SACRIFICED TO THE DEER HE HAD SLAIN: / OR THE ORIGIN OF THE SOCIETY OF RATTLESNAKES; lines 5269-5378","start":"5269","end":"5378","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two youthful War-god brothers go out hunting prairie-dogs. Rain begins, making the trail muddy, and they curse it. Seeing a great thunderstorm in the south, the younger proposes going to the Land of Everlasting Summer to steal the gods’ thunder and lightning. The elder, though cautious, agrees after they bring prairie-dogs home to their grandmother. The next morning they secretly depart, deceiving the grandmother by saying they are only going to hunt more prairie-dogs. Skirting the plains near Thunder Mountain, they reach the coral-like Land of Everlasting Summer and the red terraced House of the Beloved Gods, whose smooth high walls they cannot climb. The younger suggests seeking their grandfather, the Centipede. The brothers lay down their weapons and turn over flat stones until they find the old Centipede, who lives under one and is annoyed at being disturbed. He reproaches his grandsons, warning they are getting into trouble, but they flatter him and explain that the Rain-gods in the tremendous house guard the thunder-stone and lightning-shaft, which they wish to obtain. Centipede advises them to go home and leave these powers alone, yet agrees to help and wriggles rapidly up the terrace walls like a vine, over the roof, through a sky-hole, and along the ceiling to the altar. The beloved gods sit there in silent majesty, heads bowed in deep meditation, and do not hear him. Centipede winds down into the altar, steals the thunder-stone, carries it in his large mouth back over the roof and down the wall, and returns to the flat stone where the impatient brothers await him. The younger cries out that the grandfather has brought it; Centipede throws the stone down and it begins to sound, but Áhaiyúta seizes it and suppresses its world-stirring voice, thanking their grandfather. He then summarizes several Russian variants. In the first, an old man, his wife, and their little daughter live together; a bean dropped by the girl grows up to heaven, the old man climbs it, returns to fetch his wife, but drops her while carrying her up and she dies; a Fox is called in as Wailer. In a Vologda variant, an old couple lose a pea that later sprouts; they water it until it grows higher than their cottage, the old man climbs, harvests peas, but drops the bundle on the old woman, killing her. In another version, a grandfather and grandmother sow a bean and a pea; a hen eats the pea, but the bean grows through their table, ceiling, and roof up to heaven. The grandfather climbs to heaven, finds a hut made of foods and eats there; twelve sister-goats, each with one more eye than the last, notice the disturbance and set one goat as watch each time. The grandfather repeatedly charms the guard goat’s eyes to sleep with a formula and keeps stealing food until he fails to charm all twelve eyes of the last goat, who sees and catches him; the story breaks off. A further tale of the \"Munchausen\" type begins when a cock finds a pea under a cottage floor; the cottager waters it and it grows through the house up to heaven. A moujik decides to climb up to look for sugar, mead, and other delights; his wife assents. In heaven he finds a large wooden house and a stove loaded with pigs, geese, pies, and other food, guarded by a seven-eyed goat. He charms six of its eyes to sleep, eats and drinks, and sleeps; the goat later informs the returning master, who has servants throw the intruder out. When the moujik reaches the place where the pea-stalk had been, it has vanished. He twists floating cobwebs into a cord, ties it to the edge of heaven, and begins to descend; the cord runs out high above the earth, so he lets go, falls into a swamp, and remains there until a duck nests on his head. Grabbing the duck’s tail, he is pulled out, returns home with the duck and her egg, and recounts his content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l5047-l5153","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE MAIDEN OF THE YELLOW ROCKS / THE FOSTER-CHILD OF THE DEER / THE BOY HUNTER WHO NEVER SACRIFICED TO THE DEER HE HAD SLAIN: / OR THE ORIGIN OF THE SOCIETY OF RATTLESNAKES; lines 5047-5153","start":"5047","end":"5153","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A youth presents plumes to the Sun-father, who breathes on them and on the youth, declaring his thoughts straightened. The youth then offers plumes to the Moon-mother, the Mother of Men and wife of the Sun-father, who similarly blesses them. The Sun-father invites the youth to accompany him for four days on his circuit around the world so he may see the many towns, nations, and peoples who are the Sun-father’s children; the maiden stays safely in the Sun-father’s house. The Sun-father dresses the youth like himself, takes the sun-dress, and leads him down through four great apartments of the world into a snowy lower region where people clear snow from their houses. They travel to another House of the Sun, ascend through four rooms into the home of the Sun-father’s aunts, who receive plumes of prayer and sacrifice and give blessings. Emerging into the World of Daylight, the skies are filled with summer rain, and they cross the world seeing many cities and tribes, observing wars, famine, disease, misery, and poverty among men. The Sun-father laments that his children waste their lives and kill one another though they are brothers and he is father of all. For four days they journey, and each evening the Sun-father gives his grandmother a package of treasure sacrificed by his human children, casting the treasures of the bad and double-hearted into the great waters. On the fourth day, in his western home, the Sun-father tells the youth his task is complete and he must return to his fathers below the mountains of Shíwina. The youth expects a long journey, but the Sun-father promises he will reach the river-bank in a day, giving him a shaft of strong lightning that will pull him swiftly through water, along with a quiver of unerring arrows and a strong bow to seek life. The Sun-father urges him never to forget sacrifices, which must be made with true words and a faithful heart, and instructs him to take the Rattlesnake maiden as guide and companion. The youth is told to release the lightning at the shore of her country so it lands them high, then to visit the maiden’s home where the Rattle-tailed Serpents, called his fathers, will instruct him and receive plumes from the Prey-beings. At dawn, the youth and maiden enter a hollow house, close it, and when the youth grasps the lightning shaft, the log shoots over the great waters too fast to be seen, reaching the island of the Rattle-tailed Serpents and landing high on the bank as the Sun rises over the mountains. They enter the council of the Rattlesnakes; seeing the shining black paint on the youth’s face, the serpents ask to paint their own faces likewise but do so unevenly, which the tale explains as the origin of rattlesnakes’ uneven facial markings. The young man presents plumes to each Rattlesnake elder and announces he will return with their maiden to his father’s home; the serpents consent, saying, “Be it well, that it may be well,” and The old man then divides the money into three heaps and says the third is for whoever ate his loaves. The pope immediately claims it and confesses he ate them. The old man gives him the money, urges him to serve his parish faithfully, not to be greedy, and not to beat Nicholas with the keys, and then disappears.

An editorial note explains that the main motive of the story is the same as in “The Smith and the Demon”: a supernatural being performs a miraculous cure; a man attempts the same and fails; when he is about to be punished, the being rescues him and gives him a moral lesson. Therefore we kill them not needlessly, nor waste the lives even of other animals without cause.”","summary":"The passage explains that rattlesnakes living at Yathlpew’nan were once a community of men and women of a rattlesnake kind. Children from one house ask to go slide on nearby sand-banks and are told by their mother to protect their very small sister. While they play, the baby girl runs toward an older sister sliding down a sand-hill and is accidentally crushed to death. The grieving children carry her home on their shoulders, singing a lament that calls her “Rattlesnake little-little.” As they approach the village, the mother, grandmother, and then all the villagers repeatedly cry an archaic exclamation of grief, swoon, and writhe on the ground. When they revive, they find they can no longer stand and instead wriggle and utter faint cries like rattlesnakes, explaining why rattlesnakes behave as they do. The narrator concludes that rattlesnakes, and many animals, were once a splendid people, so humans should not kill them needlessly or waste animal lives without cause.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rattlesnakes at Yathlpew’nan are described as having once been men and women of a rattlesnake kind.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Children from one house ask their parents’ permission to go out and slide down the sand-banks south of the Bitter Pond on the other side of the river.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The mother tells the children they may go but warns them to be very careful of their little sister, describing her as young, very small, and helpless and instructing them to carry her gently on their shoulders and place her where she will be safe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The children affirm their love for their little sister, lift her in their mantles, carry her on their shoulders to the sunny side of the sand-banks, and begin sliding down one after another.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The baby girl leaves the spot where she was set, runs toward an older sister sliding down the sand-hill, clapping her hands and laughing; the older sister cannot stop and warns her, then collides with her, knocking her over and rolling her in the sand so that she is crushed to death and left very small.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The children gather around their dead little sister, cry, then lift her tenderly onto Each Blackbird plucks a feather from one wing, unfortunately all from the same side. The old Bird asks the Coyote if he is willing to undergo an operation to have the feathers planted in his skin; he agrees, sits down, steadies himself with his tail, and holds up an arm while the birds thrust feathers along his forelegs and down his back where wings should be, causing him pain but not complaints.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"public_domain"},{"id":"ev:6","type":"summary","locator":"7082-7096","quote_or_summary":"The Blackbirds declare the Coyote ready and reform on the slope, singing and hopping down before flying into the air. The Coyote, startled but brave, follows with heavy flops. Because his wings are made from feathers taken only from one side, he flies slanting and spirally and crashes against the mountain. He picks himself up, calls out to the birds that they have left him behind, and when they return they explain his wings are not thick enough and liken his poor flight to a young Blackbird’s first attempts.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"public_domain"},{"id":"ev:7","type":"summary","locator":"7097-7111","quote_or_summary":"The old Blackbird tells the flock to pluck feathers from their other sides and to select strong feathers from the tips of their wings, explaining these are used to cleave the air, guide movement, and sustain flight. He loves the Eagle intensely, constantly feeding, petting, and protecting it, neglecting all other work, so his brothers and male relatives resent both him and the bird. After another day of labor, the brothers decide to kill the Eagle to cure the youth of his infatuation. The Eagle, seemingly unaware, overhears their plan and becomes anxious. When the youth next brings food, the Eagle refuses to eat and, speaking for the first time, explains that it loves and cherishes the youth as he does it, but that the relatives, angered by the youth’s neglect of fields and duties, intend to destroy the bird. The Eagle says humans cannot really harm it if it takes flight, yet it is sad because it must leave the next day for its home in the skies. The youth weeps and insists he cannot live without the Eagle, begging to accompany it rather than remain behind. The Eagle replies that the youth has no wings and lacks knowledge of the high skies and other unknown worlds, and warns that Eagle-people eat raw prey without fire, unlike humans whose food is ripened by fire, so the youth could not survive there. The youth insists he would rather eat raw food or none at all than live without the Eagle. After repeatedly warning that such a journey would lead to the youth’s undoing and to its own sadness, the Eagle finally agrees: it tells the youth to go home for the last time, gather much sustaining food in pouches as for a long journey, make them into a pack, and return in the morning after the people have gone down to their {"record_id":"batch.motif.sufi-attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-archive-l2409-l2675","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/sufi/project-gutenberg/bird-parliament-attar-fitzgerald.md","passage_locator":{"label":"Bird Parliament; lines 2409-2675","start":"2409","end":"2675","translation":"Bird Parliament","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After the Tajidar finishes speaking, the birds’ previously abstract fears about the journey become overwhelming. Many slip away to their nests or exhaust themselves preparing and never begin. Others rise toward the first dark valley, where a fierce wind blows, only to scatter in panic, reducing the great world-assembled caravan by more than half. As the journey continues, some birds sit paralyzed by dread, others drop out quickly, and the road becomes strewn with the dead. Birds perish through exhaustion over land and sea, from heat, cold, thirst, drowning, hunger, poisoned food, terror, predators (tiger, snake, crocodile), madness, suicide, or fighting one another, until only a handful remain. This remnant climbs the mythic mountain Kaf, whose feet rest in the seven seas and whose forested slopes of light and darkness conceal a hidden Presence. On these heights, only thirty birds, battered and nearly featherless, survive a cataclysmic clash of rock, sea, and fire that darkens the sun and collapse at the threshold of the Everlasting One, barely able to cry out to the all-absorbing Reality.

A winged Harbinger of Flame, a tongue of fire, appears and demands who they are, whence they came, and why. The Tajidar replies that they are disfigured fractions of the sum of being, spent and defiled, seeking readmission at the treasury door. The angelic figure answers that the One they seek, as the Fount of universal Being, cares little for number or kind and needs no tally of the overflowing drops from His urn. The spokesman responds that they ask only to see the Fount from which they flow and to lose themselves in it. Immediately, before any formal opening of a portal, they find themselves within, before the Throne and the Majesty, overwhelmed by a blinding blaze of glory that forces their eyes downward.

Looking down, they see a scroll which flashes back to each bird the entire story of its soul, compared to the writing that Yusuf once gave his brethren, which revealed the deed by which they had sold him. Exposed memory and conscience lash the thirty; they confess fully, loathe themselves, and cast off the rags of carnal self. Their old selves, now known and rejected, give way to a new clothing in the integrity of the soul. They then dare to raise their eyes again toward the Throne and blaze, and at the center of that glory they see a transfigured figure of themselves. Looking at themselves, they behold the enthroned Figure mirrored, and vice versa, until they cannot distinguish seer from seen, experiencing an identity that is "Another, yet the Same," divided yet one.

From this Presence comes a Voice, almost indistinguishable from their own inner aspiration, declaring that the "Sun of my Perfection" is a glass in which those who reflect pass from seeing into being, seeing themselves in the One and the One in themselves. The Voice explains that their apparent selves are merely fractions of the All, like water lifted from the deep as individual drops of rain, then melting back into the universal sea. All they have been, done, and thought has in fact been the "I" speaking: the Voice is their sin and their remorse, the Tajidar who led them, the briar that held them back; pilgrim, pilgrimage, road, retribution and its cancellation are all the Self moving toward itself. Their arrival is the Self arriving at its own door, using their fractional selves as mirrors in which it beholds itself, a vision that endures even in drowning. The Voice calls the birds, as lost atoms, to draw toward their center, become the eternal mirror they beheld, and return as wandering rays subsiding back into their sun. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l13556-l13593","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 13556-13593","start":"13556","end":"13593","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"As arrows fly at a group ascending into the sky, the Sun casts his shield beneath them so the missiles glance away. They draw up the corners of a mantle and rise higher while the people below, both old and young, quarrel and fight, accusing each other of folly for attempting the life of a god. A young man declares that they will always be fools and that their father the Sun had intended all things for their good, but through their foolishness their peace and treasures will depart with him and his. The storyteller then addresses the listeners as children, explaining that the little blue stars seen at sunset beside the Sun are the result of this ancient event, and that precious jewels are now found only in the east and west at the borders of the great oceans. Since then, the world has been filled with anger, so that even brothers quarrel and spill each other’s blood. The narrator adds that if men had been more grateful and wise, the Sun-father would have freely scattered treasures and humans would have lived in mutual kindness. He ends with a blessing for long-growing corn-stalks and for the protection of the Holder of the Roads of Life, who once sheltered his children with the shield of his sunlight, and then formally closes the tale.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Arrows whistle past a group, but the Sun casts his shield beneath them so that the higher into the air.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The people on the ground, both old and young, begin to quarrel, beat, and fight one another while accusing Mythology is defined as the superstitions of the ancients and folk-lore as those of the present-day ignorant. Ancient mythology has been mined for literary ornament and then probed for hidden wisdom; modern science now compares mythologies and sets them against scientific knowledge to trace stages in human opinion. The mythology of ‘tribal men’ is described as their philosophy, explaining cosmic mysteries through tales told by wise men, prophets, and priests. This lore is said to have the same origin and significance as the myths of Hesiod and Homer, but it lacks poetic glamour and is now dismissed as folk-lore—discredited mythology—by ‘civilized and enlightened’ people. The Zuni folk-tales collected by Cushing are called a charming display of Zuni wisdom, though also of their follies from a modern point of view. The text explains that science values such material not for truth or mere literary embellishment but for understanding the evolution of pleasures, industries, institutions, languages, and especially opinions; psychologists study mythology and folk-lore as stages in the development of thought. Cushing is praised as a poetic but scientifically-minded writer who can think and speak like myth-makers, prophets, and priests while retaining scientific clarity. The introduction then outlines a Zuni-style animistic cosmology: the Zuni gods, like those of other ‘primitive’ peoples, are the ancient first animals. All entities—humans, beasts, plants, stars, lands, waters, and rocks—are animals possessing souls, which are tenuous, mist-like ghostly beings inhabiting material bodies. Souls can leave their bodies and can possess vacated ones; they are the seat of force and mind, while matter provides fixed form. The world is a universe of animals under magic: stars are animals compelled to circle the world; plants are animals under an enchantment that usually prevents movement; waters are animals sometimes enchanted, with lakes writhing in waves, the sea circling the earth, and streams running over land. Mountains and hills tremble in pain and usually cannot move, though rocks and mountains sometimes travel at night. These animal beings come in generations: the first-born are gods, called ancients or first ones, and later generations are their degenerate descendants. The world is portrayed as a theatre of necromancy in which the gods are primeval wonder-workers. The gods still live, but their descendants often die; death itself is said to arise from necromancy practiced by bad men or angry When he accidentally strikes a bone splinter, the bones and fragments of the dead rise and pursue him like a cloud of ghosts as he flees toward his Stork grandparents. His Badger grandparents instead reach him first, pull him into their burrow, and drive off the ghosts with their powerful odor, then dose him four times with a nauseating herbal medicine and scold him for having become enamored of beautiful Death and for forfeiting his life and plumage. They tell him he can no longer descend to his own people below or live among the Eagles, and send him to his Stork grandparents, who reproach him and warn that his Eagle-wife’s love is likely lost. After he goes to plead at the Eagles’ high-walled house, his wife publicly rejects him as a polluted, faithless fool and he shuttles sadly between the Storks and the Eagles. At last, elder Eagles persuade the Eagle-maid to help by returning him to his own home; despite protesting that he is polluted by Death, she agrees, finds an old ragged eagle dress for him, and, after he puts it on, tells him to follow her according to the knowledge they have taught him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The youth wakes in the morning to find that the once fine, finished room is now tottering, with winds shrieking through crevices, broken windows, and sand sifting into an old barren room.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Bones, skulls, half-buried dried faces, and mummy-like fingers and feet are strewn over the floor around the youth, making the place seem like a vast cemetery of dead from all ages.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Bones cling to the youth where maidens had lain beside him, and he stealthily picks them off and carefully steps between the scattered bones toward the broken-down doorway.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The youth trips against a splinter of bone embedded in the debris, and its whistling sound causes the bones and fragments of the dead to rise, shrieking and howling, and pursue him like a flock of vampires as he runs toward the Storks’ home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A great cloud of the dead presses nearer and surrounds the youth as he runs in terror.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"One of the youth’s grandparents, a Badger near its hole and followed by others, hears the fearful clamor, calls him their grandson, and rushes forward to save him by catching him up and casting him down into one of their holes.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Badgers bristle Dead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After driving off the ghosts, the Badgers enter the hole, lift the youth up, and scold him vigorously for his folly, saying he is not yet saved.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Badgers order water to be heated, mix nauseating herbs and other medicines into it, and direct the youth to drink the mixture four times, after which he reports feeling much better.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Badgers call the youth a fool and faithless lout for becoming enamored of Death, however beautiful, and remark that it is a wonder they have saved him thus far.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The Badgers say it will be an even greater wonder if Death, who loved the youth, still loves him enough after his faithlessness to save the life he has forfeited, asking rhetorically who would dance and take joy in Death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Badgers tell the youth that his plumage is gone and his love given up, so he can neither descend to his people below without wings nor live among the Eagles without love, and they instruct him to go live with his Stork grandparents.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At the home of the Storks, the youth’s grandparents look at him with downcast faces and repeatedly reproach him, saying there is little chance of regaining his wife’s love and affection.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The youth insists he will go plead with his wife and claims he did not know what he was doing, while the Storks remind him that they had warned him against it and he did not heed.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The youth lingers outside the great, high-walled house of the Eagles, moping and moaning, while the Eagles come and go or gather talking on the rooftop without greeting him.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"At last the Eagle-maid, his wife, appears above him with a shiver of disgust and orders him to go back to his grandparents, declaring that he has forfeited her love and will never be received among the Eagles again, calling him an example of folly and faithlessness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The youth returns sadly to the Storks’ home but continues to come back to the Eagles’ house, where he is treated as though he were not present.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"During one of the youth’s absences, elder Eagles implore the Eagle-maid to take the youth back agrees.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13","ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Eagle-maid finds an old eagle dress with broken, ragged feathers and thin wing-feathers through which the him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The passage repeatedly links the youth’s being enamored of Death with pollution, forfeiture of life, and the loss of love content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l8700-l8808","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HOW THE RATTLESNAKES CAME TO BE WHAT THEY ARE / HOW THE CORN-PESTS WERE ENSNARED / JACK-RABBIT AND COTTONTAIL / THE RABBIT HUNTRESS AND HER ADVENTURES; lines 8700-8808","start":"8700","end":"8808","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A young woman, hunting rabbits to feed her poor parents, eagerly follows rabbit trails into snowy canyons, driving several into hollow logs, killing them with a blow and stringing them together, all while ignoring an approaching snowstorm. As she thinks happily of how the meat will strengthen her father and mother and provide dried stores for later, the snow deepens, darkness falls, and she loses the trail and misjudges her direction, wandering into the Descending Plain of the Pines and becoming lost. She decides to find a sheltered spot among some rocks to spend the night until the storm passes. She sees Taiuma’s Cave with a dim light inside, assumes belated rabbit-hunters left a fire, and crawls in with her rabbits and mantle. Inside she finds a bed of hot coals and wood; she gathers more wood from outside, builds up the fire, dries her wet clothing, and cooks and eats a rabbit with corn cakes, the fire lighting the cave brightly. Just after finishing her meal she hears a distant cry of distress that comes nearer; thinking it is a lost rabbit-hunter, she goes toward the entrance and calls back. Then she hears the clatter of an enormous rattle and realizes in terror that a Cannibal Demon, perhaps the renowned Átahsaia, has seen her fire and used the cry to lure her. She retreats to the back of the cave as the Demon approaches, snapping twigs, rattling noisily, and shouting to her. Reaching the entrance, he complains of cold and hunger and demands to be let in, but the opening is too small for his giant shoulders. He then politely orders her to come out and bring him food and rabbits; she, terrified, refuses to move, saying she has eaten her food, while he insists she at least throw him a rabbit.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The maiden enthusiastically follows rabbit trails into snowy canyons, sometimes driving multiple rabbits into a single hollow log, where she splits the logs, kills the rabbits with a blow to the neck, breathes in their expiring breath, ties their legs, and strings them over her fear.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Cannibal Demon approaches the cave, snapping twigs under his feet, shouting hoarsely to her that he knows she is He and the maiden fall in love, and he visits her secretly at noon until she becomes his wife and conceives a child. Knowing she is consecrated and fearing that no one will believe her explanation of the pregnancy, she resolves to put the child away. One night she gives birth to a baby boy, wraps him in soft cotton-wool, and secretly carries him over the rooftops to the sheltered side of a refuse-heap near the stream below the village, where she leaves him and returns mourning. At dawn, a Deer with two speckled fawns comes from the southern hills to drink at the stream. Hearing the infant cry and seeing dust and cotton-wool flying, the Deer discovers the human baby. Declaring that she has found a waif and will love it as another child, she warms and caresses the infant, rewraps it, lifts it on her horns, and carries it, followed by her fawns, to her lair near the spring Póshaan among piñon and cedar trees. As he plays and runs with them, he becomes stronger and swifter than the Deer, learns their language and ways, and, being the offspring of the Sun-father, gains great vigor. When fully trained in all a deer should know, his Deer-mother presents him to the larger herd, which gladly accepts him. Later he returns with part of a nut containing fine white meat, calls the Cock \"comrade father,\" and proposes they share his nut supply from a nearby high tree he climbs each autumn. The Cock loves the nut, laments that his grandmother rarely brings him similar food, and wishes he had more. The Mouse suggests the Cock go to the tree, but the Cock explains he is trapped: his wings are worn, his beard is crumpled from pushing against the bars, and his grandmother tightly fastens the door after feeding him. The Mouse uses his strong teeth to gnaw through the holding-string on the wicket and tells the Cock to push the door open; the Cock escapes, rejoicing, and follows the Mouse to the nut-tree. The Mouse climbs to the topmost boughs and confirms the nuts are ripe, while the Cock cannot reach even the lowest branches and begs for nuts to be thrown down. The Mouse tosses a nut which the Cock devours and then greedily demands more. The Mouse positions himself directly above the Cock and drops a large nut onto his head, bruising and stunning him so that he \"dies for a short time\" and forgets. She scolds him for leaving his place, refuses to bind his head unless he gives her his bristles of manhood as a lesson, and demands at least four bristles. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l1579-l1671","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE PINNACLES OF THUNDER MOUNTAIN 344 / INTRODUCTION / THE TRIAL OF LOVERS: / THE YOUTH AND HIS EAGLE; lines 1579-1671","start":"1579","end":"1671","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A mortal youth living among Eagle people is given a fine eagle-coat and, with patient instruction from the Eagles and his Eagle-maiden wife, learns to take eagle form and fly, first inside their great house and then over the valleys and plains to the north and east. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l12751-l12867","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 12751-12867","start":"12751","end":"12867","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Two rapidly growing boys, described as children of the Sun but living with an old Badger couple, become skilled at killing small animals near their doorway and long to hunt rabbits farther away. Their Badger father crafts bows, arrows, and bark moccasins for them, while their Badger mother prepares corn-cakes for their lunch and worries they will freeze in the snowy weather. The boys set out among the hills at the foot of Thunder Mountain, successfully hunt many rabbits, and at noon climb a high hill, clear the snow, and eat. The Sun looks down, pities them, descends to earth in splendid human form, approaches the frightened boys, and tenderly claims them as his own children to whom he gave life, though they initially do not believe him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The two boys grow in one day as much as human children do in a year, so that in eight days they are as large and knowledgeable as children usually are in eight years.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The boys are described as children of the Sun.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"There is no little animal that the boys cannot kill unfailingly.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The boys grow weary of killing birds around their doorway.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Their old Badger father tells them every morning never to go out of sight of their house.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The old Badger woman keeps watching the boys for fear they will run off, get lost, or be found and claimed by somebody.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The boys want to kill prairie-dogs and cottontails but cannot get near enough to them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The boys ask their father to make them bows and arrows so they can hunt rabbits and provide plenty of food for their parents.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The old Badger father goes to the Cañon of the Woods, cuts down a small oak, and gets branches for arrows.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Using a piece of flint, the father makes each boy a bow and some arrows; being awkward without human fingers, he splits a single feather and twists it around the butt of each arrow shaft.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"That night a great deal of snow falls.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The boys say that the next day they will go rabbit-hunting and express impatience to do so.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The boys ask their mother to make a lunch for them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The mother protests that the boys will freeze to death because they have no clothes and no wool on their backs.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The boys reply that they are tough and will wait until the sun shines warm before going hunting.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The mother asks how they will carry their food since they have no blanket to wrap it in.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The boys suggest that the mother make corn-cakes, string them on a little stick, and that they will carry the stick by the middle.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The mother makes the corn-cakes, strings them on little sticks, and the boys go to bed but sleep restlessly, repeatedly waking and peeping out to see how long it will be before daylight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"In the morning the old Badger father collects bark, rubs it until soft, and weaves for each boy a pair of bark moccasins that come halfway up to the knees.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The elder brother puts on his moccasins, runs out into the snow, and exclaims that they are first-rate.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The other boy puts on his bark moccasins, and the two boys take their strings of corn-cakes and bows and arrows and start off as fast as they can.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The boys go among the hills at the foot of Thunder Mountain and soon find a rabbit trail.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Their first arrow kills a rabbit, and they continue hunting until they have a large number of rabbits and begin to get tired.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"Although snow is on the ground, the sun is very warm, and the boys forget about the snow until they grow hungry.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"The boys see that it is noon because the sun is resting in the mid-heavens.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"The boys go up on top of a high hill, carry their rabbits there one by one, find a place where the snow is shallow, brush a space clear of snow, lay down the rabbits, and sit to eat their corn-cakes placed on a bundle of grass.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"While the boys sit eating, the Sun looks down, pities his two poor little children, and decides to go down to talk to them and help them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"By his will alone the Sun descends and stands on the earth a short distance from the two boys.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The Sun appears grand and beautiful, wearing embroidered cotton garments, fringed leggings, many-colored girdles, bright buckskins, bracelets and wampum, turquoise earrings, plumes on his head, and long glossy hair bound with colored cords and macaw feathers.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"One of the boys looks up, sees the Sun-father standing there, and alerts the other boy that somebody is coming.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"The Sun approaches with stately step, dazzling the boys’ eyes with his beauty and magnificent dress.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"The boys huddle together, crouch their knees close to their bodies because they have no clothes, and watch the Sun trembling.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"One boy faintly asks, \"Comest thou?\" and the Sun replies, \"Yea, I do, my children. How are ye these many days?\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"The boys respond that they are happy, though they are almost frightened out of their wits and keep looking first at the Sun-father and then at each other.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:35","text":"The Sun-father tenderly tells the boys that they are his own children and that he gave them both life.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:36","text":"The boys gaze at the Sun-father and do not believe what he says.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:37","text":"The Sun-father repeats that they are his children; the boys ask, \"Is that so?\" and he confirms it, saying he saw them, pitied them, and came to speak with and help them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:38","text":"The boys exclaim \"Hai!\" but still look at each other and at the Sun-father and do not believe him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Elder boy, child of the Sun","description":"The elder of the two brothers,
