content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.native-american-zuni-folk-tales-cushing-gutenberg-l12956-l13078","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","passage_locator":{"label":"ITALIAN VERSION / THE GIANT CLOUD-SWALLOWER / THE MAIDEN THE SUN MADE LOVE TO, AND HER BOYS / OR, THE ORIGIN OF ANGER; lines 12956-13078","start":"12956","end":"13078","translation":"Zuni Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this part of the tale, the Sun-father explains to the boys how they can restore their dead mother to life by secretly gathering all her bones, her two dried eyes, and her heart after a dance, warning that any missing part will be absent from her revived body and that they must also obey his taboo against killing certain game animals or die with her. He then calls the younger brother, clothes and arms him in garments like his own, conjures a warm cloud of mist to cleanse and beautify both boys, and dresses the elder similarly so that they resemble the Sun. The boys realize he is their father and thank him. The Sun-father, calling them his children, says he must return to his home in the heavens and sends them back to the Badgers who reared them, instructing them to carry their bark moccasins, strings of corn-cakes, and the rabbits they have slain; he miraculously lightens the rabbits so they can be carried. When the boys reach the Badgers’ hole, their foster mother at first fails to recognize them because of their transformed beauty, but they prove their identity with the moccasins and corn-cakes and tell how the Sun is their father, their human mother once lived at the Home of the Eagles, was killed by the Twain while escaping on an Eagle, and that they were born when she fell into the Cañon of the Coyote and were found and reared by the Badgers. The Badger-father confirms this story and announces a dance to be held at the Home of the Eagles in eight days. The boys, uncomfortable in their fine clothes, remove and store them, eat with their foster parents, ask the Badger-father to count the days, and are told on the day before that the dance will occur tomorrow.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Sun-father describes that after a dance is over and someone has taken back all of the mother’s bones and replaced them in a niche.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Sun-father instructs that the designated boy must lie down and pretend to sleep while some young men go home and others sleep there.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When the others begin to snore, the boy must gather all the bones, the two dried eyes, and the heart of his mother and carry them as fast as he can to where his brother waits.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Sun-father states that when the boy brings these parts to his brother, their mother will come to life again and be as she was before being killed by the Twain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Sun-father warns that not a single bone or any part may be left behind, or the revived mother will lack that part.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The boys reply that they will do as they have been told and will certainly obey.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Sun-father says he gave the boys at their birth the power to slay all game.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Sun-father commands that they must not slay rabbit, deer, antelope, mountain sheep, or elk, and warns that if they do they will perish with their mother.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The two boys promise not to disobey, and the younger brother remarks that when a father commands, a son cannot disobey.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Sun-father summons the younger brother to come and stand before him, and the boy obeys.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The Sun-father removes the younger boy’s bark moccasins, puts beautiful fringed leggings on him, replaces the moccasins with buskins like his own, ties the leggings with many-colored garters, and places a beautiful quiver on his back, dressing him as the Sun-father is dressed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Before the transformation, the little boys are described as dark-colored, with tangled and matted hair over their heads.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The Sun-father turns about as if to summon an unseen messenger and creates a great warm cloud of mist with which he cleanses the boys.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"After being cleansed by the cloud of mist, the boys’ skins become smooth and clear and their hair falls down their backs in wavy masses.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The Sun-father arranges the younger brother’s hair, places a plume in it like his own, adds beautiful plumes on his head, and then dresses the elder brother like the first.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The two boys exclaim and look at each other and at the Sun-father, remarking to one another that they are just like Him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The boys observe that their mother’s face has a black streak down the middle and that their father’s face is similar except for a grizzly chin; from this they conclude that the Sun is their father and thank him for his goodness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The Sun-father calls the boys his children, tells them to mind what he has told them, says he must go to his home in the heavens, and expresses his love and wish for their happiness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The Sun-father instructs the boys to run home to the Badgers who reared them, warns that the Badgers will not recognize them, and tells them to roll up their bark moccasins and take their strings of corn-cakes and the rabbits they have slain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:20","text":"The boys ask how they can carry the rabbits because they are heavy.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:21","text":"The Sun-father gently passes his hands over the heap of dead rabbits, after which they become as light as dry grass-stalks and the boys can easily lift them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:22","text":"The boys bid their father farewell, start home, and when they look back after going a little way they find that he is nowhere to be seen.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:23","text":"Near their home, the two old Badgers are running around their hole; the Badger-father is about to go out to search for the boys for fear they have perished from cold and goes down to get rabbit-skins and other things to wrap them.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:24","text":"The old Badger-mother, who is above ground, shouts down to her mate to hurry and come out because somebody is coming.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:13"]},{"id":"obs:25","text":"One child points out their mother waiting for them near the hole and urges the other to hurry so their father will not come out searching.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:26","text":"As the boys approach, they address their mother, noting that she is in the cold waiting for them, but she does not recognize them and hides her face in her paws from shame because they are too beautiful, like the Sun-father.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:27","text":"When asked if she knows them, the Badger-mother replies that she does not and that her children did not look like they do now.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:14"]},{"id":"obs:28","text":"The boys insist that they are her children and show their bark moccasins and strings of corn-cakes as proof.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:29","text":"The Badger-mother exclaims \"Our poor children!\" in response to the tokens.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:15"]},{"id":"obs:30","text":"The boys say that their father is the Sun-father, that he came down to speak to them that day, dressed them like himself, and told them that their mother used to live at the Home of the Eagles, where their aunts and grandfather still live.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:31","text":"The boys recount that their mother was killed by the Twain as she tried to escape on the back of an Eagle, that when she fell into the Cañon of the Coyote they were born, and that the Badger-father found them and both Badgers reared them.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:16"]},{"id":"obs:32","text":"The old Badger-father affirms that the story is true, adds that he knows there will be a dance at the Home of the Eagles in eight days, explains that tomorrow only seven days will remain, and tells the boys that on the eighth day they will go to see it.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:17"]},{"id":"obs:33","text":"The two boys enter the Badgers’ dwelling but feel ill at ease in their unfamiliar fine clothes.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:34","text":"The Badger-mother places soft rabbit-skins on the floor; the boys remove their clothing, carefully lay it away, and the whole family eats their evening meal.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:18"]},{"id":"obs:35","text":"The boys ask their foster father to keep count of the days and to let them know when the time for the dance arrives.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]},{"id":"obs:36","text":"The days pass until the day before the dance, when the old Badger tells the boys that the dance will occur tomorrow.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:19"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Sun-father","description":"Solar being who addresses the boys as his children, gives them powers and taboos, transforms and clothes them, lightens their game animals, and then returns to his home in the heavens.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2","role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8","ev:10","ev:11","ev:12"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Younger brother","description":"One of the Two boys, initially dark-colored and poorly clothed, whom the Sun-father first summons, dresses, and cleanses; he speaks of a son’s duty to obey his His wife objects that they already have too many children but advises him to enlist allied Coyote clans and share the captives. The Coyote summons four tribal groups of Coyotes, who gather below Thunder Mountain and follow his plan to form a living ladder by standing on each other and holding tails, after belching to avoid hiccoughs. A Coyote near the top sneezes, the whole chain falls, and many Coyotes are flattened on the rocks. A fierce warrior of the Kâkâ, ‘he of the Long Horn,’ rushes from a sacred western lake to rescue the children; finding them already safe, he beats surviving Coyotes and skins them. The tale explains that Long Horn dancers now have blue faces and wear coyote-skin collars around their necks when they come to the pueblo, said to be the origin of these ritual features and their content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-myths-folk-tales-curtin-gutenberg-l3852-l3974","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/myths-folk-tales-russians-slavs-magyars-curtin.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE FEATHER OF BRIGHT FINIST THE FALCON. / WATER OF YOUTH, WATER OF LIFE, AND WATER OF DEATH. / THE FOOTLESS AND BLIND CHAMPIONS. / THE THREE KINGDOMS.; lines 3852-3974","start":"3852","end":"3974","translation":"Myths and Folk-tales of the Russians, Western Slavs, and Magyars","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ivan Tsarevich, searching for Peerless Beauty, is told by one old woman that her elder sister ahead on the road commands all creatures and may know of the bride. After spending the night, he rides to the elder sister’s vast house, where another old woman first scolds him for tying his horse to a golden ring but then hosts him. Over a meal he recounts how his father promised him Peerless Beauty—daughter of three mothers, granddaughter of three grandmothers, and sister of nine brothers—as his bride, and asks where she lives. The old woman, nearly ninety, has never heard of her but promises to ask her \"answer-givers.\" In the morning she washes and summons the fish and creatures of the water, then the beasts of the forest, and then the birds of the air; they assemble in such numbers that they cover sea, earth, and sky, yet all reply that they have neither seen nor heard of Peerless Beauty. After she says there is no one else to ask and leads Ivan indoors, the Mogol bird arrives late, darkening the window, and explains it has been arraying Peerless Beauty for mass. The old woman asks the bird to carry Ivan to her. The Mogol bird agrees on condition that it receives three forties of beef and a vessel of water. Ivan gathers the provisions, loads them on the bird, has a long iron lance forged, bids farewell to the old woman, and entrusts his steed to her. During the long flight, each time the bird looks back, Ivan feeds it meat on the end of his lance until the beef is nearly exhausted. When Ivan asks the bird to descend, it warns that below them are sleeping forests and sticky morasses they could never escape. After the beef is gone, Ivan cuts off the calves of his own legs and feeds them to the bird so they can fly on. They reach a green meadow where the bird lands, and Ivan, now lame, explains what he has done. The Mogol bird then coughs up the calves, reattaches them to Ivan’s legs, and restores them with its breath and spittle, so he regains his strength. Ivan walks on to a great town, where a grandmother living in a backyard lodges him and promises to wake him when the bell rings.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An old woman tells Ivan Tsarevich she is living toward the end of her eighth decade and has content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l11438-l11571","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"SOZH AND DNIEPER. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER IV. / MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT.; lines 11438-11571","start":"11438","end":"11571","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage concludes a tale in which a Cossack has fought a witch and severed her arm. The next morning the household master and mistress find everyone alive. The Cossack proposes to \"show Death\" by searching the village with local officers. At the Ponomar's cottage they find his daughter lying on the stove with one arm missing; the Cossack produces the severed arm, and the commune rewards him and orders the witch drowned. The editor then comments that such witch stories are widespread, often featuring witches in animal form, and cites Hertz's monograph on werewolves. He summarizes a Polish tale where the Plague, embodied as a woman called the Pest Maiden, seeks victims from house to house until a nobleman leaves a window open, cuts off her arm, and frees the village. He also gives an Indian example in which a hero watching beside a haunted princess cuts off the arm of a Rakshasa who reaches into the room. The next story, \"The Headless Princess,\" begins: a king's daughter is an enchantress. A priest's ten-year-old son, taught by an old woman, glimpses the princess through a palace window removing her head, washing and grooming it, and replacing it, and concludes she is a witch, telling others what he saw. She falls gravely ill and, before dying, instructs her father that the priest's son must read the psalter over her three nights. After her death she is placed in a coffin in the church and the king orders the priest to send his son. The boy is distressed; the old woman questions him, admits she already knew the princess was a witch, and gives him a knife and instructions to draw a protective circle in the church, to read without looking behind him, and to ignore any horrors lest he perish. On the first night he follows her advice; at midnight the coffin lid flies open, the princess rises, threatens him for peeping and gossiping, and tries to reach him but cannot cross the circle. She conjures terrifying apparitions, but he continues reading until daybreak, when she returns to the coffin. The second night is the same. Afterwards the old woman gives him a hammer and four nails to drive into the coffin corners and tells him to place the hammer before him while he reads, anticipating a more horrible third night.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The master and mistress wake in the morning, see that everyone is alive and well, and are extremely delighted.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Cossack offers to show the household \"Death\" and asks that all the Sotniks and Desyatniks be gathered so they can search the village house by house for her.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"At the Ponomar's cottage, the Cossack learns that one of the Ponomar's daughters is ill and lying on the stove.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Cossack sees that one of the girl's arms has been cut off, produces the severed arm he had taken, and the commune rewards him with money and orders the witch to be drowned.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The narrator states that stories of this kind are common in many lands and that the witches in them often assume the forms of beasts of prey, especially wolves or cats.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage refers to Dr. Wilhelm Hertz's monograph on werewolves as containing a long series of similar tales.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A Polish story is victims.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In the Polish tale, all doors and windows are barred except a single casement left open by a nobleman willing to howling and leave the arm behind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the Headless Princess story, a king has a daughter who is an enchantress, and near his palace lives a priest whose ten-year-old son goes daily to an old woman to learn reading and writing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Late one evening the priest's son passes the palace, looks through a window, and sees the princess remove her head, lather it with soap, wash it with clean water, comb its hair, plait its braid, and put it back in place; he is filled with wonder and thinks she is a witch.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"After returning home, the boy tells everyone that he has seen the princess without her head.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The king's daughter suddenly falls grievously ill and instructs her father that if she dies, he must have the priest's son read the psalter over her for three nights.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The princess dies, is placed in a coffin, and carried to the church; the king tells the priest to have his son read the psalter over her three nights in succession.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The priest's son becomes gloomy; at his lessons the old woman asks why he is unhappy, and he explains that he must read psalms over the princess, whom he knows to be a witch.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The old woman says she knew the princess was a witch already, gives the boy a knife, and instructs him to trace a circle around himself in the church, read from his psalter without looking behind him regardless of horrors, warning that if he looks back he will be destroyed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"On the first night in the church, the boy draws a circle with the knife and begins reading; at midnight the coffin lid flies open and the princess rises, leaps out, and threatens to punish him for peeping through her windows and telling what he saw.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The princess rushes at the priest's son but cannot break through the circle; she conjures various horrors, yet he continues After a comic incident where the heavy bundle falls on the younger brother, he pretends injury and insists on carrying only a small bundle while the maiden carries the large one. Before they leave, the maiden addresses the game animals as her children and releases them to roam the earth and multiply so that humans may again have their meat and pelts. The brothers and the maiden return home in a set order, and the maiden dries the meat in the upper rooms.

The brothers whisper among themselves about what the maiden will say for herself. That evening, the maiden tells them to rest and declares that she cannot yet consent to marry them because they have not shown they can dress buckskins as well as hunt. She explains that many buckskins have accumulated in the upper room and that she has no brothers to soften and scrape them. She promises to be the wife of one or both if they remove the hair from all the buckskins and scrape them thin and soft before the next sunset.

The brothers despair at the task but decide to try. They find the upper room packed with buckskins, bale them, and carry them to the river, where they realize the quantity exceeds what they could clean in a year. The younger suggests hiding some skins in rock crevices, but the elder refuses, saying the woman will have counted them. They spread the skins in the water to soak overnight and build a small dam so the skins will not float away. While working, they hear voices.

The narration explains that a nearby hill across from the Village of the Yellow Rocks is home to Field-mice, who are prolific and historically addicted to gambling, betting away their nests so that their bare young die of cold, yet continuing to gamble with model nests. These are the voices the brothers hear. They cross the river, listen to the tiny cries, and the younger descends through a hole into the hill, followed by the elder. Inside they find a large village of Field-mice in human form, with mouse-shaped clothes hanging on the walls. Some have removed their clothing to the waist and are gambling vigorously.

The mice ask who has come, and the brothers answer. The mice invite them to sit and gamble despite having nothing to bet and ask their purpose. An old Field-mouse with a broken tail questions them, and the brothers explain that they came because they heard voices and describe their task. When the mice learn that the brothers must remove the hair from many pelts, they excitedly offer to help on condition that the brothers promise to give them all the hair. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l7908-l8054","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MYTHOLOGICAL. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER III. / MYTHOLOGICAL.; lines 7908-8054","start":"7908","end":"8054","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ralston introduces Likho as a personification of evil or misfortune in Russian folklore, noting that one tale belongs to the Polyphemus-cycle and depicts Likho as a baleful one-eyed woman. In the tale, a smith who has never seen harm decides to seek out evil. A prosperous tailor joins him. They walk through a dark forest along a narrow path and reach a large, squalid cottage where they spend the night. A tall, lank, crooked one-eyed woman, Likho, enters, greets them, and implies she will eat them. She lights the stove, kills the tailor, trusses him, and bakes him. The smith, seeking to save himself, tells her he is a smith who can forge anything. She asks him to make her an eye. He ties her up with cords under this pretext, heats an awl, and pierces her sound eye while hammering with a hatchet. Likho breaks free and sits at the threshold, threatening that the smith will not escape. That night she brings in her sheep. In the morning, as she lets them out one by one by grabbing their wool and shoving them through the doorway, the smith turns his sheepskin coat inside out so the wool is outside, wears it, and creeps like a sheep. Likho handles him like the flock and pushes him out. Outside, he stands up, calls farewell to Likho, and says he has suffered much evil from her and that she can no longer harm him. Likho cries that he will still endure more and has not yet escaped. As he returns through the forest, the smith sees a golden-handled hatchet stuck in a tree and seizes it; his hand sticks fast. In a Russian variant, a prince whose sister plots against him under the influence of her demon serpent lover is sent to obtain healing and vivifying water kept between two lofty mountains that briefly part each day; he rides between them, fills flasks, and although his horse’s hind legs are crushed when the mountains close, the waters heal them. A Slovak version has a murderous mother sending her son to two mountains that open at midday and midnight, revealing the Water of Life and the Water of Death. A Ukrainian tale describes two springs of healing, life-giving water guarded by iron-beaked ravens, reached through grinding hills; a Fox succeeds in the quest but a Hare’s tail is caught between the closing cliffs, explaining why hares have no tails. The discussion then turns to the Waters of Strength and Weakness in tales where many-headed snakes abduct wives and daughters to metallic castles. In a detailed story, the golden-haired Queen Anastasia is torn from her husband Tsar Byel Byelyanin by the whirlwind demon Vikhor; her sons search for her, and the youngest, Prince Ivan, finds three metallic palaces with captive princesses and a fourth palace of diamonds where his mother is confined. In Vikhor’s cellar she shows him two tubs containing the Water of Strength and the Water of Weakness, has him drink the Strength water and swap the tubs so Vikhor will be deceived. When Vikhor returns, Ivan hides under her cloak, seizes his mace, and after an aerial struggle Vikhor drinks the weakened water while Ivan drinks the Strength water, becomes the mightiest hero, beheads Vikhor with one blow, then burns and scatters his body to prevent any return. The author compares the role of the Water of Strength to the energizing Soma drink that braces Indra for battle, and Vikhor’s debility to Indra’s when the Asura Namuchi drank Indra’s strength along One very rainy season makes the piñon trees, datila plants, and grasses on the nearby Southeastern Mesa (Shoyakoskwe) extraordinarily fruitful. An old bear claims the mesa and its produce for himself, growing fat while killing, maiming, and driving away the people of K’iákime when they try to gather food. The boy announces to his grandmother that he will go to the mesa for datilas and piñon nuts despite her pleas not to risk the bear’s violence. He follows the Road of the Pending Meal-sack, climbs the crooked trail up Shoyakoskwe, and begins eating datilas and nuts. The bear rushes out, accusing him of stealing and threatening to tear him to pieces. The boy calls the bear ‘friend’ and proposes a bargain, insisting the food is no more the bear’s than his. He suggests a test: whoever truly owns the plateau and its products must prove it by not being frightened by anything the other does, with one hiding while the other tries to scare him. The bear agrees and tries first, twice rushing out of the thicket, snapping trees and shouting fearsome cries, even grabbing the boy, but the boy remains unmoved, calmly eating. The bear concedes that the boy is \"a man\" and tells him to try to frighten the bear, warning that unless the boy succeeds he must stay away from the datila and piñon patch. The boy runs back toward his grandmother’s house, singing that the one of the piñon patch shall be frightened. His grandmother is surprised to see him alive. At his request she paints his face to look as frightening as possible, blackening one side with soot and whitening the other with ashes so he resembles a demon, and she gives him a stone axe of ancient, magically powerful origin. Armed and painted, the boy runs back to the mountain, where the bear is again eating datilas, and rushes toward him shouting a terrifying The brothers go down to the river; the elder shaves hair off the skins while the younger scrapes them thin and softens them.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain (Zuni Folk Tales, Project Gutenberg)."},{"id":"ev:3","type":"summary","locator":"lines 3968-4105 (Completion of the skins and maiden’s decision)","quote_or_summary":"The brothers work through the forenoon, and by late afternoon all the skins are finished. The Field-mice have carefully dressed most of them, even better than the men, and the skins lie spread out on the sand, white and numerous like a field. When the maiden comes at midday and again before sunset, she examines, counts, and recounts the skins, finds them all present, and, after probing the water with a long pole and finding none there, declares that the brothers shall be her husbands and that she must submit, then goes home with them.","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zuni/project-gutenberg/zuni-folk-tales-cushing.md","rights_note":"Public domain (Zuni Folk Tales, Project Gutenberg)."},{"id":"ev:4","type":"summary","locator":"lines 3968-4105 (Married life and birth of twins)","quote_or_summary":"The woman lives with the two brothers as their wife, and they manage to live together comfortably, not quarreling more than before. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-russian-fairy-tales-ralston-gutenberg-l12542-l12671","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/russian-fairy-tales-ralston.md","passage_locator":{"label":"MAGIC AND WITCHCRAFT. / FOOTNOTES: / CHAPTER V. / GHOST STORIES.; lines 12542-12671","start":"12542","end":"12671","translation":"Russian Fairy Tales: A Choice Collection of Muscovite Folk-lore","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“…a country beyond the sky, inhabited by supernatural beings of magic power and unbounded wealth… tales of the well-known ‘Jack and the Beanstalk’ type.”","summary":"Ralston first describes Russian peasant beliefs about the post-mortem habitation of the soul and associated funeral customs, noting grave goods and commemorative feasts that imply both a journey after death and continued residence of the dead at the grave, as well as attempts to reconcile these ideas with Christianity. He remarks that folk songs and stories do not speak of a heavenly home for ordinary departed spirits, but do mention a country beyond the sky inhabited by supernatural beings of great power and wealth, known from “Jack and the Beanstalk”-type tales. He then gives the tale “The Fox-Physician”: an old man’s cabbage grows from his cellar through the floor and ceiling up to the sky. Climbing the stalk, he cuts through the sky and finds a mill that produces abundant food. After eating and returning home, he tells his wife, who wishes to go there. She gets into a sack which he carries in his teeth while climbing the cabbage; the sack slips, she falls to the ground, and her body is smashed, leaving only small broken bones. A fox meets the grieving old man and offers to cure his wife, instructing him to heat a bath-room, bring the remains with oatmeal and butter, and wait outside without looking. Inside, the fox washes and eats the old woman, piles her bones in a corner, makes and eats a pudding from the provisions, lies twice about the woman’s condition, then escapes. The old man finds only picked-clean bones and no food, and is left alone and poor.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Russian peasants are described as having confused ideas about where the disembodied spirit resides after burial, sometimes placing it in the coffin with the body.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The departed spirit is also imagined as hovering around its former home or flying abroad on the wings of the winds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Food, money, and other necessities are placed in the coffin with the corpse.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Pomniki, or feasts in memory of the dead, are celebrated at fixed short intervals after a death and on its anniversary at the burial place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"These practices are interpreted as traces of beliefs in the soul’s journey after death and its continued residence at the grave, including susceptibility to physical suffering and enjoyment.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Two different beliefs about the soul’s post-mortem location run side by side, sometimes clashing and being partly reconciled with Christian ideas.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Songs and stories of the people do not mention a heavenly or upper-world home for ordinary departed spirits.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Stories do speak of a country beyond the sky inhabited by supernatural beings of magic power and unbounded wealth, associated with tales of the “Jack and the Beanstalk” type.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In the tale, an old man plants a cabbage in the cellar under his cottage floor, and an old woman plants another in the ash-hole; her cabbage withers but his grows up to the floor and beyond.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The old man repeatedly cuts holes in the floor and ceiling as the cabbage grows, until it reaches the sky.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The old man climbs the cabbage-stalk up to the sky, cuts a hole in the sky, and creeps through.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Beyond the sky he finds a mill which, each time it turns, produces a pie, a cake, and a pot of stewed
